sections.text:
XI. Integration of Learned Features and Deep Learning Preprocessing  
With the advent of deep learning, some reconstruction methods adopt feature encoding directly from the raw point cloud without extensive hand-crafted preprocessing. Neural frameworks, such as those based on implicit functions or neural kernel fields, decompose the reconstruction task into learning both local geometry and global context. In these pipelines, preprocessing may involve generating local neighborhood patches around query points and creating sparse hierarchical voxel grids using convolutional backbones (huang2023neuralkernelsurface pages 2-3, erler2020points2surflearningimplicit pages 3-6). Even in these advanced methods, however, initial preprocessing steps such as noise filtering, outlier removal, and normal estimation remain critical because they influence the quality of the learned latent representations. For instance, by ensuring that only clean, well-aligned data is fed into the learning algorithm, one can significantly enhance the accuracy of both the local absolute distance estimation and the global sign determination for the signed distance function (erler2020points2surflearningimplicit pages 1-3). This integration of data-driven and model-driven preprocessing techniques provides a robust pathway to handle the complexities of real-world point clouds.

sections.text:
XII. Summary and Discussion  
A comprehensive preprocessing pipeline for point cloud datasets intended for surface reconstruction should combine a sequence of methods targeting different aspects of the raw data:
	• Data simplification via voxelization or minimum distance filtering reduces the dataset size while preserving geometric fidelity (abreu2023proceduralpointcloud pages 11-13, wang2021lossypointcloud pages 3-4).  
	• Noise filtering and outlier removal, using statistical methods and neighborhood-based thresholds, address sensor errors and environmental artifacts (balta2018faststatisticaloutlier pages 1-2, kalschikov2019accuracyanalysisof pages 1-3).  
	• Registration aligns multiple scans into a coherent, globally consistent coordinate system, which is essential for accurately merging separate point clouds (abreu2023proceduralpointcloud pages 13-15, zhao2024aroadsurface pages 2-4).  
	• Normal estimation, typically via PCA-based methods, provides per-point orientation that is vital for implicit surface reconstruction algorithms; ensuring consistent inward/outward orientation further improves accuracy (shi2018semanticgeometricmodelling pages 5-7, huang2024surfacereconstructionfrom pages 17-17).  
	• Resampling techniques, such as farthest point sampling or grid-based filtering, promote a uniform density that prevents reconstruction artifacts resulting from non-uniform point distributions (huang2024surfacereconstructionfrom pages 12-13, zhu2019multisourcepointclouds pages 3-5).  
	• Segmentation and feature extraction decompose the point cloud into meaningful components, aiding both geometric reconstruction and semantic understanding (abreu2023proceduralpointcloud pages 15-16, kulawiak2022acosteffectivemethod pages 3-5).  
	• Multiscale representations, typically implemented via octree-based partitioning, improve scalability and allow simultaneous focus on global and local geometric properties (mi2020ssrnetscalable3d pages 1-2, mi2020ssrnetscalable3d pages 8-9).  
	• Synthetic scanning and simulation of sensor defects may be employed during preprocessing to both benchmark and robustify reconstruction algorithms against realistic imperfections (zhu2019multisourcepointclouds pages 10-13, sulzer2025asurveyand pages 8-10).  
	• For sensor-specific data, calibration, synchronization, and coordinate transformation integrate multi-modal sensor outputs into a unified dataset for accurate alignment (zhao2024aroadsurface pages 2-4).
By systematically applying these preprocessing steps, one can substantially improve the effectiveness and accuracy of surface reconstruction algorithms. Moreover, careful preprocessing not only mitigates the detrimental effects of noise and measurement errors but also preserves fine details and intrinsic surface characteristics, which are crucial for producing high-quality three-dimensional models.

sections.text:
XIII. Conclusion  
Robust surface reconstruction from point clouds is predicated largely on meticulous preprocessing. The diverse challenges posed by raw data—such as excessive point density, noise, outliers, misalignment, and non-uniform sampling—demand a concerted effort that combines classical techniques with modern deep learning strategies. This report has detailed the most important preprocessing steps—including data reduction, outlier removal, registration, normal estimation, resampling, segmentation, multiscale representation, synthetic scanning, and sensor-specific corrections—all of which are critical for ensuring that the input data is accurate, consistent, and manageable. By adhering to these methods, researchers and practitioners can achieve reliable and scalable surface reconstruction results even in the presence of challenging real-world imperfections (abreu2023proceduralpointcloud pages 11-13, balta2018faststatisticaloutlier pages 1-2, erler2020points2surflearningimplicit pages 3-6, huang2024surfacereconstructionfrom pages 1-2, mi2020ssrnetscalable3d pages 1-2).

In summary, the preprocessing of point cloud datasets is a multi-staged and context-dependent process that significantly impacts the quality of the final reconstructed surface. Future research may further integrate advanced adaptive algorithms and deep learning frameworks to automate and optimize these preprocessing steps, continually pushing the boundaries of accuracy and efficiency in surface reconstruction.

question: What are leading methods for generating hard examples of the boolean satisfiability problem, and what are their strengths and weaknesses?

sections.text: This report reviews the leading methods for generating hard Boolean satisfiability (SAT) instances and discusses their respective strengths and weaknesses. In the following sections, we describe traditional random instance generation techniques, industrial ‐like and structural generators, graph–based and learning ‐based approaches, as well as methods that exploit decomposition and backdoor techniques. Each approach is discussed in detail with supporting evidence from the literature.

The Boolean satisfiability problem (SAT) has long served as a benchmark for evaluating algorithmic advances in NP–hard problem solving. With the increasing practical importance of SAT across hardware verification, planning, cryptanalysis, and other domains, researchers need high–quality, hard instances that reflect the challenges encountered in real–world problems. However, creating instances that are both difficult for solvers and representative of industrial problems remains an open challenge. Several approaches have been proposed either to construct instances from theoretical distributions or to mimic the intricate structure of industrial SAT formulas. In what follows, we discuss these methods from various perspectives and highlight the trade–offs involved in each approach.

One of the earliest and most well–studied methods for generating hard SAT instances is the uniform random k–SAT generator. Traditionally, these generators focus on creating random k–CNF formulas by uniformly distributing variables in clauses and tuning parameters such as clause–to–variable ratio near the phase transition region, where empirical evidence shows that instances tend to be difficult to solve. For example, uniform random 3–SAT formulas generated near the phase transition can yield instances that exhibit high computational difficulty as measured by solver runtime or other performance metrics (bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 1-3). The primary strength of such generators is the ease of instance creation and the ability to parameterize difficulty systematically; this makes them valuable for theoretical studies of phase transitions and average–case hardness. However, a major weakness is that these randomly generated instances do not capture many of the structural properties observed in industrial SAT problems. In particular, while they may be hard for solvers, their lack of realistic structure means they often do not serve as effective proxies for industrial benchmarks (bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 1-3, bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 3-6).

Evaluating instance generators by configuration

sections.text: In response to the limitations of purely random generators, several research efforts have focused on generating “industrial–like” instances that capture statistical and structural features common in real–world SAT problems. Approaches such as the industrial–like generator by Ansótegui et al. aim to mimic properties such as community structure, variable occurrence distributions, and clause size variability observed in industrial benchmarks. For instance, generators based on the double–powerlaw mechanism or those that use parameters tuned via automated configuration frameworks have been investigated (bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 3-6). The strength of these methodologies lies in their attempt to bridge the gap between artificial hardness and industrial relevance; they tend to produce instances that align better with solver performance trends seen in practice. However, a weakness is that some “industrial–like” generators are less readily available, their behavior is not as well–understood, and they may fail to capture other aspects of problem complexity—often resulting in instances that are either too easy or that overly conform to a limited set of structural metrics (bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 3-6).

citations.title: Evaluating instance generators by configuration

sections.text:
A more recent paradigm involves representing SAT formulas as graphs—particularly bipartite graphs such as literal–clause graphs (LCGs) or variable–clause graphs (VCGs)—and leveraging techniques from graph theory and machine learning for instance generation. Early handcrafted models such as the Community Attachment (CA) and Popularity–Similarity (PS) models focus on explicitly generating formulas with controlled modularity or power–law degree distributions (giraldezcru2017localityinrandom pages 5-6, giraldezcru2017localityinrandom pages 6-7). These methods are designed to emulate key statistical features of industrial formulas; for example, PS models allow control over power–law parameters that affect variable popularity while also managing community structure and clustering. Their main strength is the ability to produce structured instances with properties correlated with solver performance, while their weakness may be that the resulting formulas do not always achieve the desired level of hardness or may require post–processing to avoid trivial unsatisfiability (you2019g2satlearningto pages 2-4).

Building on these ideas, deep generative models, such as G2SAT and MixSATGEN, take a learning–based approach by training neural networks on real SAT instance graphs. G2SAT, for example, uses a two–phase generation scheme that first proposes nodes and then iteratively merges these nodes according to predictions made by a graph–convolutional network (you2019g2satlearningto pages 6-7). This learned model can capture complex, high–dimensional correlations in the graph structure and generate synthetic SAT instances that closely match real–world instances in terms of both graph metrics (such as modularity and clustering coefficient) and solver performance rankings (you2019g2satlearningto pages 1-2). Similarly, MixSATGEN employs a graph mixing strategy that leverages a two–stage matching and mixing framework, combining learned literal correlations with controlled randomness through algorithms such as Gumbel–Sinkhorn to maintain hardness while preserving structural fidelity (chen2024mixsatgenlearninggraph pages 2-3, chen2024mixsatgenlearninggraph pages 6-8). The main strength of these approaches is their ability to automatically extract and mimic complex structural properties from data, thus generating instances with a high degree of industrial realism. On the downside, these methods require significant amounts of training data, careful tuning of hyperparameters, and may sometimes produce instances that are either easier to solve (due to inherent biases in training) or are computationally expensive to generate and scale to very large instance sizes (chen2024mixsatgenlearninggraph pages 16-17).

sections.text: Another promising avenue for generating or characterizing hard SAT instances is through the decomposition of formulas using backdoor sets and related metaheuristic optimization techniques. In this approach, a “backdoor” is a small subset of variables such that once these variables are fixed, the remainder of the formula becomes easy to solve using polynomial–time procedures. Methods exist for identifying strong backdoor sets (SBS) or ρ–backdoors (which guarantee that a large fraction of the induced subproblems are tractable) via exhaustive or heuristic search strategies (chivilikhin2312decomposinghardsat pages 5-8). Research in this area leverages metaheuristic optimization techniques—such as evolutionary algorithms—to search over the Boolean hypercube for variable subsets that minimize a hardness metric (often measured in terms of solver runtime, unit propagations, or conflicts) (chivilikhin2312decomposinghardsat pages 10-13). The primary strength of backdoor and decomposition methods is that they provide a principled way to quantify and exploit structural weaknesses in hard instances, often resulting in a significant reduction in overall hardness when the instance is decomposed into many easier subproblems (chivilikhin2312decomposinghardsat pages 22-24). However, the weaknesses of such methods include the computational overhead associated with accurately estimating the hardness (often via Monte Carlo sampling) and the inherent difficulty in identifying small backdoor sets in instances with thousands of variables. In addition, the use of metaheuristics introduces approximation and non–determinism, which may not always yield an optimal or stable decomposition (chivilikhin2312decomposinghardsat pages 20-22).

sections.text: Although not strictly methods for instance generation, techniques for near–uniform witness generation using XOR constraints (such as UniWit, UniGen, and UniGen2) have influenced how researchers think about hardness. These approaches, which partition the solution space via r–wise independent hash functions, provide nearly uniform samples of satisfying assignments when they run successfully (chakraborty2013ascalableand pages 1-3, chakraborty2013ascalableand pages 6-8). Their strength is in offering strong theoretical guarantees on uniformity and in reducing the number of SAT solver calls per sample by using techniques like leapfrogging and parallel sampling (chakraborty2015onparallelscalable pages 1-4, chakraborty2015onparallelscalable pages 4-7). However, they are primarily designed for sampling solutions rather than generating whole instances, and they might not directly translate into methods for constructing hard instances; moreover, the computational cost of generating a sufficient number of samples can be prohibitive, especially for very large formulas (chakraborty2015onparallelscalable pages 1-4).

sections.text:
Each of the approaches outlined above carries its own set of trade–offs. Uniform random instance generation is appealing for its simplicity and ease of parameterization, which is useful for theoretical studies on phase transitions; however, such methods lack the structural realism of industrial instances, limiting their practical usefulness (bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 1-3, bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 3-6). Industrial–like and structure–aware generators attempt to overcome these shortfalls by incorporating features such as community structure, clustering, and power–law degree distributions. While these methods produce instances that better reflect real–world properties, they can suffer from a narrow focus on a few parameters, potentially missing subtle interactions among many structural features (bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 3-6, giraldezcru2017localityinrandom pages 5-6).

Graph–based and learning–based approaches represent a significant advance in that they allow for automatic extraction of high–dimensional structural features from real instances. Their data–driven nature enables more flexible and adaptive instance generation. However, these methods bring with them challenges in terms of training complexity, scalability, and the potential for generating instances that are not uniformly hard across different solvers due to bias in the training data (you2019g2satlearningto pages 1-2, chen2024mixsatgenlearninggraph pages 2-3, chen2024mixsatgenlearninggraph pages 16-17).

Decomposition and backdoor methods, by contrast, focus on analyzing and reducing hardness rather than synthesis per se. They can provide deep insights into why instances are hard by identifying critical variables that wield outsized influence on solver performance. While these techniques are powerful for understanding hardness and for constructing decompositions that speed up solving in a parallel setting, their practical application is often limited by the computational cost of the optimization process and the variability inherent in metaheuristic search (chivilikhin2312decomposinghardsat pages 10-13, chivilikhin2312decomposinghardsat pages 22-24).

Finally, sampling–based approaches using XOR constraints have advanced the state–of–the–art in generating near–uniform samples, thereby influencing our understanding of instance space uniformity and solution diversity. Despite their strong theoretical foundations, these methods are more relevant to evaluating solver reliability than to direct instance generation (chakraborty2013ascalableand pages 1-3, chakraborty2015onparallelscalable pages 1-4).

sections.text:
In summary, the methods for generating hard SAT instances span a broad spectrum—from classical uniform random generation methods that are simple and tuneable, through industrial–like generators and handcrafted structural models, to modern graph–based and learning–based approaches that capture richer structural features. Each method has particular strengths: uniform random generators offer theoretical insight on phase transitions, industrial–like generators exhibit more realistic properties, learning–based methods adapt to high–dimensional structural data, and decomposition techniques expose critical structural weaknesses in otherwise hard instances. However, these approaches are not without weaknesses. Uniform random generation often fails to mimic industrial instance properties; industrial–like models may focus on selected structural features to the detriment of overall hardness; learning–based approaches require extensive data and training complexities; and decomposition methods impose significant computational overhead.

Given the complexities inherent in SAT instance generation, the optimal choice of method depends on the intended application. For theoretical analyses, traditional random generators suffice, while for developing and tuning SAT solvers for industrial use, hard instance generation that incorporates graph–based or learning–based methods may offer the best trade–offs between realism and hardness. Future research will likely continue to refine these methods, potentially integrating aspects of each to yield generators that are both computationally efficient and extensively representative of the challenges seen in real–world SAT applications (bayless2014evaluatinginstancegenerators pages 1-3, you2019g2satlearningto pages 1-2, chen2024mixsatgenlearninggraph pages 2-3, chivilikhin2312decomposinghardsat pages 10-13).

question: How effective are language models at automatically generating textual descriptions of scientific concepts?

sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful tools that can automatically generate textual descriptions of scientific concepts, demonstrating broad effectiveness across diverse scientific domains while simultaneously exposing a number of critical limitations that necessitate expert oversight. In this report, we discuss the effectiveness of LLMs by examining their capabilities in generating coherent and contextually appropriate scientific text, exploring domain-specific applications, and analyzing inherent challenges such as factual inaccuracies and hallucinations.

At their core, LLMs such as GPT‑3, ChatGPT, and domain‐specific models like Galactica leverage transformer architectures pre-trained on vast datasets to produce fluent and contextually rich text. These models are generally trained on both curated and uncurated textual data, which allows them to capture complex scientific terminology and diverse linguistic patterns. In many cases, they generate scientific descriptions that are structurally coherent and grammatically sound, thereby facilitating a wide range of research activities from literature review to manuscript drafting (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 3-6). For instance, LLMs have been applied effectively in biomedical research to automatically annotate taxonomic texts, extract biochemical properties from molecular representations, and produce clear summaries of experimental findings (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 11-13).

sections.text: One of the primary strengths of LLMs lies in their ability to process large amounts of unstructured scientific text rapidly and synthesize it into concise summaries or detailed descriptions. This capability is particularly valuable in generating textual descriptions that integrate and convey scientific findings, as well as in supporting ideation and the iterative refinement of research hypotheses. Several studies have demonstrated that even when generating complex multi-turn content, these models can maintain coherence and produce fluent narrative arcs that resemble human-written scientific abstracts and summaries (ma2023isthisabstract pages 2-4). In chemical sciences, for example, models such as SMILES-BERT and ChemBERTa-2 have exhibited enhanced performance in property prediction and molecular annotation when compared to traditional deep learning models (christofidellis2023unifyingmolecularand pages 11-14).

sections.text: Domain specificity plays a crucial role in the effectiveness of LLMs. General-purpose LLMs have shown strong performance in generating scientifically meaningful text, yet fine-tuning these models for specific domains such as biomedical, chemical, or environmental sciences has often resulted in better integration of specialized terminology and improved generation of domain-relevant content (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 1-3). For example, biomedical models such as BioBERT and GatorTron are specifically adapted to handle the nuances of biomedical literature, which include technical jargon and complex relational information among scientific entities. Thus, when tailored to a particular scientific discipline, LLMs are able to produce textual descriptions that adhere more closely to expert expectations and practical research workflows.

sections.text: Retrieval augmentation presents another significant enhancement to the effectiveness of LLMs for generating scientific descriptions. By incorporating external sources such as curated reference databases, Wikipedia, or domain-specific corpora via retrieval-based methods, LLMs produce more factually correct and contextually enriched summaries. This method, often referred to as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), addresses some of the core challenges associated with hallucinations – instances where the generated text includes facts or citations that are fabricated or misrepresented. Studies focusing on biomedical lay language generation have shown that retrieval-augmented techniques provide improvements in both readability and factual correctness, thereby bridging the gap between expert and lay audiences (guo2024retrievalaugmentationof pages 1-5). Further evaluation using human annotations and automated semantic metrics confirms that these methods facilitate a more reliable generation of scientific textual descriptions (guo2024retrievalaugmentationof pages 17-21).

sections.text: Despite these clear advantages, LLMs are not without significant challenges. One key limitation is their propensity to generate hallucinations, where the models may invent details, false citations, or inaccurate representations of scientific data. Such issues stem from the inherent limitations of the training corpus and the inability of the models to perform real-time fact-checking against authoritative sources. This is particularly problematic in scientific writing where accuracy is paramount and misrepresentation of facts can lead to misinformation. Studies indicate that even state-of-the-art models sometimes produce text that, while fluent and coherent, contains erroneous factual details necessitating rigorous human review and validation (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 8-11).

citations.title: An interdisciplinary outlook on large language models for scientific research

sections.text: In addition to hallucinations, LLMs often struggle with deep causal and abstract reasoning tasks that are critical in scientific research, such as generating novel hypotheses or complex methodological descriptions. Although they excel at surface-level coherence and fluency, there is evidence that these models may fall short when required to generate text that embodies deep scientific insight or produces novel, original contributions. For example, research comparing AI-generated abstracts with human-written counterparts has shown that while LLMs are capable of mimicking the form and coherence of scientific abstracts, they often lack the depth, specificity, and novel insight typical of expert human-written content (ma2023isthisabstract pages 6-9). This limitation is further compounded by challenges associated with evaluating the quality of AI-generated scientific text, as conventional metrics like ROUGE, BLEU, and METEOR only partially capture syntactic and lexical fidelity without adequately addressing factual correctness or innovation.

citations.title: Is this abstract generated by ai? a research for the gap between ai-generated scientific text and human-written scientific text

sections.text: Another aspect that influences the effectiveness of LLMs is the integration of multi-modal inputs. Modern research often demands that LLMs operate in conjunction with structured data modalities such as figures, tables, and chemical notations (e.g., SMILES strings in chemistry or protein sequences in biology). Some LLMs, like Galactica, are specifically designed to incorporate multi-modal scientific data, enabling them to generate comprehensive textual descriptions that encapsulate both numerical and qualitative aspects of scientific research (taylor2022galacticaalarge pages 1-2, taylor2022galacticaalarge pages 2-4). These models are capable of converting structured data into coherent narratives that are invaluable when interpreting experimental results or supporting data-driven scientific inquiry.

sections.text: Evaluation of LLM performance in generating scientific descriptions relies on both automated metrics and human judgments. On the automated side, metrics such as ROUGE-L, METEOR, BLEU, and BERTScore are commonly deployed to assess lexical overlap and semantic similarity between generated content and human-authored reference texts. However, these metrics are often criticized for failing to capture deeper aspects of scientific coherence, context, and factual accuracy. Human evaluations remain indispensable to ensure that the generated text is not only linguistically plausible but also factually precise and contextually appropriate, especially in the domain of scientific communication where even subtle inaccuracies can significantly detract from the value of the work (tang2023evaluatinglargelanguage pages 3-5). High-quality human evaluations often highlight that while LLMs can provide readable and grammatically sound output, there is still a critical gap in ensuring that the content is fully aligned with the latest scientific knowledge and that it meets stringent academic standards.

sections.text: Moreover, prompt engineering is recognized as a critical factor in harnessing the full potential of LLMs for generating scientific descriptions. The quality, specificity, and structure of the prompts provided to these models greatly influence the output. Carefully engineered prompts that include structured guidelines can steer the LLM to produce outputs that are more aligned with the desired format and quality expectations. Studies have shown that even slight modifications in prompt design can result in significant differences in output quality, coherence, and factual correctness (lozic2023fluentbutnot pages 1-2, ma2023isthisabstract pages 4-6). In practice, researchers often need to iterate on prompt designs multiple times, balancing between conciseness and detail, in order to generate the most informative and contextually relevant scientific descriptions.

sections.text: Further attention has been given to emerging methods such as iterative refinement, where an initial draft generated by an LLM is subsequently refined either by another pass of generation or by human editors. This iterative process can help eliminate inaccuracies, improve the flow of logic, and transform raw LLM output into publishable scientific text. While the raw output from LLMs serves as a strong starting point by providing a coherent draft, the involvement of expert human oversight remains essential to validate and edit the content, thereby ensuring its correctness and utility for scientific communication (ma2023isthisabstract pages 9-12).

sections.text: It is also important to discuss the differences in performance across various scientific domains. In chemical sciences, for example, LLMs have been effectively used in summarizing molecular properties, predicting chemical reactions, and generating natural language descriptions of visual representations like chemical structures and reaction mechanisms (christofidellis2023unifyingmolecularand pages 11-14). In the environmental sciences, LLMs have been applied to unstructured text analysis tasks, such as sentiment analysis and topic clustering, which support the generation of coherent descriptions that integrate observational data with environmental policy insights (guo2024retrievalaugmentationof pages 25-27). Similarly, in the field of biology, models are being used to automate the extraction and annotation of taxonomic descriptions, although challenges related to homonymy and synonymy in biological nomenclature require nuanced handling and domain-specific fine-tuning (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 11-13).

sections.text: While the promise of LLMs is evident, the limitations are equally significant. Technical challenges such as data bias, opaque decision-making processes, and the lack of explicit reasoning pathways contribute to occasional outputs that may be superficially coherent but are internally inconsistent or factually misleading. This has led to ongoing research aimed at improving transparency and interpretability of LLM-generated content. Techniques such as chain-of-thought prompting and semantic distance minimization have been proposed to provide structured reasoning steps that could potentially mitigate these issues; however, preliminary evaluations indicate that these methods are not yet fully effective and require further development to reliably improve factual consistency (si2409canllmsgenerate pages 75-79).

sections.text: Ethical considerations further complicate the deployment of LLMs in scientific writing. The ease with which these models can generate plausible-sounding text raises concerns about authorship, intellectual property, and the possibility of encouraging academic fraud through overreliance on machine-generated content. These concerns underscore the importance of establishing clear guidelines and ethical frameworks for the use of LLMs in scientific workflows, ensuring that the outputs are transparently attributed and rigorously verified by human experts before publication (angelis2023chatgptandthe pages 2-3).

sections.text: A particularly illuminating case study is provided by the specialized model Galactica, which was trained on a meticulously curated corpus of scientific literature, textbooks, and reference materials. Galactica not only generated highly coherent and contextually accurate textual descriptions of scientific concepts but also demonstrated an ability to handle multi-modal inputs such as LaTeX equations, SMILES representations, and protein sequences. This showcases the potential of domain-specific LLMs to overcome some of the limitations inherent in general-purpose models, although even in these cases, issues like hallucinated references still require careful post-processing and expert review (taylor2022galacticaalarge pages 1-2, taylor2022galacticaalarge pages 2-4).

sections.text: Comparative studies focused on AI-generated versus human-written scientific texts offer further insights into LLM effectiveness. Human evaluators and detection models have revealed that while LLMs like GPT‑3, ChatGPT, and even newer versions of these models are capable of producing text that is linguistically fluid and structurally coherent, they often fail to incorporate the depth of thought and the nuanced originality that characterize human scientific writing. In some cases, detection algorithms based on syntactic and stylistic cues have been able to distinguish between AI-generated and human-authored content with considerable accuracy, thereby highlighting persistent gaps in creativity and factual reliability (ma2023isthisabstract pages 1-2, ma2023isthisabstract pages 6-9). Such findings underscore that although LLMs offer a significant boost in productivity by distilling large volumes of scientific literature into readable summaries, they still function best as supplements to, rather than replacements for, human expertise.

sections.text: In addition to direct text generation, LLMs also serve an integrative role by synthesizing information that comes from multiple disciplines and data modalities. In interdisciplinary research, for instance, LLMs have been utilized to generate directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) and summary tables that capture complex causal relationships, thereby facilitating the interpretation of multifaceted scientific phenomena. Their ability to break down disciplinary jargon and reconstruct complex concepts in accessible language further highlights the value they add in supporting cross-disciplinary communication—a key requirement in modern research environments (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 15-17, boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 17-20).

sections.text: Furthermore, the effectiveness of LLMs is enhanced when they are embedded in larger ecosystems that include error detection, retrieval augmentation, and iterative refinement systems. Retrieval augmentation, as mentioned earlier, has proven particularly effective in addressing lapses in factual accuracy by grounding generated outputs in external data sources. Such hybrid systems often outperform standalone LLMs in generating high-quality scientific summaries and explanations (guo2024retrievalaugmentationof pages 14-17, guo2024retrievalaugmentationof pages 27-31). These systems, by integrating external knowledge bases, mitigate one of the inherent weaknesses of LLMs—that is, their reliance on static training data which can become outdated or incomplete.

sections.text: Another advantage of using LLMs is their capacity for rapid iteration. In fast-moving fields where new information is constantly emerging, LLMs can assist researchers by quickly assimilating new data and producing preliminary drafts of literature reviews or background sections. This rapid turnaround can help accelerate the pace of scientific discovery, although the benefits of speed must always be balanced against the potential pitfalls of reduced accuracy and the risk of propagating errors (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 1-3).

sections.text: Despite these advancements, it is clear that the generation of scientific textual descriptions by LLMs is not a fully solved problem. Ongoing research efforts are focused on developing more robust evaluation metrics that go beyond lexical overlap, incorporating semantic and pragmatic factors that more accurately reflect the quality and reliability of scientific output. Some researchers advocate for evaluation methods that include detailed human assessments, backward chaining of generated hypotheses, and even interactive systems in which users provide iterative feedback to refine the AI-generated content (lozic2023fluentbutnot pages 1-2, ma2023isthisabstract pages 2-4).

They excel in tasks such as summarization, translation of technical inputs into descriptive narratives, and initial drafting of scientific content—all of which significantly enhance the efficiency of the research workflow (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 11-13, christofidellis2023unifyingmolecularand pages 11-14). When integrated with domain-specific fine-tuning and retrieval augmentation strategies, these models demonstrate a markedly improved capacity to generate relevant, context-aware, and technically accurate descriptions that are useful across a range of scientific domains (guo2024retrievalaugmentationof pages 17-21).

Issues such as hallucinations, citation inaccuracies, and superficial reasoning persist, meaning that while LLMs are invaluable as assistive writing tools, they cannot yet replace the nuanced judgment and original creativity of human experts (ma2023isthisabstract pages 6-9, si2409canllmsgenerate pages 75-79). Yet, due to their inherent limitations, they are best regarded as complementary tools that augment human expertise rather than serve as standalone solutions. The integration of LLMs with structured workflows, advanced prompt engineering, retrieval-based augmentation, and stringent human-in-the-loop verification systems represents the most promising pathway forward in harnessing their full potential in scientific research (taylor2022galacticaalarge pages 2-4, angelis2023chatgptandthe pages 2-3).

Continued research in this area holds the promise of ultimately achieving fully automated, yet scientifically reliable and innovative, textual descriptions that can keep pace with the rapid growth of scientific knowledge. In closing, while language models are demonstrably effective at generating textual descriptions of scientific concepts with considerable fluency and breadth, their current state also mandates a robust system of evaluation and expert oversight to ensure the integrity, relevance, and originality of the generated content (boyko2023aninterdisciplinaryoutlook pages 8-11, tang2023evaluatinglargelanguage pages 3-5).

sections.text: Overall, the body of evidence reflects that LLMs are indispensable tools in the modern scientific landscape. They provide rapid, cost-effective solutions for synthesizing vast amounts of data into coherent narratives. However, achieving the dual objectives of efficiency and absolute reliability in scientific communication remains an active area of research. By addressing the challenges of factual accuracy and semantic fidelity through innovative retrieval augmentation techniques, iterative refinement practices, and domain-specific fine-tuning, LLMs may eventually reach a point where they can autonomously generate high-quality, expert-level descriptions of complex scientific concepts without the constant need for human correction.

Thus, while the current generation of language models offers exciting possibilities for automating scientific writing and knowledge dissemination, their effectiveness is ultimately contingent upon an integrated approach that combines technological innovation with rigorous human oversight. The future of automated scientific text generation will likely depend on continued research that bridges these gaps, ensuring that the benefits of LLMs can be fully realized in producing clear, accurate, and original scientific descriptions that support and enhance human research endeavors (li2024pretrainedlanguagemodels pages 1-2, li2403chatcitellmagent pages 10-12).

question: How good are LLMs at solving traditional tabular ML datasets using ICL?

sections.text:
This report examines the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in solving traditional tabular machine learning (ML) datasets via in
‐context learning (ICL). We structure our discussion into several sections: an introduction to the problem and background on traditional tabular methods, an overview of the ICL paradigm with LLMs, a detailed comparison between LLM
‐based approaches and classical methods, an analysis of key challenges and limitations, and future directions to improve LLM performance on tabular problems.

1. Introduction  
Traditional tabular data problems have long been dominated by specialized algorithms such as gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT) like XGBoost, CatBoost, and ensemble methods including random forests and support vector machines (SVM). These methods leverage decision boundaries that are specifically designed to capture the heterogeneous structure (e.g., categorical, numeric, binary) and limited sample sizes typically found in tabular datasets. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated powerful zero-shot and few-shot learning capabilities in natural language processing tasks by performing in-context learning (ICL), where they condition on a few examples to predict unseen data. This report seeks to critically examine how well LLMs perform on traditional tabular ML tasks when using ICL, and whether their innate generalization abilities can rival or complement state-of-the-art classical methods.

2. Background and Motivation  
The tabular data domain presents unique challenges that are distinct from those in image or text domains. Heterogeneous features, loss of spatial or sequential order, and the necessity for effective preprocessing (e.g., encoding, normalization, handling missing values) have traditionally made deep learning approaches less competitive than tree-based models when applied directly to structured data. Recent research has introduced specialized transformer models such as TabPFN and TabICL, which are tailored for tabular tasks through pretraining on synthetic or realistic datasets. These models exploit in-context learning capabilities to generate predictions without traditional fine-tuning. Initial work has shown that zero-shot ICL using LLMs lags behind classical algorithms, but finetuning or incorporating suitable pretraining data can substantially narrow the performance gap (bae2405finetunedincontextlearning pages 1-3).

LLMs have the attractive potential to bring transfer learning and instruction understanding to tabular tasks, as they can in principle leverage semantic information from column names and textual descriptions. However, the core challenge is that LLMs’ pretraining on large corpora of unstructured text does not inherently provide them with the numerical understanding or data inductive biases required for tabular prediction. The seminal studies indicate that while emerging LLMs show nascent promise for certain tabular tasks, they face significant hurdles in bridging the gap with specialized classical ML methods (fang2024largelanguagemodels(llms) pages 27-29).

citations.title: Fine-tuned in-context learning transformers are excellent tabular data classifiers.

sections.text:
3. In-Context Learning (ICL) with LLMs for Tabular Data  
In-context learning refers to the ability of an LLM to adapt to a new task simply by conditioning on a set of examples provided in the prompt, without gradient updates to the underlying model. Many of the recent works have attempted to serialize tabular data into natural language by generating text strings that couple feature names and values. For instance, methods explored in TabLLM and related approaches focus on varied serialization strategies that improve the model’s ability to extract relevant information from tabular rows (hegselmann2023tabllmfewshotclassification pages 2-3). Several studies have shown that such serialization, in combination with carefully engineered few-shot examples, can enable LLMs to generate reasonable predictions on tabular data. Yet, the performance of LLMs in purely zero-shot or few-shot ICL settings is very sensitive to prompt design, tokenization inefficiencies, and the limited input context of most models (ono2406textserializationand pages 1-2).

LLMs tend to underperform in direct ICL on tabular tasks relative to traditional algorithms. For example, GPT-4 and similar models, when applied in a zero-shot ICL setting, generate predictions that are inconsistent and generally poorer in accuracy than those of XGBoost or support vector machines (bordt2024elephantsneverforget pages 1-2, bordt2024elephantsneverforget pages 9-10). These performance limitations are partly due to the lack of numeric inductive biases in LLM architectures and the dramatic token inefficiencies when converting numbers into text strings. In-context examples, which serve as the sole basis for adapting the model to a new dataset, must be carefully selected to contain reliable statistical information, yet even then the performance tends to saturate well below that of finely tuned classical methods (nafar2409learningvsretrieval pages 7-9).

sections.text:
4. Comparison with Classical Tabular ML Methods  
A large body of literature emphasizes that classical methods such as XGBoost, LightGBM, random forests, and SVMs remain the gold standard in tabular prediction due to their interpretability, robust handling of feature heterogeneity, and computational efficiency. Multiple studies comparing various methods on standard tabular benchmarks consistently report that tree-based methods maintain superior performance with lower error rates (breugel2405whytabularfoundation pages 1-2, breugel2405whytabularfoundation pages 4-5).

LLMs applied to tabular data using ICL, even when combined with augmented strategies such as retrieval or specialized prompts, have not yet demonstrated clear superiority over these classical algorithms. For instance, experiments have shown that out-of-the-box LLMs often achieve accuracy and AUROC scores that are substantially inferior to classical baselines, with reported metrics for LLMs sometimes approaching random guessing in zero-shot settings (bordt2024elephantsneverforget pages 10-13, hollmann2023largelanguagemodels pages 1-3). Fine-tuning LLMs specifically on tabular data or combining them with retrieval-augmented techniques can improve their performance; nevertheless, these hybrid strategies still fall short of the sophisticated ensemble methods used by classical models (rabbani2501transferlearningof pages 1-2, rabbani2501transferlearningof pages 2-4).

One of the compelling observations is that while classical algorithms operate with strong inductive biases—for instance, tree-based models inherently partition feature spaces in a way that suits heterogeneous data distributions—LLMs must learn these patterns anew from a few examples. Even with additional pretraining on synthetic tabular data (as seen in models like TabPFN), performance gaps persist in scenarios with large sample sizes, complex feature interactions, or when the underlying data distribution deviates from the training distribution (qu2025tabiclatabular pages 7-8, ma2024tabdptscalingtabular pages 1-2). Thus, classical ML algorithms retain a competitive advantage largely because their architectures are expressly designed to process tabular data, while LLMs require further adaptation beyond simple ICL to approach similar levels of performance (ghaffarzadehesfahani2024largelanguagemodels pages 3-6, ghaffarzadehesfahani2024largelanguagemodels pages 6-9).

sections.text:
5. Analysis of Performance Variability in ICL  
The performance of LLMs using ICL on tabular datasets is highly sensitive to several aspects of prompt design and example selection. Serialization methods, which transform a tabular row into a natural language string, significantly affect how well the model can parse and leverage the numeric and categorical information embedded in the input. Studies have shown that simpler serialization templates (e.g., “[column name] is [value]”) often yield better results than more complex concatenations, likely because they minimize token overhead and ambiguity (ono2406textserializationand pages 7-8, ono2406textserializationand pages 8-9). Yet, even with optimized prompts, LLMs’ predictions tend to vary greatly based on the order and quality of the in-context examples. This sensitivity can occasionally lead to instability, where adding more examples does not linearly translate into performance improvements or can even degrade results if the ordering introduces biases (nafar2409learningvsretrieval pages 9-10, nafar2025learningvsretrieval pages 10-11).

Moreover, another critical factor is data contamination. Because many LLMs have been exposed during pretraining to popular datasets or similar statistical distributions, there is a risk that the model may “memorize” or retrieve learned patterns rather than genuinely learning from the in-context examples provided. This phenomenon can lead to inflated performance when the test set closely matches the training data seen during pretraining, but it does not provide robust generalization to novel or out-of-domain datasets (bordt2024elephantsneverforget pages 10-13, nafar2025learningvsretrieval pages 10-11). As a result, careful design of evaluation protocols is required to truly assess the ICL capabilities of LLMs on tabular prediction tasks.

sections.text:
6. Limitations of LLMs in Tabular ICL  
Several limitations of applying LLM-driven ICL to traditional tabular datasets have been identified across multiple research works. First, token inefficiency presents a significant roadblock. Numerical values in a table must be tokenized, often resulting in suboptimal representations that obscure the continuity and precision inherent in raw numeric data (fang2024largelanguagemodels(llms) pages 29-31, ono2406textserializationand pages 1-2). In addition, LLMs are generally not optimized for handling the high density of features typically seen in tabular data, as they are designed for sequential text where the ordering carries rich semantic information rather than the order-invariance of tabular data (fang2024largelanguagemodels(llms) pages 27-29).

Second, the context window limitation constrains the number of in-context examples that can be incorporated into a prompt. Although recent approaches have attempted to extend the effective context size through retrieval-augmented techniques, this remains a bottleneck that can limit the scalability of ICL with LLMs, particularly when large datasets with many features are involved (wen2502scalableincontextlearning pages 1-2, wen2502scalableincontextlearning pages 2-3).

Furthermore, LLMs inherently lack the inductive biases that classical models possess. Traditional methods, by design, embed a prior knowledge about the structure of tabular data—such as interaction terms and non-linear splitting rules—that LLMs must try to infer solely from the in-context examples provided (zhang2023towardsfoundationmodels pages 1-3, qu2025tabiclatabular pages 1-2). This gap is even more pronounced in scenarios with low sample sizes where the few-shot examples may not cover the breadth of feature interactions present in more complex datasets. As a result, even with advanced serialization and careful prompt engineering, LLMs’ predictions often fall short compared to those generated by highly tuned ensemble methods (hollmann2023largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, rabbani2501transferlearningof pages 7-9).

Another limitation is the computational cost and latency associated with deploying LLMs for ICL. Because LLMs are large and resource intensive, running them in inference mode with complex prompts can be significantly slower and more expensive than running classical algorithms that have been optimized for fast numerical computation (wen2024fromsupervisedto pages 9-9, tassini2023exploringllmsfor pages 28-31). This inefficiency further hampers the feasibility of LLMs as drop-in replacements for established methods in time-sensitive or resource-constrained environments.

sections.text:
7. Opportunities and Hybrid Approaches  
Despite these limitations, there are promising directions for enhancing LLM performance on tabular tasks through hybrid techniques and improved training methodologies. Researchers have pursued finetuning strategies whereby an LLM is further trained on a large corpus of tabular data—sometimes obtained via synthetic data generation—to imbue the model with specific numerical and statistical priors. Such methods have produced finetuned in-context learning transformers that yield better generalization and competitive performance on tabular benchmarks, particularly when sufficient training data is available (bae2405finetunedincontextlearning pages 1-3, rabbani2501transferlearningof pages 2-4).

Other approaches combine retrieval mechanisms with LLM-based ICL. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques allow an LLM to dynamically incorporate a support set of relevant examples for each test instance, thereby extending the effective context window and improving prediction quality. Such systems, exemplified by TabICL and similar models, have shown that with carefully engineered retrieval policies, LLMs can generate decision boundaries that are competitive with classical ensemble models on large-scale tabular datasets (wen2502scalableincontextlearning pages 8-9, qu2025tabiclatabular pages 8-9).

Additionally, some studies advocate for using LLMs as complementary modules in hybrid pipelines. For example, an LLM might be used to generate interpretable explanations or to perform feature engineering—such as suggesting new composite features—while leaving the final prediction to a robust classical model like XGBoost (hollmann2023largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, liu2023investigatingthefairness pages 1-2). This division of labor leverages the strengths of both approaches: the flexibility and language understanding inherent in LLMs and the robust inductive biases and computational efficiency of classical ML algorithms.

A further research avenue involves developing specialized tokenization and serialization methods tailored for tabular data. Recent work has indicated that modifications to tokenizers—for example, processing each digit separately or using templates that preserve numeric precision—can improve the representation of continuous features, which in turn enhances the model’s arithmetic and relational reasoning capabilities (fang2024largelanguagemodels(llms) pages 29-31, ono2406textserializationand pages 7-8).

sections.text:
8. Comparative Evaluation on Benchmarks  
The empirical evaluation across a wide range of benchmark datasets reveals a nuanced landscape. On one hand, LLMs in a pure ICL, zero-shot configuration consistently underperform compared to classical methods. In many studies, LLMs achieve mediocre accuracy or AUROC scores, sometimes equivalent to random guessing when no domain-specific adaptation is provided (bordt2024elephantsneverforget pages 1-2, bordt2024elephantsneverforget pages 10-13). On the other hand, when LLMs are finetuned or augmented with techniques such as retrieval or synthetic data pretraining, their performance improves markedly—even approaching or sometimes surpassing that of strong baselines under limited data regimes (wen2024fromsupervisedto pages 1-3, qu2025tabiclatabular pages 7-8).

For instance, in the context of healthcare data or other low-dimensional tabular datasets, finetuned LLMs have demonstrated notable improvements over standard ICL approaches, achieving competitive area-under-the-ROC-curve (AUROC) scores relative to classical methods (rabbani2501transferlearningof pages 7-9). However, in scenarios involving higher dimensionality or complex, multi-class classification tasks, classical algorithms such as XGBoost and random forests continue to dominate due to their well-engineered feature processing pipelines and tuning capabilities (breugel2405whytabularfoundation pages 4-5, qu2025tabiclatabular pages 2-3).

It is also important to note that the performance of ICL-based LLMs tends to be highly contingent on the similarity between the test data and the examples provided in the prompt. Where there is significant overlap in feature distributions (or if the model has been inadvertently exposed to the task during pretraining), LLMs may exhibit surprisingly strong predictive capability. Conversely, when the test dataset diverges from any domain seen during training, performance degrades rapidly (nafar2409learningvsretrieval pages 9-10, zhang2023towardsfoundationmodels pages 7-8).

9. Interpretability, Fairness, and Robustness Considerations  
Interpretability of predictions is a key consideration in many tabular applications, particularly in high-stakes domains like finance and healthcare. LLMs, with their inherent capacity to generate natural language explanations, offer the potential advantage of producing interpretable output alongside predictions. However, studies indicate that the fairness of LLMs may be compromised by residual biases inherited from the pretraining corpus, and the resultant explanations are not always faithful or consistent (liu2023investigatingthefairness pages 1-2, fang2024largelanguagemodels(llms) pages 29-31).

Moreover, classical ML methods benefit from decades of research into methods for fairness, interpretability (e.g., Shapley values), and stability. LLMs, while promising in their generative and reasoning capabilities, still require additional mechanisms—such as audit modules or post-hoc explanation frameworks—to address issues of hallucination and attribution bias. These challenges illustrate that even if LLMs continue to improve in raw prediction performance via enhanced ICL, integrating them reliably into decision-making pipelines remains a nontrivial task (bordt2024elephantsneverforget pages 10-13, tassini2023exploringllmsfor pages 28-31).

sections.text:
10. Future Research Directions  
There exists an opportunity to bridge the performance gap between LLMs and classical models by leveraging specialized pretraining and finetuning strategies. Future research should focus on:  
• Developing domain-adaptive pretraining protocols that incorporate diverse and representative tabular datasets, including both synthetic and real data, to endow LLMs with stronger numerical reasoning and inductive biases (bae2405finetunedincontextlearning pages 1-3, wen2024fromsupervisedto pages 1-3).  
• Optimizing serialization and tokenization schemes to reduce ambiguity and improve the representation of numerical features while preserving the contextual semantics found in column names and value descriptions (ono2406textserializationand pages 7-8, fang2024largelanguagemodels(llms) pages 27-29).  
• Integrating retrieval-augmented generation techniques that dynamically supply relevant in-context examples, thus extending the effective context window and improving generalization on diverse datasets (wen2502scalableincontextlearning pages 2-3, qu2025tabiclatabular pages 8-9).  
• Exploring hybrid architectures where LLMs and classical methods complement each other, such as employing LLMs for feature engineering or explanation generation and relying on tree-based models for high-precision prediction (hollmann2023largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, rabbani2501transferlearningof pages 7-9).  
• Investigating methods to mitigate data contamination and prompt bias by using datasets that are external to the LLM’s pretraining distribution, thereby ensuring that predictions arise from genuine in-context learning rather than memorized patterns (nafar2409learningvsretrieval pages 10-11, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 31-34).

sections.text:
11. Conclusion  
In summary, while large language models demonstrate promising capabilities in applying in-context learning to tabular data tasks, their performance in a zero-shot or few-shot ICL setting remains generally inferior to classical tabular ML algorithms such as XGBoost, random forests, and support vector machines. The inherent challenges stem from inefficiencies in text serialization, the lack of built-in numerical inductive biases, limitations in the context window, and sensitivity to prompt design. Finetuning LLMs on tabular data and employing retrieval-augmented techniques can mitigate some of these issues, leading to notable performance improvements and, in certain constrained scenarios, competitive results relative to classical methods. However, robust generalization across domains and complex, high-dimensional datasets remains elusive, and classical methods continue to offer superior efficiency, consistency, and interpretability in practice.

Future progress in this area will likely depend on research that combines the generative power and transfer learning capabilities of LLMs with more effective mechanisms for handling the unique challenges of tabular data. By designing dedicated pretraining strategies, refining prompt engineering techniques, and integrating hybrid approaches that leverage both LLMs and traditional models, it is possible that LLMs may eventually rival—even in some cases surpass—traditional algorithms on standard tabular ML benchmarks. Until that point, LLMs are best viewed as complementary tools that can augment classical methods with additional functionalities such as natural language explanation generation and dynamic adaptation via ICL.

Overall, while LLMs possess considerable promise and have opened new research avenues in the domain of tabular data modeling, current evidence suggests that in-context learning with LLMs alone is not yet sufficient to replace highly optimized classical ML approaches. Continued innovations in model architecture, training paradigms, and hybrid strategies will be essential to fully harness the potential of LLMs for traditional tabular machine learning tasks (bae2405finetunedincontextlearning pages 1-3, bordt2024elephantsneverforget pages 1-2, fang2024largelanguagemodels(llms) pages 27-29, wen2502scalableincontextlearning pages 8-9).

This conclusion is supported by extensive evaluations across various benchmarks and comparative studies that consistently indicate LLM-based ICL methods still struggle with scaling and achieving the level of generalization, efficiency, and robustness demonstrated by specialized classical algorithms (qu2025tabiclatabular pages 7-8, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 29-31, zhang2023towardsfoundationmodels pages 8-10, tassini2023exploringllmsfor pages 28-31).

In essence, LLMs have made significant strides toward addressing traditional tabular problems using in-context learning, particularly when enhanced by finetuning and retrieval strategies; yet, in their current state, they are complementary to rather than a replacement for established, high-performance classical tabular ML methods. Future research that successfully combines LLMs’ strengths with the robust design principles of classical algorithms holds the promise of delivering more versatile and effective tools for tabular data analysis.

question: Compare the various algorithms for compressing trees in terms of computation complexity.

sections.text: This report reviews and compares a wide range of algorithms developed for compressing trees with regard to their computational complexity. The discussion considers several families of methods, including those based on directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), grammar-based compression (including straight ‐line programs, both SLPs and tree straight-line programs, TSLPs), top tree compression, succinct data structures, and differential approaches. In what follows, we describe for each class the underlying ideas, the theoretical worst-case and average-case complexities of constructing the compressed representation, and the trade-offs that these methods exhibit between compression power and the computational overhead required for compression and query support.

Tree-structured data arise in many applications such as XML document representation, compiler syntax trees, and hierarchical data mining. Compressing trees efficiently is challenging because structures may exhibit various types of redundancy. Early methods such as minimal DAG compression reuse repeated subtrees by sharing identical substructures, which can be computed in linear time when a tree is explicitly given. However, DAG compression only handles entire repeated subtrees while missing internal pattern repetitions. More advanced methods (e.g., grammar-based compressors) can exploit tree pattern repeats even when the redundancy is not an exact subtree repeat, thereby achieving exponentially smaller representations in some cases, albeit with higher computational complexity. Techniques such as top tree compression combine ideas from both DAGs and tree grammars to deliver both effective compression and efficient navigation (e.g., logarithmic time queries). Other approaches pursue succinctness —attaining space close to the information-theoretic bounds while still supporting fast (often constant-time) navigation operations —and differential compression methods attempt to encode only changes between node codes. In the following sections we examine these methods in terms of their computational complexity.

The classical DAG compression method represents a tree by identifying all isomorphic (identical) subtrees and replacing each occurrence with a shared pointer to a unique copy. Because the minimal DAG for a tree can be built in a bottom-up pass, its overall construction time is linear in the number of nodes of the input tree. For example, Bille et al. describe DAG compression that uses subtree repeats and can be computed in O(n) time, where n is the size of the tree (bille2013treecompressionwith pages 1-3). The computational cost is low because each node is visited once and compared against previously encountered subtree representations; however, while the time is optimal, the approach is limited by the fact that it does not capture internal tree pattern repetitions. Ingels explains that efficient algorithms for computing tree equivalence classes —for example, via an AHU-inspired algorithm —can further lead to DAG constructions with complexities of O(n ·d) in the ordered case or O(n ·d ·log d) in the unordered case, where d is the maximal degree (ingels2022onthesimilarities pages 33-35). Overall, DAG-based methods are attractive for their low computational expense and linear running time, but they may miss substantial compressibility in trees with repeated patterns that do not constitute whole subtrees.

On the similarities of trees: the interest of enumeration and compression methods

sections.text: Moving beyond DAGs, grammar-based compression methods represent trees as context-free grammars, allowing for the sharing of repeated patterns even when these patterns do not occur as complete subtrees. In this framework one often distinguishes between tree straight-line programs (TSLPs) and straight-line programs (SLPs) that produce a balanced parenthesis (BP) sequence representing the tree. TSLPs can share repeated patterns with  “gaps ” in them, and while they can potentially achieve exponentially smaller representations compared to the minimal DAG, computing an optimal (or even minimal) TSLP is NP-hard (lohrey2015grammarbasedtreecompression pages 4-7). Therefore, practical algorithms resort to approximation and heuristic approaches. Many of these algorithms run in polynomial time, but the constants and degree of the polynomial vary according to the method.For example, TreeRePair —an algorithm inspired by the string compressor RePair —constructs linear straight-line context-free tree grammars in linear time in practice by repeatedly replacing the most frequent digrams, with constant time updates per replacement on average (lohrey2013xmltreestructure pages 1-4, lohrey2013xmltreestructure pages 40-44). The compression phase of TreeRePair is designed to run in overall linear time because it updates occurrence lists for the replaced digrams locally in constant time. However, additional processing such as encoding and grammar normalization may introduce overheads that affect the practical runtime leading to differences of up to an order of magnitude in running time when compared with methods such as top tree compression (hubschleschneider2015treecompressionwith pages 3-5).SLP-based approaches that compress the BP representation of a tree have another attractive property: in the worst-case, they may be exponentially more succinct than minimal DAGs. Bille et al. detail algorithms that support random access and basic navigational queries (e.g., rank, select, excess) on the SLP-compressed BP string in O(log N) time, with the SLP size being linear in the number of nonterminals produced by the compression process (bille2015randomaccessto pages 3-5). The construction of an SLP from a DAG is performed by converting each node of the DAG into several nonterminals in the SLP, maintaining the overall structure and ensuring that the final grammar captures the complete BP sequence. Although the SLP compression itself can be achieved in linear time with respect to the size of the DAG or the original tree in some cases, certain applications (like pattern matching or membership testing on SLP-compressed trees) become computationally hard (PSPACE-complete in some cases) because the operations must work directly on the compressed representation (ganardi2018treecompressionusing pages 1-2, ganardi2018treecompressionusing pages 20-22).Thus, grammar-based methods represent a trade-off: while they are capable of achieving exponential compression ratios and can be constructed in time that is polynomial (or even linear in practical scenarios with heuristics such as in TreeRePair), many algorithmic problems remain challenging on the compressed representations, with some decision problems potentially being NP-hard or PSPACE-complete (lohrey2015grammarbasedtreecompression pages 7-9).

sections.text: Top tree compression was introduced as a method that combines the benefits of DAG and tree grammar compression. The method first transforms the input tree into a top tree —a hierarchical clustering of subtrees where the repeated tree patterns become explicit subtree repeats —and then constructs a minimal DAG (called the top DAG) of this top tree (bille2013treecompressionwith pages 3-6). The construction of top trees involves a bottom-up, greedy clustering procedure that is executed in O(log n_T) iterations, where n_T is the number of nodes in the input tree; each merge operation is designed to preserve the ordered tree structure. After the top tree is built, computing the top DAG is a linear-time process relative to the number of clusters. Hence, the overall compression process is efficient in terms of time complexity. Moreover, navigation operations such as computing parent, first child, and next sibling on the compressed representation can be supported in O(log n_T) time (bille2013treecompressionwith pages 3-6). Further improvements on the top tree compression scheme were introduced by harnessing RePair-inspired heuristics. Hübschle-Schneider and Raman demonstrated that using such combiners increases the compressibility of the top tree representation —reducing overhead, though with additional computational costs due to hashing and frequency analysis of merge candidates (hubschleschneider2015treecompressionwith pages 8-10, hubschleschneider2015treecompressionwith pages 13-15). The basic top tree algorithm remains a linear-time algorithm when the merging order is fixed and executed using a simple bottom-up left-to-right scheme; however, employing the RePair-inspired heuristic introduces extra iterations and the need for hash table operations, which while still practical, raise the constant factors in the running time compared to the classical (non-heuristic) top tree compression algorithm.

sections.text: An important approach to tree compression involves representing the tree structure as a balanced parenthesis (BP) sequence generated by a depth-first traversal and then applying grammar compression techniques to the resulting string. Bille et al. (bille2015randomaccessto pages 1-3) show that an SLP can be constructed to generate the BP sequence, and such SLP-based approaches are capable of reproducing strings of length N with a representation that can be exponentially smaller than N. The compressed representation supports random access, as well as navigational queries on the tree, in O(log N) time. The conversion from DAG representation to an SLP is carried out in time that is linear in the number of nodes of the DAG, and the subsequent heavy-path decomposition required for query support typically contributes an additional logarithmic factor relative to the original tree size (bille2015randomaccessto pages 3-5). This combination is particularly effective for trees that are not well compressed by minimal DAGs, such as long chains of repeated labels.

sections.text: Another class of techniques focuses on differential compression of trees, where the idea is to store differences rather than absolute values. In the DeltaTree approach described by Wang and Deng, each node stores only the differences from its parent node rather than the full code. The underlying problem in the DeltaTree method reduces to finding a minimum spanning tree (MST) over a complete graph (called the DeltaGraph) where vertices represent tree node codes and edge weights represent the number of differences between codes (wang2020deltapq pages 5-6). Because the DeltaGraph contains O(n²) edges, applying classical MST algorithms directly would incur a polynomial time cost, typically at least quadratic in the number of nodes. However, tailored algorithms for the DeltaTree approach achieve more efficient processing, so that once the MST is computed, differential coding for search and update operations can be executed in O(n) time in certain practical scenarios. Thus, while the core problem deals with a dense graph and has a high worst-case computational complexity, subsequent compression operations leverage the MST structure to reduce redundancy effectively.

sections.text: A related line of work  “compresses ” trees in a different sense, where the objective is to represent a tree using space close to the information ‐theoretic lower bound (approximately 2n bits for a tree with n nodes) while still supporting constant-time navigation queries. The Balanced Parentheses (BP) and Depth-First Unary Degree Sequence (DFUDS) representations are canonical examples of such succinct representations. These methods are not compression in the lossless coding sense aimed at reducing file size by exploiting repetitions, but rather they are compact encodings that support constant-time rank and select operations through auxiliary data structures (이준희2021spaceefficientrepresentationof pages 74-78). In both BP and DFUDS representations, the tree can be navigated using operations that run in O(1) time, though the construction phase requires linear time and additional preprocessing to build the required auxiliary data structures. As such, the computational complexity of succinct tree representations is dominated by the O(n) preprocessing time and the O(1) per query cost, which is highly desirable for applications where frequent query operations are needed on a compact representation.

sections.text: An essential theme that emerges is the trade-off between compression efficacy (i.e., how small the compressed representation is) and the computational complexity of both compression and subsequent operations on the compressed format. Methods such as minimal DAG compression and succinct tree representations achieve optimal or near-optimal construction times (linear time) and provide fast navigation (O(1) for succinct structures and O(log n) for grammar-based methods). However, their compressibility is limited; for example, DAG compression struggles with chains of repeated labels (bille2013treecompressionwith pages 1-3).In contrast, grammar-based methods (including TSLPs and SLPs) can achieve exponentially better compression ratios for trees with significant repetitive structure. Algorithms like TreeRePair are practically linear in running time due to localized updates and constant-time digram replacements (lohrey2013xmltreestructure pages 1-4, lohrey2013xmltreestructure pages 40-44). Nonetheless, the general problem of computing a minimal grammar is NP-hard, and several associated decision problems (e.g., pattern matching within an SLP-compressed tree) have high worst-case complexities, sometimes reaching PSPACE-completeness (ganardi2018treecompressionusing pages 1-2, ganardi2018treecompressionusing pages 20-22).Top tree compression methods, by contrast, provide a compromise in which the compression ratio is provably close to the information-theoretic optimum and all navigational queries are supported in O(log n) time. Their construction is based on bottom-up cluster merging, performed in a logarithmic number of iterations, and it can be computed in linear time when using a simple left-to-right merging order (bille2013treecompressionwith pages 3-6). When augmented with RePair-inspired combiners, the quality of the compression improves while still maintaining a low asymptotic complexity —albeit with increased constant factors due to additional hashing and frequency analysis (hubschleschneider2015treecompressionwith pages 8-10).Differential compression methods such as DeltaTree reveal a different computational profile. Although the underlying MST problem on an O(n²)-edge graph suggests a potentially high worst-case complexity, the practical adaptations and domain-specific heuristics often result in efficient algorithms that are linear or near-linear after the initial heavy computations (wang2020deltapq pages 5-6).It is also worth noting that the transformation between different compressed representations may incur additional overhead. For instance, converting an SLP into a top DAG or into a balanced parenthesis SLP might involve a logarithmic or polynomial sized increase in the representation, yet these conversions are usually performed in time that is linear or near-linear in the size of the compressed structure rather than in the uncompressed tree size (bille2015randomaccessto pages 3-5, lohrey2012algorithmicsonslpcompressed pages 26-29).
