sections.text: Given the empirical and theoretical findings summarized above, several key conclusions can be drawn regarding the correlations among fairness metrics. First, while positive correlations exist for a subset of metrics—especially those that share similar error-focused perspectives (e.g., SPD, DEO, EOD, and AAOD)—this correlation is not universally strong. Empirical results indicate that metrics focusing on error rates and predictive values generally move together when data and model conditions are stable, but they may diverge under more complex scenarios involving dataset shift, varying data quality, or model architectural changes (barry2023ontheimpact pages 1-2, yang2024alargescaleempirical pages 8-9). Second, there is compelling evidence that the context in which fairness is evaluated plays a decisive role. Fairness metrics applied to image classification tasks may correlate differently than those applied to natural language processing or recommender systems. Moreover, metrics that capture intrinsic biases of models (such as those derived from embeddings) often fail to correspond accurately with extrinsic measures that capture downstream behavior (cao2022ontheintrinsic pages 1-2, cao2022ontheintrinsic pages 2-4). Similarly, studies in face recognition and medical imaging further highlight that domain-specific characteristics drive discrepancies in metric behavior (zong2210medfairbenchmarkingfairness pages 1-3, sukthanker2023rethinkingbiasmitigation pages 25-28). Third, the model architecture and training methodology significantly influence observed fairness correlations. Models trained with adversarial or regularization techniques designed to reduce bias can lead to improvements in certain fairness metrics while inadvertently worsening others, as observed in both linear and deep neural network scenarios (beutel2019puttingfairnessprinciples pages 2-3, jones2020metricsandmethods pages 4-5). The variability of these effects across datasets and architectures reinforces the notion that no single fairness evaluation is robust across all conditions, and that multi-metric, context-aware approaches are necessary. Fourth, the use of integrated evaluation frameworks that assess fairness across multiple thresholds and conditions (e.g., using fair efficiency measures) can help reconcile some of the observed disagreements. By averaging performance over different operating points, some studies have found that overall fairness improvements in one metric tend to lead to relative improvements in other related metrics, even if the correlation is not perfect at any individual threshold (jones2020metricsandmethods pages 1-2, yang2024alargescaleempirical pages 8-9). Fifth, the theoretical underpinnings of fairness metrics imply that trade-offs are inevitable. In particular, metrics such as calibration and equalized odds are mathematically constrained to diverge when base rates differ across groups, so that a model might achieve high calibration at the expense of equalized odds and vice versa. These trade-offs are not mere artifacts of experimental design but are inherent in the definitions themselves, and they naturally lead to only partial correlation between different fairness metrics in practice (barry2023ontheimpact pages 2-3, garg2020fairnessmetricsa pages 2-4).

sections.text: The considerable variability in fairness metric correlations suggests several practical recommendations for practitioners and researchers: 1. Employ a multi-metric evaluation strategy. As no single metric is universally robust, it is imperative to assess fairness using a suite of complementary measures that capture different aspects of bias. This approach helps to provide a more complete picture of a model’s fairness profile, particularly in light of dataset and architecture sensitivity (yang2024alargescaleempirical pages 2-3, pagano2023contextbasedpatternsin pages 1-2). 2. Contextualize fairness metrics based on the dataset and domain. Researchers should carefully consider the distributional properties of their datasets and the nature of the bias present. For example, bias in medical imaging may require different fairness considerations compared to bias in language models or recommender systems (zong2210medfairbenchmarkingfairness pages 1-3, delobelle2021measuringfairnesswith pages 9-10). 3. Recognize that methodological choices (e.g., data preprocessing, sampling strategies, thresholding decisions) can have substantial impacts on fairness evaluations. Therefore, sensitivity analyses that examine how fairness metrics shift under varying conditions are essential for robust evaluation (deldjoo2025cfairllmconsumerfairness pages 12-14, loureiro2024computationalmethodfor pages 37-40). 4. Consider integrated global metrics—such as fair efficiency—that average across multiple operating points and provide a more robust picture of fairness–performance trade-offs. This approach can mitigate the discrepancies observed in single-threshold evaluations and help in selecting models that generalize better across disparate groups (jones2020metricsandmethods pages 2-3, yang2024alargescaleempirical pages 8-9). 5. Finally, it is vital to align the choice of fairness metrics with the ethical and practical requirements of the specific domain. In scenarios where the consequences of bias are particularly severe, as in healthcare or criminal justice, metrics that prioritize worst-case subgroup performance (e.g., Max-Min fairness) may offer more appropriate evaluation than aggregate metrics (zong2210medfairbenchmarkingfairness pages 3-4, hinnefeld2018evaluatingfairnessmetrics pages 2-3).

sections.text: In summary, the correlation between different fairness metrics is complex and heavily context dependent. Empirical studies reveal that while certain fairness metrics—particularly those focused on error rates and predictive disparities—can show positive correlations under controlled conditions, significant disagreements emerge when intrinsic and extrinsic fairness measures are compared or when datasets and model architectures vary. Theoretical work further supports that inherent trade-offs exist among fairness metrics, particularly when base rate differences are present. The comprehensive picture that emerges from the literature is that practitioners and researchers must employ a multi-dimensional approach to fairness evaluation. Relying on a single metric is likely to yield a myopic view of bias, whereas using a carefully curated set of fairness measures provides a deeper understanding of model behavior across diverse conditions. Additionally, sensitivity to dataset properties, model architecture, and training methodologies further complicates the correlations among fairness metrics, underscoring the need for integrated evaluation frameworks. Future research should focus on developing unified fairness evaluation frameworks that not only quantify bias using multiple metrics but also reconcile the intrinsic trade-offs and domain-specific nuances that drive their divergence. Advancements in this direction—combining thorough empirical studies with robust theoretical analyses—will play a pivotal role in achieving fairer and more transparent machine learning systems across all application domains. The empirical and theoretical evidence discussed throughout this report demonstrates that fairness metric correlations are not static but instead vary according to dataset characteristics, model architectures, and evaluation protocols, with some measures reliably aligning under certain conditions and diverging under others (barry2023ontheimpact pages 1-2, cao2022ontheintrinsic pages 2-4, yang2024alargescaleempirical pages 8-9, garg2020fairnessmetricsa pages 2-4, hinnefeld2018evaluatingfairnessmetrics pages 2-3). The observed instability and context sensitivity reinforce the importance of adopting multi-metric evaluation strategies and careful methodological design in fairness research. By providing a more nuanced understanding of how fairness metrics interrelate and where discrepancies may arise, this report contributes to the broader effort of methodically measuring and ultimately mitigating bias in machine learning systems. It is only through such comprehensive and context-aware approaches that the research community can develop reliable and actionable fairness assessments—an essential step toward the ethical deployment of artificial intelligence.

question: How has literature discussed AI as a design material?

sections.text: The rapid advances in AI have transformed traditional design paradigms by introducing computational methods that enable designers to interact with and leverage emergent properties of intelligent systems, thereby positioning AI not merely as a passive tool but as an active design material (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 1-2). Designers and researchers now increasingly recognize AI’s capacity to support creative synthesis, iterative prototyping, and co-creative processes, which ultimately expand the palette of materials available for design exploration (subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 2-4). In addition, the evolving role of AI in design is characterized by its unpredictability, data-driven behavior, and dynamic learning processes, all of which are redefining both technical and aesthetic dimensions in design (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 1-3). This report surveys the diverse literature on AI as a design material, cutting across materials science, creative practice, user experience (UX), and participatory design, and it examines both the methodological opportunities and challenges that arise from treating AI as a material (holmquist2017intelligenceontap pages 1-3).

sections.text: AI’s integration into materials design represents a paradigm shift from traditional trial‐and‐error experimentation toward data‐driven synthesis and optimization, where AI algorithms unlock new design spaces by predicting material properties and discovering hidden correlations (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 1-2). Researchers have demonstrated that AI can accelerate materials discovery cycles by efficiently processing large datasets and identifying promising candidates that traditional physics‐based models may overlook (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 2-4). In the domain of bioinspired and architected materials, AI has enabled the generation of complex microstructures and hierarchical designs that serve as both design outputs and conceptual materials for further exploration (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 9-12). Moreover, the capacity of AI to act as an “intelligent design partner” in materials engineering is evident in its application to optimize mechanical, thermal, and chemical properties, thereby introducing a novel materiality that combines computational creativity with physical performance (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 23-24). These findings underscore AI’s dual role as both an analytical engine and as an emergent design material that reshapes technical innovation in materials science (jiao2021artificialintelligenceenabledsmart pages 1-3).

sections.text: In bioinspired design, AI has been widely discussed as a generative material that bridges the gap between natural phenomena and fabrication techniques, enabling the synthesis of architectures inspired by biological templates such as spider-webs, leaves, and bones (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 8-9). Techniques like generative adversarial networks (GANs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) models have been deployed to produce intricate microstructures that go beyond human intuitive capabilities, effectively positioning AI as an active design contributor (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 12-13). This generative capacity is particularly valuable when designers need to rapidly explore vast design spaces and iterate on new form solutions, ultimately allowing AI to function as an adaptable design material (jiao2021artificialintelligenceenabledsmart pages 20-21). In this context, AI is no longer merely a computational tool for analysis, but rather an integral material component that embodies creative data, computational logic, and design aesthetics (gmeiner2023exploringchallengesand pages 17-18). Such an approach redefines design by incorporating both the inherent physical properties and the latent creative potential of AI-driven systems (liao2020aframeworkof pages 11-13).

sections.text: The literature has also explored the role of AI as a design material in creative and media arts, highlighting its unpredictable, non-deterministic behavior as a source of creative surprise rather than a flaw (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 11-13). Artists repurpose AI algorithms as expressive materials that generate unexpected outputs, thereby harnessing serendipity to subvert conventional representations and open new aesthetic possibilities (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 13-15). This unpredictability is embraced as a creative asset, positioning AI as a dynamic medium that challenges traditional notions of control, authorship, and reproducibility in artistic practice (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 17-19). In these creative contexts, AI materiality is seen as an emergent process where the machine’s internal randomness and evolving behavior contribute to the material itself, enriching the dialogue between human intention and computational output (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 19-20). Overall, the aesthetic dimension of AI as a design material raises fundamental questions about the origins of creativity and the mechanisms by which digital processes can be transformed into culturally resonant artworks (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 3-5).

AI techniques such as evolutionary algorithms, supervised learning, and convolutional neural networks are being integrated into the product design lifecycle to generate design alternatives that are tailored to consumer preferences and market demands (elahi2023acomprehensiveliterature pages 17-19). By enabling designers to overcome fixation and expand the range of ideation, AI becomes a material through which human creativity is systematically enhanced, allowing for the exploration of previously uncharted design spaces (jin2021designheuristicsfor pages 1-2). Furthermore, AI’s capacity to process large volumes of unstructured data transforms it into a reflective design material that supports both the ideation and iterative refinement of product concepts (kulkarni2023awordis pages 1-3). This integration not only accelerates design processes but also democratizes access to advanced design methodologies by offering intuitive tools that bridge the gap between technical expertise and creative expression (liao2020aframeworkof pages 25-27).

sections.text: Participatory design (PD) has traditionally emphasized transparency, user agency, and the co-construction of technology through direct user involvement, yet the opacity and statistical nature of machine learning pose significant challenges when integrating AI as a design material (bratteteig2018doesaimake pages 3-4). The literature highlights that while AI systems offer personalized and context-aware solutions, their evolving behavior and reliance on hidden training data complicate the direct participatory process (bratteteig2018doesaimake pages 4-4). In response, new methodological approaches in PD have been suggested that embrace AI’s unpredictability by incorporating storytelling, scenario building, and iterative feedback loops, thereby enabling users to collaboratively negotiate the behaviors and outputs of AI systems (bratteteig2018doesaimake pages 2-3). Such approaches advocate for a rethinking of control and agency, where designers and users must learn to interpret and mediate the statistical decision-making processes of AI to ensure meaningful engagement with the technology (subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 20-21). Therefore, the challenges in PD arise from the need to balance the opacity of AI’s internal processes with the participatory demands of inclusiveness, transparency, and long-term user involvement (bratteteig2018doesaimake pages 1-2).

Literature in this area argues that the inherently dynamic and opaque nature of AI necessitates careful mediation between human values and computational processes, raising ethical concerns about bias, accountability, and control (bratteteig2018doesaimake pages 4-5). In practice, designers are increasingly called upon to develop frameworks and processes that render AI’s design decisions interpretable and contestable, thereby situating AI as a material that carries both technical capacities and socio-political responsibilities (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 22-24). These efforts have led to the conceptual framing of AI as a material that must be managed in a way that integrates ethical considerations throughout its lifecycle, from data collection and model training to interaction design and subsequent user evaluation (subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 23-23). By embedding these ethical principles into the design process, researchers and practitioners are striving to create AI systems that reflect democratic values and facilitate legitimate user control (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 24-25).

sections.text: The emergent nature of AI as a design material necessitates novel prototyping methods that integrate both design and engineering perspectives, fostering a collaborative, iterative workflow that allows for rapid experimentation with AI behaviors (subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 4-6). In these co-creative environments, AI prototypes are not only used to simulate anticipated outcomes but also to expose the underlying statistical and computational processes so that users and developers can jointly shape the final design material (subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 8-10). Data probes and designerly proxies serve as tangible representations of latent AI capabilities, enabling both rapid validation of design hypotheses and real-time negotiation between the creative and technical dimensions of projects (subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 16-18). This approach minimizes the gap between abstract AI potential and practical user experience by creating a shared language for discussing, modifying, and refining AI behaviors during early design iterations (kulkarni2023awordis pages 13-16). In addition, such iterative processes allow designers to continuously evaluate the outputs of generative systems and to adjust parameters or refine prompts in order to better align with design objectives, thereby transforming AI from a static tool into a malleable design material (kulkarni2023awordis pages 16-17). Ultimately, this iterative, co-created workflow not only validates AI’s role as a design material but also highlights opportunities for enhanced collaboration that maximizes both creative expression and technical robustness (gmeiner2023exploringchallengesand pages 18-18).

This shift challenges conventional design methodologies by framing AI as an active participant in the creative process, one that evolves over time and interacts with human designers in unexpected ways (liao2020aframeworkof pages 23-25). Consequently, this redefinition of materiality prompts the development of new design heuristics and evaluation criteria that account for the computational and sociotechnical dimensions of AI (jin2021designheuristicsfor pages 1-2). As a result, the integration of AI into design not only expands the material palette available to designers but also enriches the theoretical foundations of design practice by merging insights from computer science, cognitive psychology, and material culture (subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 18-20).

sections.text: Taken together, the literature reveals a complex, multifaceted portrayal of AI as a design material that is both dynamic and transformative, imbued with capacities for generative creativity, adaptation, and social mediation (caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 25-25). Researchers propose that future work should not only focus on refining the technical capabilities of AI systems but also on developing robust prototyping frameworks and participatory methods that ensure the technology serves as an adjunct to human creativity rather than a replacement (subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 20-21). Further, emerging studies advocate for the creation of explainable AI systems that articulate their decision-making processes transparently, thus facilitating deeper user engagement and iterative refinement during co-creation (bratteteig2018doesaimake pages 2-3). There remains a need to explore how ethical safeguarding mechanisms, such as contestability frameworks, can be integrated into AI-driven design materials to manage bias and ensure accountability in deployed systems (alfrink2023contestableaiby pages 3-6). Future research may also benefit from interdisciplinary approaches that combine insights from materials science, HCI, art practice, and UX design to develop holistic models of AI materiality that can guide both academic inquiry and practical application (liao2020aframeworkof pages 25-27). Finally, addressing the evolving nature of AI—its capacity to learn and adapt over its lifecycle—will require the continuous development of co-creation methodologies that keep pace with advances in machine learning (gmeiner2023exploringchallengesand pages 17-18).

sections.text:
In summary, the literature has discussed AI as a design material by framing it as an active, generative, and dynamic component in a wide range of design contexts. Studies in materials science have highlighted AI’s role in accelerating discovery cycles and optimizing engineered materials, while work in creative and artistic domains emphasizes its unpredictable and expressive capacities. Within UX and product design, AI is increasingly treated as a collaborative partner that supports iterative prototyping and co-creative workflows. Meanwhile, participatory design research exposes the tension between AI’s opaque, statistical mechanisms and the need for transparency and direct user engagement. Simultaneously, ethical, sociotechnical, and ethical dimensions prompt designers to negotiate issues of bias, contestability, and accountability when incorporating AI as a material. Looking forward, the field calls for innovative prototyping techniques, improved explainability, and interdisciplinary collaboration to navigate the emerging complexity of AI as an active design material that continuously co-evolves with human creative processes (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 1-2, subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 4-6, caramiaux2022"explorersofunknown pages 17-19, bratteteig2018doesaimake pages 4-5).

Overall, the literature positions AI not simply as a computational tool but as an emergent, co-creative design material that offers unprecedented opportunities for innovation while simultaneously demanding new frameworks for understanding, prototyping, and ethical integration in design practice (holmquist2017intelligenceontap pages 6-6). The field continues to evolve as researchers and designers collaboratively articulate the complex materiality of AI through iterative design processes, interdisciplinary dialogue, and critical reflection on both technical promises and sociocultural ramifications (kulkarni2023awordis pages 17-19).

This report thus presents a multifaceted view of AI as a design material, encompassing technical performance, creative generativity, and collaborative co-creation, while also highlighting the ethical and participatory challenges inherent in this new paradigm. Future academic inquiry and practical implementation will need to address these complex dynamics to fully harness AI’s potential as a material that not only augments design processes but also reshapes the very nature of creativity and technological development (elahi2023acomprehensiveliterature pages 16-17).

By integrating insights from diverse domains—including materials science, creative arts, UX design, and participatory methods—the literature collectively redefines the concept of “material” in design, positioning AI as a transformative, interactive medium that supports innovation through its inherent dynamic and collaborative properties (liao2020aframeworkof pages 13-15, subramonyam2021towardsaprocess pages 18-20). As designers continue to experiment with and refine AI-driven systems, the evolving discourse on AI materiality will undoubtedly shape future design practices and technological implementations, ensuring that AI's transformative potential is realized in ways that are both creative and ethically sound (ghoreishi2020newpromisesai pages 1-2).

In conclusion, the discussion of AI as a design material in contemporary literature emphasizes its dual role as an enabler of accelerated, data-driven material exploration and as a co-creative, expressive medium that challenges and expands traditional design paradigms. With a growing emphasis on collaborative workflows, ethical design, and agile prototyping frameworks, future research will likely continue to investigate the dynamic interplay between human creativity and machine intelligence, fostering richer, more resilient design ecosystems in which AI is not just a tool but a vital, evolving material (gmeiner2023exploringchallengesand pages 18-18).

This comprehensive survey highlights that AI, imbued with both computational power and emergent creative potential, stands at the nexus of technology, design, and human experience, constantly reshaping our understanding of what it means to work with materials in a digital age (badini2023unleashingthepower pages 23-24).

question: What are the best practices to protect a software against vulnerabilities from third party libraries?

sections.text: Third‐party libraries are integral to modern software development because they accelerate functionality by leveraging preexisting code, but their ubiquity also expands the attack surface of applications. Vulnerabilities in these libraries can be introduced both intentionally and unintentionally, as they may be released without rigorous security vetting or may become outdated before vulnerabilities are discovered. The increasing complexity of dependency networks not only poses challenges for detecting vulnerabilities in direct dependencies but also in transitive dependencies, making a comprehensive security strategy indispensable (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 25-28). Consequently, best practices to protect software must incorporate proactive vulnerability detection, continuous dependency management, automated analysis, and effective communication channels with both the developer community and maintainers of third‐party libraries (arshad2018thoushaltnot pages 1-2).

sections.text: A key best practice is to integrate robust vulnerability detection techniques into the development lifecycle. Traditional tools that rely solely on metadata often result in false positives and negatives, hence code‐centric detection is preferred. Developers should adopt techniques that analyze the actual source code or binary artifacts in use and the reachability of vulnerable constructs by combining static analysis with dynamic testing. This approach helps focus remediation efforts on vulnerabilities that are exploitable in the application's runtime context rather than merely flagged based on version numbers (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 1-3). Such code-based, fine-grained analysis leverages static analysis methods—by examining call graphs and abstract syntax trees—to comprehensively identify which portions of library code are potentially executed by the application, thus ensuring that only active vulnerabilities are prioritized (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 12-15). Furthermore, dynamic analyses performed via test suites and runtime instrumentation can confirm the execution of specific vulnerable constructs and therefore help in accurately assessing the real risk posed by a dependency (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 15-18). It is also critical to combine both analysis methods. Static analysis identifies all theoretical vulnerability paths, while dynamic analysis verifies which paths are exercised under typical application usage; the combined approach reduces false positives and aligns risk assessment with actual application behavior (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 18-20, ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 6-8). Additionally, adopting tools like Eclipse Steady, which have empirically demonstrated a reduction in overestimations of risk by using code-centric techniques, can further help in accurately localizing the vulnerabilities (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 31-33). Finally, developers must ensure that static analysis can handle inversion of control scenarios and transitive dependencies appropriately, as overlooking these aspects might leave critical vulnerabilities undetected in complex dependency trees (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 33-36).

sections.text: The automation of vulnerability scanning and dependency monitoring plays a fundamental part in maintaining a secure codebase. Automated tools such as npm audit, Dependabot, and similar third‐party scanning solutions are designed to alert developers when vulnerabilities are identified in the libraries under use (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 25-28, decan2018ontheimpact pages 7-8). In addition, automated scanning should not be limited to direct dependencies; it must include transitive dependencies, as these can often harbor vulnerabilities that propagate indirectly (duan2021towardsmeasuringsupply pages 12-13). Implementing a continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline that integrates automated vulnerability scanners ensures that each new code change is checked against the latest vulnerability databases, thereby reducing exposure time between vulnerability disclosure and remediation (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 6-7). These tools are more effective when they leverage comprehensive and updated vulnerability knowledge bases, which should be maintained collaboratively among tool developers, ecosystem stakeholders, and security researchers. Such integration not only automates detection and reporting but also helps prioritize which vulnerabilities should be fixed first on the basis of metrics such as reachability and update effort (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 20-23). Additionally, employing source code analysis tools that integrate both static and dynamic analysis can help to dynamically prioritize risk and offer a concrete action plan, rather than relying solely on statistical risk indicators (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 38-40).

sections.text: Managing dependencies is central to reducing exposure from third‐party libraries. Best practices include maintaining an inventory of all dependencies and continuously monitoring them for security vulnerabilities. The use of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is highly recommended to provide a comprehensive view of all third‐party components within an application, which in turn aids in tracking versions and vulnerability statuses (zeng2404asurveyof pages 4-6). Regular reviews of dependency graphs should be performed to identify outdated libraries or those that exhibit a long technical lag – a phenomenon wherein vulnerabilities remain undiscovered or unfixed for extended periods (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 38-39). Version pinning and the deprecation of poorly maintained libraries are also effective strategies for mitigating vulnerability risks. By pinning dependency versions, developers can firmly control the exact library versions integrated into their projects, thereby preventing unintended upgrades that may introduce vulnerabilities. In addition, deprecating libraries that have ongoing vulnerabilities or that are no longer actively maintained encourages the adoption of safer, more secure alternatives (ladisa2023soktaxonomyof pages 10-11, ladisa2023soktaxonomyof pages 18-18). It is equally important to remove unused dependencies proactively, as whittling down older or redundant libraries reduces the overall attack surface (ladisa2023soktaxonomyof pages 17-18). When an update is required, best practices call for planning dependency updates diligently; this involves assessing the impact of the changes, testing new releases thoroughly, and cautiously integrating them into the production environment. Developers should establish policies regarding how and when dependencies are updated—balancing the cost of migration efforts against the risk of retaining a vulnerable dependency (kula2017dodevelopersupdate pages 1-4, kula2017dodevelopersupdate pages 25-27).

sections.text: Introducing pre-release security vetting mechanisms into the third‐party library lifecycle can be a potent measure to minimize vulnerabilities before libraries are deployed. Pre-release vetting, analogous to the review practices used in mobile app stores, involves scrutinizing popular libraries for common vulnerabilities – such as cross-site scripting attacks – before they become part of the official repository (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 25-28). Moreover, having coordinated vulnerability disclosure practices is essential. Instead of public announcements that provide little time for affected developers to prepare their patches, a private, coordinated approach involving key users and vendors ensures responsible communication and prompt remediation (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 25-28). This strategy is particularly important in ecosystems where the majority of disclosed vulnerabilities remain unfixed at the time of public disclosure, thereby allowing attackers to exploit known issues for an extended period (decan2018ontheimpact pages 7-8). Furthermore, the establishment of standard protocols for vulnerability disclosure within ecosystem platforms, such as PyPi for Python or npm for JavaScript, can help increase transparency and reduce the risk window associated with vulnerability fixes. Vendors should adopt systematic approaches where vulnerabilities are first reported privately to mitigate immediate risks before being disclosed publicly after fix deadlines have passed (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 39-40).

sections.text: Developers play a critical role in mitigating vulnerabilities – irrespective of whether the vulnerabilities originate from third-party components or from custom code. To protect software reliably, developers need to follow secure coding guidelines and ensure that integration of third-party libraries is guided by thorough code review and security testing. Educating developers about potential vulnerabilities associated with third-party packages and training them to detect and prioritize such issues is essential (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 1-2). Developers should also demonstrate awareness by using automated tools to scan for vulnerabilities and incorporate these tools into their everyday workflow (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 9-10). Furthermore, it is advisable to leverage continuous integration environments that run security test suites along with functional tests to promptly catch regressions that might emerge from a dependency update (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 17-19). The proactive attitude should be extended to include submission of upstream patches to vulnerable libraries, rather than solely patching them locally. This not only benefits individual projects but also contributes to the overall improvement of the open source ecosystem (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 19-19). Developer communities must foster a culture of transparency regarding library vulnerabilities, where experiences with dependency failures and successful patch integrations are openly discussed via mailing lists, issue trackers, and public repositories. This collective intelligence can drive improved security practices and facilitate faster remediation times (kula2017dodevelopersupdate pages 25-27).

sections.text: Beyond initial detection, mitigation involves determining the effort required for safe dependency updates. Advanced approaches recommend the use of quantitative metrics such as callee stability, development effort estimates, and body stability measures to assess how challenging library updates might be (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 38-40). By quantifying factors like the proportion of an application’s directly called constructs that are present in a candidate library version, developers can make informed decisions about whether to update or maintain current dependencies (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 15-18). Automated tools that compute these metrics not only provide immediate feedback on compatibility but also estimate the impact on functionality due to update-induced changes (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 20-23). With such metrics in place, teams are better positioned to balance the trade-offs between upgrading a fruitful dependency and the potential risk introduced by breaking changes. Furthermore, historical analysis of dependency update patterns may reveal that certain libraries exhibit a prolonged period of vulnerability, which should prompt pre-emptive measures such as replacement or isolation of those dependencies (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 38-39). It is equally important that any vulnerability fix be validated through both automated testing and manual code inspection to ensure that the integration of the new version does not inadvertently introduce regressions or new security issues (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 5-6).

sections.text: Attacks on third-party libraries are not confined to individual developers but affect entire ecosystems. Attacks such as typosquatting or malicious injections into widely used libraries are a significant threat. Therefore, it is imperative that registry maintainers, package maintainers, and developers collaborate to institute preventive measures at the ecosystem level (duan2021towardsmeasuringsupply pages 13-14). Registry maintainers can implement controls such as multi-factor authentication, code signing, and vetting pipelines to detect abnormal publishing behavior, while also establishing policies to control the transfer of package ownership (duan2021towardsmeasuringsupply pages 12-13). At the package level, maintainers must secure their accounts and infrastructure while ensuring timely updates to address vulnerabilities reported by the community. The integration of security pull request systems and automated tools like Dependabot further enhances the collective ability to mitigate vulnerabilities across the entire dependency network (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 39-40). It is also recommended that maintainers provide clear security-related metrics—such as time-to-patch and vulnerability prevalence statistics—to give downstream users actionable insights into the risk levels associated with library updates (krasner2021thecostof pages 25-28, ladisa2023soktaxonomyof pages 17-18). Furthermore, industry-wide initiatives that build centralized and comprehensive vulnerability databases enable improved threat intelligence and facilitate rapid dissemination of patch information. Such centralized databases allow developers and security professionals to detect emerging trends in library vulnerabilities, thereby promoting a more proactive security posture across ecosystems (duan2021towardsmeasuringsupply pages 13-14).

sections.text: Different programming ecosystems pose distinct challenges with respect to dependency management and vulnerability detection. In JavaScript, dynamic and transitive inclusions of libraries such as jQuery or Angular can result in a chaotic dependency tree that is particularly susceptible to vulnerabilities (arshad2018thoushaltnot pages 14-15). Best practices in these ecosystems involve employing specialized tools like AuditJS and Retire.js, which are designed for the unique characteristics of JavaScript code—including handling inline scripts and transitive inclusions—along with adopting semantic versioning to manage updates consistently (arshad2018thoushaltnot pages 3-4, arshad2018thoushaltnot pages 13-14). In contrast, ecosystems such as Python or Java require strategies that can integrate fine-grained static analysis and dynamic assessments due to the layered complexity of dependencies, especially in mature package repositories like PyPi or Maven. Here, the integration of a software composition analysis that provides visibility on the dependency tree is paramount (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 25-28, ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 36-38). Thus, by tailoring the vulnerability detection and dependency management practices to the characteristics of each ecosystem, developers can effectively mitigate associated risks.

sections.text: While many best practices focus on the management and detection of vulnerabilities in third‐party libraries, it is also critical to implement defensive coding techniques and runtime isolation strategies to mitigate the impact of potential exploitation. Defensive coding practices, such as proper input validation, the use of safe arithmetic libraries like SafeMath in smart contract development, and rigorous error handling are indispensable to reduce the attack surface even when a library contains an exploitable flaw (pan2019securityanalysismethods pages 6-7, destefanis2018smartcontractsvulnerabilities pages 5-6). Additionally, techniques like sandboxing or isolating components—especially those imported dynamically or via advertisement, tracking, or social media widgets—help contain the spread of an exploit should one occur (arshad2018thoushaltnot pages 12-13). These runtime isolation measures, when combined with dependency scanning and code vetting, provide multiple layers of defense that greatly reduce the likelihood of a single vulnerability compromising the entire application.

sections.text: Even the most sophisticated automated tools and rigorous dependency management processes are only as effective as the developers that employ them. A culture of continuous security improvement is vital, which involves regular training sessions for developers to understand the nuances of dependency vulnerabilities and secure coding principles (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 1-2). Developers should be encouraged to share best practices and lessons learned regarding dependency updates and vulnerability remediation via internal documentation and community forums (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 17-19). Moreover, periodic security audits and cross-team reviews can improve overall awareness and help identify potentially overlooked vulnerabilities in both third‐party libraries and proprietary code. Establishing communication channels for prompt vulnerability disclosure and remediation strategies enhances the resilience of the entire organization (pashchenko2020aqualitativestudy pages 19-19, arshad2018thoushaltnot pages 15-15).

sections.text: Establishing strict governance over dependency usage is another vital aspect of minimizing the risk associated with third-party libraries. Organizational policies should mandate pre-approved lists of libraries, require rigorous vetting of new dependencies, and enforce version control strategies that incorporate version pinning to avoid unintentional upgrades that could introduce vulnerabilities (ladisa2023soktaxonomyof pages 10-11). In practice, these policies are enforced by tools that automatically check for compliance with internal standards and signal discrepancies or outdated versions (duan2021towardsmeasuringsupply pages 13-14). Additionally, clear guidelines regarding the process for updating or deprecating libraries are essential. Such policies ensure that decisions regarding dependency management are made systematically, with a clear understanding of the associated security implications and remediated in a timely manner (krasner2021thecostof pages 25-28).

sections.text: Empirical analyses have repeatedly demonstrated the risks of maintaining outdated libraries and the subsequent difficulties in mitigating vulnerabilities in a timely manner. Studies indicate that vulnerabilities in libraries tend to persist undetected for extended periods – sometimes for several years. For instance, an empirical investigation has found that vulnerabilities in Python packages remain undiscovered for a median of three years, a delay that underscores the necessity for proactive security practices and continuous monitoring (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 25-28). Empirical data from JavaScript ecosystems also reveal that a significant fraction of websites use vulnerable versions of popular libraries, thereby creating widespread exposure to exploitable vulnerabilities (arshad2018thoushaltnot pages 1-2). Such studies reinforce the need to enforce rapid patching mechanisms, maintain strict dependency inventories, and educate developers to update dependencies promptly rather than deferring critical migrations (kula2017dodevelopersupdate pages 25-27).

sections.text: A comprehensive defense strategy must integrate multiple layers of security controls, addressing vulnerabilities at different stages of software development and deployment. Each layer, starting from code scanning and dependency management to runtime isolation and governance, plays an integral role in mitigating risk. For example, pre-release security vetting filters out potentially vulnerable packages before they enter the repository, while automated CI/CD pipelines ensure that any subsequent vulnerabilities are detected as soon as new code is merged (alfadel2023empiricalanalysisof pages 25-28). This layered approach not only reduces the likelihood of vulnerabilities slipping through but also minimizes their overall impact by limiting the exploitability of the affected code in isolation (arshad2018thoushaltnot pages 14-15). Moreover, incorporating real-time monitoring for abnormal library behavior using metrics derived from automated tools can help detect unusual patterns that might signal a compromise, enabling immediate reaction before the vulnerability is exploited (ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 31-33, ponta2020detectionassessmentand pages 40-41).

question: What are some biologically-inspired robot path planning algorithms?

sections.text:
Robotic path planning in dynamic and complex environments poses significant challenges that conventional deterministic or optimization
‐based methods often struggle to overcome. Biologically
‐inspired algorithms offer alternative solutions by imitating strategies evolved in nature and found in diverse organisms. These approaches range from neural network models that mimic neuron dynamics and sensory–motor coordination, to swarm intelligence methods inspired by social insects and flocking behavior, and to evolutionary algorithms that emulate genetic adaptation. In this report we review a variety of biologically
‐inspired robot path planning algorithms, discuss their underlying principles and advantages, and illustrate their applications in scenarios such as multi
‐Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) coordination, underwater vehicle navigation, indoor cleaning, and even minimally invasive medical procedures. The report also highlights the potential of hybrid approaches that combine wireless sensor integration, reinforcement learning, and bio
‐inspired neural computation to achieve robust, adaptive, and computationally efficient path planning.

Modern robotic systems must navigate environments that are often cluttered, uncertain, and subject to real
‐time changes. Traditional path planning methods typically rely on predefined maps or global optimization routines, which may be computationally expensive or insufficiently adaptive when encountering dynamic obstacles. Biological systems, by contrast, exhibit remarkable adaptability and efficiency in navigating complex environments without complete environmental maps, prompting researchers to develop algorithms inspired by natural phenomena for robotic path planning (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 2-3). In particular, bio
‐inspired methods leverage analogies with neural dynamics, swarm intelligence, and evolutionary principles to solve NP
‐hard path planning problems. This report presents an in
‐depth survey of these algorithms, classifies them according to their bio
‐inspired paradigms, and discusses how these methods have been applied to different types of robotic platforms.

sections.text:
Biologically
‐inspired algorithms draw on various principles observed in nature. Many approaches are motivated by the collective intelligence of social animals such as ant colonies or bird flocks, which achieve coherent group navigation by simple local interactions (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 33-35). Other methods are based on the dynamics of biological neurons as described by the Hodgkin–Huxley model and Grossberg’s shunting equations, enabling robust, distributed decision
‐making processes in neural networks (glasius1996abiologicallyinspired pages 1-3). Evolutionary computation, exemplified by genetic algorithms (GAs) and related artificial immune network techniques, mimic natural selection and biological adaptation to search large solution spaces for optimal trajectories (bhaduri2009amobilerobot pages 3-4). Additionally, reactive behavior strategies inspired by insect navigation and animal locomotion have been developed to guide robots by local, sensor–based cues (teimoori2010abiologicallyinspired pages 1-3). Together these inspirations contribute to a rich set of tools for designing algorithms that overcome the limitations of conventional path planning approaches (karur2021asurveyof pages 1-2).

sections.text:
One prominent class of bio
‐inspired methods is rooted in neural network models that emulate the dynamics of biological neurons. These models represent the environment as a continuous activity landscape where the target generates excitatory signals while obstacles produce inhibitory effects. For example, models based on shunting equations derived from Hodgkin–Huxley’s membrane dynamics provide continuous signal propagation that guides the robot along collision–free trajectories without requiring explicit global optimization (glasius1996abiologicallyinspired pages 1-3). Early work utilized these continuous neural dynamics to plan smooth, real–time paths in dynamic environments, ensuring that local inhibitory effects from obstacles did not prevent global target attraction (duro2003biologicallyinspiredrobot pages 159-162). More advanced neural network models have been extended to handle nonholonomic constraints by discretizing control variables such as linear and angular velocities, enabling robots to plan feasible paths that respect kinematic limitations (yang2001realtimecollisionfreepath pages 2-3). An additional advantage of these neural network–based approaches is their suitability for real–time updates, as the network’s activity dynamically reflects changes in sensor data and environmental disturbances (li2022bioinspiredintelligencewith pages 4-7).

Recent advances have integrated neural network algorithms with reinforcement learning techniques such as Q-learning to further optimize path planning. In these hybrid models, a biologically inspired neural network conducts initial path planning based on instantaneous sensory input, while Q-learning is selectively activated in regions with high uncertainty—typically near obstacles—to reduce path repetition and avoid local minima (tan2023biologicallyinspiredcomplete pages 10-13). Such integration facilitates both rapid computation and adaptive path adjustment, allowing mobile robots to achieve complete coverage in areas with unpredictable obstacles (tan2023biologicallyinspiredcomplete pages 2-4). Complementary approaches incorporate full coverage path planning (FCPP) in indoor environments using neural networks that simulate cleaned versus uncleaned areas, where neural activities guide coverage maneuvers through locally evolving state spaces (hu2010completecoveragepath pages 1-2, qiu2006acompletecoverage pages 1-2).

sections.text:
Swarm intelligence algorithms are another widely used bio–inspired paradigm in robot path planning. Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), inspired by the flocking behavior of birds and schooling of fish, is frequently employed to optimize 3D surveillance trajectories and collision avoidance in UAV path planning (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 9-11). PSO variants such as NPSO, IPSO, DPSO, and multi–objective PSO have been developed to handle multi–UAV coordination problems by adjusting inertia weights or particle diversity to improve convergence speed and robustness (poudel2023bioinspiredoptimizationbasedpath pages 9-10). Likewise, Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) mimics the foraging behavior of ant colonies that deposit pheromone trails to reinforce successful paths; this approach is used to navigate environments with dynamic obstacles, allowing robots to generate near–optimal paths by following dynamically updated pheromone gradients (karur2021asurveyof pages 11-13).  
Evolutionary algorithms such as Genetic Algorithms (GA) have also been adapted for robotic path planning. These methods treat possible solutions as individuals in a population that evolve over time using crossover, mutation, and selection operators inspired by natural evolution. An example is the Genetic Artificial Immune Network (GAIN) algorithm, which enhances traditional GAs by applying immune network–like recombination operators to maintain diversity and generate more connected paths (bhaduri2009amobilerobot pages 3-4, bhaduri2009amobilerobot pages 4-4). These evolutionary techniques are especially useful in large, high–dimensional search spaces where traditional optimization methods may become trapped in suboptimal solutions.

Another line of research applies bio-inspired algorithms based on bacterial foraging optimization (BFO), a technique that models the chemotaxis processes in bacterial colonies to provide smooth paths and robust responses under non–linear cost functions. This method has been successfully used in mobile robots and has been shown to generate paths with fewer abrupt changes, especially in uncertain dynamic environments (hossain2015autonomousrobotpath pages 1-2). Such swarm–based and evolutionary methods offer robustness through the exploitation of distributed processing and cooperation among simple agents, an approach well suited to applications that require simultaneous coordination among multiple robots or UAVs (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 33-35).

Behavior–based strategies derive from the observation that many small animals and insects navigate complex terrains with only rudimentary sensory inputs and pre–programmed neural circuits. One notable approach in this category is the Equiangular Navigation Guidance (ENG) law, inspired by honeybee and insect navigation, which combines a goal–directed component with a sliding–mode obstacle avoidance technique (teimoori2010abiologicallyinspired pages 1-3). The ENG law maintains a constant relative angle between the robot’s movement vector and salient environmental features, thereby ensuring that the robot sidesteps obstacles while continuing its progress toward the goal (teimoori2010abiologicallyinspired pages 11-12).  
Reactive algorithms also include methods based on a “reflection cone” concept where the robot dynamically alters its trajectory by following a fixed avoidance angle relative to detected obstacles. This technique provides a local, real–time response that is computationally lightweight and can be deployed onboard robots with limited processing power (savkin2013asimplebiologically pages 1-3). In addition, reactive approaches that incorporate sensory information such as optic flow and proximity measurements allow robots to mimic animal–like collision avoidance behaviors seen in insects and small mammals, enabling efficient movement in cluttered environments without requiring comprehensive mapping (savkin2013asimplebiologically pages 7-10).

Hybrid algorithms seek to combine the best features of several bio-inspired methods to produce more adaptive and efficient path planners. One successful strategy has been to integrate bio-inspired neural network algorithms with reinforcement learning techniques such as Q-learning. In these models, the neural network rapidly computes a feasible local plan while Q-learning fine–tunes the trajectory to minimize repetition and avoid being trapped by local minima (tan2023biologicallyinspiredcomplete pages 6-8). Such adaptive systems have been shown to work well with limited movement directions (e.g., up, down, left, right), reducing the computational complexity while still providing near–optimal complete coverage in indoor mapping tasks (tan2023biologicallyinspiredcomplete pages 10-13).

Other hybrid methods combine evolutionary algorithms with swarm intelligence. For example, hybrid approaches that integrate PSO with algorithms from the harmony search family, improved bat algorithms, or grey wolf optimization have been proposed for UAV path planning in dynamic and uncertain environments (poudel2023bioinspiredoptimizationbasedpath pages 12-13). By merging the global search capabilities of evolutionary algorithms with the fine–tuning attributes of swarm–based methods, these hybrids are capable of overcoming the limitations encountered by each technique alone, such as premature convergence in PSO or slow learning in purely reinforcement–based systems (poudel2023bioinspiredoptimizationbasedpath pages 19-20).   
In addition, some researchers propose approaches that adapt the neural activity propagation based on current environmental cues, such as adjusting inhibitory thresholds near obstacles or dynamically shifting neural network connectivity. These modifications allow the bio-inspired models to preemptively adjust to local changes and maintain a balance between exploitation (following the strongest target signal) and exploration (scouting alternative routes) (li2022bioinspiredintelligencewith pages 7-9).

sections.text:
The practical applications of biologically–inspired path planning algorithms span a wide range of robotic platforms and scenarios, demonstrating the versatility of these techniques.  
For multi–UAV systems, bio-inspired algorithms have been employed to solve complex path planning problems that involve collision avoidance, multi-objective trajectory optimization, and cooperative formations. Reviews on bio-inspired multi-UAV path planning showcase various strategies such as particle swarm optimization and pigeon-inspired optimization, and they emphasize the need for enhanced coordination schemes that accommodate both centralized and distributed planning environments (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 2-3, aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 35-35). Moreover, challenges unique to three-dimensional spaces require adaptations in the underlying bio-inspired models, prompting researchers to develop novel hybrid algorithms that incorporate local planning modules for better handling of partially known or dynamic environments (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 31-32).  

In underwater robotics, potential field-based bio-inspired neural networks have been applied for Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) path planning. These methods incorporate obstacle avoidance by coupling bio-inspired neural network dynamics with potential field adjustments, thereby enabling AUVs to maintain safe distances from obstacles and adapt to disturbances such as ocean currents (cao2021auvglobalsecurity pages 1-3, cao2021auvglobalsecurity pages 13-16). The same principles have been extended to multi-AUV cooperative search and formation tasks, where self-organizing maps and neurodynamic models contribute to robust velocity synthesis and adaptive path generation (cao2021auvglobalsecurity pages 16-17).

Indoor cleaning robots provide another fertile application area for neuro-dynamics based complete coverage path planning. Biologically inspired neural network algorithms have been successfully utilized to achieve full coverage of indoor areas while minimizing overlap and deadlock situations. In these systems the environment is modeled as a grid where neural activity indicates the level of “unclean” or “to be cleaned” areas; the robot’s path is then driven by gradients in this activity landscape, leading to efficient and collision–free motion (hu2010completecoveragepath pages 1-2, qiu2006acompletecoverage pages 1-2). Enhancements such as the “fictitious frontier” concept further improve environmental perception and planning speed (hu2010completecoveragepath pages 6-6).

In the medical domain, path planning for neurosurgical probes has also benefited from bio-inspired approaches. For example, a smooth path planning algorithm for a biologically inspired neurosurgical probe modifies existing techniques to constrain curvature and its derivative, ensuring minimal tissue damage during probe steering. Although this application diverges somewhat from conventional mobile robot navigation, it clearly demonstrates the potential of biologically inspired methods to generate smooth, continuous, and safe trajectories under complex mechanical constraints (bano2012smoothpathplanning pages 4-4).

Behavior-based and reactive algorithms offer additional examples from mobile robotics. Methods based on the equiangular navigation guidance (ENG) law have been implemented for wheeled robots navigating cluttered, unknown environments. These algorithms, drawing inspiration from animal behaviors such as those seen in honeybees, rely on local sensor information to generate continuous control signals that enable robots to avoid obstacles and maintain a stable trajectory toward a target (teimoori2010abiologicallyinspired pages 1-3, teimoori2010abiologicallyinspired pages 11-12). Similarly, reactive strategies based on infinite visions cones and sliding-mode obstacle avoidance have been successfully demonstrated on platforms such as the Pioneer P3-DX robot, thus validating the practical applicability of bio-inspired reactive methods (savkin2013asimplebiologically pages 1-3, savkin2013asimplebiologically pages 7-10).

Finally, implementations of bio-inspired robotic navigation have also been influenced by studies in biological sensory–motor coordination. Researchers have designed algorithms based on insect optic flow and desert ant homing, using vision-based techniques and vector integration methods to guide robots over uneven terrain or toward landmarks in GPS-denied environments. These studies provide an important link between biological sensory processing and robotic navigation, emphasizing low computational cost and high robustness (iida2016biologicallyinspiredrobotics pages 11-12).

A detailed analysis of biologically inspired path planning algorithms reveals several strengths inherent in these methods. Neural network-based algorithms offer real-time responsiveness and adaptability by continuously updating the neural activity landscape as the robot moves, thereby effectively handling dynamic changes and local perturbations (li2022bioinspiredintelligencewith pages 4-7). Their distributed nature and local communication among “neurons” allow for scalability and robustness even when faced with sensor noise or unmodeled environmental features. However, pure neural network models sometimes suffer from convergence issues and the possibility of getting trapped in local minima, which has prompted researchers to develop hybrid approaches that blend neural computation with reinforcement learning (tan2023biologicallyinspiredcomplete pages 10-13).  
Swarm intelligence and evolutionary methods, such as particle swarm optimization, ant colony optimization, and genetic algorithms, enable the exploration of large solution spaces and offer robustness in optimization tasks. These algorithms, however, often exhibit challenges related to premature convergence, sensitivity to parameter tuning, and computational load for real-time applications (poudel2023bioinspiredoptimizationbasedpath pages 9-10). The Genetic Artificial Immune Network (GAIN) method, for example, demonstrates that combining aspects of immune system dynamics with genetic operations can yield faster convergence than classic genetic algorithms (bhaduri2009amobilerobot pages 3-4).  
Behavior-based reactive algorithms, leveraging simple yet effective local control rules, provide an attractive option for applications that require immediate responses to obstacles without relying on a complete map of the environment (teimoori2010abiologicallyinspired pages 1-3). While their simplicity is a strength, these methods may also be limited by their local scope; without a global representation of the environment, they might miss more optimal paths or become trapped in deadlock situations in complex settings (savkin2013asimplebiologically pages 7-10).  
Hybrid approaches that combine neural network planning with reinforcement learning or integrate swarm–intelligence methods offer a promising avenue by balancing fast local planning with global optimization. These methods leverage the complementary strengths of fast, reactive network responses and slower, more deliberative evolutionary or learning-based processes, thereby providing a more holistic solution to path planning problems (tan2023biologicallyinspiredcomplete pages 6-8, poudel2023bioinspiredoptimizationbasedpath pages 12-13).

Despite the significant progress achieved with bio-inspired path planning algorithms, several challenges and opportunities for future research remain. Improvements in the integration of learning techniques such as Q-learning or deep reinforcement learning with bio-inspired neural networks can further enhance the ability to adapt to unforeseen changes and unknown environments. In applications such as multi-UAV systems, standardizing benchmarks and developing robust simulation environments are essential steps to facilitate cross-evaluation of different algorithms (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 31-32). Furthermore, the extension of bio-inspired methods into fully three-dimensional spaces, as required for UAVs and underwater vehicles, calls for enhanced models that can incorporate both global and local planning techniques seamlessly (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 33-35).  
Another promising direction involves the application of biologically-inspired principles to soft robotics and medical robotics. For example, the smooth path planning methods developed for neurosurgical probes highlight how inspiration drawn from biological structures and flexible mechanisms can lead to improved safety and performance in delicate operations (bano2012smoothpathplanning pages 4-4). Research that bridges insights from computational neuroscience, such as operant and classical conditioning models, with adaptive control strategies is likely to yield even more robust robotic systems capable of operating in complex, dynamic environments (wang2012bioinspirednavigationof pages 1-4).  
Finally, the role of sensor fusion in biologically-inspired path planning is an important topic for further exploration. Integrating signals from vision, sonar, and tactile sensors to build richer representations of the environment remains a challenge but one that is essential for advancing biologically-inspired algorithms to real-world deployments. Techniques that couple multi-sensor data with self-organizing maps and dynamic neural networks could provide the robust, adaptive control necessary for next-generation robotic applications (hu2010completecoveragepath pages 6-6).

sections.text:
Biologically-inspired robot path planning algorithms represent a diverse and dynamic field of research that harnesses natural principles—ranging from neural dynamics and swarm intelligence to evolutionary adaptation and reactive behavior—to generate efficient, adaptive, and robust navigation solutions. Neural network approaches using shunting models, additive dynamics, and hybrid Q-learning integration have proven effective in offering real-time path updates and collision avoidance in dynamic environments. Similarly, swarm intelligence and evolutionary algorithms such as PSO, ACO, and the Genetic Artificial Immune Network provide robust strategies for global search and multi-agent coordination, particularly in multi-UAV and underwater applications. Behavior-based methods and reactive navigation laws, inspired by the agile movements of insects and animals, enable robots to respond promptly to changing environments. Hybrid methods that combine these diverse strategies promise to overcome individual weaknesses and yield more comprehensive solutions for the complex, multidimensional challenges encountered in modern robotic path planning.
The continued evolution of these biologically-inspired algorithms—bolstered by advancements in sensor technology, reinforcement learning, and computational modeling—ensures that future robotic systems will be better equipped to navigate unpredictable and dynamic environments, thereby expanding the frontiers of autonomous operation across various domains, from surveillance and environmental monitoring to healthcare and robotics-assisted surgery.

In summary, the diverse portfolio of biologically-inspired path planning algorithms reviewed herein—including neural network models (glasius1996abiologicallyinspired pages 1-3, duro2003biologicallyinspiredrobot pages 159-162, yang2001realtimecollisionfreepath pages 2-3, li2022bioinspiredintelligencewith pages 4-7), swarm intelligence and evolutionary approaches (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 2-3, poudel2023bioinspiredoptimizationbasedpath pages 9-10, bhaduri2009amobilerobot pages 3-4), behavior-based reactive methods (teimoori2010abiologicallyinspired pages 1-3, savkin2013asimplebiologically pages 1-3), and hybrid schemes integrating Q-learning with biologically-inspired neural networks (tan2023biologicallyinspiredcomplete pages 10-13)—demonstrates the capacity of bio-inspired techniques to address the inherent complexities of robot path planning. By emulating natural processes and behaviors, these algorithms offer flexibility, efficiency, and resilience under dynamic and uncertain conditions, paving the way for innovative applications in UAV coordination, underwater navigation, indoor cleaning, and even neurosurgical procedures. Future research, particularly that which integrates advanced learning methods and multi-sensor fusion with bio-inspired dynamics, is expected to further enhance these capabilities and drive the field toward more adaptive and autonomous robotic systems (aljalaud2023bioinspiredmultiuavpath pages 9-11, hu2010completecoveragepath pages 1-2).

This report has provided a detailed analysis of various biologically-inspired path planning algorithms, highlighting their underlying principles, key strengths, limitations, and promising avenues for future development. As robotic platforms continue to advance and operate in increasingly challenging environments, the role of biologically-inspired methods is likely to become ever more critical in delivering robust and efficient solutions to complex navigation problems (karur2021asurveyof pages 16-18, iida2016biologicallyinspiredrobotics pages 11-12).

question: how do post-quantum cryptography algorithms such as kyber/dilithium compare to corresponding non-quantum-safe methods in terms of performance and energy cost, and how could this be affected by future hardware optimizations?

sections.text: Abstract—This report examines the performance and energy cost characteristics of post‐quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms, specifically CRYSTALS‐Kyber and CRYSTALS‐Dilithium, in comparison with classical non‐quantum‐safe schemes such as RSA and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). The analysis highlights that despite the inherent computational complexity and increased energy demand of PQC schemes due to lattice operations and larger parameter sizes, targeted hardware optimizations—such as specialized accelerators, unified cryptoprocessors, and dedicated arithmetic units—can largely mitigate these disadvantages. Furthermore, the report discusses how future hardware innovations and design refinements are expected to improve performance and energy efficiency, potentially enabling PQC algorithms to surpass classical cryptosystems in constrained and high‐volume applications.

I. Introduction Recent advances in quantum computing have spurred intensive research into cryptographic algorithms resilient to quantum attacks, leading to the development of post‐quantum cryptography candidates like CRYSTALS‐Kyber for key encapsulation and CRYSTALS‐Dilithium for digital signatures. These lattice‐based schemes, which are being standardized by NIST, rely on mathematical problems such as Learning With Errors (LWE) that are believed to resist quantum algorithm attacks like Shor’s algorithm, unlike classical schemes such as RSA and ECC. (aikata2023kaliacrystal pages 10-11) As a result, the transition from classical cryptographic methods to PQC algorithms is viewed as a strategic imperative for ensuring long‐term data security, particularly in environments such as IoT and telecom networks where energy efficiency and performance are paramount. (liu2401postquantumcryptographyfor pages 4-5)

sections.text: II. Performance Comparison between PQC and Classical Cryptography A. Computational Complexity and Latency PQC algorithms such as Kyber and Dilithium inherently involve complex arithmetic operations—including number theoretic transforms (NTT) and polynomial multiplications—that lead to higher computational complexity relative to RSA and ECC, which rely primarily on modular exponentiation or elliptic curve arithmetic. (demir2503performanceanalysisand pages 1-2) However, when implemented in hardware, optimized architectures have demonstrated substantial speed improvements; for instance, dedicated hardware accelerators achieve speedups ranging from 85× to over 23,000× compared to software implementations on embedded platforms such as the Raspberry Pi 3 or ARM Cortex-M4. (aikata2023kaliacrystal pages 10-11) Hardware co-design approaches on ASIC and FPGA platforms have further narrowed the performance gap by leveraging parallel processing and pipelined arithmetic units to accelerate the NTT and other lattice operations. (banerjee2019sapphireaconfigurable pages 23-26) B. Throughput in High-Volume Operations High-volume operations, particularly in protocols like TLS, require low-latency key generation, encapsulation, decapsulation, signing, and verification, and early hardware acceleration studies have demonstrated that Kyber and Dilithium can support these requirements effectively. (buchanan2019performanceanalysisof pages 8-10) Specifically, FPGA-based implementations that batch multiple cryptographic operations have reported speedups of 3× to 9× in throughput compared to advanced CPU vectorized software implementations, with batching strategies reducing communication overhead and latency. (carril2024hardwareaccelerationfor pages 1-3) Moreover, benchmarking on constrained devices, such as the Raspberry Pi 4, reveals that despite the inherently higher cycle counts for PQC operations, optimized implementations can yield competitive handshake times compared to their classical RSA/ECC counterparts. (fitzgibbon2024constraineddeviceperformance pages 1-2) C. Comparative Execution Times Experimental results indicate that lattice-based schemes, although computationally intensive, often execute key encapsulation and signature operations faster than classical algorithms when optimized routines and vectorization are applied; for example, key generation and decapsulation in Kyber have been shown to be approximately three times faster than corresponding RSA or ECC implementations under similar security levels. (demir2503performanceanalysisand pages 3-4) Digital signatures using Dilithium also demonstrate favorable signing and verification times compared to ECDSA, especially at higher security levels where classical algorithms require longer key sizes and more complex operations. (demir2503performanceanalysisand pages 2-3) These processing time advantages are further reinforced by the use of AVX2 instructions and specialized co-design methodologies that reduce latency and enhance operational throughput. (demir2503performanceanalysisand pages 5-6)

Energy Consumption in Software-Only Implementations When benchmarked in software-only environments, PQC algorithms such as Kyber and Dilithium tend to consume more energy per operation than classical schemes due to the intensive arithmetic required by lattice problems and the larger key sizes encountered. (liu2401postquantumcryptographyfor pages 5-6) For instance, simulations and measurements on constrained devices reveal that, without hardware acceleration, operations involving PQC can result in higher energy consumption relative to optimized RSA and ECC routines running on similar platforms. (gonzalez2022kemtlsvs.postquantum pages 12-14) B. Impact of Hardware Acceleration on Energy Efficiency The integration of dedicated hardware accelerators has been shown to significantly reduce the energy consumption of PQC algorithms by leveraging architectural features such as in-memory processing, efficient modular arithmetic units, and optimized hash function accelerators. (banerjee2019sapphireaconfigurable pages 20-23) ASIC implementations employing hardware/software co-design have reported energy costs in the microjoule range for key encapsulation and decapsulation operations, thereby rendering PQC operations comparable to or more efficient than classical methods when executed on purpose-designed hardware. (dang2020implementationandbenchmarking pages 1-3) In addition, unified cryptoprocessors that support both Kyber and Dilithium have been demonstrated to use a small silicon area with energy consumption approximately half that of competing high-speed designs, underscoring the efficiency gains achievable through integrated hardware approaches. (aikata2023kaliacrystal pages 12-12) C. Energy Efficiency in Constrained Devices Benchmarking studies on devices such as ARM Cortex-M4 microcontrollers indicate that while PQC algorithms generally enforce a higher computational load, optimized hardware accelerators can reduce overall energy usage and mitigate the impact on battery-powered systems. (minhas2024postquantumauthenticationscheme pages 6-9) Furthermore, post-quantum TLS implementations incorporating Dilithium and Kyber have been shown to consume between 18% and 51% of the energy of traditional RSA+ECDHE configurations under certain authentication scenarios, highlighting the potential energy benefits in real-world applications. (tasopoulos2023energyconsumptionevaluation pages 7-8) The energy savings are primarily attributed to reductions in cycle counts and improved efficiency in arithmetic operations, as demonstrated by FPGA and ASIC implementations optimized for lattice-based arithmetic. (dang2020implementationandbenchmarking pages 21-22)
