sections.text: To reduce the space overhead associated with Sparse Table solutions, block-based techniques have been developed. These approaches partition the input array into blocks of fixed size, compute the minimum within each block, and use a combination of precomputed results and scanning within blocks to answer queries. One such approach is the Block-based Sparse Table (BbST), where the array is divided into blocks and for each block, only a concise summary (such as the block minimum) is stored. During a query, the parts of the range that are fully contained in blocks are answered using the precomputed summaries, and the remaining small segments are scanned directly. This technique often incorporates a two-level block structure, where intra-block and inter-block queries are handled separately to balance time and space (kowalski2018fasterrangeminimum pages 3-5, kowalski2018fasterrangeminimum pages 5-8). Hybrid methods combine block-based Sparse Table approaches with succinct RMQ solutions that have provable constant–time guarantees without access to the original array, achieving both high speed and minimal space overhead (kowalski2018fasterrangeminimum pages 1-3, kowalski2018fasterrangeminimum pages 10-12).

sections.text: When the number of queries is known in advance, offline RMQ processing techniques can contract the array based on the actual queries. In such cases, the array can be reduced in size (or “contracted”) to only those elements that potentially serve as minimums over the query ranges. Approaches that integrate sorting or integer sorting algorithms can then be applied to precompute answers efficiently. These offline methods are particularly useful when the query workload is predetermined and can yield significant space savings over systematic online structures (durocher2013asimplelinearspace pages 10-13, kowalski2018fasterrangeminimum pages 16-18).

sections.text: Beyond the succinct representations that aim for near–optimal space usage in bits (around 2n + o(n) bits), recent research has focused on compressed data structures for RMQ. In compressed RMQ, the input array or its associated Cartesian tree is compressed using grammar-based or tree compression techniques. One approach compresses the input string using Straight-Line Programs (SLPs) and builds RMQ data structures on the compressed representation; another compresses the Cartesian tree itself (often via DAG compression) so that LCA queries on the compressed structure provide RMQ answers with logarithmic query time in the worst case (gawrychowski2020compressedrangeminimum pages 1-2, jo2018compressedrangeminimum pages 1-3). These compressed RMQ data structures have the advantage of reducing space usage further when the input has structure or redundancy, though they sometimes incur a logarithmic slowdown in queries. Nonetheless, for many practical applications, the space savings are worth the additional query overhead (gawrychowski2020compressedrangeminimum pages 1-2).

sections.text: For multidimensional arrays, the RMQ problem becomes significantly more challenging. In one dimension, techniques such as Cartesian trees fully capture the RMQ behavior; however, in two or more dimensions no analogous construction is known. Instead, a variety of approaches have been developed. Some methods rely on range trees—data structures that recursively partition the multidimensional space into canonical intervals—while others adopt a micro-block decomposition strategy combined with permutation-type encoding. In such solutions, the array is divided into small micro blocks (whose size is typically logarithmic in n), with the distinct pattern of relative orders within each block precomputed (yuan2010datastructuresfor pages 1-2, yuan2010datastructuresfor pages 2-3, yuan2010datastructuresfor pages 3-4, yuan2010datastructuresfor pages 4-5). Although these multidimensional RMQ data structures typically incur higher query times—often O(8^d) for d dimensions—they achieve linear or near-linear space in practice. Furthermore, dynamic programming approaches based on canonical interval trees have been proposed to extend the efficiency of RMQ to multidimensional arrays even though they require additional comparisons at query time compared to their one-dimensional counterparts (yuan2010datastructuresfor pages 1-2).

sections.text: Another relevant aspect in real-world applications is the performance of RMQ structures in external memory or cache-oblivious models. In external memory, batched or static RMQ solutions have been developed based on fully balanced k-ary search trees. In these structures, internal nodes store sets of minima for the ranges of their children, enabling efficient aggregation of partial answers using I/O–optimal algorithms (arge2013on(dynamic)range pages 4-7). The underlying idea is to mimic the recursive block decomposition found in in-memory solutions while tailoring the data layout to minimize disk accesses. Similarly, in parallel external memory (PEM) models, these k-ary tree–based RMQ data structures have been extended to leverage parallelism while keeping the asymptotic I/O cost low (arge2013on(dynamic)range pages 4-7).

In many applications, it is necessary not only to answer queries quickly but also to support updates such as insertions and deletions in the input array. Dynamic RMQ data structures extend many of the static techniques, albeit with some fundamental trade-offs. One standard approach is to maintain the array with a balanced binary tree (or a variant thereof) where each leaf represents an element of the array, and each internal node stores a pointer to the leaf with the minimum value in its subtree. These trees can support updates in O(log n) time, and queries can also be answered in O(log n) time by traversing the tree structure (davoodi2011datastructuresrange pages 29-31, davoodi2011datastructuresrange pages 56-59). Some variants operate on the dynamic array using additional annotations such as subtree sizes or greedy longest decreasing sequences in the context of augmented binary trees, which can help in merging results over siblings more efficiently (liu2020lowerboundfor pages 33-36). Although dynamic solutions typically do not reach the constant query time of the static counterparts, they provide a flexible framework for applications where the data is not fixed at preprocessing time (arge2013on(dynamic)range pages 4-7).

sections.text:
The RMQ problem is fundamental in algorithmic research and practical implementations. Across the literature, a few common themes emerge. First, the use of tree-based representations—especially through Cartesian trees and their variants—provides a natural reduction from RMQ to LCA, which can then be solved using efficient techniques. Second, the quest for better space efficiency has led to numerous succinct data structure techniques that rely on encoding trees using balanced parentheses, DFUDS, or similar bit–vector representations, with operations supported by rank and select queries. Third, precomputation techniques such as the Sparse Table and modern block-based Sparse Table variants have provided practical routes to constant-time queries despite higher worst-case space overhead. Fourth, specialized schemes for dynamic settings, multidimensional problems, and external memory models illustrate that the RMQ problem is a rich source of algorithmic challenges that must be adapted according to the operational environment and input characteristics. Finally, recent advances in compressed data structures have initiated a new line of research by leveraging the redundancy in the input to further diminish space while providing acceptable query times, making the RMQ solution applicable even when the dataset is massive and highly repetitive (ferrada2017improvedrangeminimum pages 1-2, jo2018compressedrangeminimum pages 1-3).

Each of these data structures brings its own advantages and caveats. For example, while the classical Cartesian tree approach with succinct representations achieves constant query time using nearly optimal space, it can be challenging to update when the underlying array changes. Conversely, block-based and Sparse Table methods, although very effective on static data and relatively simple to implement, may use more space than is strictly necessary. Similarly, compression techniques can greatly reduce the data structure’s size when the input has inherent redundancy but might incur logarithmic query time in the worst case. Such trade-offs must be carefully balanced based on the specific requirements of the target application (durocher2013asimplelinearspace pages 1-3, kowalski2018fasterrangeminimum pages 1-3).

sections.text:
In summary, the literature on RMQ is characterized by a diversity of data structures that have evolved over the years. The most commonly used include:

•	Tree–based methods that begin with the Cartesian tree construction, which exploits the equivalence of RMQ and LCA, and its variants such as the extended Cartesian tree and 2d-Min-Heap. These structures are valued for their theoretical optimality and constant–time query performance (demaine2014oncartesiantrees pages 1-4, fischer2011spaceefficientpreprocessingschemes pages 6-7).

•	Succinct tree representations including balanced parentheses and DFUDS encode these trees nearly optimally—in 2n + o(n) bits—while still allowing rapid navigation operations essential for RMQ (fischer2010optimalsuccinctnessfor pages 7-9, davoodi2012succinctrepresentationsof pages 1-3).

•	Precomputation techniques such as Sparse Tables and their block–based variants precompute answers for subranges of the input array. These methods offer constant query time in the static case but often with increased space usage unless combined with block decomposition or hierarchical strategies (durocher2013asimplelinearspace pages 1-3, skala2013arrayrangequeries pages 3-6, kowalski2018fasterrangeminimum pages 3-5).

•	Dynamic RMQ data structures rely on balanced binary search trees augmented with auxiliary information to support updates as well as queries in logarithmic time, making them suitable for applications where the input array is mutable (davoodi2011datastructuresrange pages 29-31, liu2020lowerboundfor pages 33-36).

•	For multidimensional arrays, canonical interval trees, range trees, and micro-block decompositions—often paired with permutation-type encoding—are employed to extend the RMQ problem beyond one dimension (yuan2010datastructuresfor pages 1-2, yuan2010datastructuresfor pages 3-4).

•	Recent research on compressed RMQ structures leverages grammar-based and tree compression techniques to reduce space usage further while retaining acceptable query times, making these approaches attractive when handling large or redundant datasets (gawrychowski2020compressedrangeminimum pages 1-2, jo2018compressedrangeminimum pages 1-3).

The diversity of these approaches reflects the inherent trade-offs between time, space, and update flexibility that are typical in efficient data structure design. For many practical applications—from text indexing and succinct tree navigation to external memory processing—the choice of RMQ data structure is guided by whether the primary requirement is static speed, minimal space consumption, dynamic update performance, or multidimensional support. Future research will likely continue to blend these paradigms, striving for solutions that are both space‐optimal and flexible in handling dynamically changing, higher-dimensional, or compressed data (arge2013on(dynamic)range pages 4-7, baumstark2017practicalrangeminimum pages 1-3).

In conclusion, commonly used data structures for solving the Range Minimum Query problem are based on tree–structures (most notably the Cartesian tree and its derivatives such as extended Cartesian trees and the 2d-Min-Heap), succinct representations (balanced parentheses, DFUDS, BP), Sparse Tables with block-based precomputation, and hybrid approaches that integrate these techniques in static, dynamic, multidimensional, and compressed settings. Each methodology is supported by tight theoretical foundations and numerous practical improvements, ensuring that RMQ remains a central problem in the design of efficient data structures (demaine2014oncartesiantrees pages 7-9, fischer2011spaceefficientpreprocessingschemes pages 25-27, kowalski2018fasterrangeminimum pages 16-18).

question: how can software engineering process improvements be effectively measured in real-world settings?

sections.text: This report examines methods for effectively measuring software engineering process improvements in real world settings. The discussion integrates insights from traditional process improvement frameworks, agile and lean measurement approaches, continuous integration and continuous delivery practices, and empirical case studies from industry. The measurement of process improvements is critical because it transforms abstract quality and productivity claims into quantifiable evidence that organizations can use to guide iterative improvements and strategic decisions (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 1-2).

citations.title: Software engineering for machine learning: a case study.

sections.text: Software engineering process improvements are intended to enhance software quality, productivity, and team effectiveness by evolving development practices in response to emerging challenges. However, to realize the benefits of these improvements, organizations must deploy measurement methods that accurately reflect process maturity, efficiency, and quality outcomes in an environment characterized by complexity, context specific constraints, and varying degrees of team expertise (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 2-3). The central research question addressed in this report is: How can software engineering process improvements be effectively measured in real-world settings? This report elaborates on the necessary criteria, tools, and methodologies, drawing on empirical studies and systematic literature reviews that span traditional frameworks, agile practices, continuous software engineering, and key performance indicators (KPIs).

sections.text:
Historically, process improvement in software engineering has been driven by models such as the Capability Maturity Model (CMM) and Six Sigma, which offer structured approaches to assessing and advancing an organization’s process capability (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 2-3). These models provide staged frameworks that range from ad hoc, chaotic processes to fully optimized, quantitatively managed processes. For example, the traditional CMM framework delineates five maturity levels that help organizations benchmark their current practices while providing direction for systematic improvement (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 2-3).

While these frameworks traditionally focus on rigorous planning, documentation, and quantitative process control, their direct application in contexts such as Agile or machine learning (ML) systems can be challenging. As software systems become increasingly complex and integrated with data-driven ML components, the need to contextualize traditional process measurements has grown (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 1-2). In addition, while Six Sigma emphasizes waste elimination and quality improvement through statistical methods, its implementation often demands rigid adherence to well-defined projects and control charts that may not suit the dynamic environment of agile software development (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 2-3).

sections.text:
Agile methodologies prioritize flexibility, rapid feedback, and customer collaboration over exhaustive documentation. In Agile contexts, software engineering improvements are often measured using lightweight metrics that support sprint planning, progress tracking, and quality assurance. For instance, metrics such as velocity, burndown charts, story percent complete, and defect counts are widely used to provide both immediate feedback and longer-term trends that indicate process health (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 2-3).  
Agile metrics are purposely chosen to be simple and to motivate teams rather than control every detail, recognizing that overemphasis on numbers can lead to dysfunctional behavior or narrow optimization that undermines creativity and adaptability (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 7-8). Agile teams typically use metrics to support planning and iterative improvements; for example, velocity and effort estimates are not only used to predict work completion but also to foster team transparency and continuous learning (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 5-6).

Lean practices add another layer of process improvement by emphasizing waste reduction and continuous delivery. Lean Software Development borrows concepts from lean manufacturing, such as value stream mapping, to identify non-value adding activities and bottlenecks, thereby offering a clear path toward process optimization (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 4-5). Value stream mapping provides a visual representation of the entire software development lifecycle that highlights delays, rework, or excessive inventories of work-in-progress. By coupling value stream mapping with lean metrics like lead time and flow measures, organizations can quantitatively assess how changes in process design contribute to speed and quality improvements (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 7-8).

sections.text:
Continuous software engineering (CSE) represents an evolution from traditional and agile methods toward an integrated, end-to-end approach that covers planning, development, testing, deployment, and operations. CSE uses continuous integration (CI) and continuous delivery (CD) pipelines to provide constant, automated feedback on the state of the software system (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 8-9). In these environments, metrics derived from CI systems—such as build success rates, automated test pass rates, code coverage, and time-to-deployment—serve not just as indicators of process health but also as drivers for immediate corrective action (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 10-10).

The integrated nature of CSE emphasizes that process improvements are not isolated to the development phase alone but are distributed across multiple stakeholders and activities. For instance, effective measurement requires linking technical quality metrics with operational indicators such as customer satisfaction and business value delivery (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10). This holistic approach entails the use of multi-dimensional measurement frameworks that capture technical, process, and organizational aspects, ensuring that data from CI pipelines, testing routines, and post-deployment monitoring collectively inform improvements across the software lifecycle (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 5-6).

sections.text:
In large organizations with complex, distributed software development operations, the establishment of Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) is indispensable. KPIs provide consolidated values that synthesize disparate measurements into actionable insights that can be communicated and compared across organizational units (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 1-2). For an effective measurement framework, KPIs must be tailored to the context of the organization, aligned with strategic business objectives, and built to ensure transparency, intelligibility, quantification, and comparability (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 2-3).

The process of selecting KPIs requires active involvement from stakeholders at different levels, as well as iterative refinement based on feedback. For example, initial KPIs might include measures such as the “Definition of Ready” for requirements, the number of change requests, or the time-to-market, all of which provide insight into process delays and quality constraints (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 6-7). As KPIs are refined, organizations develop a common language and a shared understanding of what constitutes quality and progress. When KPIs are successfully implemented, they serve not only as static reports but also as dynamic tools that drive continuous improvements in process and product quality (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 7-8).

Furthermore, the balance between automation and manual data review is crucial in KPI deployment. While automated tools can provide rapid, near real-time insights into process performance, manual review remains important for ensuring data quality, contextual interpretation, and alignment with strategic objectives (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 9-10).

Process maturity models offer a structured way to measure and improve software engineering practices by providing staged benchmarks that indicate progress toward excellence. Recent research has attempted to develop maturity models tailored to the unique challenges of ML-integrated systems, reflecting the iterative, experimental nature of these projects (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 7-8). These maturity models typically assess dimensions such as goal definition, consistency in implementation, documentation, automation, measurement, and continuous improvement, offering a multidimensional view of process health (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10).

Self-assessment approaches, which rely on structured questionnaires and Likert-scale evaluations, allow teams to benchmark themselves against industry standards and identify gaps in their practices (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10). Such models are particularly useful because they enable organizations to track improvements over time, highlight diminishing challenges as teams gain experience, and provide empirical evidence of process maturity increases (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10). By combining self-assessment methods with tangible metrics from the development process, organizations create a more complete picture of their strengths and weaknesses, thus informing targeted interventions (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 2-3).

Beyond technical metrics, the quality of teamwork and communication plays a pivotal role in determining the success of process improvements. Research on teamwork quality (TWQ) has shown strong relationships between team interactions and overall project outcomes, particularly regarding product quality and team member satisfaction (lindsjørn2016teamworkqualityand pages 20-22). Although TWQ is inherently subjective, incorporating multi-rater assessments—such as evaluations from team members, leaders, and product owners—can yield actionable insights about areas needing improvement (lindsjørn2016teamworkqualityand pages 20-22).

The integration of team dynamic metrics with technical process measures enables organizations to adopt a more holistic approach to improvement measurement. For example, teams that consistently meet sprint goals and maintain high velocity are likely to report better communication and collaboration during retrospectives, which in turn leads to iterative refinements in their processes (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 7-8). Therefore, effective measurement not only considers quantitative indicators such as defect counts and test pass rates but also qualitative feedback related to teamwork, learning, and communication.

Empirical software engineering research has increasingly advocated for mixed-method approaches that combine quantitative data with qualitative insights. This dual perspective is essential for understanding the multifaceted nature of process improvements in real-world settings (garousi2019guidelinesforincluding pages 31-32). Quantitative metrics provide objective evidence of process performance, while qualitative methods—such as interviews, focus groups, and case studies—provide context, explain causality, and reveal underlying factors that numbers alone cannot capture (dikert2016challengesandsuccess pages 7-8).

For instance, a systematic literature review on the use of metrics in agile and lean development has highlighted that combining numerical data (e.g., velocity, defect counts, cycle times) with contextual information (e.g., team satisfaction, communication quality) leads to a more nuanced understanding of process improvements (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 3-3, kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 20-21). Mixed-method studies thereby enable practitioners to triangulate results, validate findings across multiple sources, and ultimately improve the reliability and generalizability of the measurement outcomes (baltes2022samplinginsoftware pages 34-37).

A key enabler of effective measurement in contemporary software engineering is the integration of automated tools that support continuous monitoring and feedback. Continuous integration systems, automated testing frameworks, static code analysis tools, and dashboards for KPI visualization constitute the backbone of an integrated measurement infrastructure (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 8-9). These tools facilitate near real-time detection of issues, promote rapid iteration, and provide objective metrics that are essential for continuous improvement.

For example, CI environments generate automated reports that detail build success rates, test results, and code quality metrics. When these metrics are embedded in a broader dashboard that incorporates business KPIs, such as customer satisfaction scores or time-to-market data, organizations gain a comprehensive view of how process improvements are translating into tangible performance gains (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 10-10).  
Moreover, automation reduces the reliance on manual data collection, minimizes errors in measurement, and supports sustained improvement by enabling frequent, low-overhead evaluations (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 3-3).

Continuous improvement is at the heart of both Agile and lean methodologies. Regular feedback loops—such as sprint retrospectives, daily stand-ups, and automated build-and-test cycles—provide the iterative insights necessary for incremental enhancements (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 4-5). These feedback mechanisms help identify not only technical faults but also process bottlenecks, communication breakdowns, and areas where additional training or process standardization may be required (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 7-8).

A process improvement measurement system that incorporates frequent feedback loops enables rapid adjustments and reinforces the idea that improvement is an ongoing journey rather than a one-time intervention. This continuous cycle of measuring, analyzing, and acting on improvement opportunities ensures that teams remain agile, can adapt to changes in requirements or technology, and ultimately deliver higher quality software (thomson2025apracticalapproach pages 8-11).

Empirical case studies provide compelling evidence of how measurement frameworks can be applied effectively in industrial settings. For example, studies conducted at large organizations have demonstrated that customized KPI systems can reveal hidden process inefficiencies, such as delays in requirement clarification or testing bottlenecks, and guide targeted process interventions (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 6-7).  
Other studies have shown that maturity models and self-assessment tools, when combined with automatable metrics from CI/CD pipelines, produce actionable insights that improve process consistency over time (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10).

Similarly, case studies in agile environments have underscored that the use of lightweight metrics—such as burndown charts and defect counts—support iterative planning and help teams to identify trends before they become critical issues (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 5-6). These real-world examples illustrate that effective measurement is not a one-size-fits-all proposition; rather, it requires tailoring to the specific context, technology stack, team structure, and business objectives of the organization (dikert2016challengesandsuccess pages 7-8).

sections.text:
Despite the benefits of integrated measurement frameworks, there remain several challenges in implementing these systems effectively. One major challenge is the potential misinterpretation or misuse of metrics, where an overemphasis on particular quantitative indicators can lead to gaming of the system or narrow optimization that neglects broader quality dimensions (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 15-16).  
Another challenge relates to data quality and consistency, particularly in large organizations where software development processes span multiple departments and rely on heterogeneous data sources (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 8-9). Balancing automated measurements with manual validation and contextual interpretation is essential to ensure reliable data that accurately reflects process performance (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 2-3).

Furthermore, measurement approaches must be flexible enough to adapt to changing organizational needs and evolving technologies. For instance, while traditional metrics may work well for mature, waterfall-based systems, they may not capture the iterative, rapid-cycle nature of Agile and continuous software engineering environments (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 1-2). This necessitates the development of adaptive measurement frameworks that incorporate both established models and emerging metrics tailored to new modes of software development (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 3-3).

sections.text:
To successfully measure software engineering process improvements in real-world settings, organizations should adopt a multi-faceted approach that incorporates the following best practices:

•	Align metrics with business value. Metrics should not be selected arbitrarily but must be closely tied to strategic business objectives and customer outcomes. This ensures that improvements in technical quality translate into measurable business benefits, such as reduced time-to-market and increased customer satisfaction (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10, surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 2-3).

•	Select context-appropriate metrics. Different software development contexts—whether traditional, Agile, lean, or continuous—require different sets of metrics. For example, while velocity and burndown charts may be effective in fast-paced Agile teams, maturity models and defect density may be more relevant in environments that require rigorous process stabilization (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 7-8, amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 2-3).

•	Integrate quantitative and qualitative data. The most effective measurement systems combine numerical metrics from automated tools with subjective assessments gathered through surveys, interviews, and self-assessments. This mixed-methods approach ensures that numbers are contextualized and that nuances related to team dynamics and communication are captured (garousi2019guidelinesforincluding pages 31-32, dikert2016challengesandsuccess pages 7-8).

•	Foster continuous feedback loops. Regular feedback is essential for driving iterative improvements. By incorporating mechanisms such as daily stand-ups, sprint retrospectives, and CI/CD dashboards, organizations can rapidly identify process gaps and immediately act on them (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 4-5, kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 5-6).

•	Customize KPIs and measurement tools. Especially for large organizations, customization of KPIs to reflect domain-specific challenges and opportunities is critical. Tailored KPI systems enable teams to monitor progress across departments and provide a unified view of overall software development health (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 7-8, surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 9-10).

•	Ensure stakeholder involvement and clear communication. Successful measurement initiatives require broad involvement from all levels of the organization—not only developers but also management, quality assurance experts, and business stakeholders. Regular workshops, training sessions, and update meetings help build consensus and ensure that metrics are correctly interpreted and acted upon (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 6-7, thomson2025apracticalapproach pages 8-11).

•	Emphasize process maturity and self-assessment. Using maturity models and self-assessment tools that are specifically designed for modern development practices can help teams understand where they are on their improvement journey. Such models also provide benchmarks against which progress over time can be measured (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10, amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 7-8).

•	Leverage automation while remaining vigilant about data quality. Automated measurement systems are indispensable for continuous improvement, yet they must be supplemented with periodic manual reviews to ensure that the data are accurate, consistent, and contextually relevant (fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 8-9, surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 3-3).

While significant progress has been made in establishing frameworks and tools for measuring software engineering process improvements, further research is needed in several key areas. For instance, new metrics may be required to better capture the impacts of emerging technologies such as machine learning, microservices architectures, and cloud-native development. Additionally, research on integrating agile, lean, and continuous improvement metrics into unified dashboards remains an important challenge, particularly for large organizations undergoing digital transformations (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 1-2, abrahamsson2017agilesoftwaredevelopment pages 105-109).

Future studies should also focus on further validating maturity models and mixed-method measurement approaches through longitudinal studies that track improvements over time. Establishing causal relationships between discrete process improvements and business outcomes would further strengthen the rationale for investment in measurement infrastructure (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10, dikert2016challengesandsuccess pages 7-8). Moreover, there is a need for improved methods to mitigate the risks of metric misuse, whereby a narrow focus on specific indicators might lead to perverse incentives rather than genuine process improvement (kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 15-16).

sections.text:
Measuring software engineering process improvements in real-world settings necessitates a multidimensional, context-sensitive approach that combines traditional process maturity frameworks with agile and lean methods, continuous integration practices, and tailored KPI systems. Effective measurement is achieved by aligning metrics with business value, integrating both quantitative and qualitative data, establishing continuous feedback loops, and ensuring stakeholder engagement across organizational boundaries. In addition, the adoption of maturity models, self-assessment tools, and automated measurement infrastructures enables teams to empirically validate process improvements and respond dynamically to challenges. Ultimately, by embedding measurement into the very fabric of software development practices, organizations can transform process improvement from an abstract goal into a disciplined, data-driven, and continuous journey toward enhanced productivity, quality, and collaboration (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 1-2, fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 4-5, kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 7-8).

The discussion presented in this report illustrates that effective measurement of software engineering process improvements is not solely a technical endeavor. It requires a holistic view that incorporates organizational maturity, team dynamics, strategic alignment, and continuous learning. Empirical studies—ranging from comprehensive literature reviews to real-world case studies—provide strong evidence that a blended approach, employing both automated quantitative metrics and qualitative feedback mechanisms, can lead to a sustainable and iterative improvement process across diverse development environments (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 9-10, dikert2016challengesandsuccess pages 7-8, lindsjørn2016teamworkqualityand pages 20-22).

In summary, the combination of traditional measurement frameworks, agile and lean practices, continuous integration methodologies, and tailored KPIs creates a robust infrastructure for gauging the success of process improvements in software engineering. Organizations that invest in comprehensive measurement systems will not only better understand their current operating state but will also be empowered to drive targeted, data-driven improvements that resonate with both technical excellence and business success (surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 1-2, thomson2025apracticalapproach pages 11-15).

As the field of software engineering continues to evolve, the methods and metrics for process improvement must also evolve in tandem. Future research and practical implementations will benefit from further integration of emerging technologies, continued validation of measurement frameworks across diverse contexts, and an unwavering commitment to aligning process improvements with core business objectives and team well-being (baltes2022samplinginsoftware pages 34-37, kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 3-3).

By fostering a culture of continuous feedback, rigorous self-assessment, and stakeholder collaboration, organizations can ensure that the improvements they implement are both measurable and meaningful. This holistic approach not only enhances software quality and development efficiency but also contributes to overall organizational agility in a rapidly changing technological landscape (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 7-8, fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 8-9).

In conclusion, effective measurement of software engineering process improvements in real-world settings is achieved through: 

	•	Combining traditional process improvement models with agile and lean metrics,  
	•	Leveraging continuous integration and automated monitoring tools to provide real-time feedback,  
	•	Defining and tailoring KPIs that align with organizational goals and business value, and  
	•	Incorporating both quantitative and qualitative data via mixed-method approaches.

This comprehensive measurement framework transforms the abstract notion of “process improvement” into quantifiable, actionable insights that drive strategic enhancements and foster a responsive, quality-oriented software engineering culture (thomson2025apracticalapproach pages 4-8, kupiainen2015usingmetricsin pages 5-6, surucu2020establishingkeyperformance pages 7-8).

Ultimately, by institutionalizing these practices, organizations not only measure improvements effectively but also create an environment where continuous evolution and excellence in software engineering processes are the norm rather than the exception (amershi2019softwareengineeringfor pages 2-3, fitzgerald2017continuoussoftwareengineering pages 8-9).

question: What interfaces have researchers developed to help people perform behavioral evaluation of ML models, and how do they accelerate annotation efforts?

sections.text: This report presents a comprehensive review of interfaces that researchers have developed for behavioral evaluation of machine learning (ML) models and examines how these interfaces accelerate annotation efforts. Behavioral evaluation refers to the process of assessing ML models by examining their responses over diverse data slices, subgroups, or modalities rather than relying solely on aggregate performance metrics. In this context, an interface is a system–software component that mediates the human–machine interaction, enabling users to inspect, correct, and annotate model outputs. The following sections describe several representative systems, discuss their design principles, and analyze the ways in which they reduce manual annotation workload, increase feedback efficiency, and ultimately accelerate the iterative model training and evaluation cycle.

One of the earliest and highly impactful innovations in this field is the Fluid Annotation interface, developed to provide a unified approach for full image annotation in lieu of fragmented micro‐task approaches. Fluid Annotation leverages the prediction output of a neural network as an initial “draft” for segmentation, which then can be edited, added, or removed by human annotators. This integration of strong machine learning assistance with flexible human correction not only provides a seamless annotation experience but also reduces the time required to produce high-quality labels considerably (andriluka2018fluidannotation pages 1-2). By presenting a single‐pass interface that unifies the entire annotation process, the system minimizes context switching costs and thus enables annotators to focus on addressing challenging cases and model errors directly. This design choice accelerates annotation because human effort is prioritized where the automated model is less certain, leading to annotation processes that require significantly less time than traditional methods.

citations.title: Fluid annotation

sections.text: Another noteworthy development in behavior evaluation interfaces is the NOVA system. NOVA is an interface that integrates explainable AI (XAI) techniques, facilitating an interactive, cooperative machine learning paradigm. In NOVA, multiple visualization algorithms—such as guided backpropagation, deep Taylor decomposition, and Layer-wise Relevance Propagation—are combined into a single interface that enables annotators to scrutinize model predictions on behavioral data such as facial expressions or speech (baur2020explainablecooperativemachine pages 17-19). The system implements a cooperative machine learning (CML) strategy whereby human raters provide feedback, and the model incrementally improves its performance by focusing on low-confidence or error-prone cases. By providing immediate visual feedback that includes prediction reliability via confidence values, NOVA directs human effort toward the annotation of only the most informative examples (baur2020explainablecooperativemachine pages 19-20). This targeted approach not only improves annotation precision but also drastically reduces manual labeling time by automating the annotation of easier cases while flagging ambiguous ones for human review.

sections.text: A more recent contribution, Zeno, provides a comprehensive solution for behavioral evaluation by combining a Python API with an interactive user interface. Zeno supports the creation of data slices, exportable reports, and unit tests for model behavior, thereby letting users delve into model performance on specialized subgroups. Its design includes a dual-interface structure: an Exploration UI that is geared toward non-technical stakeholders allowing for intuitive slicing of data, and an Analysis UI that facilitates writing tests and tracking performance over time (cabrera2023zenoaninteractive pages 1-2). In addition, Zeno offers decorator functions such as @model, @metric, @distill, and @transform which enable programmatic generation of metrics and metadata; this further accelerates annotation by reducing manual intervention in data segmentation and behavioral testing (cabrera2023zenoaninteractive pages 5-6). Through such interactive capabilities, Zeno empowers users to rapidly identify, validate, and even share common failure modes, directly speeding up the cycle of data curation and model refinement.

sections.text: Several interfaces designed for interactive machine learning (IML) aim to tightly couple user feedback with model updates. Reviews of IML interface design have highlighted various approaches in which users provide direct feedback to the system through interactive labeling and error-correction tools. These systems typically enable live annotations that are integrated into the learning loop to improve model predictions continuously, thus reducing both the cognitive load on annotators and the time-to-convergence for the ML models (dudley2018areviewof pages 14-16). For example, by embedding correction options directly within visualizations such as error-tracking charts or confusion matrices, users can quickly identify misclassifications and refine models in real time. The incorporation of interfaces that allow for hierarchical and structured feedback assignment further reduces annotation redundancy and focuses human attention on the samples that most affect model accuracy (dudley2018areviewof pages 26-28).

citations.title: A review of user interface design for interactive machine learning
A review of user interface design for interactive machine learning

sections.text: Further improvements in annotation interfaces are found in systems that draw inspiration from gamification and crowd-sourcing techniques. Interactive systems like JAABA and iHEARu-PLAY have been designed to allow multiple annotators to work concurrently or sequentially, pooling collective knowledge to label complex behaviors such as animal or human emotional expressions (dudley2018areviewof pages 28-29). By engaging annotators in a game-like or shared interactive environment, these interfaces not only motivate participants through immediate visual and statistical feedback but also drive up annotation throughput via distributed human effort (dudley2018areviewof pages 3-5). The high level of user engagement in these environments results in faster labeling cycles, as annotators are incentivized to review large volumes of data quickly while still achieving high accuracy.

citations.title: A review of user interface design for interactive machine learning
A review of user interface design for interactive machine learning

sections.text: Another pioneering interface design is Marcelle, a toolkit that supports the composition and integration of interactive ML workflows. Marcelle adopts a modular approach whereby developers can create custom pipelines by linking together a variety of components—from data ingestion and visualization to model training and error analysis—in a drag-and-drop fashion (francoise2021marcellecomposinginteractive pages 3-6). The system enables both ML experts and domain specialists to collaboratively build interfaces that are tightly aligned with their annotation and evaluation needs, thus improving flexibility and scalability. For instance, by creating customized dashboard views that display real-time training logs and classifier outputs, Marcelle allows users to quickly detect anomalies and iteratively refine the system, fundamentally accelerating the annotation process by reducing the need for extensive coding or external tooling (francoise2021marcellecomposinginteractive pages 20-22). In addition, the ability to compose workflows that integrate interactive visualization of high-dimensional data supports rapid cycle testing and user-driven model evaluation (francoise2021marcellecomposinginteractive pages 24-26).

sections.text: Explainable Active Learning (XAL) represents a critical development in interfaces designed to accelerate annotation efforts by integrating explanation-based feedback with active learning. In XAL, local explanations of model predictions—typically in the form of feature importance scores—are presented alongside query instances, offering annotators insights into the rationale behind each prediction (ghai2020explainableactivelearning pages 23-24). These explanations empower users to provide more informed corrections and reduce uncertainty, especially when the underlying ML model generates ambiguous outputs. The interface further supports the iterative refinement of models by allowing real-time modifications at the feature level, such as adjusting weights via interactive sliders, which directly reduces the overall number of manual annotations required (ghai2020explainableactivelearning pages 5-6). Subsequent developments in this area have demonstrated that interfaces leveraging explicit local explanations not only guide annotators to focus on misclassified regions, but they also help in calibrating annotator trust in the system, further expediting subsequent annotation rounds (ghai2021explainableactivelearning pages 6-8).

sections.text: Label-and-Learn is another prominent interface that integrates multiple visualization strategies to support behavioral evaluation and data labeling. Designed primarily for developers with limited ML expertise, Label-and-Learn combines intuitive displays such as confusion matrices, word clouds, and classifier performance graphs with interactive labelling tasks (sun2017labelandlearn pages 9-11). By visually communicating the impact of each new annotation on model performance, this interface encourages annotators to focus on the most informative samples. This approach not only improves the overall quality of the annotated dataset but also reduces the total number of annotations needed by dynamically converging toward a state where additional labeling yields diminishing returns (sun2017labelandlearn pages 1-2).

sections.text: Recent interfaces have begun integrating emerging ML technologies, such as large language models (LLMs), Transformers, and diffusion models, to further accelerate annotation workflows. Advanced systems leverage prompt-driven strategies to generate synthetic annotations or augment existing data by synthesizing analogies and modifications based on minimal human inputs (watson2023augmentedbehavioralannotation pages 10-12). These interfaces use minimal notation techniques—sometimes reducing complex inputs to simple point-based interactions—to decrease the cognitive burden on annotators, allowing users to efficiently mark events or objects in the data stream (watson2023augmentedbehavioralannotation pages 7-8). By automating routine aspects of labeling and facilitating the rapid creation of augmented datasets, these systems substantially reduce manual annotation time while maintaining or even enhancing the fidelity of the labels.

sections.text: For domains such as behavioral neuroscience or interactive robotics, real-time evaluation interfaces have emerged to support multimodal data analysis. For example, the BENTO interface is a MATLAB-based graphical user interface that synchronously displays neural signals, video streams, human annotations, audio spectrograms, and pose estimates (watson2024machinelearningdriven pages 11-12). By consolidating various data modalities into a unified platform, BENTO enables annotators and researchers to evaluate model behavior with high temporal precision and contextual richness. The integration of near real-time processing means that automated classifiers can generate preliminary annotations that human experts can then verify or correct, dramatically reducing the manual input necessary for high-quality annotations. Such systems are especially beneficial in domains with complex and rapidly evolving behavioral dynamics, where timing and context are critical for accurate evaluation (watson2024machinelearningdriven pages 12-14).

sections.text: In addition to the interactive approaches described above, systems like OneLabeler take a mixed-initiative approach to data annotation. OneLabeler implements default labeling, where an automated process initially assigns labels that annotators subsequently correct. This default labeling strategy is complemented by mixed-initiative sampling methods that cluster similar data objects together so that annotations can be applied to batches of items simultaneously (zhang2022onelabeleraflexible pages 12-13). Such an approach significantly reduces the amount of manual labor involved in granular labeling tasks because multiple instances are corrected in a single pass. Furthermore, by iteratively incorporating user corrections into the model’s training cycle, OneLabeler fosters continuous improvement in label accuracy—thereby accelerating the annotation process while maintaining high quality.

citations.title: Onelabeler: a flexible system for building data labeling tools

sections.text: Another strategic direction in interface design focuses on the integration of confidence metrics into the annotation workflow. Some interfaces incorporate internal measures of prediction confidence to dynamically prioritize which data samples require human review. For example, confidence values generated by a model’s label prediction are used to select only those instances that fall below a certain reliability threshold for manual annotation (baur2020explainablecooperativemachine pages 20-21). This technique ensures that annotators are not overwhelmed by redundant tasks involving highly certain predictions, thereby concentrating human effort on error-prone or ambiguous cases. The selective annotation strategy markedly reduces the overall number of annotations required while still ensuring that the ML model continues to receive the critical corrections it needs to improve.

citations.title: Explainable cooperative machine learning with nova

sections.text: A further line of research has explored the integration of rule-based (RB) models with machine learning methods into a hybrid system. In such systems, expert-driven rules based on domain knowledge are initially used to assess sample quality and flag uncertain cases; only these low-confidence examples are then forwarded for manual review (lee2022towardsefficientannotations pages 1-2). This hybrid human–AI collaboration minimizes annotation workload by leveraging expert knowledge to pre-filter data, thus ensuring that human effort is dedicated exclusively to samples that will yield the highest improvement in model performance. Interfaces incorporating such hybrid models achieve significant reductions in annotation time while maintaining high accuracy, and they are particularly valuable in safety-critical or clinical applications where errors can be costly.

citations.title: Towards efficient annotations for a human-ai collaborative, clinical decision support system: a case study on physical stroke rehabilitation assessment

sections.text: Another prevailing theme in the development of annotation interfaces is the focus on intuitive user interface (UI) design. Recent surveys and experimental studies have stressed that superior UI design can substantially reduce cognitive load and speed up annotation cycles (viana2021aninterfacedesign pages 2-3). Interfaces that incorporate layered complexity—offering both basic and advanced modes with clear iconography and guided onboarding—allow both novice and expert annotators to participate efficiently in behavioral evaluation tasks. These UI design choices, which often include immediate visual feedback and interactive sample review tools, streamline the collaboration between domain experts and machine learning models and shorten the time required to achieve reliable model behavior evaluation.

citations.title: An interface design catalog for interactive labeling systems

sections.text: The evolution of annotation interfaces has also seen the rise of platforms that support both multimodal annotation and distributed human input. Systems that integrate crowdsourcing components, often through web-based platforms, enable the partitioning of large annotation tasks among many annotators. Such distributed platforms have been designed to incorporate automated error detection and duplicate monitoring, which further refine the quality of annotations while keeping the human effort focused on unique and informative data points (watson2023augmentedbehavioralannotation pages 17-19). By combining automated pre-annotation with human verification and correction, these platforms accelerate annotation efforts for large-scale, multimodal datasets, thus addressing two key challenges: dataset quality and annotation scalability.

citations.title: Augmented behavioral annotation tools, with application to multimodal datasets and models: a systematic review

sections.text: Across the diverse range of systems described above, several common themes emerge. First, many modern interfaces are predicated on the idea of close human-system collaboration, where machine predictions serve as an initial baseline and human input is used to refine those predictions iteratively (andriluka2018fluidannotation pages 1-2, dudley2018areviewof pages 14-16). Second, the integration of explainability—whether through feature importance, visual analytics, or structured feedback loops—is a critical element that not only increases transparency but also effectively guides annotation efforts (ghai2020explainableactivelearning pages 23-24, ghai2021explainableactivelearning pages 6-8). Third, many systems are designed to be modular and customizable; frameworks such as Marcelle and Zeno illustrate that providing a toolset for composing and tailoring annotation workflows can significantly lower the overhead associated with model evaluation and make behavioral analysis more accessible and scalable (francoise2021marcellecomposinginteractive pages 3-6, cabrera2023zenoaninteractive pages 1-2). Fourth, several approaches leverage active learning and confidence-based prioritization to selectively direct human annotation where it is most needed, thereby optimizing both the speed and accuracy of human–machine interactions (baur2020explainablecooperativemachine pages 20-21, sun2017labelandlearn pages 9-11). Finally, the incorporation of modern ML techniques such as LLM-driven prompt engineering, synthesis of augmented data, and multimodal concurrency in annotation interfaces signals a transition toward more automated yet human-guided behavioral evaluation workflows (watson2023augmentedbehavioralannotation pages 10-12, watson2024machinelearningdriven pages 11-12).

sections.text: The benefits of these interface innovations extend beyond mere time savings; they also enhance model performance and data quality by ensuring that annotations are concentrated on the most informative examples. By providing interactive feedback, these interfaces support an iterative learning process in which models and annotators gradually co-adapt to each other. The result is not only a faster training process but also a higher-quality annotated dataset that can reveal nuanced model behaviors and systemic biases (cabrera2023zenoaninteractive pages 5-6, dudley2018areviewof pages 31-33). For instance, in applications where behavioral subtleties such as affective expressions are critical, interfaces that combine real-time visual feedback with interactive model correction—such as BENTO and specialized multimodal annotation tools—have been shown to achieve near real-time performance with human-level annotation quality (watson2024machinelearningdriven pages 11-12).

sections.text: Despite these advances, several challenges remain in the design and deployment of behavioral evaluation interfaces. One of the key issues is the balance between automation and human control; while high levels of automation reduce the manual annotation burden, they can also lead to over-reliance on machine predictions if not carefully monitored by human experts. In this regard, the integration of explainable interfaces and active learning remains vital to ensure that users remain engaged and aware of the model’s inner workings (ghai2020explainableactivelearning pages 3-5). Another challenge is ensuring that these systems can scale effectively across diverse data types and application domains. While systems such as Marcelle and OneLabeler exhibit considerable flexibility, further research is needed to adapt these interfaces to emerging ML paradigms such as few-shot learning and meta-learning, which require even more granular control over the annotation process (zhang2022onelabeleraflexible pages 12-13). Finally, the development of hybrid systems that combine rule-based components with deep learning models opens new avenues for inquiry, particularly in high-stakes domains such as clinical decision support, where annotation errors can be costly (lee2022towardsefficientannotations pages 1-2).

sections.text: In summary, researchers have developed a diverse array of interfaces to facilitate the behavioral evaluation of ML models, each contributing to accelerated annotation efforts in distinct ways. From the unified Fluid Annotation interface that integrates deep learning predictions with human correction, to explainable cooperative systems like NOVA that prioritize human input based on prediction confidence, to modular toolkits such as Marcelle and Zeno which empower users to design custom annotation workflows, these developments reflect a trend toward interactive, human-in-the-loop systems that enhance both efficiency and quality. Explainable active learning interfaces further reduce cognitive load by presenting local explanations that enable smarter annotations, while visualization-driven systems like Label-and-Learn make progress and performance dynamically understandable to users. Advanced platforms that support multimodal annotation and distributed human input add scalability to these methods, ensuring that even large and diverse datasets can be managed effectively. Finally, hybrid approaches that combine rule-based systems with ML models indicate a promising direction for minimizing the required human workload while maintaining high annotation fidelity. Collectively, these innovations not only accelerate the annotation process—by reducing annotation time, focusing human effort on critical cases, and integrating automated feedback loops—but also improve the overall quality of annotated datasets, thereby enhancing the robustness and fairness of ML models in practical, real-world applications (andriluka2018fluidannotation pages 1-2, baur2020explainablecooperativemachine pages 17-19, cabrera2023zenoaninteractive pages 1-2, dudley2018areviewof pages 14-16, francoise2021marcellecomposinginteractive pages 3-6, ghai2020explainableactivelearning pages 23-24, sun2017labelandlearn pages 9-11, watson2023augmentedbehavioralannotation pages 10-12).This evolving landscape of behavioral evaluation interfaces illustrates that combining explainability, interactivity, and automation not only enhances the speed of data annotation but also enriches the overall process by enabling more targeted human intervention, improved model diagnostics, and iterative refinement. Such systems represent a critical shift in how ML models are developed and evaluated, fostering a deeper collaboration between computational algorithms and human expertise that is essential for the development of trustworthy and robust intelligent systems.

question: What is the difference between FMRI datasets and MRI datasets in terms of data analysis?

sections.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) are two essential neuroimaging modalities; however, they differ fundamentally in the type of information they provide and the corresponding data analysis methods required. Structural MRI, typically acquired as T1- or T2-weighted images, captures high-resolution anatomical details and is primarily used for evaluating morphology, volumetric measurements, and tissue segmentation. In contrast, fMRI datasets capture dynamic brain activity by measuring blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signals over time, reflecting the neural activity associated with cognitive, sensory, or motor tasks, or with intrinsic resting-state fluctuations. Given these fundamental differences in the nature of the signals, the data analysis pipelines for fMRI and MRI differ substantially from one another. This report provides a comprehensive overview of the distinctions in the analysis approaches applied to each modality.

The primary distinction between MRI and fMRI datasets lies in their inherent dimensionality and the qualities of the acquired signals. Structural MRI produces static, three-dimensional volumetric images that capture detailed anatomical properties. These datasets are characterized by high spatial resolution (typically around 1 mm isotropic) and are well suited for segmentation, cortical surface reconstruction, and morphometric analysis. Conversely, fMRI datasets comprise a temporal sequence of 3D volumes acquired at intervals determined by the repetition time (TR), which can range from 1 to 3 seconds or even shorter in specialized protocols. This results in four-dimensional datasets where the time series component is critical for detecting BOLD signal fluctuations related to neural activity (lv2018restingstatefunctionalmri pages 1-3). The dynamic nature of fMRI creates inherent challenges in both acquisition and subsequent analysis, including the necessity to account for temporal signal variability and physiological noise.

citations.title: Resting-state functional mri: everything that nonexperts have always wanted to know.

sections.text: Owing to the differences in data acquisition, the preprocessing steps for fMRI and MRI datasets differ markedly. MRI preprocessing generally focuses on correcting intensity nonuniformities, skull stripping, and image registration to standard anatomical templates (wakeman2015amultisubjectmultimodal pages 1-2). These steps aim to standardize the anatomical images, segment gray and white matter, and prepare the images for morphometric analyses. In contrast, fMRI preprocessing is considerably more complex due to the additional temporal dimension. For fMRI data, preprocessing typically involves:   Discarding initial volumes to allow for steady-state magnetization,   Correcting for slice-timing differences given that the slices within a single volume are not acquired simultaneously,   Realigning the time series to correct for head motion, which is a critical factor that affects signal quality and can vary across individuals,   Correcting for susceptibility-induced distortions that are particularly common in echo-planar imaging (EPI) sequences used in fMRI,   Co-registering functional images to high-resolution anatomical images (often T1-weighted) to ensure that the functional signals are accurately localized relative to brain structure,   Spatial normalization, which transforms the dataset into a common stereotactic space (such as MNI) for group analyses, and   Temporal filtering and regressing out confounding signals such as physiological noise components (e.g., those arising from respiration and cardiac pulsations) (nietocastanon2210preparingfmridata pages 1-4, esteban2019fmripreparobust pages 1-2).Thus, while both modalities require spatial normalization and alignment, the temporal corrections for fMRI—such as motion correction and slice timing—are unique to functional imaging and are essential for isolating the relatively low-amplitude BOLD response from competing sources of noise (adhikari2019arestingstate pages 2-3).

sections.text: The strategies used for statistical modeling also reflect the nature of each dataset. Structural MRI analysis is typically focused on quantifying static properties such as volumetric measurements, cortical thickness, and tissue contrasts. These analyses frequently employ voxel-based morphometry (VBM) or surface-based techniques to study anatomical variability across individuals or populations, sometimes relating anatomical differences to behavioral or clinical measures (snoek2021theamsterdamopen pages 29-33). Such analyses are generally robust to the absence of a temporal component.In contrast, fMRI analysis tackles the challenge of modeling temporal fluctuations. For task-based fMRI, the general linear model (GLM) is frequently applied to the preprocessed time series to relate changes in the BOLD signal to experimental stimuli or task-specific events. This requires modeling the hemodynamic response using basis functions (e.g., gamma variate functions) to account for the delay and dispersion associated with neurovascular coupling (esteban2020analysisoftaskbased pages 2-5). Furthermore, individual activations are often estimated as beta coefficients that quantify the strength of the association between task events and BOLD responses. For resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI), the focus is on extracting functional connectivity patterns by examining the correlation of BOLD signals across different brain regions. Here, methods such as principal component analysis (PCA), independent component analysis (ICA), and seed-based correlation analyses are employed to differentiate between true neural connectivity and noise (lv2018restingstatefunctionalmri pages 1-3, phinyomark2017restingstatefmrifunctional pages 1-2). The temporal nature of fMRI data also makes it susceptible to spurious correlations induced by head motion and physiological artifacts, leading to rigorous regressor and filtering strategies that are not necessary in the analysis of structural MRI datasets (nietocastanon2210preparingfmridata pages 4-6).

sections.text: fMRI data introduce challenges that require advanced analytical tools beyond traditional statistical modeling. One major issue is the presence of head motion, which can both corrupt the BOLD signal and introduce artificial correlations between regions. Robust motion correction algorithms and methods for censoring high-motion time points are standard in fMRI analysis pipelines. Moreover, modern approaches may incorporate multi-echo acquisitions that enable techniques such as multi-echo independent component analysis (ME-ICA) to separate BOLD-related signals from non-BOLD artifacts such as those due to motion or scanner instability (kundu2017multiechofmria pages 12-15, kundu2017multiechofmria pages 30-33). The use of ME-ICA can improve signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) and statistical power by distinguishing neural activity from artifacts based on the echo time dependence of the signal, which is a step not required in structural MRI analysis because such datasets are not designed to capture dynamic processes (kundu2017multiechofmria pages 30-33).Another challenge in fMRI analysis is managing physiological noise—such as fluctuations due to heartbeat and respiration—which interact with the low-frequency BOLD signal. To mitigate these effects, preprocessing pipelines include physiological noise regressors derived either from concurrent physiological monitoring or from data-driven approaches like anatomical CompCor, which extracts principal components from white matter and cerebrospinal fluid compartments (nietocastanon2210preparingfmridata pages 1-4). In addition, temporal filtering (e.g., band-pass filtering) is often applied to focus analyses on the frequency bands associated with neural activity (chen2018reproducibilityofr‐fmri pages 2-3). These preprocessing techniques underline the fact that fMRI data analysis must account simultaneously for both spatial and temporal sources of noise, whereas structural MRI analysis concentrates solely on spatial accuracy and artifact removal (adhikari2019arestingstate pages 1-2).

sections.text: Although fMRI and MRI analyses are distinct in many respects, the integration of structural and functional datasets is common in neuroimaging studies. High-resolution anatomical images from structural MRI are often used as a reference for fMRI data, providing a detailed map that helps spatially localize functional activations (wakeman2015amultisubjectmultimodal pages 1-2, hagler2019imageprocessingand pages 19-22). The anatomical images facilitate coregistration and spatial normalization of the fMRI time series to a standard space, enabling group-level analyses that require precise anatomical localization of functional signals. However, while the structural MRI information is used in the preprocessing of fMRI data (by providing a target for registration and segmentation), the analytical frameworks applied remain tailored to the specific properties of the dynamic BOLD data (nietocastanon2210preparingfmridata pages 6-9).

sections.text: Given the large size and high dimensionality of fMRI datasets, which can include hundreds of thousands of voxels sampled over hundreds of time points, dimensionality reduction is a crucial step in many analyses. Techniques such as PCA and ICA are routinely applied in fMRI analysis to reduce noise, extract meaningful functional components, and facilitate group comparisons by capturing task-related or intrinsic connectivity patterns (sen2018ageneralprediction pages 10-12, phinyomark2017restingstatefmrifunctional pages 12-13). These methods decompose the fMRI time series into a set of spatial maps and associated time courses, where each map represents a putative functional network. In contrast, structural MRI datasets do not require similar dimensionality reduction methods because they consist of a single volumetric image per subject, and the analysis focuses on spatial features rather than temporal dynamics (sen2018ageneralprediction pages 2-4).

sections.text: The increasing availability of large, multi-site fMRI datasets has necessitated the development of scalable processing frameworks that can handle the computational demands of analyzing high-dimensional temporal data. Distributed computing platforms such as Apache Spark and GPU acceleration are sometimes employed to process large-scale fMRI datasets efficiently, particularly for connectivity analyses or when developing machine learning models that require processing numerous participants (boubela2016bigdataapproaches pages 1-2, phinyomark2017restingstatefmrifunctional pages 2-3). In contrast, structural MRI analyses, while also benefiting from automation and scalability, typically do not require the same level of computational intensity as the analysis of fMRI data due to the absence of a temporal component and the lower dimensionality of the data (boubela2016bigdataapproaches pages 1-2).

sections.text: Beyond standard preprocessing and GLM-based analyses, fMRI data often support more advanced analytical techniques that are designed to capture the complexity of brain connectivity and function. For example, functional connectivity analyses incorporate graph theoretical measures to examine network properties such as global efficiency, clustering coefficients, and modularity, providing insights into the organization of brain networks in both health and disease (bae2018differencesbetweenschizophrenic pages 1-2). Moreover, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) are increasingly used in fMRI studies to decode cognitive states or compare brain representations with models including those derived from deep learning (chang2019bold5000apublic pages 1-3, esteban2020analysisoftaskbased pages 2-5). These methods heavily rely on the temporal structure of the fMRI data and exploit the rich dynamic nature of the acquired signals to infer functional architecture. Structural MRI analyses, by contrast, are generally confined to univariate or simpler multivariate models that do not engage with time-series dynamics (pinho2018individualbraincharting pages 1-2).

sections.text: The software landscape supporting fMRI data analysis is vast, with popular packages such as FSL, AFNI, SPM, and more recent standardized pipelines like fMRIPrep designed to ensure reproducibility and robustness in preprocessing (esteban2019fmripreparobust pages 2-3, bowring2019exploringtheimpact pages 2-3). fMRIPrep, for instance, integrates tools from multiple neuroimaging software packages to produce preprocessed fMRI data along with detailed confound regressors, thereby accommodating the considerable variability inherent in multi-site fMRI datasets. Each of these tools incorporates specialized steps for time-series analysis, motion correction, and artifact regression that are specifically tailored to overcome the challenges posed by the BOLD signal’s temporal variability (esteban2020analysisoftaskbased pages 2-5). In contrast, the analysis of structural MRI data is more standardized, with pipelines largely focused on segmentation, cortical surface reconstruction, and spatial normalization without requiring the complexities of temporal modeling (hagler2019imageprocessingand pages 19-22).

sections.text: The differences between fMRI and MRI data analyses are particularly evident in studies of clinical populations versus healthy controls. For example, in autism spectrum disorder research, fMRI data are often analyzed using sophisticated machine learning techniques that incorporate feature extraction from the BOLD time series, connectivity patterns, and network dynamics to classify patient groups; such analyses exploit the functional nature of the data and require careful handling of multi-site variability and confounding factors (liu2021autismspectrumdisorder pages 1-2). In contrast, structural MRI studies may rely on volumetric or morphometric measures to detect anatomical differences, which are inherently less sensitive to the temporal dynamics crucial for understanding functional aberrations (sen2018ageneralprediction pages 2-4). Similarly, studies investigating psychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia have utilized fMRI to derive global and local network connectivity features, enabling the differentiation between patient groups and healthy controls based on dynamic brain activity patterns (bae2018differencesbetweenschizophrenic pages 1-2). These applications underscore the need for tailored analysis pipelines that address the unique challenges of fMRI data processing while benefiting from the spatial reference provided by structural MRI data (adhikari2019arestingstate pages 2-3).

sections.text: Despite the distinct analysis pipelines for fMRI and MRI, multimodal analysis that integrates both structural and functional information is increasingly common. Structural MRI provides an anatomical scaffold that enhances the interpretability of functional activations by offering precise localization of BOLD signals. For instance, the co-registration of fMRI data to high-resolution T1-weighted images enables researchers to map functional responses onto detailed cortical surfaces, thereby linking neural dynamics to specific brain regions and structural features that may be altered in disease states (hagler2019imageprocessingand pages 25-28, nastase2021the“narratives”fmri pages 6-7). However, even in multimodal analyses, the processing requirements remain distinct: while structural MRI analysis emphasizes steady-state, high-resolution anatomical features, fMRI analysis demands dynamic temporal modeling and artifact correction to accurately capture neural activity (adhikari2019arestingstate pages 1-2, nietocastanon2210preparingfmridata pages 6-9).
