sections.text: Reproducibility in neuroimaging research has been a major concern, especially for fMRI studies where analysis pipelines may differ substantially across research groups. Standardized pipelines such as fMRIPrep have been developed to minimize methodological variability by applying a consistent set of preprocessing steps to diverse fMRI datasets, thereby improving comparability between studies (esteban2019fmripreparobust pages 2-3, bowring2022isolatingthesources pages 4-6). In contrast, structural MRI studies have traditionally enjoyed a higher level of standardization thanks to well-established protocols for segmentation and normalization. This difference is rooted in the dynamic nature of fMRI data, which necessitates not only the correction of spatial distortions but also the accurate modeling of temporal fluctuations that could otherwise compromise the validity of statistical inferences (nietocastanon2210preparingfmridata pages 1-4).

sections.text: One of the most innovative aspects of modern fMRI analysis is the use of advanced denoising techniques. Methods such as multi-echo fMRI combined with independent component analysis (ME-ICA) selectively remove non-BOLD noise components based on their unique echo time dependencies. This refinement increases the fidelity of the extracted neural signal and mitigates the adverse effects of head motion and physiological fluctuations (kundu2017multiechofmria pages 12-15). Although similar correction procedures are not required in structural MRI analysis, the successful implementation of these fMRI denoising strategies has dramatically advanced the sensitivity of functional connectivity studies and task-based activation maps (kundu2017multiechofmria pages 30-33).

sections.text: The dynamic characteristics of fMRI data facilitate the application of network-based analytical techniques that probe the brain’s functional architecture. In task-based as well as resting-state fMRI studies, methods including graph theoretical analyses, clustering, and even topological data analysis (TDA) are employed to map the intricate connectivity patterns across brain regions (phinyomark2017restingstatefmrifunctional pages 12-13). TDA, in particular, offers a novel framework to capture the shape of high-dimensional fMRI data, providing insights that would be obscured by traditional linear approaches. Such methods are not applicable to structural MRI data, where the focus is on static anatomical features rather than on inter-regional connectivity dynamics (phinyomark2017restingstatefmrifunctional pages 2-3).

In these studies, the emphasis is on establishing reliable functional territories within a single brain rather than relying solely on group-level effects. Although structural MRI is also employed in these studies for anatomical segmentation and normalization, its analysis remains focused on identifying static patterns of brain morphology rather than on the dynamic interplay of neural networks captured in fMRI data (pinho2018individualbraincharting pages 1-2).

sections.text: In clinical and translational neuroimaging, the dynamic functional data offered by fMRI are often used to understand underlying pathophysiological mechanisms in neuropsychiatric conditions such as schizophrenia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and autism spectrum disorders (liu2021autismspectrumdisorder pages 1-2). In these instances, the analysis of fMRI data involves characterizing aberrant functional connectivity and altered network dynamics, which can serve as biomarkers for diagnosis and treatment response (bae2018differencesbetweenschizophrenic pages 1-2). Structural MRI provides complementary information, enabling the measurement of volumetric changes or atypical morphometric patterns. However, the analytic challenges in fMRI—stemming from the need to resolve temporal fluctuations and control for confounding influences like head motion—demand more advanced statistical tools and robust preprocessing protocols than those required for pure anatomical assessments (sen2018ageneralprediction pages 2-4).

sections.text: Large-scale fMRI datasets, aggregated across sites and populations, present the opportunity to study brain function with unprecedented statistical power. Such studies, however, must contend with variability in acquisition protocols, scanner types, and preprocessing pipelines. Harmonization methods—both in terms of data acquisition and preprocessing—have been developed to achieve reliable pooling across diverse cohorts, an issue less critical for structural MRI datasets that are inherently more consistent in their anatomical contrast (adhikari2019arestingstate pages 2-3, snoek2021theamsterdamopen pages 29-33). In these multisite studies, the unique challenges of fMRI data deepen the need for standardized preprocessing protocols, noise correction strategies, and post hoc statistical adjustments, thereby underscoring the fundamental differences in data analysis between the two modalities.

sections.text: In summary, the primary differences between fMRI and MRI datasets in data analysis can be delineated as follows:   fMRI datasets are dynamic, capturing time series of BOLD signals that necessitate extensive temporal preprocessing (e.g., slice timing correction, motion correction, physiological noise regression, and temporal filtering) in addition to spatial normalization and registration (nietocastanon2210preparingfmridata pages 1-4, esteban2019fmripreparobust pages 1-2). Structural MRI datasets, on the other hand, provide static high-resolution anatomical images and focus on spatial processing tasks such as brain extraction, segmentation, and registration to standard space (wakeman2015amultisubjectmultimodal pages 1-2, hagler2019imageprocessingand pages 19-22).   Statistical modeling in fMRI data analysis often involves the use of GLM frameworks to model task-related hemodynamic responses or correlation analyses to quantify functional connectivity. In contrast, structural MRI analyses rely on voxel-based morphometry, cortical thickness assessments, and other spatial analyses that do not engage temporal dynamics (esteban2020analysisoftaskbased pages 2-5, snoek2021theamsterdamopen pages 29-33).   Advanced denoising and dimensionality reduction techniques such as ME-ICA, PCA, and ICA are integral to fMRI analysis in order to separate neural signals from motion and physiological artifacts, a step unnecessary for structural MRI (kundu2017multiechofmria pages 12-15, kundu2017multiechofmria pages 30-33).   fMRI analysis pipelines must also account for high inter- and intra-subject variability related to dynamic functional activity; as a result, reproducibility and standardization have driven the development of robust preprocessing pipelines like fMRIPrep. By contrast, structural MRI data, being more stable over time, involve relatively straightforward preprocessing focused on spatial quality control (esteban2019fmripreparobust pages 2-3, bowring2022isolatingthesources pages 4-6).

sections.text: The differences between fMRI and MRI datasets are rooted in the distinct purposes and modalities of the acquired data. fMRI datasets, whether task-based or resting-state, require elaborate preprocessing workflows to manage temporal dynamics, residual motion, and physiological noise. Their analysis involves statistical modeling methods designed to capture the temporal evolution of the BOLD signal and infer functional connectivity and activation patterns. Conversely, structural MRI datasets are analyzed as static anatomical images, employing methods geared toward segmentation, volumetry, and morphological analysis. While both modalities are often integrated to provide a comprehensive picture of brain structure and function, each requires distinct analytical techniques and processing pipelines reflective of its unique characteristics. As neuroimaging research continues to push the boundaries of data integration and high-throughput analysis, understanding these differences remains crucial for developing reproducible and reliable neuroscientific findings (adhikari2019arestingstate pages 1-2, nietocastanon2210preparingfmridata pages 6-9, phinyomark2017restingstatefmrifunctional pages 1-2).This detailed report has highlighted both the theoretical and practical aspects of analyzing fMRI versus MRI datasets, covering acquisition, preprocessing, statistical modeling, and advanced computational techniques. Each stage of the processing pipeline for fMRI data is designed to address the inherent challenges of dynamic signal fluctuations and to extract meaningful neural correlates, while MRI data analysis leverages the consistency of static images to deliver precise anatomical measurements. Through the use of standardized processing pipelines and advanced denoising methods, researchers can better harness the strengths of each modality, ultimately advancing our understanding of both the structure and function of the human brain (lv2018restingstatefunctionalmri pages 1-3, sen2018ageneralprediction pages 10-12, hagler2019imageprocessingand pages 22-25).

question: What are the main challenges in adapting transformer-based models for tabular data representation?

sections.text: This report examines the primary challenges in adapting transformer‐based models for tabular data representation. Although transformers have achieved remarkable success in natural language processing (NLP) and vision tasks, their direct application to tabular data entails numerous challenges related to data heterogeneity, input preprocessing, computational efficiency, robustness and interpretability, and the incorporation of domain‐specific knowledge.

Transformer models—originally designed to process sequential tokens with positional encodings—must be significantly modified to adequately capture the structure inherent in tabular data. Unlike text or images, tables possess two‐dimensional structures characterized by rows, columns, headers, and cells. This distinct organization necessitates new approaches not only to data serialization and embedding design but also to the integration of attention mechanisms that can capture both intra‐row (sample) and inter‐column relationships. In this paper, we focus on the multifaceted challenges in effectively adapting transformer architectures—from input representation to training paradigms—to realize robust and generalizable models for tabular data tasks (badaro2022transformersfortabular pages 481-482, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 1-3).

sections.text: Tabular data are intrinsically heterogeneous. They typically comprise numerical, categorical, ordinal, binary, and sometimes even textual elements, each with distinct statistical properties and distributions. Unlike homogeneously structured data in NLP (sequences of words) or vision (arrays of pixels), tabular data require the simultaneous handling of multiple data types. In traditional deep learning models, numerical features are often fed directly into fully connected architectures after normalization while categorical features are encoded using one-hot, label, or learned embeddings. However, transformer models rely on high-dimensional token embeddings and attention mechanisms, which necessitate more sophisticated embedding strategies. For example, current approaches frequently utilize simple parametric mappings for numerical data, for which richer alternatives like piecewise linear encodings or periodic activation functions may yield more expressive representations (gorishniy2022onembeddingsfor pages 1-2, huang2020tabtransformertabulardata pages 1-2).  Moreover, categorical variables—often characterized by high cardinality and sparse distributions—require careful handling to avoid introducing artificial orderings or excessive dimensionality via one-hot encodings. The ambiguity in representing categorical information can lead to a suboptimal capture of the inter-feature relationships critical to downstream tabular tasks. Some studies have proposed using contextualized embeddings derived from attention mechanisms that incorporate column names, metadata, and cell-level context; nevertheless, designing these embeddings in a manner that preserves and highlights relevant information remains an open research challenge (badaro2022transformersfortabular pages 482-483, somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 16-18).

sections.text: One of the most fundamental challenges in adapting transformers for tabular data is overcoming the structural mismatch between the two-dimensional layout of tables and the one-dimensional sequential input that transformers are designed to process. In NLP, the ordering of tokens is essential and is encoded via absolute or relative positional encodings. In contrast, tabular data are inherently permutation invariant with regard to row order and exhibit a two-dimensional structure that is not naturally sequential. Consequently, traditional positional encodings can inadvertently introduce spurious order biases. For instance, concatenating rows or flattening a table into a single sequence may lead a transformer to rely on artificial ordering cues rather than the true semantic content of the cells (ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 22-24, yang2022tableformerrobusttransformer pages 1-2). Several approaches have been proposed to mitigate this issue. Some methods adjust the transformer’s positional embeddings to encode column and row identities separately, while others propose architectural changes that use separate self-attention modules for rows and columns or introduce structured attention biases that capture the two-dimensional layout directly (ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 24-27, yang2022tableformerrobusttransformer pages 9-10). Another strategy is to employ content snapshots or localized tokenization schemes that focus on the most relevant rows or cells for a given task, thereby reducing the sequence length and preserving structural integrity (thai2105tabbiepretrainedrepresentations pages 1-2, yin2005tabertpretrainingfor pages 2-3). Despite these innovations, finding universally optimal serialization methods remains challenging because the ideal representation may depend on the specific downstream task as well as the inherent variability in table size, density, and feature types (padhi2021tabulartransformersfor pages 1-2).

sections.text: Transformer-based models are known for their high computational cost due to the quadratic complexity of the self-attention mechanism. When applied to tabular data, this computational burden is often exacerbated because the necessary adaptations (e.g., extended input sequences due to table serialization, additional embedding layers for heterogeneous features, or dual transformer modules for rows and columns) further increase the number of parameters and operations required. This becomes particularly problematic when scaling the models to large tabular datasets, such as those encountered in healthcare or financial applications (wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 1-3, somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 3-5). Additionally, training transformer models on tabular data faces challenges related to data quality and quantity. Tabular datasets frequently suffer from missing values, outliers, and high dimensionality relative to the number of samples. These issues necessitate careful preprocessing, augmented by techniques such as data imputation, feature selection, or even specialized regularization strategies. Moreover, because many tabular datasets are relatively small compared to the massive corpora available for NLP pretraining, transformer models may not sufficiently generalize unless pretraining techniques such as self-supervised learning, masked token prediction, or contrastive learning are employed. Although these methods have increased sample efficiency and improved downstream performance, they also introduce additional hyperparameters and potential for overfitting (borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 16-17, somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 12-14). Furthermore, models such as TransTab utilize innovative training objectives like vertical partition contrastive learning to address the variable structure of tables and leverage self-supervision across multiple datasets. However, these pretraining schemes require substantial computational resources, are sensitive to hyperparameter selection, and may not transfer easily across domains with diverse table schemas (wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 13-16, yin2005tabertpretrainingfor pages 8-9).

sections.text: Robust representation learning for tabular data is particularly challenging given the sensitivity of transformer models to input ordering and structure. Many existing transformer-based approaches that linearize tables are prone to performance degradation when the order of rows or columns is perturbed. In scenarios where tabular data are rearranged—intentionally (to test model robustness) or unintentionally (due to data preprocessing steps)—models may make inconsistent predictions if they over-rely on the imposed sequential structure rather than on intrinsic feature relationships (yang2022tableformerrobusttransformer pages 1-2, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 36-39). One proposed remedy involves designing models that leverage learnable structural biases to provide order invariance. For instance, TABLEFORMER introduces learnable attention biases that capture the two-dimensional structure of tables without relying on absolute order. Such methods improve robustness by ensuring that the model’s predictions are invariant to row or column permutations, a property crucial for practical applications where table order may vary dynamically (yang2022tableformerrobusttransformer pages 9-10, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 29-31). Nonetheless, achieving this invariance while maintaining high capacity for modeling complex interactions among features is nontrivial, since overly restricting attention patterns can lead to loss of relevant information and diminished performance (ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 27-29).

sections.text: Another significant challenge is the need to balance model complexity with interpretability and the effective selection of relevant features. Transformer-based models, by design, incorporate numerous layers of attention and non-linear transformations, which can render them opaque and difficult to interpret. In contrast, classical methods such as gradient boosting decision trees are valued for their transparency and ease of interpretation. Interpreting model decisions in a transformer not only involves deciphering the learned embeddings but also understanding the contributions of individual attention heads and layers, particularly when these models are applied to data where a single feature may strongly influence predictions (somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 27-28, borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 3-4). Furthermore, tabular data are susceptible to feature noise and correlate in complex ways that require dynamic, instance-specific feature selection. Recent architectures like SAINT and FT-Transformer introduce intra-sample attention to selectively focus on critical features of each data point, and some models even incorporate intersample attention to leverage similarities among samples. While these mechanisms enhance predictive performance, they also add layers of complexity and computational overhead, thereby complicating model tuning and interpretability (somepalli2021saintimprovedneural pages 1-2, somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 5-7). The challenge is compounded when the transformer must make use of both categorical and continuous features simultaneously. Each feature type requires distinct treatment: categorical variables call for embedding techniques that capture semantic similarity, while continuous variables benefit from scaling and possibly dedicated embedding functions that capture fine-grained numerical distinctions. The differing characteristics of these data types mean that a one-size-fits-all embedding strategy is rarely effective. Hybrid solutions that combine specialized encoders for different feature types with a joint attention mechanism across all features represent promising avenues but remain challenging to design and evaluate comprehensively (badaro2022transformersfortabular pages 482-483, gorishniy2022onembeddingsfor pages 1-2).

sections.text: Real-world tabular datasets are often fraught with various data quality issues. Missing values, outliers, and inconsistent data entries can distort the training process and lead to unreliable predictions. While classical models are frequently engineered to handle these issues internally, deep learning models, including transformers, typically rely on preprocessing pipelines to fill in missing data or eliminate noise. However, such preprocessing can be lossy or introduce its own biases, thereby complicating the learning process (borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 16-17, somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 18-21). Moreover, the process of serializing a table—transforming its inherently two-dimensional structure into a one-dimensional sequence—often involves truncation or filtering steps that may remove important contextual information. Methods such as sampling content snapshots or sliding windows attempt to reduce sequence length while preserving essential relational data, but they invariably represent a trade-off between computational feasibility and completeness of the representation (huan2020tabtransformertabulardata pages 2-3, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 3-4). Developing robust preprocessing and filtration strategies that can adapt to varying data quality across tasks remains an active area of research.

sections.text: Given that large-scale labeled tabular datasets are less common than massive text or image corpora, self-supervised and semi-supervised learning have emerged as critical strategies in transformer-based tabular modeling. Techniques such as masked token prediction, replaced token detection, and contrastive learning are being adapted to learn robust representations from unlabeled or partially labeled tables. However, designing effective self-supervised objectives that capture the nuances of tabular structure—such as the relationships between column headers and cell values, or the interdependencies among rows—poses considerable challenges (yin2005tabertpretrainingfor pages 2-3, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 17-19). For example, in approaches like TABERT, content snapshots are used to integrate salient row information with textual queries, requiring a delicate balance between capturing sufficient context and keeping the input sequence within manageable lengths. Similarly, vertical partition contrastive learning in models like TransTab attempts to leverage the column-oriented nature of databases for pretraining, but such methods are highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices and can be computationally expensive (wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 4-6, yin2005tabertpretrainingfor pages 8-9).

sections.text: Another pressing challenge in this domain is the need for models to generalize across tables with different schemas and varying numbers of features. Unlike language models that are pretrained on nearly homogeneous data, tabular models must handle variable numbers of columns, differing column names, and inconsistent feature sets across datasets, which makes transfer learning and zero-shot inference strategies particularly difficult. Approaches such as TransTab propose methods to relax the fixed-table assumption by encoding column descriptions and cell values jointly, enabling transfer across tables with non-matching schemas (wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 3-4, wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 9-11). The challenge lies in capturing the semantic equivalence between columns across different tables (e.g., “age” in one dataset may appear as “years” in another) while preserving fine-grained numerical differences. This problem is compounded by privacy concerns and domain-specific variations, which necessitate robust generalization strategies that can work well even on unseen or sparsely related tables. Models must adapt to incremental feature learning, where new columns emerge over time, and maintain performance without exhaustive retraining (wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 13-16, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 29-31).

sections.text: Interpretability is another significant challenge when deploying transformer-based models in settings where decisions must be explainable—for instance, in healthcare or finance. While attention weights can be inspected to gain insight into model behavior, the sheer complexity and depth of transformer architectures often obscure the relationships between input features and output predictions. This challenge is amplified due to the fusion of various data types and the use of multiple specialized embedding strategies, which together create a “black box” effect (borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 3-4, somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 27-28). Furthermore, ensuring fairness and mitigating biases inherited from the training data remain paramount. With textual and numerical biases potentially compounded by the model’s internal representation of heterogeneous features, robust interpretability tools and counterfactual reasoning mechanisms are needed to establish trust and transparency (ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 31-34, borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 6-7).

sections.text: Beyond academic interest, transformer-based models for tabular data must meet practical deployment constraints. In many industrial scenarios, real-time inference and resource efficiency are as important as predictive performance. The complexity of transformer architectures often necessitates powerful hardware and extensive tuning, which can preclude their adoption in resource-constrained environments such as mobile devices or embedded systems (ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 34-36, wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 1-3). Hybrid approaches that combine the representation power of transformers with the efficiency of tree-based models or shallow neural networks have been explored, yet these methods still face trade-offs between accuracy, computational cost, and latency. Achieving a favorable balance near the “sweet spot” for both performance and resource efficiency is a major engineering and research challenge (somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 25-27, borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 7-8).

sections.text: The challenges outlined above suggest that adapting transformer-based models for tabular data representation requires a multi-pronged strategy that addresses both the unique structural characteristics of tables and the computational and practical considerations of deep learning. Key areas for future research include: – Developing advanced embedding strategies that maintain the richness of heterogeneous feature types while remaining computationally tractable (gorishniy2022onembeddingsfor pages 1-2, huang2020tabtransformertabulardata pages 1-2). – Designing structural inductive biases and specialized positional encodings that eliminate spurious order effects and better reflect the two-dimensional nature of tables (ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 22-24, yang2022tableformerrobusttransformer pages 1-2). – Innovating self-supervised pretraining schemes and contrastive learning objectives that can exploit the unlabeled data common in tabular domains without incurring excessive computational overhead (yin2005tabertpretrainingfor pages 8-9, wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 4-6). – Integrating robust preprocessing pipelines and noise-handling mechanisms so that models can effectively operate on real-world, low-quality tabular data (borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 16-17, somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 18-21). – Striving for interpretability and transparency in model predictions, potentially through attention visualization, instance-wise feature selection, and hybrid schemes that fuse transformer outputs with more transparent model components (somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 27-28, borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 3-4). – Pursuing scalable architectures and transfer learning methods to handle variable table schemas and continuously evolving datasets in practical applications (wang2022transtablearningtransferable pages 3-4, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 29-31).

sections.text: Transformer-based models for tabular data representation hold significant promise in bridging the gap between deep learning and structured data tasks. However, a successful adaptation of these architectures must surmount a host of challenges arising from data heterogeneity, structural mismatch, computational demands, robustness to ordering perturbations, and interpretability concerns. Addressing these challenges involves concerted efforts in designing new embedding strategies, rethinking data serialization methods, and devising self-supervised learning objectives that are tailored to the distinctive characteristics of tabular data. In addition, practical deployment considerations such as computational efficiency, scalability, and transparency remain critical to the deployment of these models in industry settings. Continued research in these domains will not only advance the state-of-the-art in deep tabular learning but may also lead to hybrid models that integrate the strengths of transformers with traditional methods in order to achieve robust, interpretable, and efficient performance across a variety of applications (badaro2022transformersfortabular pages 481-482, ruan2024languagemodelingon pages 36-39, somvanshi2024asurveyon pages 28-30). Overall, while significant progress has been made in adapting transformer architectures to the structured nature of tabular data, the challenges outlined above underscore the need for further research and engineering innovations. Achieving success in this domain could transform applications in many fields – from healthcare and finance to recommendation systems – where the ability to effectively model tabular data is critical for informed decision-making (padhi2021tabulartransformersfor pages 1-2, borisov2024deepneuralnetworks pages 5-6, huang2020tabtransformertabulardata pages 7-8). This report has provided a comprehensive overview of the major challenges, backed by empirical and theoretical insights from recent literature. Future work that addresses these issues holistically is expected to push the boundaries of what transformer-based approaches can achieve when applied to tabular data representation.

question: What are some systems papers that conduct an observational study as the formative study instead of just interviews?

sections.text: This report examines several systems papers that employ observational studies as the formative research method rather than relying solely on interviews. In systems research, formative studies are essential for understanding operational dynamics, user interactions, and contextual variables that can be difficult to capture through self‐report or retrospective interviews alone. By embedding direct observation into the formative phase, researchers can gain granular insights into behaviors, technological interactions, and process flows across diverse application domains. This report surveys examples from digital health, clinical regulation, educational innovation, and community-based public health initiatives, illustrating the breadth of observational formative research in system-level studies.

The evaluation of complex systems—whether in health care, education, or public safety—often requires formative research that captures real-time data on processes, interactions, and user behaviors. Formative studies using observational methodologies have been increasingly recognized as fundamental to systems research because they provide concrete evidence of how interventions operate in practice. Observational studies are characterized by the direct measurement of actions and events, often using structured rating scales, checklists, or time‐and‐motion analyses that yield both quantitative and qualitative data. Unlike interview-based approaches that depend on verbal self-reports subject to recall bias and social desirability, observational studies offer contextualized insights critical to the iterative design and refinement of systems. This report reviews a selection of systems papers that integrate observational methods as a core formative research strategy.

Observational studies in digital health systems have provided robust evidence regarding the usability, utility, and integration of innovative technologies into clinical workflows. For instance, in the field of eHealth for patients with Parkinson’s disease, Bendig et al. conducted a mixed methods usability study where participants interacted with three different eHealth solutions—a 3D-camera system, wearable sensors, and a tablet application. The study intentionally combined rater-based evaluations of task performance with subjective measures, demonstrating that observational methods were more sensitive in detecting usability differences than standard self-report questionnaires alone (bendig2022measuringtheusability pages 2-3). The emphasis on direct observation allowed the researchers to capture real-world interactions with the technology, providing actionable insights for iterative system design.Another example is provided by Kannampallil et al., who executed an observational formative evaluation of a virtual voice-based coach deployed as an Alexa skill. In this study, 26 participants participated in actual therapy sessions with the system while their interactions were logged in detail. The study used both quantitative workload and usability measures as well as qualitative interviews; however, the formative aspect was driven by careful observation of user behavior during system use rather than mere retrospective interview data (kannampallil2022designandformative pages 1-2). Such an approach not only enabled the identification of usability issues such as temporal workload during problem-solving sessions but also highlighted clinical challenges that might remain undetected in an interview-only paradigm.Scheder-Bieschin et al. extend this approach to the emergency department setting with their mixed methods pilot observational study of an artificial intelligence symptom-taking tool. Rather than relying solely on interviews with staff and patients, the formative evaluation method integrated real-world observational data from patient-tool interactions. This enabled assessment of nuanced changes in patient-physician conversation dynamics and facilitated iterative design improvements based on in situ experiences, demonstrating the importance of observation in validating the system’s impact within a fast-paced clinical environment (schederbieschin2022improvingemergencydepartment pages 1-2).

sections.text: Formative evaluations in regulated healthcare systems have also benefited from observational methods. In a study by Stoopendaal, de Bree, and Robben, the concept of System-Based Regulation (SBR) was evaluated using mixed methods that involved sustained participant observation during trial inspections. Observers followed inspection teams for extensive periods, gathering thick descriptive data that illuminated the interplay between regulatory processes and organizational self-regulation. The observational data were crucial to understanding how quality and safety management systems operated in practice, thereby informing the iterative refinement of the SBR framework (stoopendaal2016reconceptualizingregulationformative pages 3-5).The same group further illustrated the value of observation by complementing interview data with structured inspection observations. For example, while several interviews were conducted with quality managers and clinical staff, the evaluators also performed on-site ‘reality checks’ during inspections. This dual method approach provided a comprehensive view of the organization’s quality and safety systems, capturing both self-reported practices and observable behaviors such as adherence to protocols and document verifications (stoopendaal2016reconceptualizingregulationformative pages 5-7, stoopendaal2016reconceptualizingregulationformative pages 7-10). By integrating formative observational data, the evaluators could precisely map the maturity of quality and safety management systems within healthcare organizations, thus supporting targeted enhancements in regulation and enforcement.

sections.text: The domain of higher education has also embraced structured formative observational studies to assess and improve teaching practices. Yee et al. conducted a study focused on formative feedback to novice university mathematics instructors using a structured observation protocol. In this study, experienced graduate student instructors observed classroom teaching using a Red-Yellow-Green (RYG) feedback system. The direct and repeated observations allowed for a longitudinal tracking of pedagogical improvements rather than relying solely on instructors’ self-assessments or interviews (yee2022bridgingthegap pages 1-3). This observational approach provided tangible evidence of teaching practice changes and informed the development of more context-specific faculty development strategies.Similarly, Drew et al. examined peer observation processes in higher education through their Peer Assisted Teaching Scheme (PATS). This study analyzed approximately 71 teaching observations gathered via structured instruments and freeform notes. The researchers found that when observers used developmental prompts during classroom visits, the resulting observational data offered critical formative feedback that helped align instructional practices with teachers’ developmental goals. The combination of structured observation data, checklists, and reflective comments provided a more robust formative assessment compared to relying solely on post-observation interviews (drew2017formativeobservationof pages 1-3, drew2017formativeobservationof pages 6-7, drew2017formativeobservationof pages 7-10). This work underscores the importance of observational methodologies in capturing subtle instructional dynamics and guiding teacher professional development in a systematic fashion.Lyon et al. also contribute to the educational literature with the development of an observation protocol—the High-Impact Classroom Assessment Practices (HI-CAP) Observation Protocol. Their work systematically measured formative assessment practices by directly observing classroom interactions via video recordings and independent rater evaluations. Their methodology involved extensive training and calibration of observers, with observational data serving as the primary formative evidence for scoring the implementation quality of formative assessment practices. Compared to traditional interview approaches that might not capture the granular dynamics of classroom interaction, the direct observation protocol provided high-resolution data that could be quantified and directly linked to teaching practices (lyon2020aformativeassessment pages 1-4, lyon2020aformativeassessment pages 7-9, lyon2020aformativeassessment pages 11-13, lyon2020aformativeassessment pages 24-25).

sections.text: Observational research has long been central to ethnographic methods, which are frequently applied in community health and public service contexts. Alcorn et al. provide an example of formative ethnographic research that employed observational methods to assess the use and impact of a novel kiosk-based water system in Ghana. By embedding a researcher within the community and observing household water-collection practices, the study revealed complex behaviors—such as the simultaneous use of multiple water sources—that would have been difficult to capture via interviews alone. This immersive observational approach provided robust formative insights that informed later quantitative household surveys and intervention design (alcorn2011formativeethnographicresearch pages 1-2, alcorn2011formativeethnographicresearch pages 2-4).Andreassen and Malling further explored formative assessment in clinical settings among junior doctors by adopting focused ethnography that included passive participant observation. Their study demonstrated that even subtle forms of everyday resistance to formative assessments could be captured by systematic observation. This methodological choice offered richer context in terms of power dynamics and organizational culture than would have been possible by relying solely on interviews (andreassen2019howareformative pages 1-2).

sections.text: Observational techniques combined with other evaluative methods have also proven fruitful in assessing complex health improvement initiatives. Odendaal, Atkins, and Lewin present several formative evaluations that integrate structured observations—such as time-and-motion studies—with qualitative interviews and diary methods to capture the multifaceted nature of public health programs in South Africa. Their work on community-based lay health worker programs utilized these observational methods to gain insights into process implementation, client interactions, and logistical challenges that interview data alone could not elucidate (odendaal2016multipleandmixed pages 1-2, odendaal2016multipleandmixed pages 2-4, odendaal2016multipleandmixed pages 5-6, odendaal2016multipleandmixed pages 7-8). This comprehensive mixed-methods strategy enhances the overall formative evaluation by triangulating findings across diverse data sources, thereby offering a more complete picture of system dynamics in public health interventions.Observational findings in such studies often reveal discrepancies between self-reported and actual practices. For instance, during structured observations, evaluators in the Odendaal et al. study noted that lay health workers sometimes deviated from prescribed protocols during client visits. This nuance, only identifiable through real-time observation, was critical for refining training protocols and operational guidelines for the program. Additionally, the use of time-and-motion data provided objective measures of workflow efficiency, directly informing program adjustments to improve client service delivery.

sections.text: Observational research methods have also been instrumental in broader implementation science endeavors. Scott et al. describe a formative evaluation approach within the SCALE community health improvement initiative that integrates an Inquiry–Observation–Reflection (IOR) framework. This framework underscores the value of systematic observation combined with inquiry and reflective practices to generate real-time feedback. For example, evaluators used structured observation during capacity-building events, capturing data that subsequently informed modifications to training sessions, webinars, and technical assistance strategies. By using observational evidence alongside other evaluative approaches, the study was able to pinpoint specific barriers and enablers in real-world implementation, thus supporting continuous system learning and improvement (scott2020formativeevaluationand pages 10-13, scott2020formativeevaluationand pages 3-5, scott2020formativeevaluationand pages 8-10).Moreover, additional research by Scott et al. highlights how the systematic incorporation of observational data—such as usage metrics and real-time feedback from capacity-building settings—can drive iterative adaptations in complex community interventions. These findings further demonstrate that observational formative research is not only feasible in large-scale system initiatives but is also vital for understanding dynamic, multi-level interactions within diverse community settings (scott2020formativeevaluationand pages 17-18, scott2020formativeevaluationand pages 8-10).

sections.text: Mobile learning environments have also benefited from observational formative research. Hwang’s formative assessment design studies for PDA-integrated ecology observations demonstrated the value of embedding observation within technology-enhanced learning systems. Hwang’s work used a variety of observational methods—including paper prototyping, diary studies, and real-time performance tracking—to gauge user interaction with mobile applications in authentic settings. By tracking system usage logs and user behaviors, these studies identified critical issues such as task sequence difficulties, interface problems, and contextual mismatches that would have been undetected if only interviews were used. Instead, the direct observation of learners’ interaction with the mobile system provided empirical data to guide iterative refinements in interface design and functionality (hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 106-108, hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 122-123, hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 26-28).Further studies by Hwang, detailed across multiple sections, illustrate a robust formative design process. This process included observational diary studies and real-time demonstration of system interactions that provided precise behavioral data, enabling the researchers to optimize learning schedules, context filters, and system responsiveness. The iterative nature of this observational formative research ultimately contributed to improved system design and better learner outcomes by grounding design changes in observed user behavior rather than retrospective interviews (hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 35-38, hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 38-39, hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 46-48, hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 48-50, hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 53-56).

sections.text: Together, the systems papers reviewed here illustrate a common trend: formative observational studies provide a depth of insight that is essential for refining complex systems. In digital health and eHealth, observational evaluations expose usability issues and clinical workflow challenges by capturing authentic user interactions with technology (bendig2022measuringtheusability pages 2-3, kannampallil2022designandformative pages 1-2, schederbieschin2022improvingemergencydepartment pages 1-2). In regulated clinical settings, observational methods complement interview data by providing real-time process evaluations that reveal the intricacies of quality and safety practices (stoopendaal2016reconceptualizingregulationformative pages 3-5, stoopendaal2016reconceptualizingregulationformative pages 5-7). Educational environments have similarly benefited from observational approaches, as seen in studies of teacher professional development and formative assessment, where classroom observations link directly to instructional improvements (yee2022bridgingthegap pages 1-3, drew2017formativeobservationof pages 1-3, lyon2020aformativeassessment pages 1-4). Furthermore, community-based health interventions and ethnographic studies leverage observational data to capture the complexities of social behavior and environmental context (alcorn2011formativeethnographicresearch pages 1-2, alcorn2011formativeethnographicresearch pages 2-4, andreassen2019howareformative pages 1-2). Finally, in the field of mobile and context-aware learning, a series of observational formative studies has demonstrated how direct measurement of user behavior and performance in natural settings is crucial for effective design and iteration (hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 106-108, hwang2010formativeassessmentdesign pages 122-123).The integration of observational methods across these domains demonstrates that systems research benefits greatly from data that capture real-time, in situ behavior. In many cases, observation has been paired with other techniques, such as interviews, surveys, and diary studies, to triangulate findings and enhance the overall validity of formative evaluations. In particular, the explicit use of structured observation and time-and-motion analyses in public health settings (odendaal2016multipleandmixed pages 1-2, odendaal2016multipleandmixed pages 2-4) and in clinical regulatory research (stoopendaal2016reconceptualizingregulationformative pages 7-10) offers a model for how formative observational studies can drive both micro-level refinements and system-level adaptations.

question: What publicly available datasets are typically used for evaluating type inference systems in python?

sections.text: This report examines the publicly available datasets that are commonly used to evaluate type inference systems for Python. Because Python is dynamically typed and because the community has recognized a persistent shortage of high‐quality, large‐scale annotated corpora, researchers have progressively developed and adapted datasets to serve as benchmarks for both static and deep learning–based type inference systems. In the following sections we detail the characteristics, construction methodologies, and evaluation aims of these datasets, citing the available sources throughout.

Python’s dynamic nature and its permissive approach to type annotations create a significant challenge for both traditional static analysis and modern machine learning–based type inference systems. Effective evaluation of these systems requires benchmark datasets that capture the richness and variety of real-world code while providing adequate ground truth on type annotations. Early works highlighted the inadequacy of existing human‐labeled resources such as the annotations “mypy” and “typeshed,” which primarily focus on function signatures rather than variable-level annotations (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 1-2). This gap motivated research to construct large-scale, automatically generated datasets that can comprehensively represent type annotations in real-world Python code. Over time, several datasets have emerged as benchmarks not only for static analyses but also for deep learning implementations; among these, ManyTypes4Py, CrossDomainTypes4Py, the PYInfer dataset variants (typePY and probPY), the Typilus dataset, and Python-150K have become central to the community.

citations.title: Pyinfer: deep learning semantic type inference for python variables

sections.text: One of the most prominent publicly available datasets is ManyTypes4Py. This dataset was designed specifically for machine learning–based type inference tasks and has become a widely adopted benchmark. ManyTypes4Py comprises a collection of more than 5,000 Python projects acquired through a search for repositories that depend on the mypy type checker, ensuring the presence of type annotations (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 1-2). It includes hundreds of thousands of source code files, extracted type hints, and a rich set of metadata obtained via an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)–based processing pipeline. The dataset not only provides the raw annotated code but also includes JSON-formatted representations of source code structure, which are suitable for feature extraction in neural models (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 3-4). In addition, ManyTypes4Py incorporates preprocessing steps such as de-duplication using tools like CD4Py to remove redundancies that could bias learning algorithms (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 4-5). Because it covers both function-level and variable-level type annotations, ManyTypes4Py addresses the shortcomings noted in earlier works that relied solely on high-level function annotations and has therefore become a staple benchmark dataset in type inference research. Complementing ManyTypes4Py is the CrossDomainTypes4Py dataset, which was introduced to facilitate evaluation of type inference systems in scenarios with domain shifts. Recognizing that the characteristics of Python code can vary significantly between application domains, CrossDomainTypes4Py was specifically constructed by mining code repositories from domains such as web development and scientific computation (gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 1-2). This dataset aggregates data from over 7,900 GitHub repositories and Libraries.io entries, resulting in over one million type annotations. By structuring the dataset into domain-specific subsets that are split at the project level, the dataset not only offers insights into overall performance but also enables researchers to conduct experiments on cross-domain generalizability (gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 10-11, gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 2-3). The inclusion of domain-specific features, such as those derived via dependencies on popular frameworks for web development (e.g., Flask) or scientific computing (e.g., NumPy), further enhances its relevance for evaluating the robustness of deep learning–based type inference models across diverse practical applications. In addition to the above large-scale datasets, the PYInfer work introduced by Cui et al. has contributed two important datasets: typePY and probPY. These datasets were automatically generated by applying the static analyzer PySonar2 to a wide range of popular Python projects on GitHub. The typePY dataset, for instance, initially included over 77 million type annotations that were later refined to about 42 million valid annotations after aggressive data cleaning (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 2-3). This dataset was designed primarily to include variable-level annotations, thereby addressing previous limitations where only function parameters and return types were annotated (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 1-2). On the other hand, the probPY dataset is a merged collection that combines data from both static and dynamic analyses of Python code and is commonly used as a benchmark when assessing deep learning models such as PYInfer. Experiments conducted using probPY have demonstrated how tuning contextual margins can significantly affect inference precision, emphasizing the need for large, diverse annotated datasets to achieve robust evaluation (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 9-10). Another important dataset in the realm of type inference for Python is the Typilus dataset, which is associated with neural type hint prediction systems. Although originally tailored for the Typilus deep learning model rather than specifically for type inference, it has served as a valuable benchmark because it transforms source code into graph representations that capture not only type hint information but also semantic code structure (allamanis2020typilusneuraltype pages 12-13). By focusing on the prediction of deeply nested and compound user-defined types, the Typilus dataset provides a different perspective on the challenge of accurately predicting type annotations in environments where type usage can be intricate and heterogeneous. This dataset has been influential in highlighting the difficulties that arise with rare or heavily nested types, which are often underrepresented in larger generic datasets. An earlier dataset that continues to serve as a reference point is Python-150K. Although it is less specialized than ManyTypes4Py in terms of the density and quality of type annotations, Python-150K comprises a considerable number of Python projects collected in 2016 by Raychev et al. This dataset has been used to train and evaluate earlier machine learning models for type inference (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 3-4). However, its age and issues such as duplication and lower annotation quality compared to MoreRecent datasets like ManyTypes4Py have led researchers to prefer the newer benchmarks. Nonetheless, it remains an important historical reference in the evolution of machine learning–based type inference approaches for Python. Furthermore, the repository of standard library stubs known as typeshed is frequently used in evaluations. Although typeshed was originally developed to provide type information for the standard library and popular third-party packages rather than for dynamic type inference evaluation per se, it has become a de facto component of the evaluation process for many type inference tools. Many inference systems use typeshed as a baseline for understanding the correct type annotations of popular libraries and for validating the inferred types against the static types provided by the Python community (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 10-11).

sections.text: While many studies rely on large-scale, automatically mined datasets, some researchers have also utilized domain-specific and micro-benchmark collections. For example, the work on TypeEvalPy presents a micro-benchmarking framework that includes 154 code snippets annotated with a total of 845 type annotations spanning 18 distinct Python language constructs (venkatesh2024typeevalpyamicrobenchmarking pages 1-2). Such micro-benchmarks are useful complements to the large datasets because they are often designed to cover corner cases and specific language features that may not be extensively represented in the larger collections. These curated benchmarks are critical for understanding the limitations and strengths of type inference systems under controlled and reproducible conditions. In addition, some studies have emphasized the importance of evaluating type inference systems on repositories that have been carefully de-duplicated and filtered to remove noise. One study noted that a very high duplication ratio in GitHub projects could distort evaluation results and that de-duplication using techniques such as TF-IDF vectorization and K-nearest-neighbor clustering is essential to obtain a representative dataset (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 4-5). This kind of preprocessing ensures that when machine learning models are trained and evaluated, they are not overfitted to redundant samples, thereby providing a more realistic assessment of generalizability and in-the-wild performance. Another approach to mitigation of dataset biases is seen in projects that perform data cleaning and type normalization. The PYInfer datasets underwent significant cleaning (e.g., removal of duplicates and meaningless type annotations), which not only improved the overall quality of annotations but also enhanced the relevance of the ground truth used for model training and evaluation (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 2-3). Such efforts underscore the necessity for robust dataset construction techniques in the field of type inference research.

sections.text: Examining the characteristics of the aforementioned datasets reveals several common themes across the literature. Most datasets are built by mining open repositories from GitHub and other public sources such as Libraries.io. This broad data collection strategy ensures that the datasets reflect a wide variety of coding styles, project sizes, and annotation practices. In addition, datasets like CrossDomainTypes4Py and ManyTypes4Py prioritize the inclusion of context-rich type annotations at both the function level and within variable declarations. These datasets are split into carefully curated training, validation, and test sets—often at the project level rather than at the file level—to ensure that evaluations do not suffer from information leakage (gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 5-6). The de-duplication process is a critical step that distinguishes high-quality datasets from their earlier counterparts. For example, the ManyTypes4Py dataset explicitly addresses the problem of code duplication by employing CD4Py, which filters out redundant files using established techniques (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 4-5). This step is vital for maintaining the integrity of the evaluation process since training or testing on multiple copies of the same code can artificially inflate inference accuracy. Moreover, the domain-specific datasets, such as CrossDomainTypes4Py, enable researchers to conduct experiments that evaluate cross-domain generalizability. By splitting the dataset into subsets that represent, for instance, web development projects and scientific computations, these benchmarks allow for an in-depth analysis of how transfer learning and domain adaptation techniques perform when moving from one code domain to another (gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 10-11, gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 9-10). This is particularly important given that the type inference challenges may vary considerably between domains with different coding idioms and library dependencies. Another factor that sets apart these datasets is the balance between breadth and depth. Large-scale datasets like ManyTypes4Py and the PYInfer datasets capture extensive volumes of Python code (with millions of annotations) and provide considerable statistical power when training and validating deep learning models. At the same time, the finer-grained datasets like the Typilus dataset, which focuses on graph representations of code, and smaller micro-benchmarks allow researchers to drill down into the nuances of type inference—such as predicting user-defined types or handling nested parametric types (allamanis2020typilusneuraltype pages 12-13, mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 3-4). Notably, the datasets also differ in terms of the nature of annotations they include. While many datasets rely predominantly on static type annotations (e.g., those provided by mypy and typeshed), others incorporate annotations generated by static analyzers such as PySonar2 and then refined through additional cleaning procedures. The PYInfer approach, for instance, distinguishes between annotations at different granularities by generating an initial set of 77 million annotations before filtering them to a subset deemed valid for training (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 2-3). The use of these automated methods for generating annotations highlights the trade-offs between scale and accuracy, as manual annotations remain scarce in the Python ecosystem. Additional research has also underscored the importance of standardized evaluation metrics and reproducible training/testing splits. For instance, many works adhere to a common split—typically 70% of data for training, 10% for validation, and 20% for testing—to allow for fair comparison among different type inference systems (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 2-3, mir2022type4py pages 5-6). Standardization of evaluation protocols is instrumental for ensuring that advances in type inference models can be reliably compared and integrated into subsequent research.

sections.text: The availability of high-quality, publicly accessible datasets has profound implications for the development and evaluation of Python type inference systems. On one hand, large datasets such as ManyTypes4Py enable deep learning models to learn complex patterns associated with both built-in types and user-defined types across a diverse set of programming projects. This breadth is essential for improving system coverage and for handling the inherent variability in Python code. On the other hand, domain-specific datasets such as CrossDomainTypes4Py force models to confront the challenges of dataset shifts, imbalanced type distributions, and out-of-vocabulary tokens—issues that are frequently encountered in real-world codebases (gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 9-10). Furthermore, these datasets facilitate the benchmarking of inference systems not only in terms of overall accuracy and recall but also with respect to specific metrics that assess the prediction of rare and deeply nested types—a critical factor for the practical adoption of such systems in production code. In this regard, the Typilus dataset has provided insights into the limitations of deep similarity learning approaches particularly when handling less frequent nested type annotations (allamanis2020typilusneuraltype pages 12-13). Moreover, the integration of static analyzers’ outputs (e.g., as seen in the PYInfer datasets) illustrates one effective strategy for bootstrapping large annotated corpora from manually unannotated repositories, thus bridging the gap between automatic annotation generation and manual precision. The role of supplementary micro-benchmarks, such as the ones introduced by TypeEvalPy, cannot be understated either. While large-scale datasets ensure that models are evaluated over a broad spectrum of codebases, micro-benchmarks provide a controlled environment to evaluate how inference tools manage syntactic complexities and specific language features (venkatesh2024typeevalpyamicrobenchmarking pages 1-2). By combining both approaches, the field benefits from both high-level generalizability assessments and fine-grained diagnosis of system strengths and weaknesses.

sections.text: As research in Python type inference continues to evolve, there is growing recognition that no single dataset can comprehensively address every evaluation need. Moving forward, the emphasis is likely to shift toward integrating multiple datasets so that evaluations can capture both scale and the diversity of real-world coding practices. In particular, combining large-scale datasets such as ManyTypes4Py with domain-specific collections like CrossDomainTypes4Py, and supplementing these with micro-benchmarks and curated repositories like typeshed, provides a robust framework for evaluating type inference tools. This multi-faceted approach is essential to support not only incremental improvements in model accuracy but also to address challenges such as domain shifts, code duplication, and the inherent uncertainties associated with inferring types in a dynamically typed language (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 1-2, gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 4-5). Moreover, datasets generated through automated pipelines like those employed for creating typePY and probPY illustrate the potential for ongoing, iterative dataset enhancement. As new static analysis tools emerge and as deep learning techniques further improve their ability to capture semantic context, it is anticipated that future benchmark datasets will provide even richer representations of type annotations. Researchers are encouraged to continue sharing their datasets publicly and to adhere to standard evaluation protocols so that progress in the field can be accurately measured and compared across different approaches (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 9-10, mir2022type4py pages 5-6). In summary, the most commonly used publicly available datasets for evaluating type inference systems in Python include: •	ManyTypes4Py, which is widely adopted due to its large scale, rich annotation set, and comprehensive preprocessing steps designed to handle duplication and noise (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 1-2, mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 3-4). •	CrossDomainTypes4Py, which extends evaluation into domain-specific areas such as web development and scientific computation, thereby supporting experiments on cross-domain generalizability (gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 1-2, gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 10-11). •	PYInfer’s datasets—namely typePY and probPY—which are generated using static analysis tools and refined through cleaning processes to emphasize variable-level annotations (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 1-2, cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 2-3). •	The Typilus dataset, which is used to assess predictions of deeply nested and user-defined types and which leverages graph-based representations of code (allamanis2020typilusneuraltype pages 12-13). •	Earlier benchmarks such as Python-150K have historically been used to provide a baseline despite known issues such as high duplication and lower annotation density (mir2021manytypes4pyabenchmark pages 3-4). •	Finally, typeshed remains an important complementary resource that contains library stubs for widely used standard libraries and third-party packages (cui2021pyinferdeeplearning pages 10-11). Collectively, these datasets form the backbone of empirical evaluation in Python type inference research. They empower the community to benchmark novel static analysis and deep learning–based approaches effectively, ensuring that improvements are measured not only in controlled experiments but also in diverse, real-world coding scenarios. As the field continues to mature, further integration and expansion of these datasets will likely help overcome remaining challenges and push the boundaries of what type inference systems can achieve in the dynamically typed Python ecosystem (gruner2023crossdomainevaluationof pages 2-3, venkatesh2024typeevalpyamicrobenchmarking pages 1-2). Through the combined use of large-scale, domain-specific, and micro-benchmark datasets, current research is well positioned to address the multifaceted challenges of type inference in Python. The ongoing development and public dissemination of these resources are critical steps toward realizing more accurate, reliable, and context-aware type prediction systems that can ultimately improve code quality and developer productivity in one of the world’s most popular programming languages.

question: is there any evidence that large language models can be effectively applied to robot planning tasks?

sections.text: This report presents comprehensive evidence that large language models (LLMs) can be effectively applied to robot planning tasks by integrating modern computational linguistics with classical planning and symbolic techniques to support complex, scalable, and dynamic task execution.

In recent years, the field of robotics has increasingly encountered challenges in dealing with the limitations of traditional symbolic planning, particularly when addressing dynamic environments and human-robot collaboration, where frequent real-time replanning is necessary to handle evolving constraints and unexpected events (capitanelli2024aframeworkfor pages 1-3). LLMs such as GPT-3, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 have emerged as powerful tools that demonstrate advanced natural language understanding, generative capabilities, and commonsense reasoning, which can be leveraged to overcome the scalability issues inherent in conventional symbolic planners (capitanelli2024aframeworkfor pages 3-6).

sections.text: Fundamentally, traditional symbolic planning methods, which often rely on Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) representations, suffer from super-linear computational behavior as problem size increases, making them unsustainable for real-time robotic tasks in dynamic environments (capitanelli2024aframeworkfor pages 1-3). In contrast, approaches such as the Teriyaki framework integrate LLMs in a neurosymbolic system, where the LLM produces incremental plans that can be handed off to a robot for immediate execution while planning continues concurrently, thus reducing waiting times and improving interaction fluency with humans (capitanelli2024aframeworkfor pages 6-9).

sections.text: In one notable study, Capitanelli and Mastrogiovanni detailed how the integration of GPT-3 into symbolic planning not only preserved plan correctness comparable to established planners but also generated shorter plans while significantly reducing average waiting times, thus evidencing that LLMs can deliver both efficiency and quality in planning (capitanelli2024aframeworkfor pages 1-3). This work demonstrates that LLMs can generate partial or complete action sequences that directly correspond to high-level robot instructions, a capability that is particularly valuable in tasks where rapid response is critical and the environment is subject to rapid changes (capitanelli2024aframeworkfor pages 3-6).

Such fine-tuning has been shown to produce planners with near-optimal plan validity relative to classical counterparts, which reinforces the notion that LLMs can be embedded within existing robotic planning pipelines to enhance performance across complex domains (capitanelli2024aframeworkfor pages 3-6).

sections.text: Complementing these findings, Chalvatzaki et al. provided insights into the application of GPT-2 for planning tasks by grounding the LLM’s representations on scene graphs, thereby enabling the decomposition of complex, long-horizon tasks into manageable subgoals that can be executed sequentially (chalvatzaki2023learningtoreason pages 1-2). This work illustrates that even smaller LLMs, when properly finetuned and integrated with perceptual inputs, can effectively serve as grounding tools for semantic scene comprehension and task decomposition which are essential in robotic planning applications (chalvatzaki2023learningtoreason pages 1-2).

Their work demonstrates that LLMs, when properly interfaced with classical path-planning and evaluation algorithms, can extend the planning horizons of robots beyond the context-length limitations of traditional LLM approaches by dynamically integrating visual and spatial information (hu2023towardgeneralpurposerobots pages 9-10).

question: What are the most important open challenges in Federated Learning?

sections.text: Below is a comprehensive discussion of the most important open challenges in Federated Learning (FL). In this report, we analyze the multifaceted issues that currently hinder FL’s widespread adoption and robust deployment, including communication efficiency, data and system heterogeneity, privacy and security constraints, personalization and fairness, scalability and client selection, standardization and benchmarking, robustness against adversarial attacks, and specific domain‐related challenges. Each challenge is discussed in detail with supporting evidence from the literature.

Federated Learning is a paradigm for distributed machine learning in which many edge devices or data silos collaboratively learn a global model while keeping raw data local. FL has emerged as an attractive solution for privacy-sensitive and resource-constrained scenarios, such as healthcare, IoT, open banking, and next-generation wireless networks. However, its distributed nature introduces significant challenges that span multiple dimensions, from fundamental algorithmic design to practical deployment issues. Recent surveys and research articles have drawn attention to many obstacles—including expensive communication, heterogeneous data and systems, stringent privacy requirements, security vulnerabilities, fairness concerns in aggregation—and these continue to define active research directions in FL (li2020federatedlearningchallenges pages 1-3, kairouz2021advancesandopen pages 4-6). The following sections elaborate on these key challenges.

citations.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning

sections.text: A central challenge in FL is managing communication overhead between a large, often massive number of participating devices and the central server or aggregator. In traditional machine learning, data is collected centrally so that communication is not a repetitive burden. In contrast, FL requires iterative exchange of model updates that are sent frequently over often bandwidth-limited networks. Communication bottlenecks arise because each participating client must transmit model updates (gradients or parameters) multiple times during training, leading to substantial overhead and increased latency. This problem is exacerbated in networks where connectivity is unreliable, where devices are heterogeneous in their access to high-speed channels, and where many clients may contribute only sporadically (li2020federatedlearningchallenges pages 8-10, kairouz2021advancesandopen pages 28-30). Researchers have proposed methods such as gradient compression, quantization, and sparse updates to reduce the size and frequency of communications, but these techniques often trade off accuracy for efficiency. For example, aggressive compression can lead to a degradation in model convergence or accuracy, while quantization may introduce errors in the aggregated update (wen2023asurveyon pages 16-17, li2020federatedlearningchallenges pages 12-14). Balancing the communication cost while preserving model performance remains one of the core challenges in FL.

citations.title: Advances and Open Problems in Federated Learning

sections.text: Another central issue in FL is statistical heterogeneity, commonly known as non-IID (non-independent and identically distributed) data across clients. In typical centralized scenarios, training data is assumed to be drawn from the same underlying distribution; however, in federated environments, the data at each client can differ dramatically in terms of distribution, quantity, quality, and noise level. Some devices may collect only a narrow subset of data (for instance, due to region, user behavior or sensor variability), while others may experience label noise or sample noise skews (ye2023heterogeneousfederatedlearning pages 10-12, li2020federatedlearningchallenges pages 10-12). This data heterogeneity leads to discrepancies during the local training phase and can cause divergence during aggregation if not properly managed. Although algorithmic modifications such as FedAvg and FedProx have attempted to address non-IID challenges by incorporating regularization terms or adaptive learning rates, robust solutions that guarantee convergence under extreme heterogeneity remain an open problem (kairouz2021advancesandopen pages 15-17, jiang2020federatedlearningin pages 11-13). Moreover, techniques such as client clustering or locally personalized models have been proposed as alternatives to the classical global model paradigm, but these methods are still in their infancy and require further theoretical and empirical validation (huang2206crosssilofederatedlearning pages 1-2, bharati2022federatedlearningapplications pages 23-26).

sections.text: Closely related to data heterogeneity is the challenge of system heterogeneity. FL typically involves a vast array of devices with diverse computation capabilities, energy constraints, storage capacities, and availability patterns. In cross-device FL scenarios, these devices include smartphones, IoT sensors, or even autonomous vehicles that differ widely in their underlying hardware and software infrastructures (li2020federatedlearningchallenges pages 1-3, kholod2020opensourcefederatedlearning pages 4-6). As such, the same training algorithm may perform well on a high-performance computing node but struggle on a low-powered mobile device due to limited memory or processing power. These discrepancies can cause issues such as stragglers—devices that take significantly longer to compute local updates—and eventual dropout or intermittent participation that bias the aggregated update toward those devices that remain online. In addition, device heterogeneity results in asynchronous updates that complicate the convergence analysis. Tools and techniques such as adaptive scheduling, dynamic resource allocation, and flexible networking protocols have been proposed to mitigate these issues; however, achieving scalability with robust performance when facing millions of diverse and unstable devices is still an unresolved challenge (li2020federatedlearningchallenges pages 8-10, khan2021federatedlearningfor pages 31-33).
