sections.text: A specific challenge of extreme weather is the rapid variability of wind conditions, which can cause significant aerodynamic disturbances. To counteract this, methods for direct wind measurement and dynamic state estimation have been intensively researched. Experimental approaches that infer wind velocity from quadrotor motion—using measurements of air-relative speed, inflow angle, and sideslip angle—enable the development of robust state observers (gonzalezrocha2019sensingwindfrom pages 17-17, gonzalezrocha2019sensingwindfrom pages 7-8). These observers provide essential feedback to control loops, allowing the UAV to adjust its thrust and attitude commands in real time. The use of local exponential stability analysis ensures that the observer error converges quickly, even when environmental parameters are uncertain or rapidly changing. In essence, such wind sensing and adaptive estimation methods directly contribute to flight robustness by allowing the UAV to “learn” and adapt to the prevailing aerodynamic environment in real time.

question: what are some datasets used for evaluating variable type inference for decompiled binaries?

sections.text:
This report details a number of publicly available datasets used to evaluate variable type inference and recovery in decompiled binaries. In decompilation research, the loss of high
‐level semantic information such as variable names and types during compilation necessitates benchmarks that reproduce realistic binary conditions, thus enabling the evaluation of both classical and machine learning–based inference techniques.

One prominent dataset is the DIRTY dataset (sometimes also referred to as DIRT), which was introduced by Chen et al. In their work, the authors mined a large-scale dataset from public GitHub repositories containing C source code and subsequently compiled these projects with various optimization levels (from –O0 to –O3) using an automated build tool (GHCC) and the GCC compiler. Binaries were then decompiled using Hex-Rays, and the preserved debugging information allowed matching decompiler–assigned variable names with their corresponding original developer–assigned names to form robust training and evaluation examples. In total, the final DIRTY dataset comprises 75,656 binaries with hundreds of thousands of unique functions split across training, validation, and test sets, making it a comprehensive benchmark for variable type inference and variable name recovery in decompiled binaries (chen2022augmentingdecompileroutput pages 5-7, chen2022augmentingdecompileroutput pages 16-17).

citations.title: Augmenting decompiler output with learned variable names and types
Augmenting decompiler output with learned variable names and types

sections.text:
Another influential dataset is VarCorpus, introduced by Pal et al. to overcome the limitations observed in earlier datasets such as DIRE and DIRTY. VarCorpus was built from a broad collection of C and C++ packages harvested from Linux distributions (for example, the Gentoo repository) and compiled under multiple optimization levels, with debugging symbols preserved to ensure an accurate mapping from decompiled variable tokens back to their corresponding source-level identifiers. The extensive nature of VarCorpus
—in terms of both the number of binaries and the diversity of compilation configurations
—makes it a valuable resource for evaluating models like VARBERT that are aimed at improving variable name prediction and type inference tasks (pal2024"lenorindex pages 1-2, pal2024"lenorindex pages 7-8).

sections.text: A further dataset often cited in the literature is the one used for the evaluation of Debin. He et al. collected 9000 ELF binaries and shared libraries derived from Linux Debug Symbol Packages, with the binaries coming from popular software packages such as coreutils, dpkg, and gcc. These binaries span several architectures (x86, x64, and ARM) and were compiled with different optimization levels to reflect real-world diversity. For training purposes, 2700 binaries per architecture were utilized, with 300 reserved for testing, and the evaluation metrics included structured prediction measures such as precision, recall, and F1 scores for both variable type and name inference. This dataset is significant because it provides a controlled yet realistic benchmark for evaluating variable recovery systems on systems-level binaries (he2018debin pages 9-10).

citations.title: Debin

sections.text:
In addition to the above, the TypeMiner dataset introduced by Maier et al. serves as another benchmark specifically oriented toward type recovery. This dataset is derived from 14 widely used open-source projects
—such as bash, grep, and wget
—with the binaries compiled in release configurations. The resulting dataset includes approximately 817,000 instructions and 23,482 data objects, covering a variety of primitive types (e.g., _Bool, char, int) as well as compound types such as pointers and structs. A leave-one-out cross-validation is employed on the collected functions to ensure evaluation on unseen data, making the dataset a robust benchmark for assessing machine learning models that predict variable types from binary code (maier2019typeminerrecoveringtypes pages 11-14).

citations.title: Typeminer: recovering types in binary programs using machine learning

sections.text: Another approach to dataset construction is seen in the work by Escalada et al., where a corpus was built using a combination of real-world open-source C projects and synthetic C programs generated by their tool, Cnerator. This hybrid dataset is designed to address issues of data imbalance and a lack of rare language constructs in real-world code, and it provides ground truth annotations that link binary-level patterns (such as register usage and instruction sequences) to high-level type information. Although this dataset is not named as a single benchmark in their text, it has been used to demonstrate significant improvements in return type prediction accuracy, reaching an F1-measure of over 79%, and thereby contributes to the evaluation ecosystem for variable type inference techniques (escalada2101improvingtypeinformation pages 1-4, escalada2101improvingtypeinformation pages 10-12).

sections.text:
Some researchers have also revisited and extended previously established benchmarks. For instance, Cao and Leach re-evaluated the DIRTY approach by retraining the model on decompiled outputs generated by the open-source Ghidra decompiler rather than Hex-Rays. Their work augments the original dataset with additional binaries
—approximately 90,000 extra samples
—to generate a large-scale dataset suitable for benchmarking variable type recovery. While this work builds on the original DIRTY dataset, it also highlights challenges, such as variables losing their debug information during symbol stripping and decompilation, thereby necessitating specialized annotations (e.g., a “disappear” label) in the training data (cao2023revisitingdeeplearning pages 1-2, cao2023revisitingdeeplearning pages 4-5).

sections.text: More comprehensive benchmark frameworks have also been developed that, while primarily targeting a broader range of decompilation quality metrics, include aspects of variable type inference among their evaluation parameters. The DecompileBench framework, for example, uses a real-world corpus derived from OSS-Fuzz projects. It extracts over 23,400 functions from binaries generated by fuzzing, and it evaluates decompilers on multiple criteria, including syntactic correctness, runtime behavior, and semantic fidelity. They are crucial for conducting head-to-head comparisons between methods based on static analysis, dynamic techniques, and increasingly, deep learning approaches employing Transformer-based architectures. sections.text: It is important to note that while each dataset has its own merits, challenges remain in creating benchmarks that are both diverse and representative of real-world conditions. For example, datasets built from open-source C and C++ repositories may not necessarily generalize to binaries compiled from other programming languages or proprietary codebases. Moreover, differences in compiler optimizations, decompilers used, and the presence or absence of debugging symbols can all substantially affect the quality of decompiled output and, by extension, the evaluation of type recovery techniques. As researchers continue to refine and extend these benchmarks, a primary objective is to foster reproducibility and robust comparison across different research efforts (chen2022augmentingdecompileroutput pages 11-13, pal2024"lenorindex pages 15-15).

question: How does in-context learning for LLMs differ from traditional machine learning model training?

sections.text: Abstract—In-context learning (ICL) for large language models (LLMs) represents a fundamental shift in learning paradigms compared to traditional machine learning (ML) training methods. Rather than updating model weights using gradient-based optimization over large labeled datasets, ICL leverages the contextual input provided during inference, enabling models to “learn” tasks on the fly without explicit fine-tuning. This report examines the intrinsic differences between in-context learning and traditional training, discusses the architectural and algorithmic underpinnings that support such capabilities, and explores the implications of these differences for real-world applications. The discussion integrates insights from recent studies, highlighting factors such as dynamic adaptation, implicit meta-learning, prompt dependency, and computational efficiency.

I. Introduction  Recent advancements in natural language processing have primarily been driven by large language models that utilize the Transformer architecture. A key emergent property of these models is in-context learning (ICL), a mechanism by which an LLM is able to perform novel tasks solely by conditioning on input–output examples provided within the prompt at inference time, without any explicit parameter updates (akyurek2401incontextlanguagelearning pages 1-3). Traditional machine learning model training, by contrast, typically involves a separate training phase wherein model parameters are explicitly optimized via gradient descent over a labeled dataset before the model is deployed for inference (chan2022datadistributionalproperties pages 1-2). The paradigm shift represented by ICL challenges the conventional separation between training and inference and highlights the potential for dynamic adaptation directly at runtime (long2404doesincontextlearning pages 1-2). This report presents a detailed analysis comparing the two learning paradigms, aiming to provide experts with a granular view of their operational differences, benefits, challenges, and underlying theoretical principles.

citations.title: In-context language learning: architectures and algorithms.

sections.text: II. Theoretical Foundations and Underlying Mechanisms  A. Implicit versus Explicit Learning  Traditional machine learning relies on explicit weight updates through iterative optimization procedures such as gradient descent. In this setting, the learning process is divided into distinct phases: pre-training, fine-tuning (or supervised training), and inference. Each phase involves updating numerous model parameters from an initial random or pre-trained state toward an optimal solution that minimizes a given loss function (bucher2406finetunedsmallllms pages 4-5). In contrast, ICL does not involve any additional weight updates at inference time; instead, it utilizes the model’s pre-trained knowledge and infers task-specific behavior dynamically based solely on the context provided in the input prompt (chan2022datadistributionalproperties pages 1-2). Essentially, while traditional training builds and stores knowledge in the model parameters, ICL relies on the model’s ability to reinterpret stored knowledge in light of supportive contextual cues, enabling rapid adaptation without further parameter optimization (chu2310finetunelanguagemodels pages 4-7).  B. Meta-Learning and Dynamic Adaptation  The inherent capability of LLMs to perform ICL can be viewed through the lens of meta-learning. Meta-learning—or “learning to learn”—refers to the process whereby models learn an internal algorithm for rapid adaptation given only a few examples (chen2021metalearningvialanguage pages 1-2). In ICL, the model uses examples within the prompt to trigger an internal, dynamic reweighting or reinterpretation of its latent representation, effectively adapting its output behavior. Various studies have suggested that Transformer models may be implicitly simulating learning algorithms such as gradient descent internally during the forward pass (garg2022whatcantransformers pages 11-13). This dynamic adaptation is achieved by conditioning on both the order and content of the provided examples and is fundamentally different from the static parameter updates in traditional training (min2021metaicllearningto pages 1-2).  C. Role of Pre-Training and Data Distribution  A salient difference between ICL and traditional training lies in the role of pre-training data distributions. ICL leverages the extensive pre-training on vast natural language corpora, which inherently contain diverse linguistic patterns, rare events, and non-uniform distributions (chan2022datadistributionalproperties pages 7-9). This exposure to complex, real-world data distributions instills in LLMs a form of implicit task recognition and pattern matching that can be dynamically invoked via context (long2404doesincontextlearning pages 1-2). Traditional ML models, however, are often trained on carefully curated, labeled datasets that focus on specificity and statistically balanced distributions, which may not generalize as flexibly to new tasks without retraining (patil2024areviewof pages 23-25).

sections.text: III. Architectural Considerations and Model Behavior  A. Transformer Architecture and Self-Attention  The Transformer architecture is central to the phenomenon of ICL. Transformers use self-attention mechanisms that enable the model to directly relate different tokens within the input sequence, capturing dependencies and contextual relationships that are critical for in-context adaptation (lampinen2024thebroaderspectrum pages 2-4). The self-attention mechanism functions as an internal, context-dependent computation unit that recalibrates token representations based on the surrounding context. This process differs substantially from recurrent or convolutional models, where sequential dependencies are modeled in a more rigid fashion (chan2022datadistributionalproperties pages 1-2). In ICL, the self-attention mechanism allows the LLM to effectively “infer” the function or mapping that the prompt examples represent, enabling rapid generalization even to tasks not previously encountered during training (kodaforno2023metaincontextlearningin pages 1-2).  B. Specialized Components and Architectural Adaptations  Empirical studies have shown that certain architectural components, such as specialized “n-gram heads” or induction heads, play a critical role in facilitating ICL by encoding higher-order sequence statistics directly within the context (akyurek2401incontextlanguagelearning pages 1-3). Some research indicates that hard-wiring such algorithmic structures or incorporating prompt-tuning mechanisms (e.g., soft prompts) can significantly improve both ICL and natural language modeling performance, further emphasizing the architectural divergence from traditional training routines which update all weights across layers (huang2212incontextlearningdistillation pages 1-2). Additionally, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods, which adjust a small set of parameters, contrast with ICL’s complete reliance on frozen parameters and prompt conditioning (wang2024parameterefficientfinetuningin pages 4-5).  C. The Role of Prompt Structure and Demonstration Quality  In ICL, the format, order, and selection of examples within the prompt are critical determinants of model performance. The model does not have the opportunity to error-correct over long periods through parameter updates; rather, it must interpret the given prompt as is (pan2023whatincontextlearning pages 1-2). This sensitivity to prompt design contrasts with traditional ML training, where repeated cycles of weight updates gradually overcome suboptimal sample presentations by averaging over large datasets (min2022rethinkingtherole pages 1-2). The emphasis on demonstration quality means that even minor changes in example selection or token ordering can have significant impacts on output performance in ICL (liu2406whatdo... oh, see specific citation: pan2023whatincontextlearning pages 1-2, wei2023largerlanguagemodels pages 1-2).

sections.text: IV. Practical Implications and Performance Considerations  A. Computational Efficiency and Resource Constraints  One of the major advantages of ICL over traditional training is the elimination of costly retraining or fine-tuning cycles at inference time. Traditional ML training demands significant computational resources for gradient updates over large, curated datasets (bucher2406finetunedsmallllms pages 4-5). In contrast, ICL primarily relies on the forward pass of pre-trained models, making it computationally inexpensive during deployment. This efficiency is particularly important in applications where rapid model adaptation to new tasks is required and where retraining could be prohibitively slow or expensive (nafar2025learningvsretrieval pages 10-11). However, while inference using ICL is less computationally expensive, the pre-training phase itself remains resource-intensive, and ICL often inherits the limitations of the pre-training corpus (liu2406whatdo... again see li2406whatdolanguage pages 10-11).  B. Adaptability and Task Generalization  ICL offers unparalleled adaptability, as it allows LLMs to generalize to a wide variety of tasks without explicit retraining. This is in stark contrast to traditional models that require separate fine-tuning for each new task, often sacrificing generality for performance gains in specific domains (bucher2406finetunedsmallllms pages 4-5, patil2024areviewof pages 37-39). In the ICL paradigm, task-specific instructions and examples are embedded directly in the prompt, enabling simultaneous handling of multiple tasks with a single model instance. This dynamic multitasking capabilities underscore a fundamental benefit of ICL: the model acts as a universal learner by leveraging extensive pre-training and prompt-based adaptation (chan2022datadistributionalproperties pages 1-2, min2021metaicllearningto pages 1-2).  C. Robustness, Bias, and Limitations  Despite its advantages, ICL is not without challenges. The performance of ICL systems is highly sensitive to prompt engineering, where the selection and ordering of examples play a crucial role. Improper prompt design can lead to misinterpretations, recency biases, or even hallucinations, whereby the model generates plausible but incorrect outputs (chen2021metalearningvialanguage pages 1-2, long2404doesincontextlearning pages 1-2). Moreover, while ICL enables models to adapt quickly, it can also inherit biases present in the pre-training data and may not always override these biases even with carefully selected prompts (dong2023asurveyfor pages 2-3, yang2023supervisedknowledgemakes pages 1-2). There is also an inherent trade-off between leveraging pre-trained semantic priors and learning explicit input–label mappings from the prompt, a balance that becomes particularly challenging in cases of flipped or semantically unrelated labels (wei2023largerlanguagemodels pages 10-12).

sections.text: V. Comparative Analysis with Traditional Machine Learning  A. Training Procedure and Workflow  In traditional machine learning, the workflow is explicitly divided into a training phase where the model weights are optimized via gradient descent, followed by an evaluation phase where the trained parameters are fixed for inference. This paradigm involves multi-epoch training on task-specific datasets, typically using well-defined loss functions to update the parameters iteratively (chu2310finetunelanguagemodels pages 4-7). In contrast, in-context learning bypasses the need for such iterative weight updates, enabling the model to “simulate” learning from a few demonstration examples provided at inference time. This results in a significantly different workflow where the context itself is the mechanism for adaptation, rather than the adjustment of model parameters (min2021metaicllearningto pages 1-2, pan2023whatincontextlearning pages 1-2).  B. Learning Dynamics and Information Flow  Traditional training updates the entire network’s weights based on a global error signal computed over a batch of training examples, effectively embedding task knowledge in the fixed parameter space of the model. With each gradient descent step, the model slowly refines its internal representations to minimize prediction errors (patil2024areviewof pages 37-39). In contrast, ICL leverages the forward pass dynamics of the model’s self-attention mechanism to temporarily “store” and combine task-specific information provided in the prompt with pre-trained knowledge, without permanently modifying the weights (akyurek2401incontextlanguagelearning pages 3-4, dai2023whycl). The information flow in ICL is thus highly transient and context-dependent, relying heavily on the quality and structure of the prompt rather than on gradual evolutionary changes in the model’s parameters (kossen2307incontextlearningin pages 1-2).  C. Generalization and Overfitting  Traditional fine-tuning on small datasets can lead to overfitting, where the model becomes highly specialized to the training data and loses the ability to generalize to unseen examples. Strategies such as regularization and transfer learning are often employed to mitigate this risk (bucher2406finetunedsmallllms pages 4-5). ICL, however, sidesteps the overfitting problem associated with explicit weight updates by relying on the vast pre-trained knowledge base and dynamically adapting based on prompt examples. While ICL can also be sensitive to the particular examples chosen (thus potentially introducing its own form of bias), it generally maintains robust generalization across multiple tasks due to the inherent diversity of its pre-training corpus (dong2023asurveyfor pages 10-11, min2022rethinkingtherole pages 1-2).

sections.text: VI. Practical Applications and Future Directions  A. Rapid Task Adaptation and Zero-/Few-Shot Learning  ICL has proven particularly effective for applications where task definitions are provided on the fly, such as natural language understanding, translation, sentiment analysis, and open-domain question answering. Instead of engaging in time-consuming fine-tuning, practitioners can simply provide a few examples directly within the input prompt, enabling rapid deployment of models across diverse tasks (akyurek2401incontextlanguagelearning pages 1-3, pan2023whatincontextlearning pages 1-2). This approach not only reduces the overhead of constant retraining but also makes large LLMs accessible to users with limited machine learning expertise, as the heavy lifting is performed during pre-training and only context adaptation is required at inference (naveed2023acomprehensiveoverview pages 16-17).  B. Domain Adaptation and Multi-Task Learning  Traditional model training typically requires domain-specific fine-tuning to adapt to new application areas, which can be both resource-intensive and time-consuming. ICL, in contrast, supports flexible domain adaptation by virtue of its prompt-based mechanism. By carefully curating examples in the input prompt, practitioners can steer the model to perform accurately in highly specialized domains without changing the underlying model weights (jovanovic2404towardsincrementallearning pages 3-5, pang2023cosmicdataefficient pages 1-2). This multi-task capability inherent in ICL significantly reduces the need for multiple specialized models, thereby encouraging the development of versatile, general-purpose LLM systems (parthasarathy2024theultimateguide pages 6-8).  C. Challenges and Research Opportunities  Despite its potential, the ICL paradigm poses several challenges that warrant further investigation. The sensitivity of ICL performance to prompt design means that significant research must be directed toward developing robust methods for demonstration selection, prompt augmentation, and self-adaptive prompting techniques (panda2023differentiallyprivateincontext pages 176-177, sia2024wheredoesincontext pages 1-3). Furthermore, understanding the internal mechanisms—such as the implicit gradient descent-like behavior in self-attention layers—and their relationship to pre-training objectives remains an active area of theoretical and empirical exploration (garg2022whatcantransformers pages 11-13, wang2307learningtoretrieve pages 1-2). Future directions include refining meta-learning frameworks that can further bridge the gap between explicit gradient-based optimization and the implicit learning observed in ICL (sinha2024mamlenllmmodelagnostic pages 1-2).

sections.text: VII. Comparative Summary and Discussion  ICL differs from traditional machine learning training across several dimensions. First, while traditional models require explicit weight updates through extensive gradient descent on curated datasets, ICL leverages the forward pass of pre-trained models with no parameter updates during inference (liu2406whatdolanguage pages 10-11, min2021metaicllearningto pages 1-2). Second, the transient and context-dependent nature of ICL allows models to rapidly adapt to new tasks based solely on in-prompt demonstrations, a process that resembles meta-learning rather than conventional supervised training (chan2022datadistributionalproperties pages 1-2, kossen2307incontextlearningin pages 1-2). Third, architectural elements such as self-attention and specialized attention heads facilitate ICL by encoding information directly from the prompt, which is distinct from the static representations learned through traditional training procedures (lampinen2024thebroaderspectrum pages 2-4, huang2212incontextlearningdistillation pages 1-2). Fourth, while traditional fine-tuning can lead to overfitting and a narrowing of model capabilities, ICL maintains a broader generalization by relying on the expansive pre-training corpus and prompt variability (patil2024areviewof pages 23-25, wei2023largerlanguagemodels pages 10-12).  Moreover, ICL underscores an important shift from parameter-centric to context-centric adaptation. Traditional training methods invest substantial resources to update model weights so that the model generalizes well on specific tasks; in contrast, ICL exploits the stored latent representations acquired during pre-training and flexibly reinterprets them based on the given prompt, such that the same model can serve a wide variety of tasks on demand (wuUnknownyearwhyincontextlearning pages 1-3, yang2023supervisedknowledgemakes pages 1-2).

sections.text: VIII. Implications for Deployment and Real-World Usage  A. Scalability and Maintenance  In real-world applications, deploying multiple models fine-tuned for individual tasks can be both impractical and expensive. The ICL paradigm offers significant advantages in scalability since a single, pre-trained LLM can adapt to multiple tasks at runtime without necessitating periodic retraining or maintenance updates for each domain-specific application (naveed2023acomprehensiveoverview pages 16-17, pan2023cosmicdataefficient pages 1-2). Consequently, organizations can benefit from reduced deployment costs and simplified system architectures that do not require maintaining a suite of specialized models (patil2024areviewof pages 37-39).  B. User Accessibility and Rapid Prototyping  The ease with which users can alter task behavior simply by modifying the prompt is a major advantage of ICL over traditional methods that require deep expertise in model fine-tuning. This democratizes access to advanced language models by lowering the barrier to entry for rapid prototyping and experimentation (pan2023whatincontextlearning pages 1-2, wei2023largerlanguagemodels pages 1-2). End users can leverage natural language instructions and example demonstrations to achieve desired outputs, thereby shifting much of the burden of model adaptation from expensive computational processes to intuitive prompt editing (akyurek2401incontextlanguagelearning pages 1-3).  C. Limitations and Ongoing Challenges  Despite the versatility, ICL is not without its limitations. Its performance can be inconsistent given slight alterations in prompt structure, order of examples, or example quality, which remains a core area of active research (min2022rethinkingtherole pages 1-2, panda2023differentiallyprivateincontext pages 71-72). Moreover, while ICL shows promising generalization, it sometimes struggles with highly complex or specification-heavy tasks that require nuanced reasoning or detailed representations that traditional fine-tuning can more robustly handle (peng2023whendoesincontext pages 7-9, wei2023largerlanguagemodels pages 10-12). Therefore, a hybrid approach—where insights from traditional training methods and ICL are combined—may yield models that benefit from both explicit parameter optimization and dynamic, context-based adaptation (jovanovic2404towardsincrementallearning pages 14-16).

sections.text: IX. Future Research Directions  The differences between ICL and traditional ML training open several promising avenues for future research. One research direction involves a deeper theoretical understanding of how self-attention mechanisms simulate gradient-based learning within the forward pass (garg2022whatcantransformers pages 11-13, lampinen2024thebroaderspectrum pages 2-4). Another direction is to explore better methods for prompt optimization and demonstration retrieval, aiming to mitigate the sensitivity issues inherent in ICL while maintaining its fluid adaptability (wang2307learningtoretrieve pages 1-2, min2022rethinkingtherole pages 1-2). Further investigation into hybrid systems that integrate explicit fine-tuning with in-context adaptation may also prove fruitful, potentially yielding frameworks that balance robustness with rapid adaptability in real-world deployments (sinha2024mamlenllmmodelagnostic pages 1-2).

sections.text: X. Conclusion  In summary, in-context learning for large language models diverges from traditional machine learning model training on multiple fundamental levels. Traditional training is characterized by explicit parameter updates through gradient descent on large datasets, resulting in a fixed model that is later deployed for inference. In contrast, ICL leverages pre-trained LLMs to dynamically adapt to new tasks based on the context provided at inference time, without any weight updates. This shift is enabled by the Transformer architecture’s self-attention mechanism, which captures intricate dependencies among input tokens and facilitates implicit learning via prompt conditioning. ICL thereby functions as a form of meta-learning, where models inherently “learn to learn” from context rather than undergoing explicit re-training, offering improved scalability, rapid task adaptation, and multi-task generalization. However, the approach is also fraught with challenges—most notably its sensitivity to prompt design and potential susceptibility to biases inherent in the pre-training data. Future research will likely focus on stabilizing ICL performance through better prompt engineering, hybrid learning frameworks, and further theoretical insights into the underlying mechanisms.  The differences outlined in this report underscore a paradigm shift that has broad implications for the design and deployment of advanced language processing systems. By enabling LLMs to dynamically reinterpret pre-trained knowledge with minimal computational overhead at inference time, in-context learning opens up innovative applications that were previously unattainable with conventional ML training. This new learning paradigm not only enhances performance in flexible, rapidly changing environments but also provides a pathway to more efficient and user-accessible model adaptation, representing a significant step forward in the field of artificial intelligence.  Keywords—In-context learning, large language models, meta-learning, Transformer, prompt-based conditioning, traditional machine learning, gradient descent, fine-tuning, dynamic adaptation, scalable inference.  In conclusion, the comparison of in-context learning and traditional training methods reveals that while both methodologies aim to equip models with the ability to generalize to unseen tasks, they embody fundamentally different mechanisms. Traditional training embeds knowledge in fixed model parameters through extensive optimization cycles, whereas in-context learning leverages the rich, implicit knowledge stored during pre-training and dynamically adapts to tasks using contextual cues provided in the prompt. This distinctive approach affords significant advantages in terms of adaptability, multi-task generalization, and computational efficiency, while also presenting new challenges related to prompt sensitivity and bias management. The evolution of these methods, as documented by extensive research, represents a promising frontier that is likely to redefine how intelligent systems are built and deployed in increasingly complex, real-world scenarios (akyurek2401incontextlanguagelearning pages 1-3, chan2022datadistributionalproperties pages 1-2, min2021metaicllearningto pages 1-2, wei2023largerlanguagemodels pages 10-12).  Through continued investigation and integration of insights across these diverse research efforts, the field is poised to develop models that not only adapt to a wide array of tasks rapidly but also do so while maintaining high levels of accuracy and robustness in unpredictable environments. This report has delineated the multi-faceted distinctions between ICL and conventional ML approaches, offering a comprehensive perspective to guide future research and practical implementations in the arena of large language models.  References to specific empirical studies and theoretical analyses within this report reinforce the notion that in-context learning is not merely an alternative training mechanism but a fundamentally new paradigm. The dynamic inference capability—and inherent flexibility—of ICL, as contrasted with the computationally demanding and inflexible nature of traditional retraining, signifies a pivotal transformation in contemporary machine learning practices that will undoubtedly influence both academic inquiry and industrial application in the years to come.  Ultimately, the evolution of in-context learning paradigms is both a reflection of and a catalyst for broader trends within artificial intelligence, where the emphasis is shifting towards models that can rapidly assimilate and apply new information in situ with minimal overhead—a departure from the rigid, parameter-centric methodologies of the past. As such, the insights presented herein lay a critical foundation for the continued enhancement and integration of in-context learning strategies into next-generation intelligent systems (pan2023cosmicdataefficient pages 1-2, jovanovic2404towardsincrementallearning pages 3-5, yang2023supervisedknowledgemakes pages 1-2).  This report has demonstrated, through detailed comparative analysis and synthesis of contemporary research, that in-context learning offers a fundamentally different approach from traditional model training, with unique strengths that can be harnessed for rapid task adaptation and multi-modal integration, as well as distinct technical challenges that must be addressed to maximize its potential in practical deployments.

question: what datasets are commonly used to evaluate SLAM methods

sections.text: The rapid evolution of Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) methods has been accompanied by the development of a wealth of datasets used to evaluate algorithm performance under diverse environmental conditions and sensor modalities. This report provides an in‐depth survey of the commonly used datasets in the SLAM research community. In doing so, it categorizes datasets based on sensor modality (e.g., RGB, RGB-D, stereo, inertial, LiDAR) and application domain (e.g., indoor robotics, outdoor autonomous driving, aerial vehicles, construction sites, and even underwater scenarios). We discuss the characteristics and evaluation methodologies associated with each dataset and highlight their importance for benchmarking and advancing SLAM research.

The evaluation and benchmarking of SLAM methods are critical for ensuring the robustness, accuracy, and adaptability of localization and mapping algorithms when deployed in real-world conditions. Over the years, a number of datasets have been curated that support testing under varying conditions, sensor setups, and application contexts. These datasets have served as standard benchmarks for comparisons across methods ranging from traditional visual SLAM to cutting‐edge visual–inertial and semantic SLAM frameworks. The datasets discussed herein provide vital ground truth information, synchronized sensor feeds, and realistic environmental challenges—including dynamic lighting, textureless regions, and rapid motion—which are indispensable for evaluating performance metrics such as Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE) (altawil2024areviewof pages 11-13). In the following sections, we provide a detailed discussion of these datasets, their sensor modalities, and the scenarios they represent.

sections.text: A significant focus in SLAM benchmarking has been dedicated to datasets that primarily supply visual information and synchronized depth or inertial data. The TUM RGB-D dataset, released in 2012, is among the most influential benchmarks. It offers RGB images recorded at 640×480 resolution along with 16-bit depth maps and is extensively used to evaluate both visual and RGB-D SLAM algorithms in indoor environments featuring diverse challenges such as dynamic objects, low-texture areas, and loop closures (altawil2024areviewof pages 11-13, kasarar1811benchmarkingandcomparing pages 1-3). In addition to TUM RGB-D, similar variants such as TUM-Mono have been widely utilized to assess monocular SLAM approaches (bavle2023fromslamto pages 9-11). The TUM datasets enable researchers to reliably measure drift and accuracy through metrics like ATE and RPE, making them indispensable in SLAM evaluations. The KITTI dataset has been equally influential, particularly for outdoor autonomous driving scenarios. It integrates data from stereo cameras, LiDAR, GPS, and IMU sensors, capturing urban and suburban environments with rich details in dynamic scenes (altawil2024areviewof pages 11-13, chen2022slamoverviewfrom pages 7-7). KITTI is extensively used to benchmark visual odometry (VO) and SLAM algorithms, especially in the context of self-driving vehicles, where sensor fusion and trajectory reconstruction are essential. These datasets provide ground truth trajectories derived from high-accuracy GNSS/INS systems, making them ideal for assessing translational and rotational errors in outdoor maneuvers. In addition to these well-known datasets, the EuRoC MAV dataset offers a benchmark targeting aerial robotics. Designed for micro aerial vehicles (MAVs), it provides synchronized stereo images, inertial measurement unit (IMU) data, and accurate ground truth from motion capture systems over indoor environments (altawil2024areviewof pages 11-13, bavle2023fromslamto pages 9-11). Its sequences, which include variations in motion patterns and illumination conditions, are essential for testing visual–inertial SLAM systems, where integration of inertial data is critical for mitigating drift. Other datasets such as ICL-NUIM and Bonn RGB-D have also contributed to the evaluation landscape by focusing on indoor scenarios. The ICL-NUIM dataset offers synthetic RGB-D sequences that have been used for assessing SLAM performance in terms of camera pose recovery and map reconstruction (altawil2024areviewof pages 11-13). In contrast, the Bonn RGB-D dynamic dataset introduces dynamic elements and variations in lighting conditions, challenging SLAM methods to cope with moving objects and non-ideal sensor observations (altawil2024areviewof pages 11-13). These complementary datasets provide a spectrum of challenges that encompass static scenes as well as those with significant dynamic content.

sections.text: While classic visual SLAM evaluation predominantly focused on monocular, stereo, or RGB-D cameras, modern SLAM systems increasingly incorporate data from inertial sensors, LiDAR, and even radar. Datasets such as the Euroc MAV dataset include tightly synchronized visual and inertial data that are crucial for visual–inertial odometry (altawil2024areviewof pages 15-15, bavle2023fromslamto pages 19-19). The integration of IMU measurements helps reduce sensitivity to rapid motions and illumination changes, thus enabling robust pose estimation. In addition to visual and inertial sensors, several benchmarks have started combining LiDAR with camera data to facilitate multi-modal SLAM development. The KITTI dataset, for instance, not only provides stereo images but also incorporates LiDAR scans to support occupancy mapping and dense 3D reconstruction tasks (chen2022anoverviewon pages 7-7, helmberger2022thehiltislam pages 7-8). Similarly, the Hilti SLAM Challenge dataset is distinguished by its multi-sensor setup, including multiple cameras, LiDAR, and IMU data, captured in challenging construction environments to push SLAM algorithms toward millimeter-level accuracy (helmberger2022thehiltislam pages 1-2, kaveti2023challengesofindoor pages 3-4). These datasets exemplify the trend towards sensor fusion as a means to handle real-world complexities, such as featureless areas and dynamic obstacles. Moreover, the open-source SLAM frameworks such as ORB-SLAM3 have been benchmarked using publicly available datasets that incorporate a range of modalities (altawil2024areviewof pages 15-15, tourani2022visualslamwhat pages 13-14). The availability of these datasets has encouraged the standardization of evaluation metrics and benchmarking tools like SLAMBench, which systematically quantify performance in terms of computational efficiency, map quality, and trajectory accuracy (bujanca2019slambench3.0systematic pages 1-2).

sections.text: Given the challenges in acquiring large-scale environmental data with accurate ground truth, synthetic datasets have become increasingly popular. Synthetic environments allow researchers to generate photorealistic images and sensor data, complete with comprehensive annotations that include camera poses, depth maps, and semantic segmentations. For example, the TartanAir dataset is a synthetic benchmark created using the Unreal Engine and AirSim, providing a diverse collection of sequences across urban, rural, nature, and even sci-fi themed environments (wang2020tartanairadataset pages 2-4). TartanAir addresses some of the deficiencies of traditional datasets by featuring varied motion patterns and complex scene dynamics, thereby challenging SLAM algorithms to generalize beyond simple, repetitive trajectories (wang2020tartanairadataset pages 8-8). In addition to TartanAir, other synthetic datasets such as SceneNet RGB-D and InteriorNet offer large-scale RGB-D image streams with high-fidelity ground truth data (shi2020areweready pages 7-7, prokhorov2019measuringrobustnessof pages 3-5). These datasets are especially valuable in scenarios where real-world data would be too sparse, noisy, or expensive to capture. Synthetic datasets also enable controlled experimentation, where parameters such as lighting conditions, occlusions, and camera motion can be systematically varied to study their impact on SLAM performance (wang2020asyntheticdataset pages 2-3, wang2020asyntheticdataset pages 4-5).

sections.text: An emerging area of research is long-term and lifelong SLAM, where the goal is to maintain robust localization and mapping over extended periods despite environmental changes. Datasets such as the Oxford RobotCar dataset capture more than 1000 km of driving data over the period of a year, offering a challenging benchmark for long-term SLAM algorithms in dynamic urban environments (bavle2023fromslamto pages 9-11, schmidt2024roveramultiseason pages 17-18). This dataset addresses the challenges of varying weather, seasonal changes, and lighting conditions, which are crucial for evaluating methods designed for persistent operation. Similarly, the Lifelong Robotic Vision challenge dataset is designed to assess SLAM robustness under long-term environmental changes including variations in lighting and scene layout (bujanca2021robustslamsystems pages 2-3). These datasets not only test the accuracy of real-time pose estimation but also the consistency and robustness of the generated maps over time—which is critical for applications such as service robotics and autonomous vehicles that operate continuously in dynamic environments (tourani2022visualslamwhat pages 5-6).

sections.text: Indoor environments pose a unique set of challenges for SLAM systems, including perceptual aliasing, dynamic obstacles, and repetitive architectural features. Datasets like the Indoormcd benchmark have been introduced to specifically address these challenges in low-cost multi-camera setups where RGB-D and IMU data are acquired in typical indoor settings such as offices, kitchens, and living rooms (sewtz2023indoormcdabenchmark pages 1-2). The Indoormcd dataset is particularly geared toward service robots, providing challenges such as motion blur, occlusions, and textureless surfaces while also delivering highly accurate ground truth from motion capture systems (sewtz2023indoormcdabenchmark pages 7-8). Additional indoor datasets include those collected by institutions such as Northeastern University, which offer multi-modal data spanning several floors (kaveti2023challengesofindoor pages 2-3). These datasets often combine data from stereo cameras, LiDAR sensors, and high-grade IMUs; the resulting synchronized data streams facilitate the evaluation of SLAM performance in environments with significant spatial symmetry and dynamic phenomena such as elevator transitions (kaveti2023challengesofindoor pages 3-4). Advanced benchmarks for indoor SLAM also address scenarios affected by changing lighting conditions and feature sparsity, providing a comprehensive framework for testing algorithm robustness and real-time performance (tourani2022visualslamwhat pages 13-14).

sections.text: SLAM methods are not only targeting indoor service robotics and outdoor autonomous vehicles; they are increasingly being applied in construction site monitoring and industrial environments. Datasets such as the Hilti SLAM Challenge dataset have been created specifically to capture data in construction sites where conditions such as featureless areas, varying illumination, and dynamic backgrounds present significant challenges (helmberger2022thehiltislam pages 1-2, trzeciak2023conslamconstructiondata pages 1-5). The Hilti dataset employs a multi-sensor platform that includes high-resolution cameras, LiDARs, and IMUs, all of which are meticulously calibrated to deliver highly accurate ground truth trajectories under challenging and rapidly evolving construction site environments. To further more specialized applications, the ConSLAM dataset was designed to address the need for periodic data collection over construction sites. Unlike datasets captured in static environments, ConSLAM collects sequences over multiple time instances, thereby facilitating progress monitoring and the benchmarking of SLAM in contexts where environmental changes occur incrementally (trzeciak2023conslamperiodicallycollected pages 1-3, trzeciak2023conslamconstructiondata pages 5-8). Such datasets are instrumental in supporting the development of SLAM systems that can adapt to long-term changes in industrial and construction sites, ensuring that the maps remain consistent as the environment evolves (trzeciak2023conslamperiodicallycollected pages 3-5).

sections.text: Beyond terrestrial robotics, the expansion of SLAM into underwater environments has necessitated the development of dedicated benchmarks. Underwater SLAM datasets, although less numerous primarily due to the difficulties associated with underwater data acquisition and ground truth generation, offer sequences recorded using specialized sensors such as monocular cameras, pressure sensors, and underwater IMUs (wang2023anoverviewof pages 20-23). These datasets support applications in marine robotics, where factors such as low visibility, dynamic illumination, and the turbulent behavior of water challenge traditional SLAM methods. The underwater datasets typically include both simulated and real-world sequences to provide a balanced evaluation framework that bridges controlled experiments with field deployments (wang2023anoverviewof pages 20-23). In addition, several multi-sensor and multi-scenario datasets for ground robots have been developed to capture a wide range of sensor inputs and operating conditions. For example, the M2DGR dataset specifically targets ground robots by integrating data from cameras, LiDAR, and inertial measurement units across various urban and semi-structured environments (yin2022m2dgramultisensor pages 7-8). The diversity of sensor modalities and environmental contexts in such datasets provides rich benchmarks for algorithms that combine feature extraction, sensor fusion, and dynamic map updating.

sections.text: The datasets discussed in this report are typically accompanied by evaluation frameworks that utilize standardized metrics to measure SLAM performance. Metrics such as Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE) are most commonly employed for quantitative assessment, allowing researchers to compare improvements in drift reduction and global consistency across algorithms (sturm2012abenchmarkfor pages 1-2, prokhorov2019measuringrobustnessof pages 5-6). In conjunction with these error metrics, benchmarking platforms such as SLAMBench provide comprehensive tools that quantify not only accuracy but also computational efficiency and energy consumption (bujanca2019slambench3.0systematic pages 1-2). The integration of such metrics ensures that improvements in SLAM algorithms can be reliably reproduced and compared across vastly different datasets—be they synthetic or acquired in real-world complex settings.

sections.text: The wide variety of datasets available for SLAM evaluation reflects the diversity of application domains and sensor modalities that modern SLAM systems must address. Classic datasets such as TUM RGB-D and KITTI have dominated the evaluation landscape for over a decade, yet rapid advancements in sensor technology and computing have spurred the creation of specialized benchmarks such as EuRoC MAV, Hilti SLAM Challenge, and Indoormcd. These benchmarks not only validate improvements in localization and mapping performance but also expose the limitations of current algorithms under challenging dynamic scenarios and long-term deployments (altawil2024areviewof pages 11-13, bavle2023fromslamto pages 9-11). Looking toward the future, there is a clear trend toward fusing multiple sensor modalities—including RGB, depth, inertial, and LiDAR data—to achieve robust localization in real-world environments. Furthermore, synthetic datasets like TartanAir and SceneNet RGB-D will continue to play a pivotal role by providing detailed control over environmental variables, allowing researchers to rigorously test algorithms in conditions that would be impractical to replicate in the field (wang2020tartanairadataset pages 2-4, wang2020asyntheticdataset pages 2-3). Similarly, datasets focused on long-term and lifelong SLAM, such as Oxford RobotCar and the Lifelong Robotic Vision challenge dataset, will be critical in ensuring that mapping systems remain robust despite environmental changes over extended periods (bavle2023fromslamto pages 9-11, bujanca2021robustslamsystems pages 2-3). Specialized applications, from construction monitoring with ConSLAM to underwater SLAM, also indicate that the scope of SLAM evaluation is broadening. Emerging benchmarks in these domains will drive the development of new algorithms capable of handling specific challenges such as periodic environmental alterations, low-visibility conditions, and complex multi-floor indoor environments (trzeciak2023conslamperiodicallycollected pages 1-3, wang2023anoverviewof pages 20-23). Ultimately, the growing richness and diversity of SLAM datasets empower researchers to rigorously test algorithms not only under ideal conditions but also in complex, dynamic, and multi-sensor scenarios. This trend is expected to further accelerate the integration of SLAM into commercial products and real-world applications ranging from autonomous vehicles to service robots and beyond.

sections.text: In summary, the commonly used datasets for evaluating SLAM methods encompass a broad range of environments, sensor modalities, and application scenarios. Standard benchmarks such as TUM RGB-D and KITTI remain fundamental, with complementary datasets like EuRoC MAV and ICL-NUIM supporting indoor visual–inertial SLAM research. Multi-modal datasets—from those including LiDAR and multiple cameras to synthetic benchmarks like TartanAir—facilitate the evaluation of sensor fusion techniques and enable the development of robust long-term SLAM systems. Meanwhile, specialized datasets address emerging applications in construction, underwater navigation, and multi-floor indoor environments, ensuring that SLAM research continues to evolve in step with real-world challenges. Moving forward, sustained efforts in constructing comprehensive datasets and standardized evaluation protocols will be critical to further advancing SLAM technologies and ensuring their reliable deployment in increasingly complex operational scenarios (altawil2024areviewof pages 15-15, tourani2022visualslamwhat pages 5-6). In conclusion, the diversity of SLAM datasets—ranging from TUM RGB-D, KITTI, and EuRoC MAV for conventional visual and visual–inertial challenges, to synthetic benchmarks and domain-specific datasets such as Hilti SLAM Challenge, Indoormcd, and ConSLAM—provides the necessary ground for systematic evaluation, comparison, and subsequent improvement of SLAM systems across a wide spectrum of applications (bavle2023fromslamto pages 19-19, sewtz2023indoormcdabenchmark pages 1-2). This comprehensive benchmarking landscape ultimately drives the innovation necessary for SLAM systems to be successfully deployed in increasingly demanding real-world environments. References to evaluation methodologies based on metrics such as ATE and RPE, along with benchmarking platforms like SLAMBench, ensure that experimental results are objective, reproducible, and directly comparable across different studies. As SLAM research continues to push the boundaries of sensor fusion, dynamic adaptation, and long-term consistency, the role of well-curated benchmarking datasets will remain central to both academic research and industry innovation (sturm2012abenchmarkfor pages 2-3, prokhorov2019measuringrobustnessof pages 5-6). This report underscores the importance of datasets in driving the ongoing development of SLAM methodologies. With the continual refinement of evaluation frameworks and the introduction of new datasets that address previously underexplored challenges, the research community is well equipped to tackle diverse applications—whether in urban driving, indoor service robotics, construction monitoring, or even underwater exploration. The trend toward multi-sensor and multi-modal data fusion, combined with the systematic use of synthetic datasets as supplements to real-world data, will further support advancements in SLAM that are not only theoretically robust but also practical in complex, operational settings (helmberger2022thehiltislam pages 2-3, yin2022m2dgramultisensor pages 7-8). In summary, SLAM evaluation has matured from using a limited set of homogeneous benchmark datasets to employing a broad range of specialized, multi-range, and multi-modal datasets that capture the complexities of real-world environments. These comprehensive benchmarks provide the necessary means for quantitative evaluation of SLAM systems and will continue to drive improvement in both algorithm design and practical application across the wide spectrum of robotics and autonomous systems.

question: Can you recommend a suitable theoretical lens for qualitative research concerning robotics process automation (RPA) implementations?

sections.text:
Robotic Process Automation (RPA) has emerged as a transformative technology that automates structured, repetitive tasks by mimicking human interactions with digital systems. Its adoption, however, is not merely a technical implementation; it requires a profound organizational change in how work is understood, executed, and optimized. Qualitative research into RPA implementations must therefore delve into the socio
es-technical complexities that underpin these transitions. Among the multiple theoretical lenses available to guide such inquiry, an integrated framework grounded in Normalization Process Theory (NPT) and sensemaking/sensegiving processes stands out as a particularly robust candidate. This report examines the suitability of this lens by positioning it against alternative theoretical frameworks such as sociotechnical imaginaries, configuration theory, and established IT adoption models from organizational and technology acceptance literature.

A variety of theoretical perspectives are represented within the literature on RPA implementations. Early studies on RPA emphasize the importance of proper planning and strategic coordination when undertaking automation projects, highlighting the need for theoretical constructs that incorporate both technical and organizational dynamics (fernandez2021planningfora pages 3-6). Similarly, qualitative research in the banking sector has underscored that RPA adoption is not solely an issue of system functionality but involves complex, multi-level interactions among technicians, operational staff, and management (harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 8-12). To capture this confluence of factors, researchers have advocated for lenses that blend elements from established technology adoption models such as the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) with organizational theories like the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework (harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 28-31).A notable development is the introduction of a theoretical framework that centers on the concept of the “collective user” and integrates factors at both individual and organizational levels (harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 87-91). However, while these lenses deliver insights into acceptance and usage, they often fall short of capturing the dynamic, processual nature of RPA implementation. In contrast, the proposed framework based on Normalization Process Theory (NPT) – coupled with sensemaking and sensegiving theories – offers a process-oriented perspective that illuminates how organizational members negotiate, interpret, and embed new technologies into their daily practices (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 45-48).The concept of sensemaking, originally articulated within organizational studies, refers to the processes through which individuals interpret ambiguous or disruptive events. In the context of RPA, sensemaking helps researchers understand how employees reconcile their prior work routines with emerging automated workflows. Complementary to this is the idea of sensegiving, which is concerned with the deliberate attempts by organizational leaders or influential agents to shape the interpretation of change among stakeholders. Together, these processes are vital in explaining how a new technology like RPA is not simply accepted, but actively assimilated into the organizational fabric while provoking both support and resistance (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 43-45).Furthermore, qualitative investigations in RPA have benefited from a constructivist perspective – one that recognizes the existence of multiple subjective realities and acknowledges that knowledge is co-created in social interactions (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 7-10). Studies in the banking sector demonstrate that this approach, which combines grounded theory with pattern-matching techniques, enables researchers to capture the nuanced interpretations of organizational actors and the iterative nature of RPA implementation (harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 41-44). Parallel research has also employed configuration theory to account for the multifaceted and context-specific configurations of employees’ perceptions regarding RPA. Configuration theory highlights nonlinearity, synergistic effects, and equifinality in understanding organizational change (waizenegger2022whenrobotsjoin pages 7-9). Yet, its primary focus on employees’ subjective experiences may present limitations when the broader organizational routines and normalization practices require exploration.Sociotechnical perspectives provide another avenue for inquiry. Research on sociotechnical imaginaries, particularly in public-sector contexts, underscores that RPA adoption is as much about collectively held visions of the future as it is about technical efficiency (toll2022sociotechnicalimaginariesof pages 21-24, toll2022sociotechnicalimaginariesof pages 28-32). These lenses are extremely valuable when studying the normative and political dimensions of automation in settings such as municipalities. Nonetheless, in contexts where RPA is implemented in highly regulated and complex corporate environments, such as banking or large-scale service operations, an integrated framework that merges the processual insights of NPT with the meaning-making focus of sensemaking/sensegiving theories is more directly aligned with the empirical phenomena observed.

sections.text: Normalization Process Theory (NPT) is designed to explain how new practices become embedded and sustained within organizational routines. It comprises key dimensions including coherence (shared understanding), cognitive participation (engagement by stakeholders), collective action (practical work to implement the change), and reflexive monitoring (ongoing appraisal and adaptation). This framework is particularly adept at capturing the iterative nature of technological implementation—exactly the kind of dynamic process often encountered in RPA adoption (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 48-50).When layered with sensemaking and sensegiving theories, the combined perspective not only evaluates how new practices are normalized but also explains how meanings are constructed and communicated throughout the change process. This dual focus is crucial because RPA implementations frequently disrupt established work routines and necessitate significant reconfigurations in employees’ roles and responsibilities (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 50-54). Sensemaking, in this setting, refers to the ways in which organizational members interpret ambiguous signals, negotiate what the technology means for their work, and ultimately arrive at a shared understanding that facilitates routine adoption. Sensegiving, on the other hand, involves the communicative actions that leaders and change agents undertake to shape these understandings and foster a conducive environment for technology integration (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 45-48).

sections.text: While the NPT–sensemaking/sensegiving framework is highly recommended for its comprehensiveness, it is instructive to compare it with other potential theoretical lenses. For instance, configuration theory, as used by Waizenegger and Techatassanasoontorn, effectively accounts for multi-dimensional patterns in employees’ perceptions and reactions (waizenegger2022whenrobotsjoin pages 3-5, waizenegger2022whenrobotsjoin pages 20-22). Though particularly strong in highlighting the nuanced, context-dependent responses of employees, configuration theory can sometimes lack the process orientation necessary to explain how initial interpretations evolve into sustained practices. Furthermore, while sociotechnical imaginaries provide a rich account of collective visions and normative dimensions in public-sector automation (toll2022sociotechnicalimaginariesof pages 35-39, toll2022sociotechnicalimaginariesof pages 39-43), they are most effective when the research focus is on inter-organizational and policy-level dynamics rather than the embedded practices within a single organization.In contrast, established IT adoption models—including the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Diffusion of Innovations (DOI), and the integrated TOE framework—tend to focus on factors such as perceived usefulness, ease of use, management support, and environmental pressures (tew2020investigatingthefactors pages 15-17, tew2020investigatingthefactors pages 56-58). While these frameworks are very useful in quantitative settings and provide clarity on the pre-adoption decision variables, they are limited by their inherently linear and individualistic assumptions. The dynamic, socially complex process observed in RPA implementations requires a lens that transcends these limitations by capturing the iterative and negotiated nature of organizational change.Thus, the integrated NPT and sensemaking/sensegiving approach is particularly well-suited because it not only recognizes the role of objective factors—such as system characteristics and management support—but also foregrounds the interpretive processes through which these factors are understood and acted upon within organizations (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 48-50, tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 50-54).

sections.text: When applying the integrated theoretical lens in empirical research, qualitative methodologies such as case studies and semi-structured interviews are recommended. For instance, a retrospective case study design could be employed to explore how a major bank or large-scale service organization implemented RPA over several years (harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 41-44). Semi-structured interviews with a diverse set of stakeholders—ranging from frontline employees to senior managers and IT professionals—can capture the breadth of perspectives and unfolding narratives associated with RPA adoption. The methodological emphasis should be on theoretical sampling, ensuring that the voices included span different levels of organizational hierarchy and functional domains (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 40-43).Data analysis in this framework should utilize a pattern-matching approach, comparing emergent themes related to coherence, cognitive participation, collective action, and reflexive monitoring against existing theoretical constructs (harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 41-44). This iterative coding process, which aligns with principles of grounded theory, facilitates the identification of sensemaking and sensegiving episodes—moments when organizational actors explicitly articulate the meaning of RPA and attempt to influence others’ perceptions. Such a methodological approach is well-documented as being conducive to uncovering the subtle interactions and negotiations that define successful normalization of new technologies (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 54-57).Furthermore, this integrated lens encourages the researcher to pay close attention to communication artifacts—such as emails, meeting minutes, and internal reports—which provide supplementary insights into how managerial direction and employee interpretation are reconciled through everyday organizational discourse. The inclusion of these additional data sources not only enhances triangulation but also provides deeper contextual background that enriches the interpretation of interview data (harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 38-41).

sections.text: The theoretical contribution of adopting the NPT–sensemaking/sensegiving integrated framework is multifaceted. First, it extends traditional IT adoption theories by incorporating a temporal dimension that accounts for the evolution of meaning over time. Rather than treating acceptance as a one-off event, this lens captures the ongoing dialogue between employees and management as they adjust to new operational realities underpinned by RPA (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 45-48).Second, this approach offers practical insights for managing RPA implementations. For instance, by recognizing that sensemaking activities often begin at the grassroots level, organizations can design interventions that facilitate bottom-up communication channels, thereby accelerating the normalization of automated practices. The framework also underscores the importance of reflexive monitoring, suggesting that continuous feedback loops help organizations adapt and refine RPA deployment in response to emerging challenges and opportunities (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 50-54).Moreover, the integration of NPT with sensemaking and sensegiving theory fosters a more human-centered approach to RPA implementation. This is essential because the success of automation not only rests on technological adequacy but also on how well human actors can integrate these technologies into their routines while preserving job satisfaction and organizational cohesion. The insights gained from these qualitative investigations can inform training programs, communication strategies, and change management practices to mitigate resistance and enhance overall performance (harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 34-38).Finally, by situating RPA within a broader constructivist paradigm, this integrated lens challenges deterministic views of technology adoption. Instead of perceiving RPA merely as a tool imposed by managerial fiat, the framework emphasizes the agency of employees who co-construct the meaning of technology through everyday interactions. This perspective not only yields richer empirical insights but also aligns with contemporary calls for more inclusive and participatory research approaches in the field of digital transformation (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 7-10).

sections.text: While the integrated lens offers significant advantages, it is important to recognize its boundaries. For example, the framework may require adaptation when applied to organizational contexts that differ substantially from those examined in previous case studies, such as public-sector environments with strong bureaucratic control (toll2022sociotechnicalimaginariesof pages 21-24). In such cases, researchers might consider complementing the core framework with additional sociotechnical or institutional theories to fully capture the external pressures and normative dynamics at play.Furthermore, while NPT and sensemaking/sensegiving theories provide a robust structure for examining the normalization of technology, the inherently iterative and context-specific nature of these processes means that generalization across different industries may be challenging. Future research could therefore aim to conduct comparative case studies across sectors—such as banking, health care, and public administration—to test the applicability of the integrated lens under varying conditions. Such investigation would also benefit from exploring how digital platforms, evolving regulatory frameworks, and emerging workforce demographics interact with RPA implementations, potentially leading to the refinement of the theoretical framework (tew2020investigatingthefactors pages 58-61).Moreover, integrating quantitative measures with the qualitative insights derived from an NPT–sensemaking/sensegiving approach may yield a mixed-methods framework that further enhances our understanding of RPA outcomes. For example, subsequent studies could test whether organizations that exhibit higher levels of coherent sensemaking and effective sensegiving are statistically more likely to achieve sustained RPA adoption and improved operational metrics. This integration would not only validate the qualitative findings but also offer practical metrics for organizations to monitor during the implementation process.

sections.text: In conclusion, the integrated framework that combines Normalization Process Theory with sensemaking and sensegiving theories is a highly suitable theoretical lens for qualitative research on RPA implementations. This lens is particularly adept at capturing the dynamic, processual nature of technology adoption by uncovering how new practices become embedded in organizational routines through iterative, socially negotiated meaning-making. Unlike traditional IT adoption frameworks that often focus solely on tangible system attributes or individual-level acceptance factors, the NPT–sensemaking/sensegiving approach provides a holistic view that reflects the complex interplay between technology, organizational structure, and human agency.By emphasizing the importance of coherence, cognitive participation, collective action, and reflexive monitoring, this framework enables researchers to systematically explore how RPA is understood, communicated, and normalized over time. Empirical studies implementing this lens can draw upon qualitative methods such as in-depth case studies and semi-structured interviews, supported by triangulation through supplementary documents. These investigations not only enrich theoretical understanding but also yield practical recommendations for change management and organizational design in environments undergoing digital transformation.Given the extensive evidence in the literature and the close alignment of this approach with the observed challenges in RPA implementation, it is recommended as a valuable theoretical instrument for qualitative research in this domain (tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 45-48, tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 50-54, harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 41-44). Researchers who adopt this integrated lens will be better equipped to unravel the nuanced social and cognitive dimensions of RPA adoption, thereby contributing to more effective implementation strategies and a deeper understanding of the socio-technical dynamics that shape contemporary organizational change.This recommendation builds on a robust body of research that highlights the limitations of traditional, linear models of technology adoption, while simultaneously demonstrating the value of interpretive, constructivist paradigms in explaining complex digital transformations. In the context of RPA implementations—characterized by their inherent ambiguity, dynamic change processes, and significant organizational impact—the combined NPT and sensemaking/sensegiving lens offers a comprehensive framework that addresses both the technical and human dimensions of change.Ultimately, the insights derived from applying this integrated framework have significant implications for both researchers and practitioners. For researchers, it opens pathways to more nuanced investigations that can bridge the gap between theory and practice. For practitioners, understanding the underlying meaning-making processes and normalization strategies provides actionable guidance for managing change more effectively, thereby increasing the likelihood of successful and sustainable RPA deployments.By favoring an approach that respects the complexity of human-technology interactions and the layered nature of organizational change, the integrated theoretical lens recommended herein represents one of the most promising directions for future qualitative research on RPA implementations.(fernandez2021planningfora pages 3-6, harning2020managingroboticsprocess pages 8-12, tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 45-48, tasdogan2021implementationofrobotic pages 50-54)

question: What are metrics to mesures the quality of human robot communication?

sections.text: Human–robot communication quality represents a multidimensional construct that encompasses not only the efficiency and fluency of task-related exchanges but also the affective and social components of interaction. In this context, quality refers to how naturally a robot can communicate its intentions, respond to human cues, and participate as a collaborative partner—a task that involves both verbal and nonverbal modalities, including speech, gestures, facial expressions, gaze, and timing cues (abich2017theimpactof pages 1-2). Ambiguous terms such as “multimodal communication” denote the integration of several communicative channels simultaneously, while “fluency” or “engagement” refers to the smooth coordination and rhythm of turn-taking and joint attention between human and robot (hoffman2019evaluatingfluencyin pages 1-2). The overall goal of establishing reliable metrics in HRI is to provide a quantifiable means of assessing these aspects, thereby facilitating comparisons across different robotic systems and interaction scenarios.

sections.text: Subjective metrics are based on human self-reports and assessments and involve evaluating parameters such as perceived mental workload, usability preference, communication clarity, trust, and expectations of robot behavior. For example, Abich and Barber emphasize that mental workload, usability, and behavioral expectations are key indicators used in studies on human–robot multimodal communication, as these subjective evaluations help determine how taxing the communication process is for users and how they perceive the robot as a collaborator (abich2017theimpactof pages 1-2). Research in this area often makes use of standardized questionnaires such as the NASA Task Load Index (NASA TLX) to capture cognitive load and various Likert-scale based surveys to measure attributes like satisfaction, trustworthiness, and clarity of communication (hamacher2016believinginbert pages 2-3). In addition, assessments such as the Godspeed questionnaire and other validated scales have been deployed to gauge anthropomorphic perceptions, friendliness, and social intelligence exhibited by robots, ensuring that the subjective experience matches the intended design of robot behavior (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 278-280).
