sections.text: Objective metrics focus on quantifiable, observable aspects of human–robot interactions. These metrics include timing-related measurements such as task execution time, idle times for both humans and robots, and metrics related to reaction and response durations. For instance, Gombolay et al. measured team fluency by analyzing assembly time, rescheduling time, and idle time to infer the efficiency and smoothness of human–robot collaboration (gombolay2015decisionmakingauthorityteam pages 11-12). In dynamic settings, metrics related to turn-taking, such as the latency between a robot’s cue and the human’s response, as well as the degree and duration of concurrent activity, serve as reliable proxies for evaluating communication fluency (hoffman2019evaluatingfluencyin pages 9-10). Other objective measures include tracking gaze behavior by analyzing both the frequency and duration of looks toward the robot’s face or hands and monitoring nonverbal cues such as body posture stability and head movements, which are critical indicators of engagement (anzalone2015evaluatingtheengagement pages 5-7).

sections.text: Given that human–robot communication is inherently multimodal, effective evaluation relies on metrics that capture behaviors across several channels simultaneously. Nonverbal cues such as gestures, facial expressions, and gaze are essential for signaling intent and managing turn-taking in communication. Anzalone et al. describe how the measurement of static posture and dynamic synchrony (e.g., motor imitation and joint attention) provide quantifiable insights into how receptive humans are to robot signals (anzalone2015evaluatingtheengagement pages 10-12). Metrics such as gaze clustering—the analysis of focused regions and head orientation—and measures of gesture frequency and duration in naturalistic settings help discern the quality of implicit signals, allowing researchers to evaluate not only the presence of such cues but also their timing and coordination with verbal modalities (ivaldi2017towardsengagementmodels pages 2-3). By capturing the interactions through video recordings and using specialized software for behavioral coding, one can determine the extent to which nonverbal synchrony correlates with increased social presence and perceived reliability of the robotic agent (ivaldi2017towardsengagementmodels pages 9-13).

sections.text: One critical dimension of human–robot communication is fluency, which reflects the seamless coordination between participants. Fluency metrics are designed to capture temporal dynamics, including turn-taking durations, delays in response, and the proportion of idle times. Hoffman’s work on fluency in human–robot collaboration introduces objective measures such as human idle time (H-IDLE), robot idle time (R-IDLE), and functional delay (F-DEL), each of which correlates with subjective impressions of overall fluency (hoffman2019evaluatingfluencyin pages 1-2). In practical terms, a reduction in functional delays and a balance in the distribution of idle times can indicate effective communication and synchrony between agents, which is perceived by users as smooth interaction flow (hoffman2019evaluatingfluencyin pages 7-9). Furthermore, concurrent activity metrics—capturing the extent of parallel motion or simultaneous engagement in a shared task—serve as objective indicators of joint collaboration efficacy and assist in benchmarking different communication strategies in collaborative environments (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 257-259).

sections.text: In settings where robots perform complex tasks in coordination with humans—such as assembly operations, object handovers, or navigation—the quality of communication is inherently tied to measurable task performance. For example, Lasota and Shah analyzed the effects of human-aware robot motion planning and assessed metrics such as task execution time, concurrent motion, and spatial separation to evaluate collaboration quality (lasota2015analyzingtheeffects pages 4-6). Similarly, in handover tasks, metrics extend beyond simple task success rates and include measures such as transfer time, waiting time, applied force, and post-handover usability. Ortenzi et al. propose that evaluating the clarity of communication signals—both explicit, such as spoken instructions, and implicit, such as gaze and body movements—can determine if a robot’s intention in a handover is properly conveyed, thereby ensuring that the recipient is able to engage seamlessly with the object (ortenzi2021objecthandoversa pages 8-9). These metrics are essential because an effective handover not only depends on successful object transfer but also on the natural continuation of task progression post-transfer, which hinges on clear, well-coordinated communication (ortenzi2021objecthandoversa pages 13-15).

sections.text: Beyond behavioral and performance-based measures, psychophysiological metrics offer additional layers of insight into the quality of human–robot communication. These include physiological responses such as heart rate, skin conductance, and facial electromyography, which can reflect the level of stress, engagement, or comfort experienced during interaction (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 144-146). Observational techniques, such as video coding of interaction sessions, further allow for the analysis of spontaneous behaviors—including reaction times, synchrony of movements, and even subtle cues like micro-expressions—that are not easily captured by self-report instruments (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 404-406). These mixed-method approaches are particularly valuable because they provide a richer understanding of how participants experience and respond to robot communication under varying conditions (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 417-418).

sections.text: Trust is a critical component of effective human–robot communication and is influenced by multiple dimensions including reliability, transparency, and emotional expressiveness. The work with BERT, a humanoid robot, highlights that communicative expressiveness—through both speech and facial cues—can enhance trust even when the robot makes errors, and that self-reported trust ratings combined with behavioral measures (such as willingness to continue interaction) serve as useful metrics for evaluating communication quality (hamacher2016believinginbert pages 2-3, hamacher2016believinginbert pages 6-7). In addition, multi-dimensional trust scales that assess both performance-based aspects (such as robot accuracy and consistency) and moral or social characteristics (such as politeness and perceived empathy) are increasingly being recommended to capture a fuller picture of the quality of interaction (malle2021amultidimensionalconception pages 9-11). These metrics ensure that the evaluation of communication does not solely focus on task efficiency but also on the relational dimensions that underlie sustained human–robot partnerships.

sections.text: When robots engage in tasks that involve navigation in shared human spaces—as well as in scenarios of human–robot teaming—the quality of communication becomes interwoven with factors such as safety, legibility, and social acceptance. In such instances, metrics must capture not only the technical aspects of motion planning but also the communicative intent behind navigational behaviors. Francis et al. discuss how social navigation metrics include measures of comfort, legibility, and the degree to which the robot conveys its intentions through movement patterns that comply with social norms (francis2025principlesandguidelines pages 12-13, francis2025principlesandguidelines pages 13-14). Furthermore, these metrics are often derived from both direct human feedback—via questionnaires that assess perceived safety and approachability—and algorithmic evaluations such as the minimum time to collision and personal space compliance, which serve as proxies for effective communication of intent in dynamic environments (francis2025principlesandguidelines pages 16-17).

sections.text: No single metric is able to capture the full spectrum of human–robot communication quality, and thus researchers advocate for a combined, multimodal approach. Integrating subjective user ratings, objective behavioral data, and psychophysiological responses helps create a more comprehensive evaluation framework (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 31-36). For example, combining metrics such as NASA TLX scores for mental workload, observed idle times for turn-taking efficiency, and gaze tracking for attentional focus provides a robust basis for comparing different communication strategies and robot designs (abich2017theimpactof pages 1-2, hoffman2019evaluatingfluencyin pages 1-2). This ensemble approach not only enhances the reliability of the evaluation but also helps mitigate the limitations inherent in each individual measurement method by validating subjective findings with objective indicators (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 257-259).

sections.text: The experimental design plays a crucial role in the effective measurement of communication quality in HRI. Researchers stress that valid and reliable metrics often require rigorous protocols that combine multiple data collection techniques, including questionnaires, direct behavioral observations, video recordings, and sensor-based tracking (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 404-406). Moreover, approaches such as “Wizard of Oz” studies are frequently used in early-stage research to simulate naturalistic interactions that might otherwise be challenging to program fully autonomously, thereby enabling the capture of rich communication data in controlled environments (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 54-57). It is also critical to account for context-specific variables such as the setting (laboratory versus field), the familiarity of participants with the robot, and cultural factors that may influence communication styles and expectations (gasteiger2023factorsforpersonalization pages 6-6). The integration of these considerations ensures that the chosen metrics are both sensitive and specific to the intended application of the HRI system.

sections.text: A particularly illustrative example of applying communication quality metrics can be found in object handover tasks, where the successful transfer of an item depends on both physical coordination and effective communication cues. In these scenarios, performance metrics such as success rates, transfer times, and force measurements (e.g., applied force during grasping and load detection) play a critical role in evaluating the interaction (ortenzi2021objecthandoversa pages 8-9). Furthermore, subjective assessments—including evaluations of how natural the handover felt and whether the receiver needed to adjust the object post-handover—are often collected through participant questionnaires, thereby providing insight into the perceived clarity and effectiveness of the robot’s communicative actions during the handover (ortenzi2021objecthandoversa pages 12-12). Such case studies underscore the importance of integrating both objective technical metrics and human-centered evaluations when assessing communication quality in task-specific contexts (ortenzi2021objecthandoversa pages 13-15).

sections.text: Despite the progress made in identifying and applying metrics for human–robot communication, significant challenges remain. One major issue is the standardization of measurement methods across different studies and applications—a challenge that stems from the diverse nature of HRI contexts and the inherent subjectivity of some key indicators, such as engagement and trust (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 417-418). Another challenge is the integration and synchronization of multimodal data; as human–robot communication often involves parallel channels (verbal, visual, tactile, etc.), ensuring that all these data streams are accurately captured, aligned, and interpreted requires both sophisticated sensor technologies and advanced data analysis techniques (ivaldi2017towardsengagementmodels pages 9-13). Future research directions are likely to involve the development of adaptive learning models that combine hand-crafted and learned metrics to provide real-time feedback on communication quality, as well as efforts to validate comprehensive measurement frameworks across varied interaction contexts (ajoudani2018progressandprospects pages 11-12). The ultimate goal is to create evaluation protocols that are both reproducible and sensitive to the nuances of naturalistic human–robot interactions.

sections.text: In summary, the quality of human–robot communication is best captured using a multidimensional suite of metrics that encompass subjective evaluations (mental workload, trust, satisfaction, perceived usability), objective behavioral measures (turn-taking, idle times, task completion times, gaze tracking, gesture synchrony), and psychophysiological indicators (heart rate, skin conductance, facial expressions). Furthermore, application-specific metrics that evaluate the naturalness and efficacy of interactions—for example, in object handover tasks or social navigation scenarios—are essential for a complete assessment. By employing a combined approach that integrates multiple measurement modalities, researchers can obtain a robust, comprehensive understanding of how effectively robots communicate with human partners, thereby informing the design of more intuitive and socially competent robotic systems (abich2017theimpactof pages 1-2, anzalone2015evaluatingtheengagement pages 1-3, hoffman2019evaluatingfluencyin pages 1-2). This report has discussed metrics spanning subjective self-assessments, objective timing and synchrony data, and task-specific performance indicators, emphasizing the need for standardization and multimodal integration in future research efforts. The challenges identified—including the need for adaptive measurement techniques and standardized evaluation protocols—suggest promising avenues for advancing the field of human–robot communication evaluation (lindblom2020evaluatingtheuser pages 285-287, francis2025principlesandguidelines pages 14-15). Overall, the integration of these multidimensional metrics plays a crucial role in optimizing human–robot interactions by ensuring that robots are not only mechanically efficient but also capable of effective, trustworthy, and natural communication with their human collaborators (tabrez2020asurveyof pages 4-5, hamacher2016believinginbert pages 7-8, ortenzi2021objecthandoversa pages 11-11). Future research will continue to refine these measures and explore novel ways of assessing communication quality, ultimately contributing to more successful and acceptable human–robot systems in diverse real-world applications.

question: In auditory speech perception using iEEG, I will use Temporal Response Function (TRF) to determine correlations between stimulus characteristics (variations in the acoustic signal envelope, for example) and characteristics of recorded neuronal activity. I would like to fully understand the different stages of data processing carried out, as well as the reasoning and hypotheses behind them.

sections.text: The goal of this report is to provide a comprehensive overview of the various stages involved in processing intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) data when using Temporal Response Function (TRF) analyses to determine correlations between continuous speech stimulus characteristics—such as fluctuations in the acoustic envelope—and recorded neuronal activity, with a focus on the auditory speech perception paradigm (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 1-2).

sections.text: In this work we describe an end‐to‐end data processing pipeline that spans from stimulus design and feature extraction to neural data preprocessing, TRF model estimation, and subsequent validation of the inferred brain–stimulus relationships in iEEG recordings during auditory speech perception (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 2-2). The pipeline begins with the extraction of perceptually relevant acoustic features that capture both the general envelope dynamics as well as finer aspects of the speech signal (bolt2024auditoryencodingof pages 3-5). Subsequent preprocessing of the neural data, which includes sophisticated artifact rejection and filtering, ensures that only the relevant neural signals are analyzed (bolt2024auditoryencodingof pages 5-6). Following preprocessing, multivariate regression techniques—with emphasis on regularization approaches such as ridge regression and boosting—are employed to estimate the TRF that characterizes the linear mapping between time‐lagged stimulus features and the neural response (crosse2016themultivariatetemporal pages 1-2). Dynamic modifications to the TRF—including single‐trial, context‐dependent adjustments—facilitate capturing rapid, adaptive, and task-dependent changes in neural responses (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 20-22). The processing sequence is supported by insights from computational auditory neuroscience, which hypothesize that the brain can be approximated as a linear time‐invariant system under controlled conditions, albeit subject to adaptive nonlinearities (donhauser2020twodistinctneural pages 15-17). Ultimately, the TRF framework provides a window into the hierarchical processing of speech from the acoustic periphery to higher cortical and subcortical regions, offering both temporal and spatial resolution in the analysis (gillis2022neuraltrackingas pages 19-20). Our discussion synthesizes strategies from past studies and integrates them with current hypotheses regarding the functional significance of specific TRF components (lindboom2023incorporatingmodelsof pages 1-4).

sections.text: Auditory speech perception is a complex process that invokes a cascade of neural events beginning from the initial encoding of acoustic signals in the peripheral auditory system and culminating in high-level linguistic interpretation in the cortex (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 1-2). The use of intracranial EEG (iEEG) provides exceptionally high temporal resolution that is crucial for elucidating the rapid dynamics of neuronal activity in response to continuous natural speech (bolt2024auditoryencodingof pages 3-5). A major challenge in this field is accurately mapping the detailed temporal structure of continuous speech—particularly its envelope fluctuations—to the time‐locked features of the iEEG response, which necessitates advanced analytical techniques (crosse2016themultivariatetemporal pages 2-3). Temporal Response Function analysis, which relies on the convolution of stimulus features with an impulse response kernel, has emerged as a powerful strategy to establish such mappings without resorting to traditional averaging methods that obscure dynamic changes (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 2-2). In the TRF framework, the brain is modeled as an essentially linear system that transforms various aspects of the acoustic stimulus into measurable evoked responses while acknowledging that additional nonlinear transformations occur at subcortical levels (bolt2024exploringcognitivedecline pages 35-37). This linear modeling approach is particularly appealing because it enables single‐trial analyses and captures rapid shifts in neural response properties that have been linked to attention and plasticity mechanisms (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 4-7). The motivation behind applying TRF analysis to iEEG data lies in its potential to uncover fine-grained, time-resolved correlations between specific acoustic parameters—such as amplitude modulations, onsets, and spectro-temporal representations—and neural activity (crosse2021linearmodelingof pages 7-9). Furthermore, advanced data processing techniques, including stimulus-aware spatial filtering and robust regression methods, are employed to address the inherently low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) typical of intracranial recordings (das2020stimulusawarespatialfiltering pages 1-4). These methodological choices have been shaped by a series of hypotheses that posit the existence of distinct neural response components—each associated with particular time lags and stimulus features—that underlie auditory perception (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 22-24). The following sections describe in detail the data processing stages, from stimulus feature extraction and neural recording preprocessing to the precise estimation of TRFs and the interpretation of their temporal structure (crosse2016themultivariatetemporal pages 1-2).

sections.text: The data acquisition phase involves recording high-fidelity intracranial EEG signals from subjects engaged in naturalistic speech listening tasks, thereby ensuring that the neural responses reflect real-world auditory processing (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 1-2). Stimuli are typically derived from continuous speech streams such as audiobook excerpts or competing-speaker scenes, ensuring that the acoustic signal contains naturally varying temporal envelope characteristics (bolt2024auditoryencodingof pages 3-5). In these experiments, speech is presented under controlled conditions with precise synchronization between stimulus onset and neural data acquisition, often using trigger pulses embedded in the audio stream for accurate alignment (commuri2023corticalresponsestimelocked pages 3-4). Calibrated sound pressure levels (SPL) are maintained throughout the experiment to minimize confounds related to intensity variations and ensure that measured responses can be reliably linked to acoustic characteristics (kulasingham2024leveldependentsubcortical pages 1-4). The selection of stimulus materials is guided by the need to maintain a high degree of ecological validity, thereby mimicking natural listening conditions while also controlling for potential confounding variables such as talker accent, prosody, and lexical difficulty (bolt2024exploringcognitivedecline pages 70-72). Participants are often instructed to perform attentional tasks—such as responding to forced-choice questions or target detection—to guarantee that neural responses are modulated by cognitive processes like selective attention (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 2-2). This data acquisition protocol is designed to capture rapid changes in neural response timing, which are crucial for evaluating the TRF models that will later be applied to the data (donhauser2020twodistinctneural pages 15-17). High sampling rates for both the iEEG recordings and the stimulus playback are critical, with typical sampling frequencies ranging from 4,096 Hz to over 8,000 Hz, ensuring that even millisecond-scale dynamics are preserved (kulasingham2024leveldependentsubcorticalelectroencephalography pages 1-2).

sections.text: The extraction of accurate and perceptually relevant stimulus features is a cornerstone of the TRF approach, as it bridges the gap between the continuous acoustic signal and the neural dynamics recorded via iEEG (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 1-2). A primary feature of interest is the speech envelope, which captures the slow amplitude modulations and temporal energy fluctuations inherent to natural speech and can be derived using the Hilbert transform followed by low-pass filtering to isolate modulation frequencies in the range of a few Hz to tens of Hz (crosse2016themultivariatetemporal pages 1-2). Additional processing often involves decomposing the speech signal into multiple frequency bands using cochlear-inspired filterbanks, such as gammatone filterbanks, which simulate the frequency selectivity of the peripheral auditory system and allow for the extraction of band-specific envelopes (lindboom2023incorporatingmodelsof pages 4-8). These multiband representations are then combined—either through summation or weighted averaging—to produce a broadband envelope that reflects global speech dynamics while preserving important spectral cues (mai2019deltaandtheta pages 7-9). To capture transient events such as phoneme or syllable onsets, derivative-based processing methods (e.g., half-wave rectification or neural edge detection) are applied, generating “onset” predictors that highlight rapid changes in the acoustic signal beyond mere amplitude fluctuations (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 2-2). Some approaches further incorporate higher-level linguistic features, such as word or phoneme onsets and lexical surprisal values obtained from language models (e.g., GPT-2), to account for top-down influences on speech processing (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 22-24). The design of these predictors is guided by hypotheses regarding the neural encoding of acoustic versus linguistic elements, with the assumption that low-level features (e.g., envelope) primarily drive early auditory responses, while higher-level features modulate later, more cognitively mediated responses (gillis2022neuraltrackingas pages 6-8). Combining these diverse predictors allows the construction of a high-dimensional stimulus feature matrix that serves as the input to the TRF estimation algorithm (kulasingham2024predictorsforestimating pages 1-2).

sections.text: Prior to TRF estimation, the raw iEEG data must undergo rigorous preprocessing to enhance the SNR and remove artifacts that could confound the subsequent analysis (bolt2024auditoryencodingof pages 5-6). This preprocessing often begins by re-referencing the data to a common reference—such as the mastoid electrodes or an average reference—to reduce spatial noise and increase sensitivity to the underlying neural sources of interest (das2020stimulusawarespatialfiltering pages 4-6). Artifact detection is then performed using automated and/or manual methods to identify and eliminate segments contaminated by artifacts such as eye blinks, muscle activity, or electrical interference, often by applying threshold criteria or independent component analysis (ICA) to isolate non-neural components (mesik2023theeffectsof pages 3-4). Filtering is a critical step in which bandpass filters are applied to retain frequencies relevant to speech processing (typically in the 1–8 Hz range for cortical speech envelope tracking, but sometimes extending to higher frequencies for subcortical responses), while suppressing unrelated slow drifts and high-frequency noise (crosse2021linearmodelingof pages 7-9). Downsampling the data to a manageable rate—such as 128 or 256 Hz—ensures computational efficiency during TRF estimation while still retaining the temporal fidelity required to capture rapid neural dynamics (mesik2023theeffectsof pages 4-6). Spatial filtering techniques, such as stimulus-aware spatial filtering or denoising source separation (DSS), may also be applied to further enhance stimulus-specific neural components, thereby reducing the influence of uncorrelated background activity (das2020stimulusawarespatialfiltering pages 1-4). Throughout the preprocessing pipeline, normalization procedures (e.g., z-scoring) are typically applied on a per-subject basis to account for inter-subject variability—due to factors such as electrode impedance or individual differences in skull conductivity—and to ensure that model fitting is not biased by absolute amplitude differences (bolt2024exploringcognitivedecline pages 35-37). The cumulative effect of these preprocessing steps is to produce a high-quality, artifact-reduced iEEG dataset that faithfully reflects the underlying neural activity elicited by natural speech (kulasingham2024leveldependentsubcorticalelectroencephalography pages 2-4).

sections.text: The core of the TRF approach involves constructing a linear model that relates the time-varying stimulus predictors to the recorded iEEG signal through convolution with a temporal kernel, known as the TRF (crosse2016themultivariatetemporal pages 1-2). Mathematically, the TRF is conceptualized as an impulse response function that quantifies how changes in the stimulus at various time lags contribute to the neural response at a given moment, often expressed as y(t) = Σ_τ TRF(τ) * s(t – τ) + ε, where y(t) is the recorded signal, s(t) is the stimulus feature, and ε represents noise (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 4-7). Estimation of the TRF typically employs regularized linear regression techniques such as ridge regression, which introduces a penalty term to constrain the model weights and prevent overfitting given the high dimensionality and correlation structure of the stimulus predictors (crosse2016themultivariatetemporal pages 2-3). In many cases a boosting algorithm is also utilized to iteratively select and update filter weights in a sparse manner, which enhances model interpretability by emphasizing only the most statistically significant time-lag components (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 20-22). The resulting TRF consists of a set of beta coefficients corresponding to different time lags that collectively describe the neural response function to the acoustic features, such as the envelope and onsets (donhauser2020twodistinctneural pages 15-17). This estimation procedure is typically performed on a trial-by-trial basis, thereby allowing the examination of rapid, task-dependent dynamics without relying on extensive trial averaging that can mask transient neural effects (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 2-2). Model fitting is further validated via cross-validation methods, wherein the TRF model is trained on a subset of the data and then used to predict unseen iEEG segments, with performance typically assessed by computing the Pearson correlation or mean squared error between predicted and actual signals (crosse2021linearmodelingof pages 7-9). Optimal regularization parameters are chosen through grid or nested cross-validation to balance the trade-off between bias and variance in the TRF estimates (kulasingham2022algorithmsforestimating pages 12-14).

sections.text: A recent extension of the traditional TRF framework involves dynamic TRF estimation, which acknowledges that the brain’s response to a given stimulus feature may vary over time and across contexts (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 22-24). This approach incorporates additional parameters to modulate the canonical TRF for each stimulus event, such as amplitude scaling, time shifting, and even temporal stretching, thereby capturing subtle variations in neural processing due to factors like lexical predictability or attention (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 20-22). These dynamic models are implemented using gradient descent-based optimization within neural network architectures that take into account both the current and recent history of stimulus features, effectively “warping” the TRF in a context-specific fashion (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 4-7). Such modeling innovations are predicated on the hypothesis that predictable or highly familiar words trigger earlier or attenuated neural responses—as evidenced by shifts in TRF latency and amplitude—which are not adequately captured by static TRF models (karunathilake2025neuraldynamicsof pages 1-3). These dynamic modifications therefore provide enhanced insight into the adaptive nature of the auditory system, which can rapidly adjust its processing parameters in the face of changing acoustic or linguistic contexts (karunathilake2025neuraldynamicsof pages 28-30). Experimental comparisons have demonstrated that dynamic TRF models outperform static counterparts in terms of predictive accuracy, particularly when assessed on single-trial data where rapid neural adjustments are most pronounced (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 22-24). This integration of stimulus dynamics and context-dependent modulation is a natural progression from traditional TRF approaches and represents a state-of-the-art method for investigating the temporal evolution of speech processing in the human brain (brodbeck2023eelbrainapython pages 21-25). Overall, dynamic TRF estimation reinforces the idea that the auditory system operates in a flexible and adaptive manner, continuously recalibrating its response to accommodate the fast-changing nature of natural speech (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 20-22).

sections.text: The performance of the TRF model is typically evaluated by comparing the predicted iEEG signal—obtained by convolving the stimulus predictor with the estimated TRF—with the actual recorded neural response (crosse2016themultivariatetemporal pages 2-3). Quantitative metrics such as Pearson’s correlation coefficient and mean squared error are commonly used to assess the fidelity of the prediction and to determine the optimal regularization parameters used during model fitting (mesik2023theeffectsof pages 4-6). Furthermore, statistical significance is established using cross-validation techniques and permutation tests which verify that the observed correlations between the predicted and measured signals are not due to chance (crosse2021linearmodelingof pages 7-9). An important aspect of interpretation is the temporal profile of the TRF itself, wherein distinct peaks (for example, early components corresponding to subcortical activity and later components reflecting cortical processing) are mapped onto known neurophysiological markers such as the M50 and M100 responses (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 1-2). These temporal characteristics provide direct evidence for the sequential processing stages in auditory perception, from the initial encoding in subcortical nuclei to the more integrative cortical representations (deoisres2023auditorycorticalresponses pages 53-56). In addition to global performance metrics, researchers often perform channel-wise and region-of-interest analyses to localize the neural sources that contribute most substantially to the observed TRF components (donhauser2020twodistinctneural pages 15-17). Such analyses have demonstrated that while early, rapid responses are often widespread and bilateral, later components tend to exhibit lateralization consistent with language-specific processing in the left auditory cortex (bolt2024exploringcognitivedecline pages 70-72). Ultimately, the evaluation of the TRF model not only validates the linear modeling approach but also provides a mechanistic interpretation of how acoustic variations in natural speech drive specific patterns of neural activity (dieudonne2025neuraltrackingof pages 8-11).

sections.text: A key hypothesis driving recent advancements in TRF analysis is that incorporating models of subcortical processing—such as auditory nerve and inferior colliculus simulations—can improve the accuracy with which neural data are predicted from continuous speech stimuli (lindboom2023incorporatingmodelsof pages 1-4). These models incorporate nonlinearities and adaptation effects that are inherent to the auditory periphery, thereby transforming raw acoustic features into representations that more closely resemble the neural signals observed in higher brain regions (kulasingham2024predictorsforestimating pages 1-2). For example, simulated responses from the inferior colliculus have been shown to account for frequency-dependent response characteristics and temporal integration properties that are not captured by a simple envelope representation (lindboom2023incorporatingmodelsof pages 8-12). Combining these subcortical predictors with traditional acoustic features into a composite model can yield superior predictive performance, indicating that multiple levels of auditory processing contribute additively or interactively to the eventual neural response (lindboom2023incorporatingmodelsof pages 12-15). This hierarchical approach supports the idea that auditory perception is not the result of a single linear pathway but relies on the integration of complex, time-varying representations that arise at different stages of the auditory hierarchy (karunathilake2025neuraldynamicsof pages 1-3). Such integrated models have important clinical implications, as they provide a more nuanced understanding of deficits in speech perception that may arise from peripheral or central dysfunctions (kulasingham2024leveldependentsubcortical pages 4-6). In summary, the incorporation of subcortical processing models into the TRF framework represents a significant methodological advance that enhances the biological plausibility and overall performance of stimulus-to-neural response mappings (lindboom2023incorporatingmodelsof pages 4-8). The hierarchical perspective encapsulated in these models underscores the multifaceted nature of auditory processing and aligns well with longstanding theories in auditory neuroscience (brodbeck2023eelbrainapython pages 3-7).

Our analysis demonstrates that by employing rigorous preprocessing, careful feature extraction, and state-of-the-art regression techniques, it is possible to reliably track rapid neural responses in iEEG recordings during naturalistic auditory tasks (crosse2016themultivariatetemporal pages 2-3). The dynamic TRF models, in particular, lend strong support to the hypothesis that adaptive neural mechanisms operate on a fine time scale to optimize the integration of acoustic and linguistic information (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 22-24). These findings challenge traditional notions of auditory processing as strictly time-invariant, suggesting instead that the brain flexibly modulates its responses according to both the ongoing stimulus context and internal cognitive states (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 4-7). Future research will likely focus on combining TRF analysis with complementary imaging modalities, such as magnetoencephalography, to further elucidate the spatial distribution of the identified temporal components (commuri2023corticalresponsestimelocked pages 3-4). There is also considerable interest in refining subcortical predictors by incorporating more sophisticated models of auditory nerve and midbrain function, which should further improve the fidelity of TRF predictions (kulasingham2024predictorsforestimating pages 14-15). Moreover, recent advances suggest that real-time TRF estimation may soon be feasible, opening up possibilities for applications in brain-computer interfacing and smart hearing aid technologies (akram2017dynamicestimationof pages 2-2). It is anticipated that these advances will enable more precise diagnostics of auditory dysfunctions in clinical populations, as well as better tailored cognitive and rehabilitative interventions for hearing-impaired individuals (lindboom2023incorporatingmodelsof pages 12-15). Additionally, future work might explore the integration of linguistic predictors, such as phoneme surprisal or word-onset markers derived from language models, to further dissect the contribution of high-level language processes to the overall neural response (dou2025dynamicmodelingof pages 22-24). Finally, the continued development, validation, and application of TRF analysis across diverse auditory paradigms will be critical for advancing our understanding of the neural bases of speech perception in both health and disease (mesik2023theeffectsof pages 4-6).

question: Describe what is known about overfitting in in-context learning.

sections.text: This report examines current understanding of overfitting in in-context learning (ICL), a phenomenon wherein pretrained language models adapt to new tasks solely through the provision of context examples without parameter update. The body of work reviewed here spans both empirical studies and theoretical analyses. In particular, research has explored how overfitting in ICL differs from classical overfitting seen in fine-tuning or supervised learning and has begun to illuminate conditions under which models either memorize in-context examples or generalize effectively despite potential overfitting tendencies.

The distinguishing characteristic of in-context learning is that the model’s parameters remain fixed during task adaptation while only the input prompt is modified. This property underlies one of the main advantages of ICL: it inherently limits many of the overfitting risks that arise from updating billions of parameters on limited training data. For instance, studies have noted that fine-tuning strategies, such as prompt tuning or instruction prompt tuning, can suffer from overfitting when only a few examples are available because even the parameter-efficient methods update model weights, whereas in-context learning (ICL) relies solely on the input context without altering the pretrained weights (blau2024contextawareprompttuning pages 1-2).

citations.title: Context-aware prompt tuning: advancing in-context learning with adversarial methods

sections.text: Empirical investigations of transformer classifiers in an ICL setting reveal a particularly interesting phenomenon termed “benign overfitting.” In this regime, models are capable of memorizing all in-context training examples—including noisy or corrupted labels—yet still achieve nearly optimal generalization performance on unseen test data. Analyses have demonstrated that even when a model exhibits perfect interpolation of the in-context examples, the test performance does not degrade as one might expect in classical overfitting scenarios (frei2410trainedtransformerclassifiers pages 1-3, frei2410trainedtransformerclassifiers pages 5-8). This benign overfitting is further supported by detailed theoretical bounds that employ probabilistic tail estimates and risk decompositions, showing that the probability of misclassification remains low even when the training examples are exactly memorized (frei2410trainedtransformerclassifiers pages 32-35).

sections.text: Another line of research investigates the dual operating modes of ICL—the “task retrieval” mode and the “task learning” mode—and their impact on overfitting dynamics. When only a few examples are provided, models tend to rely more on pretraining priors by retrieving a task that closely resembles the in-context examples, which can result in an initial phase of overfitting to an incorrect prior (lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 1-2). This behavior is characterized by an “early ascent” in prediction risk as the model overcommits to spurious patterns in the limited context. As the number of in-context examples increases, however, there is a transition from task retrieval to task learning. In this phase, the model begins to align its predictions more closely with the target task distribution, and the risk decays approximately at a rate proportional to the inverse-square of the number of examples (lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 15-17, lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 2-3). Nonetheless, if too many examples are provided—particularly when the examples are biased—the model may start to overfit to these biases, leading to bounded efficacy where the additional context ceases to improve performance and may even degrade it (lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 8-9).

sections.text: A complementary perspective comes from theoretical analyses that examine the stability of the ICL procedure through the lens of generalization bounds. One study developed a bound showing that excess risk of the Transformer-based in-context learner scales inversely with the number of context examples, as well as other factors such as context window size and pretraining diversity (liu2405towardsbetterunderstanding pages 1-3). Such bounds, which are derived under assumptions of Lipschitz continuity and bounded loss functions, suggest that when task diversity is sufficient and the context window is properly managed, the model is less likely to overfit even as it interpolates the provided examples. In effect, these guarantees indicate that the limited capacity for additional parameter updates, when combined with the large pretrained priors, provide a form of implicit regularization that helps mitigate overfitting.

sections.text: Comparative studies between in-context learning and traditional supervised learning also provide valuable insights into overfitting. In supervised learning, where the model is explicitly trained with gradient descent on a set of labeled data, overfitting is often exacerbated by high model complexity and limited data. In contrast, in-context learning leverages the pretrained representations and, by not updating weights, circumvents many of the pitfalls related to memorization-induced degradation on out-of-distribution or noisy test examples. For example, empirical work shows that ICL is less sensitive to label corruption than supervised learning methods, which tend to sharply degrade in performance when trained on noisy examples (wang2023investigatingthelearning pages 3-4, wang2023investigatingthelearning pages 5-7). This difference reinforces the idea that the mechanism of simply “reading” and “copying” information within a prompt provides an inherent robustness against classic overfitting, as the model does not adjust its internal representations in response to the noise.

sections.text: Another angle is provided by research examining the phenomenon of “noisy ICL” where noise is deliberately injected into the model’s parameters to calibrate confidence and mitigate overfitting effects in confidence estimates. Although this approach does not directly add new knowledge to the model, it shows that overfitting can also manifest in the form of overconfident predictions when models are exposed to familiar contexts. By introducing noise into the parameters, the study observed improvements in calibration and robustness, suggesting that one proxy for overfitting is not only generalization error but also the misalignment of model calibration with true uncertainty (cho2402noisyiclalittle pages 5-6).

sections.text: In contrast, some investigations highlight that overfitting may not be the most pressing challenge in ICL. Certain studies, particularly those focusing on the architecture and the prequential (online coding) perspective of ICL, argue that underfitting, rather than overfitting, is the dominant issue because models often fail to fully capture the contextual signals provided by limited examples. For instance, advanced work on minimizing the prequential code length shows that ICL tends to achieve lower training error when sufficient context is provided, thereby reducing traditional train–test error gaps that would indicate overfitting. In these scenarios, the model’s inability to capitalize on context is posed as an underfitting issue rather than overfitting, with the underlying complexity–accuracy tradeoff being a key design consideration (elmoznino2024incontextlearningand pages 7-8, elmoznino2024incontextlearningand pages 8-10).

sections.text: A crucial aspect of overfitting in ICL concerns the interplay between memorization and generalization. The benign overfitting phenomenon, as discussed earlier, suggests that a model can achieve perfect interpolation on the provided in-context examples while still generalizing well to unseen data. This behavior is in stark contrast to traditional overfitting in which merely memorizing training data leads to poor generalization. It has been argued that the implicit regularization offered by gradient descent during pretraining, combined with the fixed nature of the model parameters during ICL, leads to the emergence of solutions that are robust against overfitting. Detailed probabilistic analyses have shown that the risk associated with these models is tightly concentrated around their training performance, indicating a stable tradeoff between bias and variance even when the training data is fully memorized (frei2410trainedtransformerclassifiers pages 32-35, li2023transformersasalgorithms pages 1-2).

sections.text: Another notable insight comes from studies focusing on meta-learning aspects of in-context learning. Meta-learned black-box models exhibit regimes of transition from mere memorization of tasks to genuine learning of task identification and algorithm execution. In these cases, overfitting may manifest as excessive memorization of training tasks; however, this is usually observed in smaller models or when the number of training tasks is insufficient. With an increased capacity and a broader diversity of tasks, the model is more likely to learn generalizable strategies rather than simply encoding the training examples verbatim. These findings underscore that overfitting in ICL is not an intrinsic flaw but one that depends strongly on the training regime, task diversity, and model capacity (kirsch2022generalpurposeincontextlearning pages 1-2, kirsch2022generalpurposeincontextlearning pages 8-9).

sections.text: Further complexity arises when considering the effect of biased or noisy in-context examples. Certain studies have shown that in-context learning exhibits a bounded efficacy effect when exposed to biased labels: as more context examples are added, the risk of overfitting to these biases increases after a certain optimal number is reached. This non-monotonic behavior—where initial increases in the number of examples reduce error, but beyond an optimal point the error begins to rise—provides concrete evidence that the tradeoff between leveraging context and overfitting to in-context noise is delicate. Such results have been theoretically captured with upper bounds on ICL risk that depend on the number of in-context examples and the degree of bias present, illustrating that performance can ultimately degrade if the model overfits to misaligned or biased prior signals from the context (lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 8-9).

citations.title: Dual operating modes of in-context learning

sections.text: The role of data contamination and prompt design is also significant when discussing overfitting in ICL. Some recent explorations note that the distinction between genuine in-context learning and rote knowledge retrieval can be blurred in scenarios where the training corpus overlaps with the evaluation domain. In such cases, the model might appear to generalize well simply because it is retrieving memorized information rather than performing true adaptation, a situation that, while not classical overfitting in the sense of poor generalization, can be thought of as a form of overfitting to the prompt distribution. This phenomenon has practical implications for the design of evaluation datasets and prompt engineering strategies, where care must be taken to ensure that the in-context examples are representative of the task distribution without inadvertently reinforcing spurious patterns (nafar2025learningvsretrieval pages 7-9).

sections.text: The theoretical literature on overfitting in ICL has also introduced the concept of risk bounds that decay with increasing in-context sample size. By providing a mathematical framework in which the error risk decreases as more consistent context is added but then levels off or increases beyond a point, these works underscore that while ICL is generally resistant to overfitting due to its reliance on fixed pretrained weights, it is not immune to the effects of overfitting induced by excessive or biased context. Such analyses reinforce that careful selection of context examples and limiting the context window to an optimal size are critical to maintaining the balance between leveraging memory and avoiding overfitting (liu2405towardsbetterunderstanding pages 5-7, lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 33-35).

sections.text: In summary, what is known about overfitting in in-context learning can be distilled into several key observations. First, the absence of parameter updates during ICL provides an inherent mechanism that reduces classic overfitting risks associated with fine-tuning large models on sparse data (blau2024contextawareprompttuning pages 1-2). Second, empirical evidence indicates that models can exhibit benign overfitting—memorizing all in-context examples while still generalizing effectively to new data (frei2410trainedtransformerclassifiers pages 1-3, frei2410trainedtransformerclassifiers pages 5-8). Third, the dual operating modes of ICL, which include an initial task retrieval phase followed by a task learning phase, reveal that overfitting may transiently occur when inadequate context causes the model to overcommit to an incorrect task prior; however, this effect diminishes with the addition of more in-context examples up to an optimal point (lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 1-2, lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 15-17, lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 8-9). Fourth, theoretical risk bounds and stability analyses suggest that overfitting is largely mitigated by the fixed pretrained weights and the implicit regularization effects they induce, although careful management of context length and quality remains necessary (liu2405towardsbetterunderstanding pages 1-3, li2023transformersasalgorithms pages 1-2). Fifth, the impact of biased or noisy examples in the context provides evidence for a bounded efficacy effect where excessive context can lead to overfitting to the biases, thereby increasing risk beyond a certain example count (lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 8-9). Finally, while some investigations raise concerns about contamination and the potential for models to retrieve memorized information rather than generalize properly, the overall literature suggests that the design of the prompt—its length, diversity, and example quality—plays a crucial role in ensuring that overfitting phenomena in ICL are minimized (nafar2025learningvsretrieval pages 7-9, wang2023investigatingthelearning pages 3-4).

sections.text: Taken together, these insights frame overfitting in in-context learning not as a pervasive flaw but as a nuanced interplay between memorization, retrieval, and the effective leverage of pretrained knowledge. The emergent behavior of ICL demonstrates that while models can reach perfect interpolation of contextual examples, the careful design of in-context prompts and the large-scale pretraining regime help ensure that such memorization does not translate into poor generalization performance. Continued research in this area is essential to further refine our understanding of the optimal tradeoffs and to develop guidelines for prompt engineering, which will ultimately lead to more robust and reliable in-context learners (frei2410trainedtransformerclassifiers pages 32-35, kirsch2022generalpurposeincontextlearning pages 1-2, lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 2-3).

sections.text: In conclusion, the current state of the literature suggests that overfitting in in-context learning manifests differently from conventional overfitting in supervised learning scenarios. The absence of parameter updates during inference, combined with the robust priors established during pretraining, underlies a resistance to overfitting that is characteristic of ICL. However, nuances such as the optimal number of provided in-context examples, the quality and representativeness of these examples, and the potential for biased or noisy contexts to degrade performance illustrate that overfitting is not entirely absent in ICL; rather, it is moderated by a complex set of factors that interplay to yield either benign overfitting or, under adverse conditions, performance degradation. Ongoing theoretical investigations and empirical validations continue to refine our understanding of this tradeoff, highlighting avenues for further research into prompt optimization, stability bounds, and the precise conditions under which benign overfitting prevails. This comprehensive picture contributes to the broader goal of developing more refined, context-aware prompt-tuning techniques and improving the generalization abilities of large language models in diverse application domains (blau2024contextawareprompttuning pages 1-2, lin2024dualoperatingmodes pages 33-35, liu2405towardsbetterunderstanding pages 5-7).

question: What are leading approaches for evaluating complex scientific question answering systems in NLP?

sections.text: Abstract—In recent years, scientific QA has evolved from retrieving simple factual answers to addressing multifaceted, domain‐specific, and multi-hop reasoning challenges. Evaluation of complex scientific QA systems requires tailored benchmarks, metrics that capture semantic similarity and reasoning accuracy, and hybrid evaluation methods that blend human judgment with automated scoring. This report synthesizes contemporary approaches by reviewing domain‐specific benchmarks, automatic evaluation metrics, and human-centric as well as hybrid methodologies. The discussion spans work in scholarly QA benchmarks that leverage knowledge graphs, biomedical QA evaluations that use both IR and machine reading comprehension techniques, and emerging frameworks that incorporate explanation logic, dynamic data, and interactive evaluation protocols.

Complex scientific QA systems are distinguished by their need to understand specialized terminologies, perform reasoning over heterogeneous knowledge graphs, and capture multi-step inferencing that goes beyond simple fact retrieval. Traditional question answering evaluations—often based on encyclopedic datasets and surface-level lexical matching—fall short when assessing these systems. The pioneering work on the SciQA benchmark, for example, leverages an extensive scholarly knowledge graph (the Open Research Knowledge Graph, ORKG) that exposes complex query structures including aggregations, comparisons, and temporal reasoning (auer2023thesciqascientific pages 1-2, auer2023thesciqascientific pages 3-4). Modern evaluation now must blend several approaches, including specialized benchmarks, traditional IR metrics, deep learning–based semantic similarity, and human evaluation. This report presents an integrated view of leading methodologies for evaluating complex scientific QA systems in NLP.

sections.text: A key aspect of evaluating scientific QA systems is the availability of benchmarks that reflect the complexity of scholarly domains. The SciQA benchmark is one such resource, which is constructed by combining 100 handcrafted complex questions with thousands of machine‐generated queries using eight question templates, and executed over the ORKG (auer2023thesciqascientific pages 1-2). This benchmark not only features factoid and non‐factoid questions but also stresses queries that require multi-hop reasoning and advanced SPARQL query formulation (auer2023thesciqascientific pages 3-4, auer2023thesciqascientific pages 6-7). Similarly, domain evaluation in biomedical QA leverages datasets from BioASQ challenges where models benefit from domain-specific pre-trained models like BioBERT and SciBERT, evaluated using metrics such as exact match and F1 score (jin2022biomedicalquestionanswering pages 11-13, jin2022biomedicalquestionanswering pages 13-15). Multi-modal benchmarks, such as M3SCIQA, further extend evaluation to include visual reasoning and multi-document synthesis (li2024m3sciqaamultimodal pages 7-9). In addition, other evaluation platforms such as SciEval incorporate dynamic data and multi-level evaluation based on Bloom’s taxonomy to assess not only knowledge retrieval but also reasoning and research skills (sun2024scievalamultilevel pages 1-2, sun2024scievalamultilevel pages 2-3). These benchmark datasets provide the infrastructure necessary for extensive, domain-specific assessment and reproducible comparisons across differing methodologies (usbeck2019benchmarkingquestionanswering pages 2-3).

sections.text:
A. Lexical and N-gram Matching Approaches  Lexical matching metrics remain important components in evaluation pipelines due to their ease of calculation and interpretability. Traditional metrics like Exact Match (EM), precision, recall, F1 score, BLEU, ROUGE, and METEOR have been extensively used in QA systems (farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 4-6, saikh2022scienceqaanovel pages 8-9). These metrics are effective for factoid questions provided the reference answers cover the lexical variations observed in system outputs. However, establishing equivalence for paraphrased and contextually correct answers through strict n-gram overlap remains challenging. For complex scientific QA, where multiple valid formulations exist and scientific language exhibits high lexical variability, these metrics can underestimate true performance (kamalloo2023evaluatingopendomainquestion pages 1-2).

B. Semantic Similarity Metrics Based on Pre-trained Language Models  To overcome the limitations of strict lexical matching, more recent evaluation techniques leverage contextual embeddings from pre-trained language models. Metrics such as BERTScore and BARTScore compare cosine similarities between token embeddings of generated answers and reference responses, thereby capturing a deeper level of semantic similarity (daull2023complexqaand pages 13-16, farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 47-50). These methods have shown improved correlation with human judgments, especially when evaluating long-form or generative answers that span multiple sentences (kamalloo2023evaluatingopendomainquestion pages 2-3). Composite metrics that combine multiple measures have also been introduced, reflecting aspects of fluency, adequacy, and factual consistency (farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 4-6).

C. Untrained Versus Machine-Trained Evaluation Scores  The literature distinguishes between Untrained Automatic Evaluation Scores (UAES) and Machine-Trained Evaluation Scores (MTES). UAES include metrics that do not require further training and are based solely on direct comparisons (e.g., EM, BLEU, ROUGE), while MTES combine features learned from large annotated data and integrate multiple dimensions of answer quality (farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 4-6). Learning-based scores such as BLEURT and ADEM are designed to encapsulate semantic and contextual nuances, making them particularly useful for evaluating the subtle aspects encountered in complex scientific QA systems (daull2023complexqaand pages 13-16).

sections.text: Given the inherent complexities and ambiguities of natural language, human evaluation remains an essential component of assessment for complex scientific QA systems. Human evaluators are tasked with judging fluency, correctness, informativeness, and coherence of answers, particularly in cases where automatic metrics struggle to capture context or deal with ambiguous references (farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 50-52, saikh2022scienceqaanovel pages 8-9). Different human evaluation methodologies include absolute rating (where evaluators score outputs on predefined scales) and relative comparative assessments via pairwise comparisons (sai2022asurveyof pages 10-12). Along with numerical scoring, providing evaluators with detailed guidelines and rationale can reduce subjectivity and improve inter-annotator agreement. For example, in scientific domains where answers span multi-paragraph explanations or require integration with figures and equations, human judgments become invaluable because automatic metrics may fail to distinguish between superficially similar but factually divergent outputs (singh2411scidqaadeep pages 8-9, farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 52-55).

sections.text: A promising avenue for evaluating complex scientific QA systems is the combination of automated metrics with human oversight—a hybrid approach that integrates quantitative scores with qualitative assessments. Recent evaluations of large language models for scientific QA have demonstrated that while automatic metrics provide rapid and objective insights (for instance, precision, recall, and F1 scores measured within controlled settings), the final assessments significantly benefit from human validation (lermann2024largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, daull2023complexqaand pages 16-17). Hybrid approaches may involve “soft” reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), where human judgment is factored into model training and subsequent evaluation to reduce hallucinations and improve factual correctness (daull2023complexqaand pages 32-34, daull2023complexqaand pages 35-37). Such methods combine the scalability of automatic evaluation with the nuanced understanding provided by expert assessors, ultimately yielding a more balanced measure of system performance (farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 19-21, farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 21-24).

sections.text: An emerging research direction for complex scientific QA evaluation emphasizes the need for systems to provide structured explanation logic and validated reasoning paths. Systems that generate entailment trees or explanation chains can be automatically fact-checked using metrics designed for consistency and coherence (daull2023complexqaand pages 32-34, daull2023complexqaand pages 38-40). Automated fact-checking tools, combined with metrics that assess the internal consistency of generated explanations, help ensure that complex multi-hop questions are addressed in a transparent and reliable manner. This not only supports the evaluation of answer correctness but also encourages accountability and interpretability in scientific scenarios (daull2023complexqaand pages 35-37).

sections.text: Scientific QA systems are increasingly expected to function in open-domain and interactive scenarios, where user inputs may be ambiguous or require clarification. Evaluation protocols for open-domain QA, as examined in recent work, involve formulating the assessment as a binary classification task where the correctness of each answer is evaluated against gold standards that consider multiple plausible formulations (wang2023evaluatingopenqaevaluation pages 4-6, kamalloo2023evaluatingopendomainquestion pages 1-2). In addition to answer correctness, interactive evaluation looks at the system’s ability to maintain dialogue context, ask clarifying questions, or leverage user feedback. Approaches in complex knowledge base QA leverage metrics such as Hits@1 and the F1 score to capture the system’s precision in ranking correct answers while concurrently evaluating robustness over compositional questions (lan2023complexknowledgebase pages 14-15, lan2023complexknowledgebase pages 15-16). Incorporating interactive elements into benchmarks—where models are evaluated on conversational task performance—remains an area of active research, pointing to the future necessity of multi-turn evaluation methodologies that capture evolving query contexts (lan2023complexknowledgebase pages 16-17).

sections.text:
Despite substantial advances, several challenges persist in evaluating complex scientific QA systems. First, handling the diversity of answer types—from concise facts to long-form, multi-paragraph explanations—places a demand on evaluation metrics to capture both surface-level correctness and deep semantic validity (farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 24-26, farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 47-50). Second, data quality and domain adaptation remain challenging when the training and evaluation datasets fail to fully reflect real-world scientific discourse (daull2023complexqaand pages 17-19, jin2022biomedicalquestionanswering pages 7-9). Third, automatic metrics sometimes fail when faced with non-literal, paraphrased, or contextually inferred answers—a limitation that necessitates further refinement of embedding-based approaches (daull2023complexqaand pages 13-16, kamalloo2023evaluatingopendomainquestion pages 2-3). Moreover, while RLHF and explanation-based approaches have shown promise, incorporating user-interaction and iterative human evaluation in a scalable manner remains a significant research frontier (daull2023complexqaand pages 32-34, farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 50-52).

Future directions include the development of composite evaluation frameworks that can integrate standardized automatic metrics with targeted human evaluations, advanced semantic similarity measures that are robust to domain-specific terminologies, and interactive assessments that simulate real-world scientific inquiry. Researchers are also exploring the use of domain-adaptive pre-trained models and leveraging structured knowledge graphs not only for question answering but also for internal reasoning evaluation, ensuring that the systems’ reasoning process is both replicable and transparent (lehmann2024largelanguagemodels pages 6-9, sun2024scievalamultilevel pages 8-9).

sections.text:
Evaluating complex scientific question answering systems in NLP requires a multi-dimensional approach that bridges standard automatic metrics and comprehensive human evaluation. Leading approaches include: (i) the use of domain-specific benchmarks like SciQA and SciEval that capture the intricacies of scholarly knowledge through advanced query types, (ii) automated evaluation metrics ranging from simple n-gram overlap measures (EM, BLEU, ROUGE) to sophisticated semantic similarity metrics (BERTScore, BARTScore), (iii) hybrid methodologies that combine machine-trained metrics with human-centric evaluation to mitigate issues such as hallucination and lexically divergent yet correct answers, and (iv) novel evaluation strategies focusing on explanation, reasoning, and interactive dialogue across complex and heterogeneous scientific domains. Together, these evaluation methods help ensure that scientific QA systems not only retrieve facts but also demonstrate deep reasoning, contextual understanding, and robust generalization. Ongoing research efforts in reinforcement learning from human feedback and neural-symbolic hybrid approaches promise to further enhance the fidelity of these evaluations, paving the way towards truly reliable and interpretable scientific QA systems (auer2023thesciqascientific pages 9-11, daull2023complexqaand pages 38-40, farea2022evaluationofquestion pages 21-24).

By synthesizing state-of-the-art benchmark datasets, developing robust automatic and human evaluation techniques, and aligning evaluation with the intrinsic complexities of scientific information, the community is steadily advancing toward more accurate, transparent, and effective QA systems in scientific domains.

This report has provided a comprehensive overview of current leading evaluation approaches, highlighting the intricate balance required to measure not only answer accuracy but also the quality of reasoning in complex scientific question answering systems (chang2024asurveyon pages 23-24, lehmann2024largelanguagemodels pages 1-3, kamalloo2023evaluatingopendomainquestion pages 1-2).

question: What are the key differences between participatory design and co-design?

sections.text: This report examines in depth the key differences between participatory design and co-design, two approaches that have evolved in response to the need for renewed user involvement and democratization in design processes. Both methodologies emphasize the engagement of end‐users in the design process; however, they diverge significantly in their underlying principles, processes, and outcomes, as detailed in the literature. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 2-4)

sections.text: The challenge of accurately involving end-users in the design process has given rise to a variety of approaches that seek to balance technical expertise with community input. Participatory design emerged as an early response grounded in democratic ideals and the empowerment of marginalized or frontline groups, whereas co-design represents a more recent evolution that focuses on joint creation between users and designers. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 1-2) The purpose of this report is to provide a detailed comparative analysis of these approaches by synthesizing insights from multiple research studies published in IEEE and related journals. (burkett2012anintroductionto pages 1-7)

sections.text: Participatory design (PD) originated in Europe during the early 1970s as a movement aimed at enabling social empowerment through enabling the direct involvement of users in decision making, channeling democratic processes into design practices. (burkett2012anintroductiontoa pages 1-7) In contrast, co-design builds upon these democratic aspirations but extends them by emphasizing equal collaboration between designers and users in every phase of the design process, thereby transforming users into active co-creators rather than passive informants. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 2-4) Historically, participatory design is associated with the ideological underpinnings of workplace democracy and has been deeply rooted in sociopolitical practices that emerged from labor movements. (smith2017participatorydesignin pages 1-3) The method promoted mutual learning and aimed to address power imbalances by ensuring that all stakeholders, especially those affected by technological change, had a say in the design process. (hansen2019howparticipatorydesign pages 1-2) Co-design, while sharing common elements with participatory design, evolved in part within contexts that demanded greater responsiveness and alignment between design outcomes and user needs, emerging prominently in urban development, service design, and educational contexts. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 1-2, gomez2018participatorydesignand pages 428-430)

sections.text: The philosophical foundations of participatory design are situated in theories of deliberative democracy and social emancipation, with a strong focus on ethical practices and the redistribution of power between professional experts and end-users. (burkett2012anintroductionto pages 14-16) Participatory design emphasizes the need for mutual reflection and learning, and it frames technological artifacts as shaped by both user experiences and political engagement. (hansen2019howparticipatorydesign pages 1-2) Conversely, co-design is frequently grounded in design thinking and constructivist theories that view knowledge as co-constructed through iterative processes and shared experiences between participants with varied levels of expertise. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 5-7) In a co-design framework, the focus shifts from merely validating user needs to actively harnessing users’ creative capacities in joint ideation, prototyping, and iterative refinement. (steen2013codesignasa pages 10-13) While participatory design historically privileges sustained dialogue around democratic values and user empowerment, co-design tends to emphasize co-creation and shared ownership over the design outcomes, often integrating techniques from ethnography and social sciences to account for users’ cultural contexts. (burkett2012anintroductiontoa pages 16-18) This theoretical divergence influences the selection of methods and the degree of collaboration expected in design processes. (busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 13-14)

sections.text: Participatory design involves a variety of methods such as workshops, focus groups, and storytelling sessions that invite users to contribute insights into both the context and values that underlie design challenges. (velden2015participatorydesignand pages 3-5) A frequent criticism, however, is that PD sometimes limits the role of users to information providers, resulting in processes that can become tokenistic if not carefully managed. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 9-11) In contrast, co-design is explicitly structured to ensure that users move beyond the role of informants to become active partners in problem definition, idea generation, and decision-making. (burkett2012anintroductionto pages 7-14) Co-design initiatives frequently feature iterative cycles of ideation and prototyping, incorporating visual and physical artefact-based methods to capture the experiential knowledge of users. For example, in museum contexts, co-design has been implemented by engaging cultural heritage professionals in creating prototypes that embody both divergent and convergent design phases. (ciolfi2016articulatingcodesignin pages 3-4) Similarly, projects in healthcare have used experience-based co-design (EBCD) methodologies to facilitate continuous interaction between patients, caregivers, and professionals through structured workshops. (donetto2015experiencebasedcodesignand pages 7-9) These methods contrast with more traditional participatory approaches in which users’ input is predominantly solicited in early research stages rather than integrated throughout every phase of design. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 5-7) The deployment of co-design methods is often accompanied by a deliberate effort to manage role ambiguity among participants. For instance, designers in co-design projects are encouraged to transition from being sole creators to facilitators who enable and galvanize collective creativity, deliberately blurring traditional boundaries between experts and non-experts. (busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 10-11) Participatory design, while supportive of user involvement, sometimes maintains clearer distinctions between the roles of designers and participants, focusing more on extracting user insights rather than on shared co-creation. (gomez2018participatorydesignand pages 424-426)

sections.text: One of the central distinctions between participatory design and co-design lies in their treatment of power within the design process. Participatory design has long advocated for a redistribution of power, emphasizing participatory spaces where users have a substantive say in shaping design outcomes and where organizational hierarchies are flattened to some degree. (burkett2012anintroductiontoa pages 14-16) Nevertheless, in practice, PD has sometimes struggled with ensuring that the influence of users is not overshadowed by dominant expert opinions or institutional agendas. (jiang2022understandingpowerdifferentials pages 15-15) Co-design explicitly focuses on power-sharing mechanisms that support shared decision-making and collective ownership of the design process. This approach is characterized by continuous negotiation and an emphasis on creating balanced partnerships where users—as co-creators—are given both responsibility and authority. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 2-4) In environments where power dynamics are particularly challenging, such as in urban regeneration or with marginalized populations, co-design seeks to provide a more structured framework for ensuring equitable participation and the mitigation of conflicts. (gaudio2020codesignfordemocratising pages 1-4) By employing iterative and transparent decision-making processes, co-design fosters an atmosphere in which users can lead aspects of the process, thereby directly influencing final outcomes, rather than merely validating decisions made by design experts. (burkett2012anintroductiontoa pages 16-18) Moreover, while participatory design is sometimes critiqued for potentially reinforcing tokenistic roles despite its democratic aspirations, co-design intentionally seeks to counteract such limitations by embedding shared power and continuous re-negotiation of roles throughout the design cycle. (vargas2022cocreationcodesignand pages 2-3) This is particularly evident in examples where co-design methodologies have been nested within broader co-production frameworks to empower service users and community members as genuine leaders of the process. (benz2024communitybasedparticipatoryresearchthrough pages 1-2)
