sections.text: Participatory design is traditionally aimed at ensuring that the outcomes of a design process adhere closely to the needs, values, and cultural contexts of users by simply integrating their feedback and perspectives in a consultative manner. (ventesen2015participatorydesignand pages 3-5) As such, PD has been successfully applied to develop information technologies and workplace systems where user needs must be rigorously understood and addressed. (smith2017participatorydesignin pages 1-3) However, its outcomes can sometimes be limited by the extent to which the input provided by users is systematically integrated into the final design, rather than attached as a guiding philosophy throughout the process. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 9-11) Co-design, on the other hand, aims not merely to collect user input but to integrate users’ experiential knowledge and creative capacities into every stage of the design process, ensuring that the outcomes are co-owned and co-created. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 5-7) This results in initiatives that often transcend mere product or service refinements to become platforms for innovation, social transformation, and empowerment. (vargas2022cocreationcodesignanda pages 3-5) In practice, co-design projects have produced outcomes that are demonstrably more responsive to local contexts and more sustainable over time due to the deep level of user investment and ownership. (steen2013codesignasa pages 13-13) The objectives of participatory design emphasize democratic participation and voice, often prioritizing process over outcome, whereas co-design focuses on tangible outputs crafted through iterative cycles of shared creation that reflect both user expertise and professional design expertise. (busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 8-10) Consequently, co-design can be perceived as a more outcome-oriented approach that still retains the democratic spirit of participatory design while ensuring that the process actively produces novel, contextually relevant solutions. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 2-4)

sections.text: A key difference between the two approaches lies in how they define and configure the roles of designers and users. Participatory design traditionally positions users as knowledgeable contributors who provide insights, contextual expertise, and feedback, with designers retaining considerable authority over final decisions. (yalmAn2015codesignpracticein pages 7-7) While PD fosters collaborative dialogue, it often does so within established roles that separate idea generation from technical implementation. (gomez2018participatorydesignand pages 428-430) Co-design, by contrast, reconfigures these roles to a degree that the boundaries between designers and non-designers become markedly blurred. In co-design environments, users are invited to assume roles that were once reserved for professional designers, engaging in concept formulation, prototyping, evaluation, and even project management. (busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 13-14) This role reconfiguration is central to the co-design ethos, as it is based on the belief that users possess unique experiential knowledge that is as critical to the design process as technical expertise. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 1-2) The resulting process is marked by a shared responsibility for both problem framing and solution delivery, a notable departure from more hierarchical approaches typically seen in traditional participatory design. (ciolfi2016articulatingcodesignin pages 12-13) This redefinition of roles extends to the responsibilities of facilitators as well; in co-design settings, facilitators are charged with not only gathering insights but also empowering participants, mediating conflicts, and ensuring that the creative process is equitable and genuinely collaborative. (busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 10-11) Such practices underline the notion that co-design is not just a set of techniques but also a mindset that prioritizes distributed authorship and shared ownership over design decisions. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborative pages 15-18)

sections.text: Both participatory design and co-design must contend with inherent challenges arising from the inclusion of diverse stakeholders; however, the ways in which they manage complexity and conflict differ significantly. Participatory design tends to emphasize processes of consensus building and mutual learning, often employing techniques intended to minimize conflict and align diverse points of view toward a common goal. (burkett2012anintroductiontoa pages 14-16) Yet, critics note that such approaches may sometimes gloss over underlying tensions or power imbalances by prioritizing surface consensus over deep engagement with conflicting perspectives. (jiang2022understandingpowerdifferentials pages 15-15) The co-design approach, while also valuing consensus, explicitly acknowledges conflict as a potential source of creative tension and as a necessary part of the iterative design process. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborativea pages 19-21) Co-design methodologies are often designed to incorporate structured methods for addressing disagreements, such as clearly defined roles, iterative prototyping sessions, and reflective practices that encourage participants to "walk in each other’s shoes." (burkett2012anintroductionto pages 16-18) Such practices do not simply aim to eliminate conflict but rather to harness it constructively, using divergent perspectives to foster innovation and enrich the design solutions through rigorous debate and re-negotiation. (gaudio2020codesignfordemocratising pages 1-4) Furthermore, co-design projects are more likely to include built-in feedback loops and iterative evaluation cycles that allow for ongoing adjustment of both process and outcomes in response to emerging conflicts. (donetto2015experiencebasedcodesignand pages 7-9) This stands in contrast to many participatory design initiatives where conflict resolution tends to be addressed primarily in the early stages, and subsequent phases may reinforce existing power hierarchies if not adequately managed. (hansen2019howparticipatorydesign pages 11-12)

sections.text: The distinctions between participatory design and co-design are reflected not only in their theoretical underpinnings but also in their applications across different sectors. In the realm of information technology and service design, participatory design has been used effectively to gather user requirements and ensure that digital systems reflect the practices and needs of their users. (gomez2018participatorydesignand pages 428-430) In such contexts, PD methodologies have contributed to the development of systems that are more usable and contextually appropriate, albeit occasionally limited by the degree of user involvement in decision-making. (smith2017participatorydesignin pages 1-3) Co-design, on the other hand, has seen broader application in fields such as urban planning, healthcare, education, and cultural heritage, where the complexity of stakeholder relationships demands a more integrative and iterative design approach. For example, in architectural projects, co-design has been used to challenge traditional notions of architectural authorship by actively involving community members in shaping spatial arrangements and social outcomes. (combrinck2021codesigninthe pages 1-3) In public health initiatives, co-design has been employed as a tool within co-production frameworks to ensure that intervention strategies are co-developed with patients, service providers, and policymakers, thereby increasing the likelihood of sustainable implementation and social inclusion. (vargas2022cocreationcodesignand pages 1-2) Similarly, in educational contexts, co-design initiatives have fostered collaborative curriculum development and innovative teaching practices by engaging teachers and administrators as equal partners in ideation, prototyping, and refinement. (gomez2018participatorydesignand pages 424-426) The outcomes achieved through co-design frequently reflect a higher degree of personalization and adaptability to local contexts compared to those achieved by more conventional participatory design approaches. (vargas2022cocreationcodesignanda pages 2-3)

sections.text: A further distinguishing factor lies in the emphasis on capacity building and sustainability within co-design initiatives. While participatory design focuses on the immediate inclusion of users to improve design outcomes, co-design is often conceived as a process that builds long-term capacities within communities. (burkett2012anintroductiontoa pages 7-14) This is achieved by engaging participants not only in the generation of ideas but also in the development of skills, shared knowledge, and the organizational structures necessary to sustain the design improvements beyond the project lifecycle. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborative pages 23-25) By contrast, participatory design, although it may engender user involvement and foster democratic practices, has sometimes been critiqued for producing outcomes that are less robust in terms of building an enduring collaborative culture. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 9-11) Co-design initiatives, through their iterative nature and emphasis on shared responsibilities, create a dynamic where participants can continue to evolve and adapt design strategies in response to future challenges, thus ensuring that the empowerment and social capital generated during the process are maintained over time. (benz2024communitybasedparticipatoryresearchthrough pages 1-2) This focus on long-term social innovation, capacity building, and sustainable change represents a key evolution from traditional participatory design, which while valuable in promoting democratic engagement, may not always provide the structural support necessary for continuous innovation. (vargas2022cocreationcodesignanda pages 3-5)

sections.text: Despite the many advantages of both approaches, each faces its own set of challenges. Participatory design is sometimes criticized for being overly consultative, where user participation is reduced to an initial set of inputs without ensuring continued influence on final decisions. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 9-11) Moreover, issues related to tokenism and insufficient integration of user expertise have been noted as potential pitfalls. (hansen2019howparticipatorydesign pages 1-2) Co-design, while offering greater promise in terms of sustained participation and collaboration, is not without its challenges. The complexity of co-design processes, in which multiple stakeholders with differing agendas must negotiate, can lead to protracted decision-making cycles and occasional conflict that, if not properly managed, might undermine project outcomes. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborative pages 21-23) The intensive resource requirements in terms of time, facilitation, and commitment also represent a barrier to scaling co-design processes, particularly in contexts where organizational cultures are not accustomed to such deep forms of collaboration. (busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 8-10) Nonetheless, proponents of co-design argue that these challenges are offset by the long-term benefits of building genuine creative partnerships and producing outcomes that are more contextually relevant and socially transformative. (steen2013codesignasa pages 10-13) Critiques of both methodologies also highlight the need for clearer theoretical frameworks and terminological consistency. Participatory design, for instance, has been variably defined across contexts, leading to a sometimes fuzzy understanding of its scope and methods. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 9-11) Co-design, while more clearly demarcated in some studies, also suffers from ambiguity in how it is articulated relative to similar concepts such as co-creation and co-production. (vargas2022cocreationcodesignand pages 3-5) Researchers continue to debate the optimal balance between structure and flexibility, the precise roles of users versus experts, and the most effective ways to manage power imbalances within these collaborative frameworks. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborativea pages 19-21)

sections.text: In synthesizing the literature, several critical differences between participatory design and co-design become apparent. First, the historical and philosophical roots distinguish the two; participatory design is fundamentally oriented around democratic participation and has its genesis in labor and social movements, whereas co-design is more recent and embraces design thinking as a means of jointly creating solutions through iterative, egalitarian collaboration. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 2-4, burkett2012anintroductionto pages 14-16) Second, the scope and process of user involvement differ considerably. Participatory design often focuses on involving users primarily to gather insights and elicit feedback, sometimes limiting their role to that of secondary contributors in a process still led by professional designers. (gomez2018participatorydesignand pages 428-430) In contrast, co-design explicitly incorporates users as equal co-creators at every stage, thereby fostering mutual learning, shared ownership, and higher levels of creative engagement. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 5-7, busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 13-14) Third, the treatment of power dynamics is a crucial area of divergence. Participatory design aims to democratize the design process by giving voice to users but can sometimes fall short in truly redistributing decision-making authority, whereas co-design explicitly structures its processes to ensure equitable power-sharing, ongoing negotiation, and the empowerment of all stakeholders. (gaudio2020codesignfordemocratising pages 1-4, burkett2012anintroductiontoa pages 16-18) Fourth, the methodological approaches differ. Participatory design often relies on established methods such as workshops, interviews, and focus groups to incorporate user feedback, while co-design employs iterative cycles of generative research, prototyping, and reflective practice to continuously integrate user contributions. (donetto2015experiencebasedcodesignand pages 7-9, ciolfi2016articulatingcodesignin pages 3-4) This difference in process is closely linked to the desired outcomes, with co-design projects typically resulting in solutions that are more robust, contextually aligned, and capable of evolving over time. (steen2013codesignasa pages 13-13) Finally, the fields of application underscore additional distinctions. Participatory design has proven effective in the development of information technologies, workplace systems, and other areas where a clear representation of user needs is essential. (smith2017participatorydesignin pages 1-3) Co-design, in contrast, has been leveraged across a broader spectrum, from urban planning and health services to education and cultural heritage, where complex social, cultural, and political factors necessitate a deeper, more sustained form of user collaboration. (combrinck2021codesigninthe pages 1-3, vargas2022cocreationcodesignanda pages 3-5)

sections.text: Looking ahead, both participatory design and co-design are likely to continue evolving in response to changing technological, social, and organizational environments. Researchers in the field are increasingly calling for more rigorous empirical studies to ground the theoretical distinctions between these approaches and to better understand the conditions under which each can yield the most effective results. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 9-11, busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 13-14) In particular, the need to integrate power-analysis frameworks and to develop clearer guidelines for role negotiation and capacity building has been emphasized as critical for ensuring that both PD and co-design can live up to their democratic and transformative potential. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborative pages 23-25) The evolving digital landscape and the advent of global communication technologies further complicate the landscape of participatory practices. Design research is increasingly addressing how digital tools can mediate collaboration while simultaneously reinforcing or challenging existing power structures. (hansen2019howparticipatorydesign pages 1-2) In these contexts, co-design methodologies may offer significant advantages by enabling diverse and distributed actors to work together synchronously and asynchronously, thereby fostering inclusiveness and shared creativity on a scale that traditional participatory design might find difficult to achieve. (vargas2022cocreationcodesignand pages 2-3) Moreover, the integration of co-design within broader co-production and co-creation frameworks represents an important theoretical shift, emphasizing that design is not an isolated technical endeavor but rather a holistic, socially embedded process that requires multi-stakeholder partnership from problem definition through to implementation and evaluation. (vargas2022cocreationcodesignanda pages 2-3) This perspective not only redefines the role of the designer but also challenges the notion of design as a linear, top-down process, suggesting instead that innovation is best achieved through sustained, egalitarian collaboration over time. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborative pages 25-28)

sections.text: In summary, while both participatory design and co-design share an overarching commitment to embedding user perspectives into the design process, they diverge significantly in their philosophies, methods, and outcomes. Participatory design is historically rooted in democratic, user-empowerment traditions with an emphasis on inclusive engagement and mutual learning, yet it sometimes limits user involvement to consultative roles. (burkett2012anintroductionto pages 1-7, smith2017participatorydesignin pages 1-3) Co-design represents an evolution of these ideas by seeking to fully integrate users as co-creators in every phase of the design process, employing iterative and reflective methods that facilitate power-sharing, capacity building, and sustained innovation. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 2-4, busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 8-10) The key differences can be summarized as follows. First, the historical origins and philosophical underpinnings of participatory design and co-design set them apart, with the former focusing on political emancipation and the latter on collaborative co-creation. Second, the processes underpinning each approach differ markedly: participatory design relies on early-stage input and consultative methods, whilst co-design advocates for ongoing, iterative collaboration that integrates creative contributions directly into design outcomes. Third, the management of power dynamics is more explicitly negotiated in co-design, ensuring a more equitable distribution of decision-making authority throughout the process. Fourth, the outcomes of co-design projects tend to be more innovative, contextually tailored, and sustainable due to the deep integration of user expertise and the iterative nature of the methods employed. (steen2013codesignasa pages 10-13, vargas2022cocreationcodesignand pages 3-5) Future work in this space will likely focus on refining these methodologies further and investigating the long-term impacts of these collaborative practices on innovation, social inclusion, and sustainable development. In doing so, researchers and practitioners alike will continue to explore how best to harness the collective creative capacities of diverse stakeholders in the service of designing more effective, socially responsible, and resilient solutions. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborative pages 21-23, benz2024communitybasedparticipatoryresearchthrough pages 1-2) Ultimately, while participatory design and co-design are interconnected within the broader spectrum of user-centered approaches, their key differences—ranging from the depth and nature of user involvement to the structures for managing power and conflict—highlight distinct pathways for achieving design outcomes that are both innovative and socially meaningful. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 9-11, burkett2012anintroductionto pages 16-18) By critically understanding these differences, designers, researchers, and policymakers can more effectively choose or integrate methodologies that best suit the specific challenges of their projects, enabling a more responsive, democratic, and impactful design process that not only addresses immediate user needs but also fosters long-term capacity building and social transformation. (busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 13-14, zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborativea pages 19-21) This report has argued that the evolution from participatory design to co-design marks a significant turning point in the field of design research—one that emphasizes not only the importance of involving users in the design process but also the necessity of rethinking traditional roles, power structures, and methodological approaches in order to fully benefit from collective creativity. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 2-4, donetto2015experiencebasedcodesignand pages 7-9) Although both approaches have their respective strengths and challenges, the move toward more integrative and collaborative design practices underscores the need for ongoing dialogue, reflexivity, and innovation in methodologies that aim to democratize design and empower users as true co-creators of their futures. (zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborative pages 25-28) In conclusion, the distinctions between participatory design and co-design are evident not only in their theoretical and methodological orientations but also in their practical implementations and outcomes across different sectors. The participatory design model, with its roots in political democracy and user specification, provides a vital foundation for ensuring that technology and service design remain responsive to human needs. Co-design builds on this foundation by transforming user participation into an active, equal, and continuous collaboration that fosters empowerment, innovation, and sustainable change. (hansen2019howparticipatorydesign pages 1-2, vargas2022cocreationcodesignand pages 2-3) As the complexity of societal challenges continues to grow, the move toward integrative, co-creative methodologies is likely to become ever more central to the practice of design in a range of contexts, from urban planning and healthcare to education and cultural heritage. (combrinck2021codesigninthe pages 1-3, gomez2018participatorydesignand pages 424-426) Through this detailed exploration, it is evident that while both participatory design and co-design share common goals of enhancing user involvement and democratizing design, they each offer unique strategies for harnessing the creative potential of all stakeholders. This analysis underscores the importance of selecting, adapting, and sometimes blending these approaches according to the specific challenges and objectives of any given design initiative. (busciantellaricci2024researchthroughcodesign pages 13-14, steen2013codesignasa pages 10-13) By fostering an understanding of these key differences, this report aims to contribute to the scholarly dialogue on design methodologies and provide practical insights for practitioners seeking to implement more effective, democratic, and transformative design processes in their work. (antonini2021anoverviewof pages 5-7, zamenopoulos2018codesignascollaborative pages 15-18)

question: Does active learning work well when fine-tuning large language models?

sections.text: This report examines the efficacy of active learning when applied to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). The analysis synthesizes empirical studies and methodological developments from recent literature to provide a comprehensive evaluation of active learning paradigms in the context of LLM fine-tuning. Active learning (AL) has long been recognized as a promising strategy in machine learning to reduce annotation costs by selectively prioritizing data that promise maximal model improvement. In the era of large language models, such as BERT, GPT-4, and Llama, the utility of traditional active learning approaches is questioned by researchers investigating issues such as the cold start problem, model mismatch, and enormous computational overhead during iterative fine-tuning (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 1-2). Simultaneously, recent work has proposed novel AL frameworks that leverage LLMs’ zero-shot and few-shot abilities to guide data selection without constant retraining, thereby rebalancing the cost-performance trade-off (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 8-11).

sections.text: Active learning seeks to identify the most informative samples based on uncertainty, diversity, or surrogate signals, ultimately reducing the required volume of labeled training data (griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 1-2). However, classical AL strategies encounter challenges when employed for fine-tuning large-scale models because iterative retraining of deep transformers is computationally expensive and subject to retrieval delays, thereby hindering practical application in real-world scenarios (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 1-2, griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 8-10). Moreover, issues such as the cold start, in which an initial set of labeled data is insufficient to yield reliable uncertainty measures, complicate the active learning process for models like BERT and its variants (yuan2010coldstartactivelearning pages 1-2). In response, researchers have worked to decouple querying from full model retraining, employing methods like using LLMs as query agents to select training examples without fine-tuning the large models at every iteration (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 8-11). Meanwhile, studies employing Monte-Carlo Dropout to estimate uncertainty, as well as evaluating the benefit of layer freezing and uncertainty propagation, have provided evidence that traditional AL can indeed enhance fine-tuning, particularly in low-resource settings (griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 2-4, griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 7-8).

sections.text: A. LLM-Based Query Models  One recent innovation is the ActiveLLM framework, which leverages instruction-tuned LLMs such as GPT-4 and Llama 3 as oracles that perform instance selection based on designed prompts. Unlike conventional AL techniques that require iterative fine-tuning during data acquisition, ActiveLLM utilizes these models’ zero-shot capabilities to assess the informativeness of unlabeled instances, thereby bypassing the need for costly iterative retraining (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 1-2, bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 13-14). This decoupling of the query process from the successor model fine-tuning not only reduces computational overhead but also mitigates the model mismatch problem—a phenomenon wherein the AL query mechanism (often based on a smaller or distilled model) does not faithfully represent the uncertainty of the final, fine-tuned model (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 4-6). B. Techniques for Cold Start Mitigation  Traditional AL strategies such as Least Confidence or Prediction Entropy face challenges in a cold start, where insufficient labeled data yields unreliable confidence estimations. Innovative methods like ALPS (Active Learning by Processing Surprisal) exploit the intrinsic language modeling loss from the pre-training phase to select informative samples before any task-specific fine-tuning begins (yuan2010coldstartactivelearning pages 1-2). In doing so, these methods leverage self-supervision to generate a surrogate measure for uncertainty, thereby ensuring that the initial training set is strategically chosen to maximize knowledge gain even in the absence of labeled data (yuan2010coldstartactivelearning pages 1-2). C. Efficient Representation-Based Approaches  Another line of research focuses on reducing the computational cost during AL iterations. Techniques such as PRepAL precompute fixed representations from large transformers and use lightweight classifiers (e.g., logistic regression) for determining uncertainty on unlabeled data, thus cutting down the time and resources needed for full model fine-tuning (vysogorets2402towardsefficientactive pages 8-10). While full fine-tuning may provide slightly superior performance, methods like PRepAL offer a scalable alternative for settings where time is critical or computational resources are limited (vysogorets2402towardsefficientactive pages 6-8).

sections.text: A. Performance Improvements in Low-Resource Scenarios  Empirical studies on datasets such as GLUE and various sentiment classification tasks have shown that AL-guided fine-tuning of models like BERT can achieve comparable or even enhanced performance relative to baselines using random data selection (griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 7-8). In these experiments, by selectively querying data points that maximize an uncertainty-driven knowledge gain, models exhibit improved accuracy with far fewer labeled examples, especially when combined with strategies like layer freezing to alleviate overfitting (griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 10-12). B. Active Learning Combined with PEFT Strategies  Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques, such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), have been investigated in combination with AL. Nevertheless, naive coupling of AL with PEFT often yields inferior results when uncertainty estimates are derived from full-model behavior while only a subset of parameters is updated (zhang2403starconstraintlora pages 1-2, zhang2403starconstraintlora pages 2-3). To address this gap, the STAR method was developed to incorporate dynamic uncertainty measurements and calibration techniques such as Monte-Carlo dropout and weight regularization. The STAR approach bridges the uncertainty gap between the full model and its parameter-efficient variants, thereby enabling data-efficient fine-tuning through active sample selection (zhang2403starconstraintlora pages 7-9). C. LLM as Annotation Oracles  Active learning frameworks leveraging LLMs as annotators have also been explored in recent work. In scenarios where the cost and effort of human annotation are prohibitive, large language models such as GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 have been utilized to provide pseudo-labels for the active learning loop. Studies demonstrate that by applying a mixed annotation strategy—where confident predictions from LLMs are accepted while uncertain samples are deferred to human experts—accuracy can be sustained while reducing annotation costs dramatically (wang2401activelearningfor pages 1-2, wang2401activelearningfor pages 4-6). Additionally, frameworks such as FreeAL have been introduced to envisage a human-free active learning loop where a large LLM acts as an active annotator and a smaller model filters the outputs, demonstrating promising performance gains in cost-effectiveness and efficiency for downstream tasks (xiao2023freealtowardshumanfree pages 8-10).

sections.text: Notwithstanding its promise, there are significant challenges when applying active learning to large language model fine-tuning. First, the iterative nature of traditional AL—whereby each active learning cycle requires partially retraining the model—poses a severe computational bottleneck given the immense size of contemporary LLMs (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 2-4, griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 8-10). Moreover, the cold start dilemma remains a critical issue in the early phases of fine-tuning where a minimal labeled set limits the reliability of uncertainty estimates and hinders the ability of the model to differentiate between easily learnable versus ambiguous examples (yuan2010coldstartactivelearning pages 1-2). Furthermore, model mismatch between the query mechanism and the final fine-tuned model continues to undermine the potential gains of active learning (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 4-6). This phenomenon is pronounced when a smaller or distilled model is used to estimate uncertainty for the selection process while the full LLM is employed for the final task, leading to suboptimal data selection (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 4-6). Equally, recent empirical findings highlight that conventional uncertainty metrics, such as entropy-based scoring, may fail to capture the true “informativeness” of data for LLM fine-tuning, thus necessitating novel metrics that account for the model’s special architecture and context limitations (margatina2104ontheimportance pages 1-2, margatina2104ontheimportance pages 5-6).

sections.text: Given these challenges, several lines of investigation have sought to enhance AL methodologies in the context of LLM fine-tuning. One promising direction is the refinement of prompt engineering, wherein the design of the prompt used to query the LLM is optimized to encourage structured reasoning (e.g., “think step by step”) and to explicitly incorporate labeling guidelines. Such refined prompts have been shown to yield superior performance in terms of sample selection and informativeness, thereby enhancing the overall utility of AL in few-shot scenarios (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 8-11). Parallel to prompt optimizations, augmentation of AL with complementary techniques such as ensemble sampling has been explored, especially in domains where task-specific considerations are paramount. For instance, when fine-tuning scientific text classifiers, ensemble sampling strategies have been shown to boost performance over single-criterion uncertainty sampling by integrating multiple uncertainty and diversity measures (hu2024promptbasedactivelearning pages 1-2). These strategies ensure that the selected training instances not only reflect high uncertainty but also capture diverse facets of the data distribution, which is essential for robust fine-tuning of large models. Moreover, techniques from active representation learning, where a fixed pre-trained representation is leveraged and only a lightweight classifier is retrained during each AL iteration, provide additional avenues to mitigate the computational overhead associated with continuous full-model fine-tuning (vysogorets2402towardsefficientactive pages 1-2, vysogorets2402towardsefficientactive pages 6-8). This representation-based approach is particularly attractive when large LLMs are employed in resource-constrained environments, as it offers a pragmatic solution to balancing annotation efficiency and computational expense.

sections.text: Comparative studies have also been conducted to evaluate whether active learning truly confers benefits over random data selection when fine-tuning LLMs. Empirical evidence indicates that while active learning has the potential to improve data efficiency, its performance gains can be context-dependent. For example, experiments on multi-class textual classification tasks have shown that AL strategies can yield superior accuracy in low-data regimes—typically when fewer than 100 examples are available (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 11-13). Beyond such regimes, however, the performance differential between AL and random sampling may diminish, suggesting that active learning is most beneficial when labeled data are extremely scarce (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 11-13). Additionally, studies that compare AL-fine-tuned models to those fine-tuned using all available data indicate that while AL can achieve near state-of-the-art performance with substantially fewer labeled examples, the incremental gains become less pronounced as the volume of labeled data increases (griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 7-8, margatina2104ontheimportance pages 5-6). This nuance underscores the importance of strategically deploying active learning in scenarios where annotation costs are prohibitive rather than as a universal substitute for comprehensive labeling.

sections.text: A. Domain-Specific Tasks  Active learning combined with LLM fine-tuning has been extensively evaluated in domain-specific contexts such as biomedical natural language processing and legal document classification. In these tasks, fine-tuning smaller models with carefully selected training data via active learning has often yielded performance that rivals or exceeds that of larger LLMs operating in a zero- or few-shot manner (lu2023humanstillwins pages 1-2). Domain-specific models benefit particularly from AL since specialized tasks require precise, high-quality annotations, and expert involvement remains a critical component in mitigating errors (lu2023humanstillwins pages 3-5). B. Safety-Critical Applications  For safety-critical scenarios, such as generating robust and representative scenarios for self-harm or offensive speech mitigation, active learning has been explored to guide LLMs in producing less typical yet important examples (hassan2410activelearningfor pages 1-2, hassan2410anactivelearning pages 1-2). These frameworks ensure that LLM-based systems are exposed to a wider range of edge cases and can thus generalize more safely to critical tasks. The interplay between AL and LLM fine-tuning in these domains illustrates that while active learning can effectively target rare but consequential examples, the challenge lies in ensuring the data remain balanced and representative of the underlying distribution. C. Text Classification and Generation Tasks  Several studies have incorporated LLMs into active learning loops to improve performance in text classification tasks. For instance, research employing a mixed annotation strategy—with uncertain instances verified by human experts and confident cases generated by LLMs—has demonstrated that models can achieve competitive accuracy while substantially reducing annotation costs (wang2401activelearningfor pages 1-2, wang2401activelearningfor pages 4-6). Similarly, frameworks such as FreeAL adopt a human-free paradigm in which LLMs serve as both annotators and selectors, reinforcing the idea that active learning can be adapted to reduce dependence on costly human labeling while still maintaining fine-tuning effectiveness (xiao2023freealtowardshumanfree pages 8-10).

sections.text: The literature presents a multifaceted picture of active learning in the context of LLM fine-tuning. On one hand, theoretical arguments and empirical results illustrate that active learning can substantially reduce the number of labeled samples required to achieve comparable performance, particularly in low-resource settings and for domain-specific tasks (griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 1-2, margatina2104ontheimportance pages 5-6). On the other hand, the computational demands associated with iterative full-model fine-tuning often necessitate the development of alternative strategies, such as representation-based learning and LLM-based querying, to make active learning a viable tool for large-scale models (vysogorets2402towardsefficientactive pages 1-2, bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 4-6). In addition, the active learning literature reveals that the effectiveness of AL is intimately linked to the choice of acquisition function. Uncertainty-based methods, while widely used, may not always capture the true informativeness of a sample, particularly in scenarios where label uncertainty is poorly calibrated—a common issue in deep neural networks and large language models (zhang2403starconstraintlora pages 1-2, margatina2104ontheimportance pages 1-2). This has led to the exploration of hybrid strategies that combine uncertainty metrics with diversity measures and incorporate dynamic calibration procedures to yield a more robust selection mechanism (zhang2403starconstraintlora pages 7-9, yu2022actuneuncertaintybasedactive pages 8-10). Furthermore, the inherent variability in LLM outputs, especially when using chat-based interfaces where hidden system parameters cannot be fully controlled, adds another layer of complexity. As researchers note, while LLMs may perform well during active learning iterations, issues related to context length limitations and difficulties with handling long contexts may affect reasoning and data selection quality (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 13-14). Therefore, while active learning holds significant promise for fine-tuning LLMs, its success hinges on careful integration, including prompt optimization and the potential decoupling of query and successor models.

sections.text: Based on an extensive review of recent literature, active learning proves to be a powerful methodology when properly integrated for the fine-tuning of large language models. Although traditional active learning approaches encounter significant challenges—such as the cold start problem, computational costs associated with iterative retraining, and issues related to model mismatch—innovative frameworks that leverage LLMs themselves as query models, employ precomputed representations, and integrate dynamic uncertainty calibration have demonstrated promising improvements in both sample efficiency and model performance (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 8-11, yuan2010coldstartactivelearning pages 1-2, vysogorets2402towardsefficientactive pages 6-8). In summary, while active learning works well in scenarios where it is enhanced by appropriate methodological refinements and careful prompt design, the benefits are most pronounced in domains with low available labeled data or where annotation is prohibitively expensive. The recent advances in frameworks such as ActiveLLM, STAR, and FreeAL offer tangible evidence that well-designed active learning strategies, when combined with state-of-the-art LLM architectures, can effectively address the inherent challenges in fine-tuning large language models (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 1-2, xiao2023freealtowardshumanfree pages 8-10). Future research that continues to refine uncertainty metrics, integrate human oversight in adaptive ways, and optimize prompt engineering will likely further enhance the practicality and efficacy of active learning for LLM fine-tuning (hu2024promptbasedactivelearning pages 1-2, margatina2104ontheimportance pages 5-6). Ultimately, the convergence of active learning and large language model fine-tuning represents a promising frontier for improving training efficiency and achieving high model performance with minimal annotated data, albeit with the necessary caveats regarding computational feasibility and selection biases. Continued interdisciplinary research combining insights from natural language processing, experimental design, and machine learning theory will be essential to fully harness the potential of active learning in this rapidly evolving landscape (rouzegar2024llmpoweredactivelearning pages 50-54, margatina2023activelearningprinciples pages 1-2). This report concludes that active learning can work well when fine-tuning large language models—provided that challenges related to uncertainty calibration, computational efficiency, and effective data representation are adequately addressed through innovative methodologies and adaptive strategies (bayer2405activellmlargelanguage pages 8-11, griesshaber2012finetuningbertfor pages 1-2, yuan2010coldstartactivelearning pages 1-2).

question: With respect to signal processing which operator is more sensitive to noise detection, first order or second order and why?

sections.text:
Edge detection in signal processing relies fundamentally on the estimation of derivatives in an image or signal, and the choice between using first
‐order differential operators (which typically compute the gradient or rate of change) and second
‐order operators (which focus on the curvature or change in gradient) has significant consequences in terms of noise sensitivity. In general, second
‐order operators tend to be more sensitive to noise than first
‐order operators, and this difference stems primarily from the mathematical properties inherent in differentiation. Specifically, differentiation acts as a high
‐pass filter, and the higher the order of the derivative, the more strongly it amplifies high
‐frequency components—including noise—that are present in the signal.

From a mathematical point of view, first
‐order operators compute the rate at which intensity changes from one pixel (or sample) to the next. This is typically expressed as the image gradient, which can be approximated by operators such as Sobel, Prewitt, or Roberts. These operators estimate the slope of intensity variation and, although they are sensitive to any rapid change in pixel values, their operation generally only boosts frequencies proportional to ω (the angular frequency) (gao2010animprovedsobel pages 1-2, chaganti2005edgedetectionof pages 33-38). In contrast, second
‐order operators, such as the Laplacian and Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG), involve taking the derivative of the gradient. Their Fourier response is proportional to ω²; hence, they amplify high frequency components to a greater extent (canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 12-14, nalwa1986ondetectingedges pages 1-2). This quadratic amplification of high
‐frequency components results in a stronger response to noise, since noise typically resides in the high frequency region of the spectrum and manifests as rapid, spurious intensity changes.

sections.text:
The implications of these properties become particularly evident when the operators are applied directly to noisy signals. For instance, studies on edge detection comparing various operators have consistently shown that first
‐order methods—especially when coupled with smoothing filters—present a more favorable trade
‐off between edge localization accuracy and noise robustness (ahmed2018comparativestudyamonga pages 1-3, bhardwaj2012asurveyon pages 1-3). In contrast, second
‐order operators, such as those detecting zero crossings from the second derivative (Laplacian based), tend to generate numerous false edges when the underlying image or signal contains even moderate levels of noise (banerjee2015noisesensitivityof pages 1-2, canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 1-2).

sections.text:
A key technical reason for the discrepancy lies in the nature of noise amplification due to differentiation. When a signal is noisy—say, with additive white Gaussian noise—the high
‐frequency components introduced by this noise are naturally accentuated during derivative computation. A first
‐order derivative will boost these components linearly (proportional to ω), whereas a second
‐order derivative boosts them quadratically (proportional to ω²). Consequently, features that originate purely from noise may end up with magnitudes that are comparable to or even exceed the response from a true edge in a second
‐order detection scheme. This phenomenon is well documented in classical texts and comparative studies wherein it is observed that second derivative methods require a substantial pre
‐smoothing operation to reduce noise effects, typically using a Gaussian filter (canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 12-14, bhardwaj2012asurveyon pages 3-6). However, this smoothing step, while mitigating noise, can also lead to blurring and loss of fine edge detail, illustrating the inherent trade
‐off involved (chaganti2005edgedetectionof pages 38-44).

sections.text:
Several experimental and theoretical studies further reinforce the notion that first
‐order operators are less susceptible to noise. For example, in work comparing the performance of edge detection operators on noisy images, it was observed that the Sobel and Prewitt operators (typical first
‐order operators) tend to manage noise somewhat better than second
‐order methods like the LOG operator, even if both must contend with some noise-induced false detections (ahmed2018comparativestudyamong pages 1-3, bhardwaj2012asurveyon pages 1-3). Although the Sobel operator itself is not entirely immune to noise, due to its built-in averaging (which partially acts as a smoothing operation), its fundamental first
‐order nature leads to a lower amplification of noise compared to second
‐order counterparts (gao2010animprovedsobel pages 1-2, chaganti2005edgedetectionof pages 33-38).

sections.text:
The role of smoothing is critical in all edge detection schemes. Given that both first
‐ and second
‐order operators are vulnerable to noise, it is common practice to apply a pre
‐smoothing filter. For first
‐order operators, even a moderate Gaussian smoothing can significantly improve their noise performance, as the gradient detection is performed on a more isotropic, low-noise representation of the image (canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 1-2, kumar2017fractionalfouriertransform pages 1-3). With second
‐order operators, pre-smoothing is indispensable because the subsequent second derivative operations would otherwise greatly magnify the residual high-frequency variations (canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 12-14, vliet1989anonlinearlaplace pages 3-5). However, the necessary level of smoothing for second
‐order operators is generally higher, further complicating the balance between noise suppression and edge localization precision (lunscher1986optimaledgedetector pages 1-2, shen1992anoptimallinear pages 17-19).

sections.text:
Another important aspect to consider is the localization precision of edges. First
‐order operators typically identify edges by locating local maxima of the gradient. While this method is computationally efficient and reasonably robust to moderate noise levels, it may sometimes produce less accurately localized edges when the gradient magnitude is distorted by noise. Nevertheless, when paired with adaptive thresholding and non-maximum suppression—as seen in the widely acclaimed Canny edge detector—the method can provide excellent localization with controlled noise sensitivity (canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 1-2, lyvers1988precisionedgecontrast pages 5-6). On the other hand, second
‐order operators, though theoretically capable of sharper localization due to their ability to identify inflection points (zero crossings), often suffer from spurious responses in noisy conditions, because the noise-induced fluctuations in curvature lead to false zero crossings. In fact, a common observation in studies comparing noise performance is that despite their potential for more precise edge pinpointing, second-order operators consistently yield a higher rate of false detections under even moderate noise (banerjee2015noisesensitivityof pages 1-1, chaganti2005edgedetectionof pages 38-44, nalwa1986ondetectingedges pages 1-2).

Comparative analyses have further quantified these observations. For example, in research on medical images where noise types such as Rician or speckle are prevalent, evaluations have shown that first
‐order operators (such as those derived from gradient masks used in the Canny method) outperform second
‐order operators (like the Laplace operator) in terms of maintaining edge detection robustness at various noise intensities and image complexities (maksimovic2024comparativeanalysisof pages 1-2, maksimovic2024comparativeanalysisof pages 15-18). These studies typically demonstrate that noise intensification in second
‐order operators leads to either the detection of numerous false edges or the requirement for more rigorous thresholding strategies to suppress such artifacts. In contrast, first
‐order operators, because of their lower sensitivity to high-frequency noise, tend to provide a more stable edge detection performance across a range of SNR conditions (chaganti2005edgedetectionof pages 33-38, ahmed2018comparativestudyamonga pages 1-3).

Moreover, in signal processing applications where the goal is to interpret real-world signals that inherently contain noise (such as in speech processing or character recognition from noisy video data), first
‐order differentiation has been preferred in many instances. For example, in research on digit recognition from street view house number images, first
‐order operators such as the Roberts or Sobel operator (particularly in their improved variants that include pre-processing steps like bilateral filtering) have been shown to yield better overall system performance by reducing the incidence of noise-induced false detections, as the noise amplification is less severe relative to second
‐order methods (fawwaz2019noiseeffectanalysis pages 1-4, gao2010animprovedsobel pages 4-5). The relative simplicity of first
‐order operators also contributes to their robustness, as the associated computational mechanisms involve fewer operations that could themselves be influenced by noise.

sections.text: In addition to the classical derivative-based edge detectors, alternative approaches have been explored that attempt to harness the benefits of fractional differentiation, which can be viewed as operating between first and second order operators. Fractional-order edge detectors provide an additional degree of freedom, allowing the order of differentiation to be tuned to balance edge sensitivity and noise suppression. While these methods can outperform classical operators under certain conditions, the general trend remains that as the order of differentiation increases, so does the amplification of noise components (kumar2017fractionalfouriertransform pages 1-3, kumar2017fractionalfouriertransform pages 9-13). Thus, even in these advanced approaches, operators that lean closer to first order tend to exhibit lower noise sensitivity.

sections.text: From a practical standpoint, when designing edge detection systems for applications where noise is a significant concern, it is common to adopt a multi-stage processing strategy. This strategy typically involves first applying a smoothing filter, such as a Gaussian or a wavelet-based denoiser, then computing the first-order derivatives to estimate edge locations, and finally refining the detection through adaptive thresholding and non-maximum suppression. This cascade approach leverages the lower inherent noise sensitivity of first-order operators while mitigating their weaknesses through careful fusion with pre- and post-processing operations (canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 1-2, chaganti2005edgedetectionof pages 38-44, bhardwaj2012asurveyon pages 3-6). In contrast, systems that attempt to use second-order methods without sufficient smoothing tend to experience degraded performance in noisy environments, as illustrated extensively in both theoretical analyses and empirical studies (shen1992anoptimallinear pages 17-19, vliet1989anonlinearlaplace pages 11-14, vriendt1995effectofsampling pages 15-18).

sections.text: Furthermore, research on energy operators such as the Teager Energy Operator (TEO) reinforces this conceptual framework. The TEO, which inherently combines both first and second derivative components in a nonlinear manner, demonstrates superior performance in capturing instantaneous energy and frequency modulations in signals; however, its operation over very short time windows renders it especially susceptible to noise. The sensitivity of the TEO is largely attributable to its reliance on second-order differences that exacerbate the influence of noise (kvedalen2003signalprocessingusing pages 77-82, kvedalen2003signalprocessingusing pages 87-89). Modifications to the TEO often involve filtering or band-limiting strategies to improve noise robustness, and these modifications further illustrate that the trade-off between capturing fine signal details (which benefits from higher derivative orders) and avoiding noise amplification is a critical design consideration in edge and energy detection.

Wavelet-based edge detectors can offer superior noise robustness by selectively analyzing frequency bands and rejecting those components associated with noise. Nonetheless, even in these methods, the analogous distinction remains: operators that effectively emphasize second-order differences (or their wavelet equivalents in high-frequency bands) are more likely to be corrupted by noise unless significant additional measures are taken (chaganti2005edgedetectionof pages 79-87).

sections.text: Cumulatively, the theoretical analyses, Fourier-based interpretations, and empirical evaluations all converge on the conclusion that second-order operators, because of their quadratic amplification of high-frequency signal components, are inherently more sensitive to noise than first-order operators. First-order operators, though not entirely noise-immune, provide a more stable response under typical noise conditions with the aid of minimal smoothing, and therefore serve as a preferable basis for robust edge detection in many practical signal processing applications (canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 1-2, ahmed2018comparativestudyamonga pages 1-3, nalwa1986ondetectingedges pages 1-2).

This inherent noise amplification in second-order methods necessitates significantly stronger smoothing to avoid spurious edges and false detections, a requirement that often leads to a trade-off with edge localization accuracy. In contrast, first-order operators, particularly when paired with appropriate pre-smoothing techniques, strike a more effective balance between detecting true edges and suppressing noise. This conclusion is supported by both theoretical analyses of the Fourier responses of these operators and empirical studies across various implementations and applications in image and signal processing (canny1987acomputationalapproach pages 12-14, bhardwaj2012asurveyon pages 1-3, kumar2017fractionalfouriertransform pages 1-3, vliet1989anonlinearlaplace pages 3-5, shen1992anoptimallinear pages 17-19).

question: how can RRT-based path planning be adapted to efficiently handle narrow pathways

sections.text: This report examines the adaptation of Rapidly‐exploring Random Tree (RRT)–based path planning methods to efficiently navigate narrow pathways, a longstanding challenge in robotic navigation. Conventional RRT algorithms are valued for their ability to rapidly generate feasible paths in high‐dimensional free spaces; however, when confronted with narrow passages, the uniform random sampling intrinsic to these methods results in infrequent sampling within critical constrained regions, leading to inefficient exploration, slow convergence, and paths that often require significant post–processing. This report synthesizes multiple advanced strategies from recent literature that modify RRT‐based methods to overcome these shortcomings.

Traditional RRT methods incrementally expand a tree through random sampling across the configuration space with a bias toward unexplored regions. Although this global strategy lends itself well to high–dimensional coverage, it suffers from severe performance degradation in environments characterized by narrow channels or passages, where the volume available for free movement is limited relative to the entire search domain (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 1-2). In such scenarios, a significant proportion of random samples fall outside the narrow corridor, leading to inefficiencies in tree growth and a heightened likelihood of redundant sampling in open areas. Consequently, researchers have introduced several modifications aimed specifically at improving sampling efficiency and convergence speed in these constrained environments.

sections.text: Narrow passages introduce multiple challenges in path planning. The inherent randomness of traditional RRT algorithms means that sampling inside these confined regions occurs with very low probability, which can lead to extensive computational times and suboptimal path quality when a viable solution is eventually discovered (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 3-5). Additionally, the inability to directly capture the geometry of narrow passages not only results in paths that are highly suboptimal in length and smoothness but also requires extensive post–processing such as path pruning and curve fitting to produce robot–executable trajectories (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 5-7). Moreover, for systems with kinematic constraints (for example, car–like robots), it becomes imperative to generate feasible paths with bounded curvature and adherence to dynamic constraints. These aspects motivate the development of tailored strategies that focus sampling density in critical narrow areas and dynamically refine tree expansion.

sections.text: One widely adopted approach to address the narrow passage problem is the introduction of informed or targeted sampling strategies. For example, algorithms such as RE–RRT* modify the sampling process by focusing node generation on regions deemed more relevant for connectivity between the start and goal, effectively shrinking the sample space to include only regions close to obstacle boundaries or along a direct corridor between endpoints (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 1-2). By sampling only along a prospective displacement vector or within a predefined “tube,” these methods dramatically reduce redundant exploration of wide open spaces and concentrate computational resources on the narrow, critical areas (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 3-5). In a similar vein, some researchers have employed Gaussian mixture models to probabilistically identify and generate samples that are more likely to fall within narrow passages, thereby improving the likelihood of early convergence (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 2-3). This method reduces both the number of needed samples and overall planning time compared to classical RRT-based exploration.

sections.text: Another effective adaptation is to employ adaptive step size strategies in conjunction with bias–controlled steering. In narrow passages, the opportunity for collision is high, and a fixed step size may either overshoot or fail to generate nodes sufficiently close to obstacles while maintaining safe clearance. To resolve this, multi–strategy fusion approaches such as the Multi–Strategy Fusion RRT (MSF-RRT) adjust the expansion step size dynamically based on local map complexity and obstacle density (lei2025researchonimproved pages 5-6). When the tree encounters regions of high obstacle density that are indicative of narrow corridors, the step size is reduced to enable precise navigation along obstacle boundaries, while in open areas the tree can expand more aggressively by increasing the step size (lei2025researchonimproved pages 6-7). Alongside adaptive step sizing, a target bias strategy is often integrated whereby a higher sampling probability is assigned to nodes that are in the direction of the goal, ensuring that the tree remains focused even as it locally refines its structure through narrow passages (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 1-2).

sections.text: Bidirectional approaches, such as the RRT–Connect algorithm, have been shown to offer substantial improvements in planning time by simultaneously growing trees from both the start and the goal configurations. In challenging scenarios involving narrow passages, bidirectional expansion increases the probability of intermediate node connections in the confined area by directing growth from both ends (meng2025efficientcollisionavoidancenavigation pages 2-3). Furthermore, the incorporation of multiple trees, as demonstrated in multi–RRT or multi–tree–connect algorithms, can foster local exploration within various subregions of the narrow passage before merging them into a coherent global path (wang2018alearningbasedmultirrt pages 1-2). The multi–tree approach distributes sampling effort across several candidate trajectories, which increases the rate of discovering feasible connections in critical narrow areas. Learning-based tree selection methods further improve performance by framing tree expansion as a reinforcement learning problem, where the algorithm updates the probability of extending the most promising trees based on past successes (wang2018alearningbasedmultirrt pages 15-16).

sections.text: Another promising strategy centers on dynamic bridging techniques. DBR–RRT, for instance, incorporates a heuristic discrimination process that assesses whether sampled points represent “bridge” candidates between distinct regions of free space (qiu2024efficientpathplanning pages 1-2). By dynamically generating additional samples near nodes that expand slowly in narrow areas, DBR–RRT enhances the local connectivity and accelerates the extension of trees through confined passages (qiu2024efficientpathplanning pages 3-5). Furthermore, these methods are typically coupled with local path optimization procedures. Curvature–based smoothing and selective node replacement techniques—often implemented via algorithms that assess turning angles and enforce maximum curvature thresholds—further refine the planned paths. This local refinement is critical for ensuring that the resulting trajectory is smooth and dynamically feasible, a necessary requirement for nonholonomic vehicles and platforms with significant kinematic limitations (qiu2024efficientpathplanning pages 12-14).

sections.text: Beyond targeted sampling and adaptive step size, additional improvements have been developed by integrating auxiliary methods with RRT-based frameworks. For example, combining Rapidly-exploring Random Trees with artificial potential fields (APF) can provide an attractive force toward the goal while repelling the tree from obstacles, thereby further focusing the sampling process in narrow passages (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 2-3). Although APF methods on their own may increase planning time in highly complex settings, their integration with RRT* – which includes tree rewiring to guarantee asymptotic optimality – has shown to accelerate overall convergence (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 3-5). Additionally, methods from other domains, such as the use of bridge tests in sampling, identify regions where free space “bridges” exist between clusters of obstacle–adjacent points. These techniques systematically increase sampling density in the neighboring regions of obstacles, ensuring that the critical narrow passages are more robustly explored (noreen2016optimalpathplanning pages 7-8).

sections.text: Another aspect of adapting RRT-based planners for narrow passages involves post–processing the initially rough tree to generate an executable path that meets practical constraints of the robot’s dynamics. RRT* variants inherently improve path optimality by rewiring the tree iteratively during its expansion; however, the resulting paths are often highly jagged due to the arbitrary nature of the random samples. Techniques such as path pruning and smoothing—using methods based on cubic B–spline interpolation or Bezier curves—remove unnecessary nodes and smooth out abrupt direction changes to produce continuous trajectories (kiss2024pathplanningfor pages 56-58). Such post–processing is particularly important in narrow environments where even small oscillations or redundant reversals in the path may lead to infeasible trajectories when accounting for the robot’s physical constraints (kiss2024pathplanningfor pages 63-65). By combining an initial RRT-based exploration with an efficient post–processing scheme, the final trajectory becomes both optimal in path length and compliant with the vehicle’s kinematic requirements.

sections.text: The challenges posed by narrow passages have also motivated the formulation of hybrid planners that blend multiple strategies into a unified framework. Multi–Strategy Fusion RRT (MSF–RRT) is one such approach that combines target bias, bias expansion, and adaptive step size strategies to improve tree growth in confined environments (lei2025researchonimproved pages 1-2). By concurrently employing these mechanisms, MSF–RRT reduces unnecessary sampling in free space, directs the tree toward the goal, and dynamically adjusts the exploration parameters in response to local obstacle density. The combined effect is a substantial reduction in computation time, path length, and the overall number of nodes generated, while simultaneously ensuring that the final path is smooth and collision–free (lei2025researchonimproved pages 5-6, lei2025researchonimproved pages 6-7). Such fusion methods exemplify the practical benefits of integrating complementary techniques, ultimately enabling RRT-based path planners to robustly handle the stringent demands imposed by narrow passages.

For instance, experiments have demonstrated that dynamic bridging and heuristic-driven sampling significantly reduce the number of nodes required to find a feasible path through narrow passage scenarios, while maintaining nearly 100% success rates in highly constrained environments (meng2025efficientcollisionavoidancenavigation pages 11-12). Furthermore, multi–RRT–connect approaches that generate multiple trees and subsequently merge them have been shown to decrease planning times dramatically compared to standard RRT-based methods, particularly when navigating through cluttered spaces (meng2025efficientcollisionavoidancenavigation pages 2-3, meng2025efficientcollisionavoidancenavigation pages 3-4). The integration of local path smoothing techniques further enhances the applicability of these methods by producing trajectories that are not only collision–free but also dynamically feasible, ensuring that vehicles such as autonomous cars or drones can traverse narrow passages without encountering abrupt maneuvers (qiu2024efficientpathplanning pages 12-14).

First, the computational overhead induced by adaptive sampling, multi-tree management, and post–processing must be balanced against the available processing power, particularly in real-time applications where delays may have safety implications. In many cases, dedicated hardware acceleration or parallel processing architectures are employed to mitigate these issues and ensure that the planning algorithm operates within acceptable time constraints (wang2018alearningbasedmultirrt pages 15-16). Second, the precise tuning of bias parameters—such as the probability of goal bias, the threshold for adaptive step size reduction, and the criteria to trigger dynamic bridging—is often application–specific, requiring an iterative design process that frequently utilizes simulation before field deployment (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 2-3, lei2025researchonimproved pages 6-7). sections.text: While significant progress has been made in adapting RRT-based methods for narrow passage navigation, opportunities for further enhancement remain. Future work may explore the integration of advanced machine learning techniques that predict narrow passage locations based on prior experience and environmental features. For example, reinforcement learning methods can be used to optimize tree selection and parameter tuning on the fly, enabling the planner to dynamically adjust its behavior as the robot encounters previously unseen or dynamically changing environments (wang2018alearningbasedmultirrt pages 1-2, xu2024recentadvancesin pages 9-11). In addition, hybrid approaches that combine RRT with other planning paradigms—such as graph-based methods or evolutionary algorithms—could be further refined to leverage the strengths of each technique while mitigating their respective weaknesses (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 3-5, noreen2016optimalpathplanning pages 7-8). Another promising direction lies in the development of algorithms that blend global exploration with local refinement seamlessly. Methods like Informed–RRT* use a focused sampling subset defined by geometric heuristics, but further research is needed to extend these ideas to high–dimensional constrained spaces where the definition of “informed” regions becomes more complex (xu2024recentadvancesin pages 2-4, xu2024recentadvancesin pages 4-5). In addition, the use of dynamically adjustable sampling domains, possibly guided by real–time computational geometry methods such as Voronoi diagrams, could further improve sampling efficiency in narrow pathways (muhsen2024asystematicreview pages 8-9, szkandera2020narrowpassageproblem pages 1-3).

sections.text: In conclusion, the adaptation of RRT-based path planning for efficient navigation through narrow pathways requires a multi–faceted approach that directly addresses the inherent limitations of uniform random sampling strategies. By focusing sampling efforts on critical regions through informed and dynamically biased strategies, employing adaptive step size modulation, and leveraging multi–tree or bidirectional expansion techniques, it is possible to considerably enhance both the efficiency and reliability of the planned path. Supplementary methods such as dynamic bridging, local path smoothing, and intelligent post–processing further ensure that the resulting trajectories satisfy dynamic and kinematic constraints while maintaining safety margins. Collectively, these adaptations significantly reduce the computational time, improve convergence rates, and produce smoother, more robust paths in environments characterized by narrow passages, thereby broadening the applicability of RRT–based planning to complex, real–world problems (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 1-2, islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 3-5, lei2025researchonimproved pages 5-6, qiu2024efficientpathplanning pages 12-14). The extensive research in this area—from modifications that dynamically restrict the sampling zone to strategies that fuse global exploration with local, heuristic–guided refinement—demonstrates that RRT-based path planning can indeed be adapted effectively for narrow pathway navigation. As robotic platforms are increasingly deployed in complex, cluttered, and confined environments, these adaptations are not only beneficial but necessary to ensure safe and efficient autonomous operation (meng2025efficientcollisionavoidancenavigation pages 2-3, xu2024recentadvancesin pages 6-7). Future work in this domain is likely to focus on integrating machine learning for predictive sampling, further optimizing multi–strategy fusion approaches, and enhancing real–time responsiveness through the use of parallel processing and sensor integration. Such improvements will continue to expand the operational envelope of RRT-based path planning, enabling advanced navigation in even more challenging dynamic environments while ensuring that narrow passages are navigated not only safely but also efficiently and optimally (wang2018alearningbasedmultirrt pages 15-16, muhsen2024asystematicreview pages 9-10). In summary, by adopting targeted sampling strategies, adaptive expansion techniques, multi–tree exploration, dynamic bridging, and post–processing refinements, RRT-based path planners can be effectively tuned to overcome the challenges posed by narrow passages. These integrated strategies produce smoother, more feasible trajectories with improved convergence speed and reduced computational overhead, ultimately enabling robust autonomous navigation in complex, constrained environments (islam2024trajectoryoptimizationand pages 2-3, kiss2024pathplanningfor pages 56-58, lei2025researchonimproved pages 1-2, qiu2024efficientpathplanning pages 1-2).

question: How can the integration of GIS spatial analysis techniques with economic modeling improve the accuracy and effectiveness of environmental policy ?

sections.text: Abstract—The integration of Geographic Information Systems (GIS) spatial analysis techniques with economic modeling provides a powerful approach to enhance the accuracy and effectiveness of environmental policy by capturing spatial heterogeneity, quantifying ecosystem services, and evaluating trade‐offs between environmental quality and economic development in a spatially explicit framework (andrew2015spatialdataanalysis pages 12-14, andrew2015spatialdataanalysis pages 18-20).

sections.text: I. Introduction  Environmental policymaking faces complexities arising from the inherently spatial nature of natural resources, pollutant dispersion, and socio-economic activities; therefore, traditional analyses that neglect spatial dimensions often yield oversimplified insights that may not capture localized externalities and varying risk profiles (andrew2015spatialdataanalysis pages 6-8, banzhaf2019environmentaljusticethe pages 4-7). GIS spatial analysis techniques enable the detailed mapping and modeling of environmental phenomena—such as land use/land cover, air quality, and ecosystem service supply—while economic models quantify costs, benefits, and trade-offs associated with policy interventions, resulting in more robust policy frameworks (andrew2015spatialdataanalysis pages 8-10, banzhaf2019environmentaljusticethe pages 7-10). This paper details the mechanisms by which integrating GIS spatial analysis with economic modeling improves policy accuracy and effectiveness, drawing upon empirical examples and methodological advances from ecosystem service assessments, environmental justice analyses, and land-use change modeling (bielecka2020gisspatialanalysis pages 12-14, boggia2018spatialmulticriteriaanalysis pages 1-2).

sections.text: II. Conceptual Framework and Definitions  GIS is defined as a system that captures, stores, analyzes, and visualizes spatial data, thereby allowing researchers to dissect geographic phenomena using high-resolution maps and spatial statistics (andrew2015spatialdataanalysis pages 6-8). Economic modeling, on the other hand, uses mathematical formulations to simulate and predict the behavior of economic agents and to evaluate the outcomes of policy interventions under various assumptions (andrew2015spatialdataanalysis pages 8-10). When integrated, these techniques provide policymakers with a decision support toolkit that explicitly links location-specific ecological aspects with economic indicators and socio-demographic data (banzhaf2019environmentaljusticethe pages 7-10).

sections.text: III. Enhancing Spatial Resolution and Data Integration  The integration process begins with the incorporation of diverse spatial datasets—such as land use/land cover maps, soil and climate data, remotely sensed productivity indicators, and socio-economic demographics—which are critical for assessing both the supply and demand sides of ecosystem services (andrew2015spatialdataanalysis pages 12-14). For instance, ecosystem service assessments use GIS to spatially quantify key environmental processes (e.g., carbon sequestration, hydrological regulation), while economic models translate these physical measures into monetary valuations that inform conservation priorities (andrew2015spatialdataanalysis pages 18-20). The fusion of economic data with spatial datasets permits a more detailed, location-specific analysis of environmental challenges, reducing the errors induced by spatial generalizations and aggregated measures (bielecka2020gisspatialanalysis pages 10-12).
