sections.text: The trend towards hybrid architectures is another emerging technique for ensuring P2P storage reliability. Many modern systems do not rely solely on one mechanism; instead, they combine replication, erasure coding, cryptographic proofs, and blockchain-based consensus into a cohesive framework. For example, while systems like Filecoin and Storj primarily use replication combined with PoRep and PoSt schemes for fault tolerance (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 10-11, daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 11-12), others like BFT-DSN merge erasure coding with a storage-weighted BFT consensus protocol to achieve both efficiency and Byzantine resilience (guo2024bftdsnabyzantine pages 1-2, guo2024bftdsnabyzantine pages 7-8).Hybrid systems often adopt a multi-layer approach. At the lower level, data is split into chunks and encoded; then, cryptographic proofs including Merkle tree paths and homomorphic fingerprints are generated to verify chunk integrity. At a higher level, a blockchain or distributed ledger provides an immutable audit log to enforce incentives and manage trust. This layered architecture not only provides end-to-end protection against data corruption and malicious behavior but also aids in fast recovery and verification processes in the event of node failures (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 19-20, xu2024filedesasecure pages 6-7).

sections.text: Finally, evolving economic models and adaptive recovery protocols directly contribute to the reliability of P2P storage systems. By incorporating real-time performance monitoring and dynamic adjustment of replication factors based on network conditions, systems can proactively manage the trade-off between storage overhead and access latency. Trigger-based ARQ mechanisms exemplify these adaptive techniques by reducing retransmission overhead through early signaling and selective chunk retransmission in response to identified failures (park2025achievinghighefficiency pages 7-9, park2025achievinghighefficiency pages 9-11).Incentive schemes that reward storage reliability over long operating periods are similarly designed to keep nodes engaged and proactive. These economic models—coupled with advanced verification techniques to ensure that only verified data is used to compute rewards—help to align the interests of all network participants with the reliability and security goals of the system (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 17-18).

sections.text: The reliability of modern P2P storage systems is achieved through the judicious combination of several advanced techniques. First, blockchain-based trust management enables decentralized reputation systems and economic incentives, which together drive honest behavior and robust peer selection. Second, efficient data redundancy is achieved using erasure coding and replication strategies that greatly reduce storage overhead while ensuring that files remain accessible under adverse conditions. Third, the integration of Byzantine fault tolerance with storage-weighted consensus mechanisms guarantees system resiliency in adversarial environments. Fourth, advanced cryptographic techniques—including homomorphic fingerprinting, threshold signatures, content-addressable storage, and zk-SNARK-based batch proofs—ensure that data integrity is maintained even under attack. Fifth, dynamic and adaptive recovery protocols such as trigger-based ARQ and multi-path transfer methods further enhance data availability and retrieval performance. Finally, hybrid architectures that blend multiple replication and verification mechanisms, alongside modern network and hardware technologies, establish a highly reliable, scalable, and efficient P2P storage environment.Together, these techniques form a comprehensive strategy for ensuring the reliability of P2P storage systems. They address challenges at every layer—from data encoding and storage to network consensus, from verification and auditing to economic incentivization—and thus provide a resilient infrastructure capable of withstanding node churn, Byzantine failures, and performance bottlenecks while maintaining end-to-end data integrity and availability (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 20-21, daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 21-22, guo2024bftdsnabyzantine pages 12-12).In summary, the state-of-the-art in ensuring P2P storage reliability involves:1. Blockchain-based reputation systems and smart contracts for trust management and economic incentivization (bellaj2022btrustanew pages 16-21, bellaj2022btrustanew pages 25-28).2. Advanced peer selection mechanisms that utilize trust metrics and pertinence ratios to balance load (bellaj2022btrustanew pages 16-21).3. The application of erasure coding techniques to split and redundantly encode data, thus reducing storage overhead while achieving high fault tolerance (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 11-12, park2025achievinghighefficiency pages 2-4).4. Integration of Byzantine fault tolerance protocols and storage-weighted consensus models to achieve optimal data consistency and reliability under adversarial conditions (guo2024bftdsnabyzantine pages 1-2, guo2024bftdsnabyzantine pages 7-8).5. The use of cryptographic verification methods—including content-addressable storage, Merkle trees, and zk-SNARK-based proofs—to ensure that data has not been tampered with (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 4-5, xu2024filedesasecure pages 6-7).6. Adaptive recovery protocols such as trigger-based ARQ that optimize data retransmission and ensure efficient file retrieval even amid high node failure rates (park2025achievinghighefficiency pages 7-9, park2025achievinghighefficiency pages 9-11).7. Hybrid multi-layer architectures that combine replication, erasure coding, cryptographic proofs, and blockchain immutability to provide end-to-end security and reliability (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 19-20, xu2024filedesasecure pages 9-10).Each of these techniques, supported by extensive experimental research and simulation studies, demonstrates that the reliability of P2P storage systems can be significantly enhanced through a multipronged strategy. These systems now incorporate both robust technical mechanisms and carefully designed economic incentives, ensuring that, even in the presence of network churn, malicious behavior, and high failure rates, data integrity, availability, and timely retrieval remain preserved.The convergence of blockchain technology, advanced erasure coding, and Byzantine fault tolerance—supplemented by innovative cryptographic and recovery protocols—represents a new era in decentralized storage. This comprehensive approach not only increases network resilience but also unlocks new possibilities for distributed data sharing in environments ranging from IoT and sensor networks to large-scale distributed cloud services, where reliability and scalability are paramount (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 2-3, daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 22-22, giantsidi2023flexlogashared pages 3-4).In conclusion, the latest techniques for ensuring the reliability of P2P storage systems constitute a robust and interconnected framework that spans trust management, data redundancy and recovery, Byzantine fault tolerance, cryptographic verification, and economic incentivization. This integrated approach is a cornerstone for next-generation distributed storage systems, meeting the rigorous demands of modern applications while fostering an environment of trust, efficiency, and resilience (daniel2022ipfsandfriends pages 20-21, guo2024bftdsnabyzantine pages 9-10).This report illustrates that by combining these state-of-the-art techniques—each addressing specific challenges at various layers of the storage stack—it is possible to build highly reliable P2P storage systems that are resilient to failures, scalable in terms of storage overhead, and secure against adversarial corruption. As research continues to evolve, further refinements are expected in facilitating even lower latencies, more efficient recovery protocols, and enhanced security guarantees, thereby pushing the boundaries of what decentralized storage can reliably achieve.

question: What principles of interactive machine teaching can be applied to interactively curating social media feeds?

sections.text: Question: What principles of interactive machine teaching can be applied to interactively curating social media feeds? This report examines the principles of interactive machine teaching (IMT) that can be applied to the interactive curation of social media feeds. It discusses how an iterative, human ‐centered, and transparent approach to machine learning can empower end ‐users to actively shape, refine, and personalize the content they view. The report is organized into an introduction that outlines the challenges inherent in contemporary feed curation, a background section defining critical concepts in IMT and social media curation, a detailed presentation of IMT principles with relevance to feed personalization, a discussion on integrating these principles into social media system design, and concluding remarks on future directions.

Social media platforms are increasingly criticized for opaque content filtering and recommendation processes that limit user agency and reinforce echo chambers. Traditional recommender systems often operate as black boxes, where users passively receive content without insight into or control over the underlying algorithms. Recent advances in interactive machine teaching (IMT) offer an opportunity to address these issues by reconceptualizing users as active teachers who iteratively guide and refine machine learning models to better align with their personal preferences and social values. This report aims to explore a range of IMT principles that can be seamlessly integrated into social media feed curation systems, thereby enhancing personalization, transparency, and user satisfaction (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 1-2).

citations.title: Mapping the design space of teachable social media feed experiences

sections.text: A. Interactive Machine Teaching  Interactive machine teaching is a human-in-the-loop approach in which non-experts or domain experts directly shape the learning process by providing explicit, iterative feedback to an algorithmic learner. Unlike traditional machine learning, which relies solely on pre-collected training data, IMT exploits a cyclical “teaching loop” comprising planning (selecting examples or defining objectives), explaining (providing explicit teaching signals), and reviewing (assessing the system’s performance and correcting errors) (ramos2020interactivemachineteaching pages 7-9). This paradigm emphasizes the importance of human agency, transparency, and bidirectional communication between teacher and learner to achieve a model that is both adaptive and interpretable (ramos2020interactivemachineteaching pages 1-3).  B. Social Media Feed Curation  Social media feed curation involves both productive curation—where users shape their digital identities through the content they produce—and consumptive curation—where users selectively engage with available content based on personal and algorithmic mediated filters (davis2017curationatheoretical pages 5-7). In this context, algorithms (curatorial code) and human network decisions (network curation) collaboratively shape the visible pool of content, yet often without explicit user input into the learning process (davis2017curationatheoretical pages 7-9). The combination of human choices with algorithmic filtering calls for interactive systems where users can learn about, influence, and adjust the models that drive feed personalization (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 18-19).

sections.text: A central tenet of applying IMT to social media feed curation is recognizing that users are not merely recipients of curated content but can be active teachers who guide recommendation algorithms. The following principles, drawn from diverse research contributions, elucidate the key elements required for effective interactive curation.  A. Iterative Human-In-The-Loop Feedback  One foundational principle of IMT is to incorporate an iterative feedback loop where users continuously provide explicit signals—ranging from simple binary evaluations (like/dislike) to complex, nuanced annotations—that directly influence content ranking and visibility. This iterative cycle involves planning teaching strategies, explaining content preferences through the selection of examples or tagging relevant features, and reviewing system recommendations to further adjust the model’s behavior (ramos2020interactivemachineteaching pages 9-11). By fostering a cyclical exchange, the system encourages users to actively engage in the personalization process and correct misaligned recommendations as their preferences evolve (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 2-3).  B. Direct Manipulation and Expressive Teaching Languages  IMT systems benefit from interfaces that allow users to directly interact with and teach the underlying machine learning models. “Exploded UI” views, which visually separate components of a post (such as author, text, media, and hashtags), empower users to indicate granular preferences for each content feature rather than relying on aggregate signals like a simple “like” (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 13-13). Such direct manipulation interfaces enable a rich, expressive teaching language that supports both structured inputs—such as selecting from predefined tags—and unstructured inputs—such as natural language annotations (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 12-13). This dual modality ensures that teacher signals capture the complexity and nuance of user judgments, thereby providing the system with high-quality training data for iterative model refinement (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 13-15).  C. Adaptivity and Real-Time Model Refinement  Real-time adaptability is a critical IMT principle for social media feed curation, where content streams are dynamic and user preferences may vary according to context and mood. The algorithm must update its predictions continuously, incorporating immediate feedback to adjust feed recommendations, and doing so in a manner that minimizes delay and interruption to the user’s browsing experience (he2023curacurationat pages 11-13). This fast, interactive retraining process ensures that the system remains responsive to the evolving signals of user input while simultaneously maintaining stability in content delivery (he2023curacurationat pages 6-9). Adaptive learning builds user trust by demonstrating that their feedback has a measurable and perceptible impact on the content curation process (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 16-17).  D. Transparency and Model Interpretability  Transparency is essential for establishing user trust, a prerequisite for successful interactive teaching. In many IMT systems, explicit explanations of how user-provided feedback influences feed ranking are offered through visual summaries, annotated examples, or explainer interfaces (he2023curacurationat pages 25-27). By making the decision-making process of the recommendation algorithm visible and interpretable, the system empowers users with the knowledge of how their inputs change the model’s outputs and helps build accurate mental models of the underlying algorithm (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 18-18). Transparent systems allow users to verify that their teaching signals are being absorbed correctly, and they enable users to correct any misinterpretations of their preferences, thereby reducing feelings of opacity that are common in black-box systems (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 19-20).  E. Balancing Human Agency with Algorithmic Assistance  Interactive curation systems should support a balanced distribution of decision-making power between human teachers and automated content filters. Users need the freedom to overtly guide their feed preferences while also benefiting from the algorithm’s ability to generalize from sparse or noisy inputs (davis2017curationatheoretical pages 7-9). Empowering users with direct teaching capabilities—so they can, for instance, create multiple thematic feeds or toggle the influence of certain feedback signals—supports user agency and self-causality, enhancing the overall satisfaction with the curation process (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 10-12). This balanced approach ensures that while the system uses automated learning to scale the curation process, final decisions remain rooted in user-defined values and preferences (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 15-16).  F. Granular, Multimodal, and Nuanced Feedback Channels  Standard like/dislike mechanisms, although commonly used, do not capture the full spectrum of user evaluations. IMT principles advocate for richer feedback channels that allow users to rank, sort, categorize, and even comment on content, thereby providing detailed signals about individual feed items (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 107-109). Feedback can be collected through multiple interaction types—such as demonstration (showing), labeling (categorizing), and evaluative ranking (sorting)—to gather information that reflects the multi-dimensional nature of user preferences (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 14-19). These varied feedback interactions help the algorithm to disentangle complex factors, like emotional impact, topic relevance, and stylistic preferences, which are critical in refining the personalized feed (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 19-21).  G. Minimizing Cognitive Load and Enhancing Usability  For an interactive teaching system to be effective, it must not impose excessive cognitive burden on the user. Designing intuitive and minimalist interfaces that integrate feedback mechanisms directly into the feed view minimizes disruption to the user’s habitual browsing behavior (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 3-4). By offering “availability without intrusion,” where teaching opportunities are accessible yet unobtrusive, the system reduces cognitive load and refrains from overburdening the user with unnecessary controls (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 4-5). Additionally, adaptive query timing—where feedback is solicited only when it is likely to be most informative and least disruptive—ensures that users remain engaged over time without experiencing feedback fatigue (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 109-111).  H. Incorporating Contextual and Temporal Factors  User preferences are inherently dynamic and context-dependent; they can change according to mood, time of day, or situational factors such as the desire for lighter versus more serious content (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 10-12). Interactive machine teaching systems for feed curation must, therefore, support teaching at varying timescales. This involves both micro-interactions for immediate adjustments and macro-level teaching for long-term model refinement (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 16-17). Such multi-temporal teaching interfaces enable users to modify feed behavior in real-time while also building a historical record of their preferences, which can be revisited or reset as needed (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 13-15).  I. Community-Driven and Collaborative Curation  While individual agency is paramount, social media platforms typically involve multiple users whose aggregate actions inform content recommendations. Techniques drawn from interactive teaching, such as those implemented in systems like Cura, suggest that community feedback can serve as an implicit teaching signal to approximate expert curator judgments (he2023curacurationat pages 3-4). By allowing selected users to act as expert curators whose voting behavior shapes the overall feed, platforms can combine individual machine teaching with collaborative curation, thereby integrating diverse perspectives and mitigating the effects of filter bubbles (he2023curacurationat pages 15-17). Such collaborative models emphasize the synthesis of heterogeneous teaching inputs to form a more representative, fair, and context-aware curation process (he2023curacurationat pages 27-29).  J. Adaptive Query and Interaction Strategies  Recent advances in interactive machine teaching research emphasize the importance of adaptive query strategies where the system dynamically selects the most informative feedback modality based on current performance and the teacher’s mental model of the learner (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 27-30). By balancing the efforts required for diverse interaction types against the anticipated information gain, adaptive systems such as INQUIRE demonstrate that dynamic modulation of query formats can lead to more efficient and robust learning (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 54-61). This principle is especially relevant for social media feed curation, where changes in content patterns and user behavior necessitate agile adjustments to the teaching strategy (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 30-33).

sections.text: Having outlined the core principles of interactive machine teaching, we now consider how these concepts can be integrated into the design of social media feed curation systems to empower users and enhance personalization. A viable design approach incorporates the following features:  A. In-Feed Teaching Interfaces  The integration of teaching instruments directly within the feed interface—such as widgets allowing for granular feedback on specific post elements—ensures that users can modify content recommendations without leaving the primary browsing experience (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 13-13). For example, an “exploded UI view” might break down a post into discrete components (author, text, media), allowing users to annotate each component with positive or negative signals (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 12-13). Such an interface not only fosters precise feedback but also reinforces transparency by visibly linking user input to the subsequent behavior of the recommendation algorithm (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 13-15).  B. Multi-Feed Curriculum Organization  Interactive systems may support the creation of multiple thematic feeds or curriculum folders that let users organize content by topic, mood, or interest. These separate feeds serve as distinct teaching curricula that collectively guide the overall personalization of content (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 15-16). By iteratively teaching the model through the organization of feeds—where each feed represents a set of curated teaching examples—users can influence the recommendation algorithm in a nuanced and context-sensitive manner (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 16-17).  C. Feedback Transparency and Explanations  To build and maintain trust, the system must provide clear explanations linking user feedback to feed outcomes. Transparent feedback mechanisms, such as visual annotations that explain why a certain post was recommended or how a change in feed structure affects content visibility, help users understand the causal impact of their interactions (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 18-18). Explanatory feedback thereby aligns with the principle of model interpretability, ensuring that the teaching process remains both intelligible and empowering (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 19-20).  D. Adaptive Interaction Modalities  Integrating multiple feedback channels—ranging from simple binary signals to complex natural language inputs—allows the system to adapt to individual users’ teaching personas. Adaptive interaction modalities enhance the richness of feedback by accommodating various user preferences and cognitive styles while optimizing the data acquisition process (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 107-109). The system might adopt an active learning strategy, dynamically selecting the type of query (e.g., ranking, labeling, or demonstration) that offers the highest potential for information gain with minimal user effort (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 14-19).  E. Incorporation of Community Signals  Beyond individual teaching, the system can leverage aggregate community inputs to refine content curation. For example, employing models that predict curator approval based on the voting behavior of trusted community members (as implemented in collaborative systems like Cura) ensures that the feed reflects both individual and collective tastes (he2023curacurationat pages 3-4). This community-driven approach not only scales the teaching process but also introduces diversity in the teaching signals, promoting fairness and mitigating the risk of echo chambers (he2023curacurationat pages 15-17).

sections.text: Implementing IMT principles in social media feed curation entails several design challenges and opportunities. First, designers must carefully balance the frequency and intensity of feedback queries with the need to maintain a low cognitive load for the user (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 109-111). Overly frequent interruptions or overly detailed queries could lead to engagement fatigue, while insufficient interaction might result in an under-adaptive system. The inclusion of adaptive query strategies and low-intrusive interface elements is therefore critical (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 111-115).  Second, the system must ensure that user feedback is interpreted in a semantically rich manner. This requires the development of expressive teaching languages and user interfaces that allow users to communicate preferences at a granular level (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 12-13). By enabling feedback that reflects nuances such as emotional tone, topic emphasis, or content clarity, the system can better align recommendations with complex real-world user preferences (koppol2023interactivemachinelearning pages 19-21).  Third, transparency and feedback mechanisms are paramount for maintaining user trust. When users can see how their input shapes feed content—through direct explanations, visual annotations, or post-feedback summaries—they gain a sense of control and validation (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 18-18). This transparency also supports the iterative refinement process, as users can detect and subsequently correct errors or misinterpretations in the recommendation model (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 19-20).  Fourth, the integration of community-driven signals helps to bridge individual teaching with broader social norms and values. As social media feeds are inherently social, leveraging the wisdom of the crowd alongside individual inputs can enrich feed curation. This collaboration between individual and collective teaching enables the system to capture a more diverse range of preferences and mitigate biases that result from isolated feedback (he2023curacurationat pages 27-29).  Finally, accommodating temporal and contextual shifts in user preferences requires the system to support both micro-level updates (for immediate feed adjustment) and macro-level curriculum refinement (for long-term content personalization). The design must embrace the non-stationary nature of social media consumption by continuously learning from feedback that reflects changes in mood, context, or emerging interests (feng2024mappingthedesign pages 16-17).

By reimagining feed curation as a collaborative teaching endeavor, designers and researchers can address pressing challenges in content personalization, mitigate issues related to algorithmic opacity, and foster trust through transparent and adaptive human-machine collaborations. Such transformative approaches have profound implications not only for individual user satisfaction but also for the broader dynamics of information dissemination and social discourse in digital environments (he2023curacurationat pages 21-23, davis2017curationatheoretical pages 7-9). question: What kinds of coverage motion planning algorithms are effective for floor-cleaning robots?

sections.text:
This report presents an in

‐depth review of coverage motion planning algorithms that have been demonstrated to be effective for floor

‐cleaning robots. The field has evolved from early heuristic methods relying on random movement to sophisticated, systematic algorithms that exploit environment decomposition, graph

‐based techniques, and advanced strategies tailored to the robot’s morphology. Numerous studies show that efficient coverage is not merely a matter of traversing every accessible location, but also of balancing energy consumption, path redundancy, and adaptability to obstacles and dynamic changes. This report categorizes the effective approaches into several groups, including heuristic methods, cellular and grid

‐based decomposition techniques, graph

‐based and spanning tree methods, bio

‐inspired neural network algorithms, and evolutionary optimization methods. In addition, special emphasis is placed on algorithms that can accommodate reconfigurable robot designs, such as those inspired by tetromino tiling theory.

Floor

‐cleaning robots require algorithms that can generate complete and non

‐repetitive paths through varied environments. Owing to challenges such as limited battery capacity, inaccuracies due to sensor noise, and dynamic obstacles, the quality of the cleaning path directly impacts operational efficiency and user satisfaction. Early generation robots, for example, used randomized and heuristic strategies for coverage; however, these strategies are often suboptimal with regard to coverage completeness and energy consumption. In response, a range of modern algorithms has emerged that emphasize systematic area coverage by decomposing the environment into smaller, manageable regions or cells, planning optimized routes for each region, and even adapting the morphological configuration of the robot itself for better accessibility (bhanushali…2020autonomousfloorcleaning pages 2-4, bormann2018indoorcoveragepath pages 1-2).

sections.text:
One of the earliest strategies in floor

‐cleaning robotics is based on random walk algorithms. In these algorithms, the robot travels forward until encountering an obstacle and then randomly changes its direction. Although the random algorithm minimizes the need for pre

‐known maps or complicated sensor systems and can be effective in low

‐complexity environments, it tends to produce repeating trajectories that increase redundancy and prolong coverage time (edwards2018acomparisonof pages 1-9, gunning2018aperformancecomparison pages 17-31). Randomized methods may yield effective coverage in open spaces, but simulations have shown that these approaches are particularly inefficient in later correction phases when many redundant passes occur (edwards2018acomparisonof pages 30-34).

On the other hand, spiral motion algorithms have been introduced to create a systematic outward growing path. The spiral algorithm is especially viable when the robot is located in an unobstructed area; however, it tends to perform poorly near corners or in complex environments where obstacles interrupt the spiral’s progression. Improvements incorporating wall-following techniques have been proposed to mitigate these corner inadequacies, yet spiral methods still lag behind more robust strategies in dynamic or cluttered environments (edwards2018acomparisonof pages 34-37).

sections.text:
A predominant class of effective coverage algorithms for floor

‐cleaning robots is based on cellular and grid

‐based methods. These techniques involve decomposing the workspace into a finite number of cells or grid units that the robot can cover sequentially. One of the classical approaches in this domain is the Boustrophedon Cellular Decomposition (BCD). In the Boustrophedon method, the environment is partitioned using a sweeping line that divides the space into cells that are subsequently covered using back

‐and

‐forth sweeping motions. A key advantage of this method is its ability to drastically reduce the number of turns required, thereby conserving energy. Boustrophedon strategies also excel in minimizing redundant paths and achieve high coverage percentages in structured indoor environments (bormann2018indoorcoveragepath pages 3-4, bormann2018indoorcoveragepath pages 4-5).

Grid-based planners typically represent the environment as a two-dimensional array of cells, where each cell's status (free, occupied, or already cleaned) is tracked during navigation. Techniques such as the Wavefront method propagate distance fields through the grid to generate smooth paths, while spanning tree methods directly generate a tree structure that guarantees complete coverage of the grid cells. Like Boustrophedon methods, grid-based approaches are systematic and perform particularly well in indoor environments where the floor plan is known or can be accurately built via SLAM (lund2017autonomousrobotcoverage pages 13-19, lund2017autonomousrobotcoverage pages 25-29).

Cellular decomposition strategies can be divided further into approximate and exact cellular decompositions. Approximate methods divide the environment into uniform cells, which may sometimes leave small gaps or introduce redundant overlaps. Exact cellular decomposition, by contrast, breaks the free space into non-overlapping cells based on the geometry of obstacles, which is then augmented with optimization techniques such as the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for short path generation. Such approaches ensure near-complete coverage with minimized overlaps and reduced turning angles (bormann2018indoorcoveragepath pages 7-8, bormann2018indoorcoveragepath pages 8-9).

sections.text:
Another highly effective approach in coverage motion planning is the use of graph-based methods, notably the Spanning Tree Coverage (STC) algorithm. These methods view the workspace as a graph where nodes represent waypoints or grid cells, and edges represent feasible transitions between cells. Algorithms such as STC, which build a spanning tree over free space points, facilitate systematic traversal of the environment with minimal repeated visits. An essential benefit of spanning tree approaches is their guarantee to cover every accessible area while allowing path optimization to minimize overall travel distance (nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 2-3, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 5-6).

Spanning tree approaches are especially beneficial when paired with algorithms that differentiate between exploration and cleaning phases. In these hybrid algorithms, the robot initially constructs a basic map of the environment through a frontier-based approach, generating local spanning trees that are later merged into a global structure representing all accessible regions. This method not only facilitates complete coverage but also addresses energy constraints by allowing the robot to deactivate power-intensive sensors during the systematic cleaning phase, thereby minimizing battery usage (nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 6-7, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 7-8).

Furthermore, some researchers have extended this approach by integrating continuous mapping updates during the cleaning operation. These continuously updated maps enable dynamic re-planning of the coverage path in response to changes in the environment or the discovery of previously unknown obstacles, ensuring that the algorithm remains robust in dynamic scenarios (nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 9-11).

sections.text:
Neural network-based planners, often inspired by biological processes, represent another prominent category of coverage motion planning. Bio-inspired methods mimic the activation dynamics of neurons across a grid representation of the environment. For instance, Glasius Bio-inspired Neural Network (GBNN) controllers have been implemented in various cleaning robots to manage coverage. These approaches inherently lend themselves to decentralized planning and the avoidance of deadlock situations in complex environments. Still, while classical neural network methods can produce erratic paths with many unnecessary turns, modifications involving heuristics have been proposed to mitigate these issues and enhance overall efficiency (bormann2018indoorcoveragepath pages 5-7, wan2024completeareacoveragepath pages 2-3).

Evolutionary algorithms have also been employed to improve coverage. Genetic Algorithms (GA) and Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) are two heuristic approaches that search for near-optimal coverage paths by simulating natural evolutionary processes. These techniques iteratively improve a population of candidate solutions based on objective criteria such as minimizing traveled distance and reducing the number of turns. By iterating over large search spaces, evolutionary algorithms can be adapted to capture additional costs like energy consumption due to rotational and reconfiguration maneuvers (le2019realizationenergyoptimization pages 1-3, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 2-3). Such approaches have the advantage of addressing complex cost functions that go beyond mere path length, making them practical in scenarios where energy optimization is crucial.

A unique subclass of coverage motion planning algorithms is designed specifically for reconfigurable robots. Reconfigurable floor-cleaning robots, such as the hTetro robot, employ a novel approach that leverages polyomino tiling theory to optimize area coverage. These robots can transform between different configurations based on the cleaning task or environmental constraints (bhagya2020htetroinfiareconfigurable pages 1-2, prabakaranUnknownyeartowardsdevelopingefficient pages 36-39).

The hTetro robot, for example, is inspired by Tetris pieces and can reconfigure into any of seven one-sided tetromino shapes to navigate narrow spaces or rooms with complex geometries. Motion planning for such robots involves decomposing the cleaning area into tiled subregions that meet the criteria of polyomino tiling theorems. This guarantees that the area can be tiled exactly by the robot’s configuration blocks, allowing for complete coverage without overlaps or missed spots. In addition to monochromatic tiling, the algorithm involves switching between configurations to traverse areas that may be inaccessible to a fixed shape robot, ultimately enhancing both the efficiency and completeness of cleaning paths (bhagya2020htetroinfiareconfigurable pages 1-2, prabakaranUnknownyeartowardsdevelopingefficient pages 36-39).

Furthermore, advanced algorithms for reconfigurable robots are often hybrid in nature; they combine classical techniques such as zigzag and spiral motions with shape-changing rules. For instance, the revised zigzag and spiral patterns for the hTetro robot allow multiple grid cells to be covered simultaneously when the robot reconfigures to increase its effective cleaning width. Comparative studies have shown that these revised algorithms are superior in complex environments as they allow the robot easier navigation around obstacles and more efficient coverage of large areas (veerajagadheswar2020motionplannerfor pages 16-20, veerajagadheswar2020motionplannerfor pages 24-26).

A critical aspect of effective coverage motion planning is the combination of exploration and cleaning phases into an integrated framework. In environments that are initially unknown or partially mapped, a hierarchical algorithm may first perform exploration using sensor data to build an accurate map. Methods based on Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) enable the robot to dynamically identify frontier cells—the boundaries between explored and unexplored areas—and direct the robot’s movement accordingly (joon2021designofautonomous pages 11-12, lund2017autonomousrobotcoverage pages 19-25).

Once sufficient information about the environment is available, the algorithm switches to a systematic coverage mode, wherein complete coverage is obtained via techniques such as spanning tree coverage or cellular decompositions. This dual-phased approach reduces computational overhead during cleaning, as the sensors are strategically deactivated during the systematic cleaning phase to conserve battery power (nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 7-8, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 8-9). The integration of exploration and exploitation allows the algorithm to adapt dynamically to changes in the environment, such as moving obstacles or unanticipated structural irregularities, ensuring that the cleaning trajectory is both comprehensive and energy-efficient.

Apart from achieving complete coverage, it is crucial that the path planning algorithm minimizes unnecessary path length and rotations, which directly influence energy consumption. Some coverage algorithms incorporate an energy optimization component by considering not just the Euclidean path length but also the cost of rotation and reconfiguration maneuvers. For example, methods reformulating the complete path coverage problem as a Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) with additional constraints—such as rotational costs—have shown promise in reducing energy consumption (le2019realizationenergyoptimization pages 1-3, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 12-12).

Furthermore, selective sensor activation has been demonstrated as an effective technique to balance the trade-off between continuous obstacle detection and battery conservation. In several hybrid algorithms, sensors are activated only during exploration phases to construct or update the environment map, and are subsequently deactivated during the planned cleaning phase. This selective approach not only reduces the overall power draw but also simplifies the path generation process by reducing the frequency of sensor-triggered corrections (nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 6-7, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 7-8).

In addition to the conventional approaches detailed above, recent research has focused on advanced methods that incorporate fuzzy logic and meta-heuristic optimization. Fuzzy logic controllers have been used to handle uncertainties inherent in sensor data and environmental variations, enabling the robot to make decisions regarding turning, obstacle avoidance, and path rectification in a more adaptive manner (simsek2023afuzzylogic pages 1-3).

Meta-heuristic algorithms—including particle swarm optimization and predator–prey based methods—have been adapted to the cleaning context with the aim of reducing redundant coverage while ensuring that energy is used efficiently. These algorithms combine the exploration strengths of randomized methods with the systematic coverage of more structured algorithms. For instance, modifications to bio-inspired neural networks using heuristic enhancements (GBNN+H) have produced planners that perform better in complex, obstacle-rich environments compared to classical versions (wan2024completeareacoveragepath pages 2-3).

Empirical evaluations and simulation studies across various algorithmic approaches have provided insights into the trade-offs between path generation time, travel distance, and percentage of area coverage. For small, simple environments, deterministic patterns such as fixed zigzag or spiral motions can be computed very rapidly and achieve high coverage with minimal rotations (gunning2018aperformancecomparison pages 1-11, edwards2018acomparisonof pages 9-14). However, as the complexity of the environment increases with more obstacles or irregular room shapes, the performance of purely deterministic methods diminishes. In these cases, hybrid approaches that combine systematic motions with real-time exploration, such as the frontier-based spanning tree coverage framework, offer superior performance by dynamically adapting the cleaning path to the updated map (nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 9-11, veerajagadheswar2020motionplannerfor pages 2-3).

Comparative studies have also demonstrated that reconfigurable robot platforms employing modified tiling motion algorithms outperform traditional fixed morphology robots in cluttered spaces. The hTetro robot, for instance, using revised zigzag/spiral algorithms alongside novel polyomino tiling approaches, achieves lower overall travel distances and higher coverage percentages by reducing grid revisitation and improving maneuverability near obstacles (veerajagadheswar2020motionplannerfor pages 16-20, prabakaranUnknownyeartowardsdevelopingefficient pages 34-36).

While significant progress has been made in the development of coverage motion planning algorithms for floor-cleaning robots, several challenges remain open to research. One challenge is ensuring that algorithms remain robust in the presence of unpredictable obstacles and dynamic changes in the environment. Although hybrid exploration–coverage frameworks provide a degree of adaptability, sensor noise and rapid environmental changes may still lead to incomplete coverage or inefficient path corrections (sivanantham2021adaptivefloorcleaning pages 2-3).

Another challenge lies in the optimization of computational efficiency alongside energy consumption. Many advanced algorithms that provide near-optimal paths in simulation—such as those based on TSP formulations or evolutionary optimization—remain computationally intensive in real-time settings. Scaling these methods for practical deployment on low-cost, energy-constrained hardware continues to be an active area of research (le2019realizationenergyoptimization pages 1-3, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 2-3).

For reconfigurable robots, further work is needed to integrate shape-changing capabilities seamlessly with path planning. While the polyomino tiling theory provides a strong mathematical foundation, real-time control and transition between different configurations under dynamic conditions require advanced modeling of the configuration space and robust control strategies (bhagya2020htetroinfiareconfigurable pages 1-2, prabakaranUnknownyeartowardsdevelopingefficient pages 36-39).

Future avenues for improvement include the integration of deep learning methods with traditional coverage algorithms to further enhance adaptability. For example, reinforcement learning approaches could be used to fine-tune the switching criteria between exploration and cleaning phases or to adaptively adjust the robot’s behavior in complex, unpredictable environments. Moreover, multi-robot coordination and collaboration remain promising directions that can leverage cooperative coverage strategies to further reduce cleaning times in large-scale environments (sivanantham2021adaptivefloorcleaning pages 2-3).

In conclusion, an array of coverage motion planning algorithms has been developed for floor-cleaning robots, each with their own strengths and trade-offs. Heuristic approaches like random walk and spiral motion provide simplicity but often lack efficiency in complex scenarios. Cellular decomposition along with grid-based methods, including Boustrophedon and exact cellular decomposition, represent a major step forward by offering systematic coverage that minimizes redundant passes. Graph

‐based methods, particularly spanning tree coverage algorithms, ensure complete coverage and efficient path generation by exploiting a structured representation of the workspace.  

Bio-inspired neural networks and evolutionary algorithms introduce adaptive mechanisms and optimization capabilities to address the nonlinearity and dynamic constraints of real-world floor-cleaning tasks. In addition, advanced hybrid approaches that integrate exploration with systematic coverage techniques and selective sensor management strategies have demonstrated significant benefits in terms of energy optimization and overall efficiency. Finally, reconfigurable platforms that employ polyomino tiling theory exemplify the innovative directions taken to accommodate various environmental constraints using flexible robot morphologies. Overall, effective coverage motion planning for floor-cleaning robots is achieved through a blend of systematic decomposition methods, real-time adaptive strategies, and energy-conscious sensor management that not only guarantee complete coverage but also minimize redundant motion and conserve energy.

This report, supported by numerous studies and simulation results, underscores that the choice of coverage algorithm depends on the specific constraints of the deployment environment, the robot’s sensor and computational capabilities, and the operational objectives such as minimizing battery consumption and reducing cleaning time. Continued advancements in sensor technology, computational hardware, and adaptive control methods promise to further enhance the efficacy of these coverage motion planning algorithms, ultimately leading to more intelligent, energy-efficient, and reliable floor-cleaning robotic systems (bormann2018indoorcoveragepath pages 1-2, edwards2018acomparisonof pages 9-14, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 7-8, veerajagadheswar2020motionplannerfor pages 26-27).

Through comprehensive analysis and comparative evaluations, it is evident that a combination of classical coverage techniques with novel hybrid and reconfigurable strategies provides the greatest promise in optimizing floor-cleaning performance and operational efficiency. As robotic platforms become increasingly sophisticated and adaptive, future research will likely focus on the seamless integration of these diverse methodologies into unified frameworks that can autonomously adjust to the complexities of real-world cleaning environments while ensuring complete area coverage and efficient energy utilization (lund2017autonomousrobotcoverage pages 19-25, nair2024efficientpathplanning pages 8-9, prassler2016domesticrobotics pages 6-8).

In summary, effective coverage motion planning algorithms for floor-cleaning robots include:  
• Heuristic methods such as random walk and spiral motion, particularly useful in open or less cluttered environments;  
• Cellular and grid-based decomposition techniques, including Boustrophedon cellular decomposition for systematic back-and-forth paths;  
• Graph-based approaches such as spanning tree coverage, which guarantee complete coverage with reduced redundancy;  
• Bio-inspired neural network algorithms and evolutionary strategies (GA, ACO) that optimize complex energy and efficiency considerations;  
• Hybrid exploration–exploitation frameworks that incorporate SLAM and frontier-based methods to dynamically adapt to environmental changes; and  
• Novel tiling-based algorithms for reconfigurable robots, which adapt robot morphology to enhance access and coverage in constrained spaces.

Collectively, these approaches form a robust toolkit for addressing the varied challenges inherent in robotic floor-cleaning applications, enabling systems to operate in both structured and dynamic environments with high efficiency and reliability (bhanushali…2020autonomousfloorcleaning pages 2-4, veerajagadheswar2020motionplannerfor pages 2-3, simsek2023afuzzylogic pages 1-3).

Through continuous advancements in robotics and optimization methods, the next generation of floor-cleaning robots is expected to combine these algorithms in increasingly sophisticated ways, leading to improvements in cleaning efficacy, energy efficiency, and overall reliability in domestic, commercial, and industrial settings.

question: What are good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots?

sections.text:
This report presents a comprehensive discussion of good benchmarks and evaluation strategies for comparing obstacle avoidance strategies in mobile robots. In recent years, the rapid progress in both classical and learning

‐based methods for mobile robot navigation has made it imperative to develop standardized evaluation protocols that combine simulation, real

‐world testing, and human

‐centered performance indices. Such benchmarks must encompass not only quantitative measures (e.g., collision rates, success rates, path efficiency, and smoothness) but also qualitative social metrics in scenarios where robots interact with people or complex dynamic environments. In what follows, we detail the rationale, components, simulation platforms, performance metrics, and evaluation methodologies gleaned from recent state-of-the-art literature.

A core principle emerging from prior research is the need to evaluate obstacle avoidance in controlled and repeatable simulation environments as well as in real-world testbeds. For instance, Dong et al. (dong2021realtimeavoidancestrategy pages 6-7) used Gazebo simulation along with real-world experiments on a Turtlebot-2 with a Hokuyo 2D laser scanner to assess a novel obstacle avoidance approach. This dual-pronged strategy illustrates that simulation ensures repeatability and statistical significance through large numbers of trials, whereas in situ experiments capture real-scenario complexities and sensor noise not always present in simulation.

citations.title: Real-time avoidance strategy of dynamic obstacles via half model-free detection and tracking with 2d lidar for mobile robots

sections.text:
Simulation environments have been central in benchmarking obstacle avoidance strategies because they allow for systematic manipulation of parameters such as obstacle density, static versus dynamic behaviors, and sensor noise. Several authors have provided comprehensive guidelines for designing artificial test environments that mimic real environments. Francis et al. (francis2025principlesandguidelines pages 1-2) recommend the integration of simulation environments with controlled scenario cards that define starting conditions, context, and expected human behavior, thereby enabling comparisons across different algorithms under identical conditions. These simulation scenarios should include both simple static maps as well as complex dynamic environments that challenge the robot

’s reactivity to moving obstacles.

citations.title: Principles and guidelines for evaluating social robot navigation algorithms

sections.text: A key feature of any benchmark is the use of quantitative performance metrics that capture the essential trade-offs in obstacle avoidance. In simulation, metrics such as the collision rate, completion time to reach the destination, path length, velocity profiles, trajectory smoothness, and clearance distances have been extensively used (dong2021realtimeavoidancestrategy pages 6-7). In particular, by running thousands of simulation trials, it becomes possible to evaluate not only average performance but also robustness under rare and adverse conditions. Further, advanced benchmarks like Arena-bench (kastner2022arenabenchabenchmarking pages 1-2, 3-4) incorporate a full suite of metrics covering both safety (collision metrics, clearance, slip) and efficiency (path optimality, travel time, energy consumption). Similarly, DynaBARN (nair2022dynabarnbenchmarkingmetric pages 1-2, pages 4-5) exemplifies an evaluation framework that categorizes environments by difficulty based on obstacle motion profiles and provides a pipeline for comparing classical planners with learning-based methods.

Comprehensive benchmarks should ideally consist of a two-stage evaluation where initial simulation testing is followed by field tests

Similarly, CrowdBot provides a simulation platform where dynamic crowd behaviors can be systematically varied, and its extensive parameterization allows for testing against varying densities and motion patterns. These benchmarks help in assessing the robustness of navigation algorithms when obstacles exhibit unpredictable behaviors, such as abrupt accelerations or changes in direction. Similarly, Perille et al. (xu2023benchmarkingreinforcementlearning pages 1-2, pages 6-7) highlight that RL policies tend to perform better when trained on a diverse set of simulation environments, but still show a domain gap when transferred to the real world. These findings indicate that in benchmarks for learning-based methods, diversity in simulation is key, and that metrics should capture not only the success rate and navigation smoothness but also the extent of overfitting to simulation environments. Reinforcement learning benchmarks, as highlighted by Xu et al. (xu2023benchmarkingreinforcementlearning pages 1-2, pages 6-7), also underscore the significance of expanding the diversity of training environments. They report that RL algorithms trained on a larger number of distinct environments generalize better to novel obstacles but still face a performance gap when transitioning from simulation to real-world deployments. Therefore, continuous benchmarking efforts must incorporate both simulation environments that include a wide variety of obstacle configurations as well as real-world tests. This dual approach helps to ensure that performance improvements are not artifacts of overfitting to a narrow set of simulation conditions.

High-fidelity simulation environments that focus on vision-based obstacle avoidance, such as AvoidBench, further demonstrate how simulation fidelity can bridge the sim-to-real gap. According to Yu et al. —are transferable to ground mobile robots. This high-fidelity simulation mitigates discrepancies between simulated and real-world conditions by incorporating realistic visual and physical interactions, which is critical when evaluating obstacle avoidance strategies. Benchmarks must also account for multimodal sensor fusion and the impact of limited sensing capabilities. Xu et al. (xu2020collisionavoidanceof pages 10-12) emphasize that real-time collision avoidance strategies must account for limitations in sensor range and resolution. For example, experiments involving holonomic and non-holonomic platforms showed that kinematic constraints and sensor field-of-view limitations significantly affect navigation performance. Consequently, benchmarks should incorporate simulated sensor models (such as LiDAR, RGB-D cameras, and ultrasonic sensors) with realistic error profiles, as demonstrated in studies using ROS-integrated simulators and controlled test environments (dong2021realtimeavoidancestrategy pages 6-7, xu2020collisionavoidanceof pages 10-12). When addressing vision-based obstacle avoidance, reliable benchmarking needs to account for variations in visual input and perspective distortions. Dang and Bui (dang2023obstacleavoidancestrategy pages 10-14, pages 16-19) demonstrated a method based on monocular camera input that uses perspective correction via a calibrated checkerboard pattern to improve obstacle localization accuracy. This approach is particularly valuable in scenarios where vision-based methods are sensitive to lens distortions and perspective ambiguities. In such cases, benchmarking may include assessing the accuracy of obstacle detection and the quality of the resulting trajectory, measured in terms of smoothness, clearance from obstacles, and response latency. Real-world experiments validating these vision-based methods thus add another layer of reliability to the overall evaluation framework.

Standardized benchmarks must also consider the computational efficiency and real-time performance of the obstacle avoidance algorithms. Many practical mobile robots have limited onboard computing resources, and as such, evaluation strategies should include processing time measurements and memory usage analyses. Xu et al. In these scenarios, metrics such as iteration counts, average distance traveled, and failure rates are effective in quantifying the computational as well as navigational complexity encountered by different algorithms. Such grid-based benchmarks can be extended by incorporating dynamic obstacles and evolving environmental conditions to mirror real-world challenges. Evaluating dynamic obstacle avoidance also benefits from difficulty metrics that capture the intrinsic challenge of an environment. Perille et al. (perille2020benchmarkingmetricground pages 1-2, pages 4-5) introduced a set of difficulty metrics

These metrics not only help in designing more challenging test scenarios but also allow for meaningful comparisons between different settings by quantifying environmental complexity in a dimensionless manner. When a robot

question: What is a good Ontology semantic similarity measure that considers multiple inheritance cases of concepts?

sections.text: This report provides an in‐depth discussion of ontology semantic similarity measures with a specific focus on methods that well accommodate multiple inheritance cases of concepts. In ontologies represented as directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), many concepts inherit properties from more than one parent. Because conventional similarity measures based solely on tree‐structured taxonomies (which assume a unique parent for every node) tend to overlook the challenges introduced by multiple inheritance, advanced measures have been proposed that explicitly integrate all relevant ancestral information. This report surveys key approaches from the literature, examines their underlying principles, and argues that node‐based, information theory–driven approaches that leverage all disjunctive common ancestors—such as GraSM and its derivative, DiShIn—are particularly appropriate for handling multiple inheritance scenarios.

Ontology‐based semantic similarity measures have become fundamental in many domains, including biomedicine, natural language processing, and linked data integration. The central goal is to quantify how close in meaning two concepts are based solely on the structured background knowledge provided by an ontology. However, ontologies such as the Gene Ontology (GO), WordNet, and others commonly feature multiple inheritance where a given concept is connected to several parents. This complex structure poses challenges to traditional similarity measures predicated on single inheritance assumptions, such as those that rely solely on the shortest path or on the information content (IC) of the most informative common ancestor (MICA). As a result, numerous studies recommend measures that incorporate all taxonomically relevant ancestral nodes to better capture semantic commonality and nuance. In this report we review key literature that has modified traditional measures to account for multiple inheritance, and conclude that a good ontology semantic similarity measure for multiple inheritance cases is one that combines node‐based information content with a treatment of disjunctive common ancestors.

Traditional edge‐counting methods that measure semantic similarity by counting the number of edges along the shortest path between two concepts rely on the assumption of a tree-like structure. This assumption does not hold for many modern domain ontologies, which are more accurately represented as DAGs where a concept may inherit from more than one parent. As explained by Gan et al. (gan2013fromontologyto pages 3-4), these methods neglect the fact that multiple paths exist and that different ancestors bring different semantic contributions to the compared concepts. Similarly, methods using a single LCA (or Most Informative Common Ancestor) such as those proposed by Resnik, Lin, and Jiang-Conrath tend to ignore the presence of alternative yet equally relevant common ancestors that are essential in multiple inheritance contexts (pesquita2009semanticsimilarityin pages 1-2, pesquita2009semanticsimilarityin pages 2-4).Multiple inheritance leads to a scenario in which multiple disjoint common ancestors (DCAs) of two terms exist. Under such circumstances, it becomes insufficient to rely on a single node’s information content because that approach may ignore significant semantic evidence contributed by additional ancestors (couto2007measuringsemanticsimilarity pages 12-14). As a consequence, newer methodologies focus on exploiting all unioning superconcepts of the compared terms, instead of isolating a sole common ancestor. Batet et al. (batet2013semanticsimilarityestimation pages 7-8) and Couto and Silva (couto2011disjunctivesharedinformation pages 1-3) have both demonstrated that measures explicitly considering multiple inheritance can yield improved accuracy, particularly in biomedical applications where ontological annotations are sparse and the specificity of information holds critical importance.

sections.text: A. GraSM: Averaging Over Disjunctive Common AncestorsOne well-regarded approach that addresses multiple inheritance is the Graph-based Similarity Measure (GraSM) as proposed by Couto et al. (couto2007measuringsemanticsimilarity pages 12-14). Unlike the classical reliance on the MICA, GraSM calculates the semantic similarity by averaging the information content of all disjunctive common ancestors (DCAs) shared by compared terms. This averaging provides a better representation of the rich semantic context due to multiple inheritance. In situations where a concept has several parents, GraSM leverages these multiple semantic contributions to produce a similarity score that reflects not only the most informative single branch but the entire taxonomic neighborhood (pesquita2009semanticsimilarityin pages 4-5).Moreover, node-based measures inherently depend on the measured specificity of individual terms. As the probability of occurrence decreases with increasing specificity, leveraging the aggregated IC values of all relevant ancestors allows the measure to compensate for the distribution of information within the ontology (couto2007measuringsemanticsimilarity pages 3-5). This strategy mitigates biases introduced by uneven link densities and structurally unbalanced ontologies.B. DiShIn: Enhancing Shared Information in Multiple InheritanceBuilding on the ideas of GraSM, Couto and Silva (couto2011disjunctivesharedinformation pages 1-3, couto2011disjunctivesharedinformation pages 5-7) later introduced the DiShIn method, which stands for “Disjunctive Shared Information”. The main innovation in DiShIn is that it not only relies on aggregating information content across multiple disjunctive ancestors but also redefines the notion of disjunctiveness by comparing the number of distinct paths from the concepts to each common ancestor. When the differences in path contributions are symmetric across the concepts, DiShIn selects the ancestor with maximal information content, thereby avoiding penalization due to redundant inheritance paths. This refined approach ensures that multiple inheritance is properly captured without diluting the semantic contributions of highly specific common ancestors (couto2011disjunctivesharedinformation pages 14-15).Experimental evaluations in DiShIn have demonstrated that this method significantly improves the correlation between semantic similarity and biological sequence similarity when compared to traditional Resnik-based similarity measures (couto2011disjunctivesharedinformation pages 7-10). DiShIn also avoids the computational complexity issues that other methods such as GraSM sometimes encounter, making it both robust and efficient for large-scale ontology-based similarity computations.C. Batet’s Multi-Ontology ApproachAnother promising contribution comes from Batet et al. (batet2013semanticsimilarityestimation pages 5-6, batet2013semanticsimilarityestimation pages 7-8) who propose a method designed specifically to work across multiple ontologies. Their approach is particularly important in domains like biomedicine where knowledge about a concept is often distributed among several overlapping ontologies with different design principles and levels of granularity. Batet’s method computes similarity values for each ontology independently and then selects the maximum as the final similarity score. This means that when a concept appears in multiple ontologies (thus involving multiple inheritance not only within a single hierarchical structure but across different ontological sources), the method prioritizes the strongest semantic evidence from the most appropriate representation (batet2013semanticsimilarityestimation pages 6-7). Such an approach leverages the best aspects of node-based and path-based features by integrating multiple inheritance both within and across ontological structures.

sections.text: A critical insight from the literature is that the best similarity measures for multiple inheritance cases do not depend solely on a single metric (e.g., shortest path length or maximum information content) but instead combine structural (graph-based) and statistical (information content) evidence. As Gan et al. (gan2013fromontologyto pages 4-5) remark, the integration of multiple types of evidence—from edge weights and path lengths to aggregated IC contributions—is essential to accurately reflect the nuanced relationships in complex ontologies.Furthermore, methods that exclusively rely on edge-counting metrics typically assume equal semantic distance between hierarchical levels. This assumption inherently fails in DAGs where, because of multiple inheritance, edge weights can be highly variable (pesquita2009semanticsimilarityin pages 5-6). Hybrid approaches such as those referenced by Harispe et al. (harispe2022semanticsimilarityfrom pages 66-68, harispe2022semanticsimilarityfrom pages 74-76) integrate both path length considerations and IC-based adjustments which better account for overlapping parental contributions.Other techniques, such as relation-based measures, extend the traditional node-based methods by incorporating explicit information about diverse relationship types (e.g., is-a, part-of) to fine-tune the similarity assessments. Sheehan et al. (sheehan2008arelationbased pages 1-2, sheehan2008arelationbased pages 4-6) discuss the need for relation-based measures that weight both node properties and edge semantics. While these methods are computationally more intensive and require careful empirically determined parameters, they bolster the robustness of the similarity measure in the face of complex multiple inheritance scenarios.Moreover, the empirical evidence drawn from evaluations in the biomedical domain confirms that node-based approaches (particularly those considering all relevant ancestors, such as GraSM and DiShIn) perform consistently better than methods based solely on a single common ancestor. In biomedicine, where the Gene Ontology encodes multiple facets of gene function with complex interdependencies, these approaches yield superior performance in tasks like gene clustering and protein function prediction (couto2007measuringsemanticsimilarity pages 12-14, couto2011disjunctivesharedinformation pages 7-10).In addition to the inherent merits of these methods, one must also consider computational scalability and ease of integration. GraSM’s requirement to average over multiple ancestors can lead to increased computational cost, particularly in very large ontologies. DiShIn addresses this challenge by reusing precomputed information content values and by normalizing shared information in an efficient, linear-time implementation when stored in relational databases (couto2011disjunctivesharedinformation pages 7-10). Batet’s multi-ontology approach, by partitioning the similarity computation per ontology and then selecting the maximum value, further simplifies the problem by exploiting the advantages of specialized similarity measures tailored to the strengths of each ontology (batet2013semanticsimilarityestimation pages 3-5).

question: Suggest some ways in which precise positioning and context-aware networking can be achieved in 6G mobile communication?

sections.text: Precise positioning and context-aware networking in 6G mobile communications are expected to be transformative enablers for a wide range of emerging use cases such as autonomous vehicles, industrial automation, immersive extended reality, digital twins, and countless other location    sensitive applications. This report outlines several promising technical approaches to achieve these objectives by leveraging advanced radio technologies, joint sensing–communication functionalities, novel hardware and waveform designs, distributed edge intelligence, and integrated system architectures.

The evolution from 5G to 6G emphasizes dramatic improvements in key performance indicators (KPIs) such as sub-centimeter positioning accuracy, ultra-low latency (in the order of milliseconds or less), and highly reliable connectivity over dense and heterogeneous networks. In 6G systems, precise positioning is not only an end in itself but also an enabler for context-aware networking in which the accurate, real-time knowledge of users, devices, and the surrounding environment informs network decisions and resource allocations. This transformative shift is underpinned by the convergence of communication, sensing, and localization functionalities. By unifying massive bandwidths associated with higher frequency bands (e.g., mmWave and terahertz), large-scale antenna arrays, and enhanced signal processing techniques, future 6G networks will become capable of directly sensing their physical environment and adapting network behavior accordingly (behravan2023positioningandsensing pages 1-2, wang2022visionapplicationscenarios pages 1-2).

sections.text:
A critical foundation for achieving precise positioning is the use of expansive spectrum ranges. By exploiting wide bandwidths available at mmWave and terahertz frequencies, 6G systems can obtain ultra-fine time resolution for delay measurements. These high-frequency bands facilitate sophisticated time-of-arrival (ToA) and round-trip time (RTT) estimation methods that underpin centimeter-level accuracy. Moreover, the shorter wavelengths at these frequencies enable the deployment of ultra-massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) antenna arrays with thousands of elements that form extremely narrow beams, dramatically enhancing the spatial resolution of angle-of-arrival (AoA) and angle-of-departure (AoD) measurements (behravan2023positioningandsensing pages 1-2, wang2022visionapplicationscenarios pages 15-16).

Reconfigurable antenna systems such as ultra-massive MIMO and distributed cell-free MIMO architectures, where antennas are spread over a geographic area rather than concentrated at a single site, can reduce the distances between transmitters and receivers. Doing so decreases path loss and minimizes interference, which are critical for reliably achieving sub-meter and even sub-centimeter resolution in diverse environments (niemann2023nextgenerationpositioningwithin pages 5-7, taleb20226gsystemarchitecture pages 8-10).

Furthermore, the introduction of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) or reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RIS) provides new degrees of freedom in managing the radio environment. These surfaces can be programmed to introduce controllable phase shifts that create virtual line-of-sight (LoS) paths, mitigating the effects of obstacles and non-line-of-sight (NLoS) conditions. By dynamically shaping the propagation environment, IRSs not only enhance data rates but also improve positioning accuracy by augmenting geometric measurements using additional reflective paths (behravan2023positioningandsensing pages 5-6, lima2021convergentcommunicationsensing pages 7-9).

sections.text:
A central theme in 6G research is the integration of sensing and communication functionalities into a unified framework, commonly referred to as Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC). In conventional networks, positioning and communication are treated as separate functions; however, in 6G these functions are tightly integrated so that the same hardware, spectrum, and radio signals serve dual roles. For example, signals used for communication can simultaneously be exploited for radar-like sensing to generate high-resolution maps of the environment and detect the presence and motion of objects (behravan2023positioningandsensing pages 4-5, zeng2024atutorialon pages 2-3).

This integration enables the development of “digital twins” of the physical environment—a continuously updated 3D representation that captures both spatial and contextual information. Such digital twins facilitate context-aware networking by providing the network with real-time knowledge about channel conditions, obstacles, and user distributions, which in turn informs dynamic resource management, adaptive beamforming, and mobility control decisions (kaushik2024towardintegratedsensing pages 1-3, niemann2023nextgenerationpositioningwithin pages 10-12).

The use of advanced sensing modalities—including radar, lidar, and passive radio sensing—further enriches the dataset available for precise positioning. For instance, radar-based sensing can provide both range and Doppler information, which is critical for detecting moving targets and accurately estimating their speeds, while optical sensors (cameras and lidars) add geometric and texture information beneficial for fine-grained localization in indoor and cluttered outdoor environments (behravan2023positioningandsensing pages 1-2, chorti2022contextawaresecurityfor pages 3-4).

At the heart of precise positioning lie the capabilities of the physical layer, where waveform design and signal processing play pivotal roles. Traditional waveforms such as OFDM, widely used in 4G and 5G, are being reexamined and optimized for 6G applications. In 6G, waveform designs must balance the high data throughput needs of communications with the requirements for fine temporal and spectral resolution needed for accurate ranging and mapping. Consequently, joint design approaches that consider both data transmission and positioning performance are explored to optimize parameters such as sidelobe levels, ambiguity functions, and robustness to hardware impairments (behravan2023positioningandsensing pages 4-5, lima2021convergentcommunicationsensing pages 17-18).

Advanced signal processing techniques—including super-resolution algorithms such as Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC) and Estimation of Signal Parameters via Rotational Invariance Techniques (ESPRIT)—enable the extraction of fine time and angle details from the received signals, even in the presence of multipath interference. Such methods are particularly important in complex propagation environments where line-of-sight conditions are not guaranteed (mogyorosi2022positioningin5g pages 15-17, niemann2023nextgenerationpositioningwithin pages 12-15).

Moreover, carrier-phase-based positioning techniques, similar to those employed in GNSS Real-Time Kinematics (RTK), exploit the phase information of the carrier wave to resolve positioning ambiguities with extremely high precision. These methods require high stability in oscillators and sophisticated algorithms for distinguishing between line-of-sight and multipath components, which are central to reducing errors in delay and angle measurement (mogyorosi2022positioningin5g pages 15-17, niemann2023nextgenerationpositioningwithin pages 12-15).
